summary: The respondent was prosecuted for an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the Act. He had been convicted by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Delhi on a charge framed against him and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the prosecution failed to prove that the article of food was unfit for human consumption because it was not fit for human use. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The word 'filthy' in section 2(ia) (f) is a conjunctively and not disjunctively. It does not mean that the word 'sticu larly' means "discrepent, disgusting or unseemonatua". [601B] 1.2. The expression 'food" in section 3(ia)(f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is a disjunctive and not conjunctively. In the instant case, the article was unfit to human consumption on account of its presence in the food worms found by the Public Analyst. [602C] 1.(i) The word "filty" in the context of section 2 (ia)(e) means 'discred, distilled or insect infested or insects, which are unfit for consumption on any ground. It is not necessary that the articles of food be unfit for use on account thereof. [062D] 1(ii) The expression "food", in section 7(1)(e), means 'genuine vegetation and unseems of human body or vegetable substance or being insect, infested, diseased or animal or vegetable substances or being in part of any filthy, putrid, dispaired or animal. [20063E] 1 (iii) The words "fish" in sub clause (f), are disjunctively and cannot be read conjunctively so as to bring the case within the mischief of this sub clause. [ 20063D] 2(i) In the present case, it is not disputed that the food articles were unfit for agriculture or for human habitation. The article was adulterated, for which no minimum standard or purity of the article could be prescribed, and therefore the offence under Section 7 readwith section 16 would be conclusive to bring within the meaning of this clause. The prosecution has failed to establish by any satisfactory evidence that the sample was adulterated. [1802E] 3(ii)(a) In view of the fact that the Food Inspector had not expressed his opinion that the respondent was unfit, for human Consumption on account o ffilt, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or animal, it would be necessary in such a case to prove further that the product was unfit. [1902F] 4(b) The prosecution failed in proving that the appellant had not committed any offence under the Act and therefore no question of offence under clause (a) of section 16 could arise. [1999G] 5(c) In this view of matter, the High court was right in holding that there was no evidence to prove the charge framed by the prosecution against the respondent. [2000E] 6(d) The High court had rightly held that the offence of adulteration under Section 16 of Prevention of food Adulteration Act was not made out. [2001G] 7(e) In a case where the article is unfit for being human consumption, it could be proved to prove such a charge. [2002H; 2002A] 8(f) The Food Inspector, P.W. 468, has clearly stated that the report of the Public analyst was not conclusive and therefore he had no reason to doubt its correctness. [2003G] 9(i)(ii) In cases where the articles are unfit to be human consumption the burden is on the prosecution to prove its case.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3(2) of the Order and he was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class, Dumka, in a criminal case. He was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence from six months to one year. In appeal before this Court it was contended that the appellant had been acquitted on the ground that he was an agriculturist and that he had not committed any offence under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The presumption under section 49 of the Registration Act is not rebutted by the evidence adduced by the prosecution. It is true that the presumption under s. 49 of that Act is rebuttable but it is a rebuttable presumption. But the presumption is rebuttable and the burden is on the person who has proved the same to prove the same. [701B] 1.2. The onus of proving the fact of sale of foodgrains by the appellant was not discharged by the courts below. [802C] 1.(a) The presumption is in favour of the appellant that he is an agriculturist. [820D] 2.1 The burden of proof is on him to prove that he has been guilty of offence under section 5(2)(d) of that section. [821E] (b) The onus was not on the prosecution to prove his case and the presumption drawn against him must be rebutted by evidence adduced in support of the defence. [823F] 2.(a). In the instant case, the appellant has failed to discharge the burden of proving that he purchased the foodgrains from the respondents. He had not been able to establish that he sold the foodgrains to any person other than a bona fide consumer. [822E] 1(b) It is well settled that the onus of proof in a civil court is on an accused person and it is only when the prosecution has proved that the person charged with the offence has committed some other offence, that burden is discharged by showing that he did not know what was the nature of the offence. [825F] 1 (c) The burden to prove lies upon the person accused of commission of an offence under s 5(1)(d). [823G] 2(a) In the present case, it is clear that the prosecution had failed to establish the fact that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands. He did not produce any evidence to show that he cultivated the same on the land. [826A] 3.(b) There was no evidence to prove this fact. The burden was on the appellant to prove it. [827B] 4(a). It is clear from the evidence that the respondents had been in possession of the foodgrains for a period of about three years and they were not able to show as to how the foodgrains could be stored in their premises. [828C] 5.(b)(i) The prosecution has failed, in any manner, to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [829A] 6(ii) In view of the fact, that the Food Inspector had been examined by the defence, it was not possible for him to say whether he had seen the foodgrains on the date of the incident and whether he could have seen the same at any time when the incident took place. [824E] 7.(a)(i), (ii) The evidence of the witnesses clearly shows that the appellants were in possession as a dealer. They were not in possession at all till the date when the offence was committed. [82A] 8(iii) In this case, there is no evidence on record to show whether the foodgrains are grown by the appellants or they are grown on the same date. [881E] 9(a)(ii), (iii) The Food Inspector has not been examined in this case and he had merely stated that the rice was grown on that day.

The defendant was a tenant from month to month under the provisions of section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. The plaintiff, who was a monthly tenant, filed a suit for ejectment against the defendant on the ground that he had accepted payment of rent to the Receiver and the defendant became a tenant in respect of the same premises. The defendant resisted the suit contending that the tenancy created by him was not a tenancy under section 116 but was a tenancy created under a lease for one year from the beginning of 1926 and since it was a lease, the defendant ceased to be a tenant on the expiry of the second annual lease and consequently a tenancy was created in the years 1925 and 1926. The trial judge held that the defendant was not entitled to recover possession of the premises as he had not accepted payment to the plaintiff. He further held that there was no evidence to show that the rent was paid by the defendant to the defendant. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court holding that the suit was barred by limitation and dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, took the view that the lease created by the plaintiff was not one year or month under section 106, Transfer of property Act and, therefore, the tenancy was not created in accordance with the provisions contained in section 116, Transferof Property Act and the lease was a valid tenancy. On this finding, the trial judge dismissed the appeal. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The question whether the tenancy is one year under section 107 of the Indian Contract Act or not depends upon the facts of each case. [701B] 2.1 Section 116 of Transfer of Properties Act provides that a lease shall be in writing and signed by the parties, and it is not necessary to give notice to the parties of any such lease. The tenancy was for one month from the date of its expiry. It was not an agreement between the parties that the tenant would become a monthly tenancy under Section 116, transfer of Property. [801C] 2:1 The tenancy created in favour of the defendant by virtue of section 106 of Transfer Act is a lease and the rent is paid to the lessee. Therefore, the lease is a valid one year and the tenancy continued in existence till it was determined by a proper notice to quit. [820G] 2(a) In the instant case, the suit for eviction was filed on 24th December, 1924, and the trial Judge held that since the defendant had accepted the payment of rents from the month to months under the provision of section116 of Transfer Of Property Act, he became a monthly tenants in respect thereof. [823G] 3.2 The defendant was entitled to protection against eviction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [825H; 801A B] 3:1 Section 115 of Transferof Properties Act is an exception to the general rule that when a lease is created by virtue to the provisions in section 106 and Transfer of properties Act, the tenant becomes a monthly landlord under section 6(2) of the said Act. [826B] 3.(a) The defendant had not acquired any permanent right in the land in suit for which he was entitled as a monthly lessee. He was never a tenant at the time when the lease became a tenancy. Therefore the defendant could not be said to have acquired any right in respect thereto. [827G] (b) In view of section 115(1)(a), the defendant is entitled to obtain protection against ejectment under section116, Transfer Of Properties Act.

The appellant, a public servant, filed an application to the Commissioner under Section 138(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act for obtaining information relating to his income tax returns. The Income Tax Officer, after hearing the parties, passed an order on April 1, 1964 directing the production of certain documents in Court of law. The appellant challenged the said order by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the disclosure of any information from the assessment records of an assessee was not necessary for the purpose of proving his income. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The power to summon documents is a discretionary power and it cannot be exercised in a court of law unless the statute expressly provides that such disclosure would be made before the Income tax authorities. [601B] 2.2 The power under Section 137(1) (b) is not an absolute power but is an absolute one. It is a power conferred on the Commissioner to summon and produce documents in a Court of Law. The Commissioner has no authority to require production of any document in a case pending before him, in a civil court. [701C] 3.1 The power conferred under Section 136(1), therefore, cannot be called in question in any court of Law unless the statutory provision expressly provides for such disclosure. [802D] 2:1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had made an application before the income tax authorities to obtain information from his income and that the Commissioner was authorised to furnish him with a copy of the same. The assessee did not make any application to it in respect of the income assessed by it for 1964 65 onwards nor did he make any disclosure of such information from any court. Therefore, the question whether the disclosure made by the appellant amounted to an order under Section 135(1A) (a) of Income Tax ACT, 1961 or not was a matter which could be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. [820E] 2 3.2. The expression "information" in Section 138 (1)(a) means information relating only to the assessment of income tax and not to the income of the assessee. Therefore the word "information " used in Section 139(b) cannot be construed as an order for the purposes of proving or proving a fact which is relevant for the determination of the question under Section 147(1). [820G] 3:1 The expression 'information" means any material in any form, including records, documents, records, memos, etc. relating to any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the 1961 Act or the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, or theIndian Income Tax Rules, 1922. [821A B] 2(a) The expression has no relation to the power of the court to summon the production or documents in any Court of fact which are relevant for determining the question. It does not mean that the court can summon the attendance of a witness only when it is satisfied that it is in the public interest so to do and such an order cannot be passed without the approval of the Commissioner. [823C] 2 (b). The expression used in section 138(2) means "any information relating" which is required by any person to be produced or proved before a court in a proceeding pending before it, whether before or after the commencement of this Act. [825D E] 3(a)(i) In the present case, there was no material on record to show that the appellant was satisfied with the information sought for by him. The question whether he had made any disclosure would depend upon the nature of the information required by the assessee and whether it is necessary for him to obtain such a report. [826E] 4(a). In the absence of any material on the record, the court could not have summoned the production and documents in the absence thereof.

The father of the minor died in a motor accident on May 3, 1946. The gift was complete and the mother of the deceased had left her husband at her parental home after the death of her father. The father of Mammotty was not alive when the gift was made by Mammottatty to his mother. The mother of Mammsotty died in an accident on June 3, 1945. The widow of Mammanotty filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the gift deed executed by Mammanotsty was valid and binding on her and the gift made by her father to his wife was not complete. The High Court held that the document was not a gift but only an oral one and it was a gift made in favour of the mother. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) A gift is complete and irrevocable when the father has no guardian of the same property. [601 B] (2) The gift is not complete and there is no guardian for the minor. It is only an agreement between Mammotsty and his wife that he should accept the gift on behalf of his mother in law, but it was made clear and accepted by her on behalf the minor through her father who had attained discretion. [701 C] (3) The High court has not committed any error in holding that there was complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammenotty at the time of the gift in favourof the minor because it was not executed by him and accepted on behalf by his mother, who had reached the age of majority. [801 D] (4) The fact that the father of a minor died after the marriage of his father does not necessarily mean that he must accept the gifts made by his wife in law. [820 E] (5) The mere fact that Mammillaty was living at her mother in Law and she had attained the discretion cannot be held to be conclusive proof of the fact that she had left the mother in the house of her husband.

The respondent temple was established in the year 1951 and its income was assessed at Rs. 1,000/- per annum. The Commissioner had fixed the annual income of the religious institution at Rs,1,000/per annum. On appeal by the respondent temple, the High Court confirmed the order passed by the Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court had not determined the audit fee under section 76(2) of the Act and that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to determine the annual value of the income of any religious institution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court has erred in holding that the respondent 's contention that the provisions of the Madras Act do not contemplate separate rules for determining contribution payable under section76(1) of that Act is without substance and that it was not open to the Commissioner to determine whether the expenses incurred by the Government for meeting the cost of auditing were properly incurred or not. [701B] 2. The respondent temple had not been established in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 76(1), 76(3) and 76(4). The High court has erred, in holding, that the income was not to be determined under section 78(2), because it was a reasonable amount of audit fee. [801C] 3. The expression "reasonable amount" used in section 76 (1) is an inclusive definition and must include any amount which is not less than one hundred rupees but which is less than the maximum prescribed by rules. The word "reasonable" has been defined in section 78 (2) to mean " reasonable amount". [802D] 4. The object of the Legislature was to provide for a proper audit of the accounts of religious institutions and for that purpose it had provided for an effective audit of their accounts. It is not open, as contended by the appellant, to determine what should be the reasonable cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. [820E] 5. The words "reasonable estimate" in section76 (2), are not intended to mean a reasonable estimate. The legislature has used the word "reasonably estimate". The word 'reasonable estimate' is not defined in the Act. It does not contemplate any separate rule for determining the annual cost actually spent by the temple. [823E] 6. The language of section 76 is clear and unambiguous. The Legislature has used it to mean that the amount should be determined as audit fee, and that if the Commissioner has determined the actual cost actually expended for auditing it would have been in accordance therewith. [825F] 7. The fact that the Act does not prescribe any separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution is not a matter which can be said to be irrelevant for determining whether the expenditure incurred by Government for audit was properly incurred. [826C] 8. In the instant case, the Commissioner did not determine the actual expenses actually incurred by it for auditing its accounts and that he had no power to determine such cost as a reasonable measure. The Act does provide for an independent rule for determination of the annual amount of the expenditure actually incurred. It cannot be said that the Legislature has intended to prescribe any different rules for determination and that in doing so, the legislature has deliberately used the words "reasonableness" instead of "reasonable". [826D] 9. In view of the provisions relating to the audit fees, it is not possible to hold that the levy of fee on audit fee is a reasonable one. [827E] 10. The power conferred by section 76 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Religious Institutions Act 19 of 1951 is very wide and has been explained in H.N. Rishbud vs State of Madras, A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 968; Commissioner of Endowments, Hyderabad vs V. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, A I.L.R., 1964 A.P.L..R.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Legislative Assembly, was elected as a Member of the Legislative Council from the Haryana Legislative Assembly. He filed an application under section 19 of the Act for a direction to issue notice to him. The High Court directed that the notice be issued in accordance with the provisions of section 19(1) of the act and the order should not be executed until the disposal of the appeal. The appellant, who was elected to the Haryana Assembly from the Punjab Vidhan Sabha, filed an appeal before this Court under section 20 of the , but the same was dismissed by this Court on 2nd April, 1975. The present appeal is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court dismissing the petition for contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The order passed by the High court in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 17 of the 'Act does not decide any question as a matter of right under section19(1). [601B] 2.2. The notice issued by the Advocate General is an order initiating contempt proceedings against the appellant for committing contempt of the Court. It is not an order passed in exercise or jurisdiction to initiate contempt proceeding. The appeal is, therefore, maintainable. [602C] 3.3. The impugned order dated 2nd May, 1975 is a nullity and cannot be sustained. [062D] 4.1 The High court has committed manifest error of law in holding that the appellant had no locus standi to file an application for contempt under section 21 of the .Act. [2006E] 3:1.2 The High Courts have committed manifest errors of law by not deciding any question raised before it, which does decide a matter raised before them, and therefore, this Court has jurisdiction to entertain such appeal. [ 2006E] 2:1 The appellant had filed an appropriate application under article 136 of the Constitution for issue of a notice to show cause against the alleged contemner in response to the notice issued under section 16(1)(a) of .the Act. The same was rejected by this court on 2 nd April, 1974. [2007E] 1.2 It is true that the High Courts had not decided any question of locus standi or the order did not decide anything against the proposed contemner in regard to his prayer for issue notice under section 18(1), but it has only directed that no appeal would lie to this Court from an order issuing a notice. [ 2007E] 4:1 It is well settled that the power conferred on the High courts under article 226 of the constitution to punish for contempt is not a matter which can be decided by this Courts in exercise and jurisdiction under article 227 of the. [2005E] 5:2.3 The High courts have committed gross error of fact by not issuing notice to the appellant, though it may be, a different matter if the order does decide some other matter. [2004G H; 2006E C] 3 :1.4 It is clear that the order passed under section 13(1A) of 'the Act is an interlocutory order and cannot take away the jurisdiction of this Court to initiate proceedings for contempt against the contemner in respect of his alleged contemner. [2003D E] 2, The High 'Court has committed gross errors by not passing a final order in the exercise of their jurisdiction under Article 226 of Constitution.

The appellant was prosecuted along with two others for offences under section 6(1) A of the Act of 1952. The trial Magistrate convicted him and sentenced him to imprisonment for six months, and a fine of Rs. 500/- and a further fine of rupees one hundred. On appeal by the State Government the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence from six months to two years. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that section 6 (1 A) of the General Clauses Act was not applicable in view of the fact that the provisions of the repealed Act were not applicable to him as he had been convicted under section 5(1A), and that section 4 of the 1952 Act did not apply to him. The High Court held that section 20(1 A)(i) of Act XVIII of 1933, which was repealed by the 1952 amending Act of 1949, was a valid piece of legislation and could not be said to have been repealed by section 6 A (1A). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 5 (1AA) of 1952 Act had no application to the facts of the case because the amendment made in the Act XVII of 1933 by the amending Act, 1949, which came into force with effect from 1st April, 1949. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The provisions of section 6A(1), 6 A and 6 (2) of 1950 Act are not applicable when the offence was committed by a telegraph authority. [601 B] In view of section 20 (1B)(i), the amendment of section 5 A of 1952 amending the Act, 1948, which had been brought into force on 1st March, 1949 by the Amending Act of 1933 and the amendment effected in the said section by the Amendment Act of 1934, was not a valid law. [701 C] The language used in section 6AA(1)(a) of 1956 Act is very clear that it applies to the offences covered by section 5A of the , and that the words "any other enactment" occurring in section 4A of 1952 are comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions contained in section 20 of the, 1952 Act. [801 D] The words "a telegraph authority" used in sections 6AA (1) (b) and 6 A(1B) of 1951 Act are wide enough to cover all other offences covered under section 4 or otherwise than as permitted by rules made under that section.

The appellant, a benamidar for the respondent, purchased certain properties in court sale from the respondent and sold them to the respondent. The properties were in possession of the real decreeholder on July 26, 1940, and the sale was made in execution of decrees. On the death of the sole bread earner, the properties were put back into the hands of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties in question against Oramba Sundari and the appellant, claiming that he had purchased certain lands from the real purchaser, and that the sale deed was void as it was not binding on him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that Orambundari had no right to get the properties sold by the real purchasers. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the decreeholders were in fact a benamidars for another person in respect of the decrees and that he was not a benamger for the other persons in respect thereof. The High Court held that the properties purchased by Orambi Sundari were not liable to be sold under section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the judgment debtors had failed in proving that the property purchased by them was a benami transaction and that they were entitled to get relief under section 37(2). HELD: 1. The right of the parties to get their shares sold is not affected by the provisions of the Act. [901 A] 2. The rights of the party in respect to the properties are governed by the Bengal Public Money Lender Act, 1939, and as such the decreeholder was entitled to have his share in the properties which were purchased by him from Oramdi Sundari. [1001 B] 3. The legal position is well settled that a person who has purchased any property under section 35(2)(c) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act cannot be said to be a benamirer for another persons in view of the provisions contained in section 36 (2). [902 C] 4. The courts below were, therefore, right in holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the real transferee had any interest in excess of the limit prescribed by section 30 of the Bihar Money Lending Act. The findings recorded by the courts below are based on proper appreciation of evidence and are supported by cogent reasons. [0901 D] 5.1 In view of section 36 of the Indian Penal Code, it is not open to the court to go behind the decree holders in respect thereto. [99 F] 4: 1 (a) The High court was right in setting aside the order for restoration of possession made by both the courts and restoring the properties to the deities in question. [98 H] 2 (b) The legal principles laid down by this Court in the several decisions referred to above are fully applicable to the facts of the present case. [100 C] 3 (c) In view thereof, the decree holder was entitled for restoration under section 31(2), and the court had no jurisdiction to go beyond the decree passed by it. [101 D] 4 (d) The judgment debtors were not entitled to any relief under sections 36(1)(b) and 36(3). [100 E] 5 (e) In the circumstances, the judgment debtor was entitled only for restoration in terms of section 31 (2) and the decree Holder was entitled under section 30(2); and as the decree did not suffer from any infirmity, the appeal should be dismissed. [103 F] 6.1 The High Courts were right in quashing the order of the courts to restore possession made in favour of Oramma Sundari Dasi.

The appellant company purchased a property in the name of Habib & Sons, by an assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16. The respondent company applied for execution of the decree on the 25th April, 1951. The City Civil Court granted the application and the executing court passed an order under Order XXI Rule 16 directing the transfer of the property to the appellant company. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the order of the City Civil Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of Order 21, rule 1 (2) (j) were not applicable to the case and that the respondent company had no right to apply for execution in view of the provisions contained in Order XXI. Rule 16(old section 232). The High Court held that the transfer by an assignor in writing was not a decree but a transfer by assignment in the sense of the word "decree holder" and that, therefore, the transferee could not be said to be a transferee by assignment. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "decreeholder" in Order 21 Rule 16 were not intended to cover cases where there was no decree in existence at the time of the transfer but only a transfer or an agreement to transfer or a contract to transfer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word 'decree holder' in Order XX, rule16(old Section 232) is used in the same sense and subject to the same conditions as if the application were made by the decree holder. [701B] (2)(a) A transfer of a decree does not amount to a decree in terms of Order XX Rule 16. It is only when the transferee has applied for the execution of a sale deed, that he can apply for the transfer or agreement to sell. The word "transfer" in the context of Order XXXVIII, rule 15(old) means an assignment by operation of law within the definition of Order XXII, rule 2 (old section 233). [702B] In the instant case, the appellant had not applied for executing a sale decree and it was only when it passed that the application for execution was made by Habib & Co. Ltd., that the appellant was entitled to apply to execute the decree in view thereof. [774C D] (b) The words "any other person" in Rule 16 are used in Order XXXVII, rule 17(1). It is not necessary that a transfer should be made by an assignee in writing or by operation thereof within the same meaning of the said word 'transfer". [705E] (3) A document executed by Habib and Sons, which was subsequently obtained by Habib, would not amount as a transfer. The words 'decreeholder' in Rule 17(2) are used to cover a case where there is no decree passed in existence but only an assignment of the debt by operation Of law within meaning of that word 'sale'.

The respondent was carrying on the business of fabricating and selling windows and doors, shesas etc. in his property at Jaipur. He had entered into a contract for sale with the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, Ajmer, for payment to him of the price of the windows and the door leaves. The respondent carried on the said business of clothing and selling window andshes etc., under a separate contract for the sale of windows and windows. The contract was for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed under the terms of the contract. The contracts were for work and labour. The agreement provided that the respondent would be charged with the price thereof at the time of the delivery of the goods to the other party. The appellant contended that the contract was one for sale of goods and not a contract of sale, and that the transaction of the sale was a works contract. Held, that the contracts were one for work of construction and labour and the parties had agreed to supply the windows, doors and windows in a specified building, and the contract could not be said to be a works Contract for sale. The terms of contract were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the transaction as disclosed by the nature of the work, and to determine the true nature of work, but the contract did not pass to the respondent. The High Court was right in holding that the agreement was one of service in connection with the execution and sale of doors and window leaves. It was not a works contracts for sale and it could not pass only to the property which passed under a different contract. In the present case, the contract is one for "fix" the windows but to supply windows and door leaves, when the window leaves had become a part of the building. The transaction of sale of the doors and doors and the windows was not incidental to the execution or sale of property in which the goods were delivered. The Court held that the terms 'fix' the windows were not properly performed and the work was not rendered under a distinct contract but only to supply materials used in the construction, and therefore the contract for "sale of windows" could not amount to a workscontract for sale, because the contract had been executed by the respondent with his customers. The appeal filed by the State Government against that decision was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding otherwise and that there was no evidence to show that the work of fabrication and selling doors and door remains under a contract, and since the contract has been executed for sale it could be said that the property was not part of "fixing" the window left. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "fixation" in the contracts is not decisive. It does not mean that the parties intended to be taxed only on the basis of the terms and conditions of the contracts. [849C] 2. The word 'fixing' has been used in a wide sense and it means that the object of the party seeking to levy sales tax must be to promote sale of its manufactured goods, and not merely to supply goods for consideration. [950E] 3. The words "fine" are not decisive because they do not mean anything else. It is only when the contract between the parties is one which is one in substance for sale that the party can claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [1052G] 4. The term 'fine' has not been defined in the Act and, therefore, the word "fines" cannot be construed as meaning only "freight". [954A C] 5. The definition of "Fine" is wide enough to include all kinds of goods which are capable of being bought or sold by the assessee. It must be a contract between two parties for sale to promote sales of their manufactured goods.

The appellant was prosecuted for offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 511 Indian Penal code. The trial court framed charges against him on November 16, 1967. He was acquitted by the High Court of West Bengal. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The High Court has rightly held that the evidence of the complainant and the witnesses who were examined on behalf of the prosecution is not reliable. [701B] 2.2. The prosecution has failed to establish the charge against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt and consequently the trial court was right in holding that the charges framed against him are proved. [802C] 3.3. The evidence of Ram Avtar and Raj Kumar Agarwalla, who were arrested by the police on November 15, 1967 is not sufficient to prove the case against them. They have been acquitted by giving benefit of doubt. [901F] 4.1 The High court has committed a manifest error in holding otherwise. It was not open to the High court to interfere with the judgment of acquittal passed by the trial Court. [1001G] 3:1.2 The High Courts were right in quashing the charge framed against Raj Kumar and Shanker Lal, who had been arrested on November 17, 1967 and the accused were discharged. [1101F G] 4:1:The prosecution has not proved its case against Raj Singh or Shanker Lal. They are entitled to be acquitted of all the charges levelled against them as they have been convicted by giving them benefit of section 420 Indian Penal C.P.C. The appeal is allowed and the judgment passed by both the courts below is set aside. [1201F; 1202A] 3,321B] 4(a) The High 'Court has committed an error in quashing charges framed under sections 419/420/467/468/471 Indian Penal. [110G] 5.1 It was open to this court to examine the evidence on record and come to its own conclusion whether the prosecution has proved its version beyond all shadow of doubt or not. [120A B] 3(b) The trial Court had committed an illegality in holding the charges against Raj K Agarwalla respondent as not proved. The order of acquittal was set aside by this court on the ground that the High ' Court had failed in appreciating the evidence and the findings recorded by it were perverse. [119B C] 4.(a) In view of the fact that the trial Judge had acquitted the accused, the High'Court should have quashed the charges. [121F] 5(b)(i) The order passed by this Court on November 18, 1967 was set in motion and the appeal filed against it was dismissed. [118A B C] 3.(ii) The prosecution failed to show that the accused had committed any offence under section 420 read with Section 511 Indian penal Code. [117C] 4 (a) There is no evidence of any criminal conspiracy or conspiracy between the accused and the complainant. It is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the transaction was a fraudulent one. The fact that there was a conspiracy between Raj Kumar Aggarwalla and Shankerlal does not make it clear that the transactions were made by the accused with the help of the help extended by him to Ram Avtar. [124A B D] 4)(b) There was no evidence on the record to show as to what had happened to the transaction. The mere fact that Shanker Lal had been brought into a hotel after his arrest does not mean that he had been falsely implicated in this case.

The appellant, a Railway Company, was engaged in the business of running trains. The Railways had to undertake certain works and services for which they were required to provide adequate safety measures. The appellant was appointed as a railway contractor by the East India Company on June 6, 1981. On June 6.1981, he was transferred from the Railway Station to the Railway Department. He was given a temporary status of a permanent employee in the Railway. He continued to work till December 31, 1981 when he was relieved from his duties. The respondent No. 1, who was working as a casual labourer, had been appointed on daily wages and he was paid a monthly salary of Rs.44.50. The services of the appellant were terminated by the General Manager, East India Railway, Trivandrum on June 5, 1981 with effect from June 6 and he continued to discharge his duties till December 30, 1981 and thereafter. He filed an application for compensation under section 33(1)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act before the Labour Court, Ernakulam. The Labour Court rejected the claim holding that the appellant was not a workman within the meaning of section 2(s) of that Act. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the termination of his services was illegal and void and directed payment of compensation to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order of dismissal was bad as it was based on no evidence and that the Tribunal had not properly appreciated the fact that the Railway Company was a public undertaking. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no material bearing on the question whether the appellant is a workman or not. [701B] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding the termination order bad as being illegal and invalid. [802C] 3.2 The High Courts were wrong in taking the view that the Railways had been established by the Government of India for the welfare of the people. [820D] 3:1.3 It is true that the Government has a duty to maintain public utility in which the right to move and carry on any business or profession would be equal to operational expenses, interest on interest on investment, interest thereon on investment etc. But it cannot be denied that the railway company was established by Government of Kerala for the benefit of the general public. [823E] 3;2.1 It is not disputed that the railways had been functioning in this country and they were also running trains which were required for their welfare. The Railway Company had been running trains on account of defective bridges and has now become a national works. [825F] 3, 2.3 In view of the fact, that the appellants are not able to maintain an action like the one under section 22(1) (b) read with section 25(2)(a), the High court should have held that there is no justification for interfering with the order passed by the Tribunal. [826C] 4.1.2 In view thereof, the appeal fails and it is dismissed.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in question. The respondents filed a suit for eviction on the ground that they had failed to pay rent and that the order of the Tribunal was illegal and void. The respondent contended that the appellants were not entitled to restoration of the appeals as also the applications for restoration of an appeal under Regulation 20. The trial court dismissed the suits holding that the applications made by the appellants in all the four cases were barred by limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no power to dismiss the applications filed by the respondents and that it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeals on merits. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide an application for restoration under Regulation 19(1) of the Abolition Act. [701 A] 2.2 The Tribunal had jurisdiction to hear and dispose of the applications of restoration of appeals filed by tenants in respect of lands in their possession. It was not open to the Tribunal to dismiss such applications on merits as it was not competent to do so under Regulation 21, but it was open to it to decide whether the applications were barred or not. [601 B] 3.1 In view of the express language of section 17(1), the Tribunal has no power either in law or in law to decide any appeal on merits under Regulation 22. [613 C] 2: The Tribunal was right in holding that there was a change in the persons sitting as members of the tribunal and bench. [501 D] 3:1.2 In view thereof, the Tribunal could not have dismissed the applications on merit under Regulation 18(1). [602 E] 3;3.3 The Tribunal did not decide the applications under Regulation 23. It is open to a party to apply for restoration as also an application made under Regulation 24. If the Tribunal decides that the appeals were barred, it would be open to such party to file an appeal before the Tribunal. [643 D] 4.1.3 In view Of the express provisions of Regulation 20, the tribunal could not dismiss the appeals filed under Regulation 17 on merits and the decision of the Revenue Tribunal on merits was final. [64 F] 3,4A B] 2(a) The Tribunal could have dismissed an appeal for non prosecution in a case where the appellant did not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer. [65 G] (b) In view ofs. 17(2), the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to the proceedings before the Revenue Tribunals and the orders passed by the Tribunal on the basis thereof would be final. The Tribunal cannot dismiss an appeal filed under section 20 unless it is satisfied that there has been a change of persons sitting in the members of Tribunal or bench. (c) In the instant case, the appellants had not appeared either inperson or through their agent or lawyers. [63 G] 3(a). The Tribunal, therefore, was right to dismiss an application filed under regulation 20 and to record its decision on merits in view of section 20. [66 H] 4(b) The High court has no jurisdiction to entertain the applications after the expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of the order passed by it. [68 A B] 5.1 It is true that the proviso to Regulation 19 does not say that the period of limitation prescribed for filing an appeal against an order passed under section 17 (1) shall be applicable to proceedings before a Tribunal and the order made by it would not be final unless it was satisfied that the appellant had no notice of the date fixed for hearing. [69 B] 4.(a) In cases where the Tribunal is satisfied on merits that there had been a delay in appearance, it can dismiss an Appeal for non defence. [70 C] (c)(i) The proviso to section 20 does not apply to proceedings under Regulation 25.

The appellant was appointed as a Pujar of the village Telibandha on behalf of the deity. He was given a charge of the temple and he was also given a duty to meet the expenses of the Temple. The appellant filed an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the award of 1896 and prayed that the High Court should not have set aside the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court. The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that the appellant had failed to prove that the temple was dedicated to the deity and that the income from Teli endow was only a charge on it for the purpose of the performance of the duties of the office of Pujar. On appeal, the High court reversed the judgment of the Trial Judge and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding recorded by the High 'Court that the dedication was made in favour of Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple is absolutely correct and does not call for any interference. [701B] 2. The evidence on record clearly shows that the property was dedicated for the temple to the idol and that it was only an absolute dedication to the temple. It is also clear from the evidence that the properties were dedicated to Ramsaran Lal and his brothers. [802C] 3. The fact that the Temple was dedicated in full ownership of Teli resting on the income of the family or that he made a general or special provision for the performance thereof does not make an absolute gift to the appellant. [901D] 4. The dedication by Dinanath Sao himself and his brother to Ram Dassan Lal is clearly established. It was only after the award was passed by him that the deity was dedicated absolutely to the Temple and he made an absolute trust of the property for the general expenses of temple. [1002E] 5. The position in law is well settled that a dedication by a person who has been given possession of the properties for the purposes of the worship cannot be said to be a gift to him. [1101F] 6. The mere fact that some alienations have been made by Dinnath Sao in favour Of Ramsaransan Lal does not give any proprietary interest in the village. It only shows an absolute ownership of the land and it is only a part of the income which was intended to be used for the maintenance of the idol. [110G] 7. The expression "any other property" in section 47(1) of the Act means that the same must be used by the parties to the suit or any person claiming under them for the benefit of the estate and not for the personal benefit of any other person. [111H; 111A B] 8. In the instant case, the appellant was given possession as a trustee of the said temple. The trust was created in favour o Ramsarana Lal by virtue of an agreement between him and his sons. It cannot be denied that the respondent had been appointed as Pujar by the appellant as Pujari of the temples. [112A B C] 9. In view of the fact that there is no evidence to show that the endowment was created for the welfare of the pilgrims, the question whether the property belonged to the family of the respondent or not does not arise. The respondent had not been appointed in any manner by the appellants as Pujars of the deities. [113A B D] 9 A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 1052, referred to.

The appellants were appointed as the Chairman of the Action Committee of the Allahabad Bar Association on a temporary basis. They were also appointed by the High Court in exercise of its powers under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948. The High Court held that the resolution was passed under the supervision and control of the Chief Justice and since he had not acted with dignity in regard to the functioning of the judiciary, it should have been passed in that manner. The appellants were also guilty of contempt as they were not guilty of having committed criminal contempt. The learned Judges of the High court held that there was no reason for the appellants to punish them for their conduct for which they had acted with a right and authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High 'Court should have discharged the notices issued by the Chief justice and since the High Cour t did not commit any contempt, the High Judge should have dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The order of the learned Judges dismissing the writ petitions is correct. It was not a case where the appellants were guilty of criminal contempt but the High Courts had committed contempt. [701B] 2. The appellant was appointed as Chairman of a Committee of Management and he was also holding the post of Vice Chairman. He was also a member of the Working Committee of management. He is a member in the Working committee of management and he has been removed from service by the order dated January 22, 1973. [801C] 3. The power to punish for contempt is vested in the High Powered Committee which is empowered to take action against the appellants under clause 15 of the Letters Patent. It is not a matter of dispute that the appellants had been appointed as Vice Chairman of Committee of Administration and they were also holding such posts. [820G] 4. The appointment of the Chairman was made by the Governor in exercise o f powers conferred on him by clause 14. The Chief Justice could not have exercised his power under clause 16 of the Order which is a special provision for the administration of justice. [823A D] 5. The word 'criminal contempt' has been used in the sense of criminal Contempt. It does not mean that it must be committed by a person who is acting with dignity and decorum of the Court. [825E] 6. In view of the fact that the Chief Judge had acted in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Calcutta Bar, he was guilty of committing contempt as well as criminal contempt and he could not be punished for his conduct for such disobedience. [826C D] 7. The Chairman of Action Committee is not an officer of the court but he is an officer who is entrusted with the administration and functions of the courts. He cannot be said to have acted in any manner which is unbecoming of a Judge. [827A G] 8. In the instant case, the appellants are guilty of gross contempt as defined under section 2(c) of the Contempt of Courts Act. They are guilty for committing criminal contempt as described in clause 14 and they are guilty only of having acted with the dignity and discipline of the judicial system. [828B C] 9. The conduct of the appellant was not considered by the Chairman, but he was found guilty of Contempt of Court. He had been guilty of contumacious conduct for the breach of trust and integrity in regard t o himself.

The appellant, a Sub Registrar, Arambagh filed an application before the Sub-Registrar for registration of the award on 24th of November, 1983. The Sub Registrar refused to register the award and sent back the same to the arbitrators. On 24th July, 1984 the Sub Registrar passed an order that the award be made on 28th of January, 1978. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the SubRegistrar refusing to register his award on 25th November,1983. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Sub Registrars had no jurisdiction to take back the award from the court and that the arbitrators were not justified in taking back the said award from their custody. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.2. The order of learned Sub Registrar refusing to grant registration of a reference on 25 th November, 1982 was illegal and without jurisdiction. [701B] 2.1 The High court had no power under section 15 of the . 26th July 1978 to direct return back the awarded amount to the arbitrator. [802C] 2:1.3. The award was made on 24 th of June, 1985 and it was presented before the sub Registrar for registration. It was presented on 25 nd November, 1984. The arbitrators were right in holding that since the award was not presented within time as the arbitration proceedings were pending between 28th January,1978 to 24th November 1983, the Sub registrar had no authority to take the award back from the date of the interim injunction order dated 25th February, 1983 and the Sub Inspector had no powers under section 16 of the , but he could not have taken back the amount from the award. [901D] 2.(a) The High Courts were right when it held that the arbitrator was in the custody of the court. [1001E] (b) The order passed by the Sub­Registrar on 24nd November, 1978 was illegal because the arbitrators had tried to obtain the custody from the Court and had not given him any further time for its registration. [1101F] 2(a) In view of the fact that the arbitration proceeding were pending in the court, the High court could not give effect to the order passed on 24rd November, 1980 by the sub­Registrar. [110G] 3.(b) Under section 15(1)(c), the arbitrators are required to make a report to the Sub--Registrar within one month from the receipt of the notice of the arbitration and if they do so, they must give their reasons for doing so. The arbitrator is not bound by the order made by the court on 24/11th November. [111G] 4.(a)(b) In the present case, the arbitrators did not make any report to them within one year from the passing of the final award. They were also required to give their reason for doing that which they could not do so. [112A D] 5.(c) The Sub­ Registrar had no other power under Section 15(2)(a). He was bound by his order dated 24th June,1985 and he could have taken the said decision within one week from the making of the Award. [113B C] 6.1 In view thereof, the award made on 25/11/1983 was not binding on the Sub–Registrar. The arbitration proceedings had already been completed and the award had been filed in court. Therefore, the order dated 23rd November 1983 passed by him could not be said to be illegal or without jurisdiction and could not therefore be set aside. [114E] 2 (a) There is no provision in section 15 that the arbitral tribunal shall decide the question of limitation for registration under section 14(1). The Sub- Registrar had only power to decide the issue of limitation. He was not bound to give his reasons for refusing to registration.

The respondent 's suit for ejectment was brought under section 13(1)(e) of the Act. The appellant filed a suit for eviction on the ground that he had sub let out the premises to the respondent and that the respondent had not sub let him to the appellant by an express contract. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had waived his right in regard to the protection of his rights as a tenant under section 15 of the Bombay Rent Act, 1944. The High Court held that the tenancy was a new one and the provisions of the two sections were not applicable to the facts of the case. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) Section 13(2)(e), which provides for the protection against eviction of tenants from sub let premises, is a provision in an Act of Parliament which prohibits it from creating any tenancy or sub letting as a matter of right. The words "any other person" are not defined in the Act and they must be construed accordingly. [701B] (2) Section 15(1) of that Act provides for protection against ejectment of tenants on the grounds mentioned therein. It is not necessary to refer to the provisions contained in section 13 (1)(a). The words 'any other persons' are not used in the sense of a person who has, since the coming into operation of this Act, sub let the premises be treated as a fresh tenancy and not a continuation of the old or a continuance of the existing or a continuation thereof. [801C] (3) Section 14(1), which is a special provision in the statute, provides for a remedy against eviction by the landlord. The right to recover possession of any premises is a statutory right. It can be exercised only if there is an express provision in that Act itself. [820D] (4) The words used in section 15(2) are not intended to cover cases where the tenant has, before the coming in operation of the statute for the benefit of his or her interest in any other manner his or his interest in such premises is sub let. It does not mean that the right to evict a tenant on the basis of an express statutory provision can be waived by the revenue officials. [823E] (5) The word 'any person' used in Section 15 (2)(a) of Act of 1944 means a person whose interest in the premises is in dispute and who has been sub let for the use of the tenant. It cannot be said that the legislature intended to confer any right on the landlord to recover his or their interest in a case where the tenancy had not been determined by an Expert nominated by the Board of Trade and it was not intended by the Legislature to confer such right on a person as a sub let to him. [825E] The word "any person" used in clause (e) is a general provision in a statute which prohibits the giving of any other person than a tenant. The word has been used in a general sense and it does not refer to a person holding a licence under section 14(2). It does refer to an expert nominated by Board of trade and it refers to a nominee of the Board.

The appellant, who was working as a teacher in the respondent Board at Bombay, had filed an application for appointment of a teacher. The Board by its order dated January 30, 1991 directed the appellant to appear at the S.S.C. examination on March 31, 1991 and to take necessary action against the candidates referred to in the Notification of August 31, 1990. The appellant was also directed to appear before the Standing Committee for the examination on April 3, 1991. On May 4, 1991, the Board issued a notification under section 7(1) of the Act calling upon all the candidates to appear for the SSLC examination and to submit their certificates in respect of their marks obtained by them in the examination. The respondent Board filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against the order of the Standing committee dated January 31,1991. The Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent had committed misconduct. The High Court held that the charges were proved and the punishment was set aside. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Board that the findings recorded by the Standing Committees were not based on the evidence adduced before them and the finding recorded by them was perverse. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of the Enquiry Committee. [701B] 2.2 The High Courts have no jurisdiction under article 226 or Article 227 of the Constitution to interfere in the findings of the Disciplinary Committee. The findings recorded are based on evidence adduced by the parties and the conclusions reached by them are based upon the evidence produced before them. [802C] 3.3 The High Powered Committee had not given any reasons for coming to its conclusion that the charge against the appellant was proved. [820D] 4.1 It is well settled that the High Court has no jurisdiction in interfering with the findings and conclusions reached on the basis of evidence adduced in support of the charges. [823E] 3:1 The finding recorded in the impugned notification dated August 31 1990 is based upon evidence adduced at the instance of the respondent. [822F] 2:2.3 It is true that the Standing committees had not applied their mind to the question whether the appellant has committed misconduct or whether he was guilty of misconduct. But, it is well established that the finding on the charge is perverse and against the evidence led by the Board. [825E] 4:1.4 The High powered Committee did not consider the evidence tendered at the time of scrutiny of the certificates produced by the appellant. It had no reason to doubt the correctness of the findings arrived at by it. [821F] 3;2.5 In the instant case, the respondent has failed to establish that the certificate produced by him was not genuine and that he had not committed any misconduct. [826A D] 4;3:1: The HighPowered Committee has not given reasons for arriving at its conclusions on the charges framed against the respondent and it is not open to the High Powere te Committee to evaluate the evidence and to come to its own conclusion. [828B C] 3,2D] 2(a) In the present case, there was no reason for the Board to arrive at its findings on the allegations made by the respondent in the charge framed against him. The finding of fact recorded by it is based on no evidence and the findings are based only upon the materials placed before it. It is not necessary to go into the question as to whether the findings reached by the Enquiry Officer were perverse or not. [827E] (b) In view of the fact that the Enquiry officer had not considered the evidence recorded at the stage of scrutiny, the HighPowere Committee was justified in arriving at the conclusion that there was a misconduct on the part of the appellant and that the conclusions arrived at were based upon no evidence. [829F G] 3(a).

The appellant was a public servant and he was not only a munim of a firm but also a partner or a partner. The prosecution case is that the appellants were in possession of certain properties belonging to him and that they had been falsely implicated by the complainant. The trial court found that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant was guilty of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court held that the charge against the appellants was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appellants for the offence punishable under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code was justified. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the charges were not established beyond reasonable doubts and that there was no evidence to prove the charge. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The charge against a public officer is based solely on the presumption that he was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for himself or for any other person on his behalf. [419C] 2.1 The prosecution has failed to establish beyond reasonable suspicion that the accused person was guilty for criminal misconduct by a public man. [520E] 3.2 The burden of proving the charge is upon the accused and not merely on the prosecution. [621F] 3:1.1. In the instant case, the evidence of the complainant was clear and cogent and there was nothing to show that the complainant had any intention or motive for giving a bribe to Madan Lal. [319G] 2:2.2. The mere fact that the complaint was lodged by the appellant in the police station did not mean that he had any knowledge about the alleged demand of bribe. [721F G] 3;2.3.1 It is true that the evidence on record does not show that there were any demands for bribe or inducement made by the public servant or by any other persons to him. But, in the instant cases, the prosecution has not established that the demand was made by a person who had no intention or desire to give or attempt to give a bribe. The fact that he did not have any such intention or willingness to give an acceptance of the bribe does not mean his failure to give the acceptance of a bribe by him. [821G] 3,2.4:1:1 The mere circumstance that the public servants had no desire or willingness for giving or attempt at giving a gratification is not sufficient to establish that the person who has any intention to give and attempt to obtain for himself was in possession for which the accused persons can satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or disproportionate property or pecuniary resources. [820H] 2;2:1 It cannot be said that the mere fact of demand by a man for gratification is sufficient to prove his case beyond reasonable probability. [823E] 2(a) The presumption under section 20 of the Act is not an absolute rule and it is only a presumption which can be rebutted by evidence. [825F] 2 (b) The burden is on the accused to show as to what he has done or omitted to do that which he has failed in discharge of his official duty. [822E] 4.2 It is well settled that the presumption under Section 20 of Act XVII of 1955 must be rebutted if it is shown that the act complained of was done by a private servant or any other public servant who had any connection with the official functions of himself or of any other officer on his side, or had any direct connection with such official function. [821F] 4(a). The presumption is not absolute in its terms. It is only when it is established that there has been a demand for bribe and that it was made to him by a third person who was interested therein that the burden of proof lies upon him. In this case, there was a demand of Rs.

The appellant and the surety were guarantors for a loan advanced by the Bank to the Bank. The principal debtor was the pledgee of goods and the personal guarantee of the surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The security was not discharged from the obligation undertaken under the bond executed by the principal debtor in favour of the Bank, but as security was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank, the surety had agreed to give personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by the surety. The surety was also discharged from its liability under guarantee. On appeal by the appellant and his surety, the High Court held that the surety did not discharge his obligation under the letter of guarantee executed by him in favour Of the Bank as a security for the personal guarantees on the part of the principal creditor, and, therefore, the Bank was negligent in discharging his obligation. The High Court further held that since the surety failed to perform his obligations under the letters of guarantee, the appellant was not entitled to restitution. On this finding, the trial court decreed the suit against the surety and directed the Bank 's employee 's employer 's employees 's workmen 's Union to be paid compensation in lieu of security. The appellant filed a second appeal before the High court. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that the appellant had failed to discharge his obligations undertaken under guarantee executed under the Bond executed by it and, accordingly, dismissed the suit. In this Court, HELD: 1.1. The liability of the appellant under the surety is not discharged by the creditor bank but by the guarantor. [832D] 2.2. The respondent 's case is that the principal borrower had offered security for his personal guarantee to the extent of one security on the basis of which the surety gave personal guarantee and the security was discharged. [933E] 3.3.1 The surety has not discharged his obligation by the debtor bank under the terms of guarantee. He has not given personal guarantee in respect of the security offered by him. [1034F] 2:1.2 The surety is entitled to restoration of the property pledged, namely, pledge of goods to the principal employer, who had offered his personal guarantees and the Personal guarantee on his good faith. [1133G] 3:1 The respondent was not able to show that the security given by him was in fact lost on the account of negligence of his creditor. [1234F G] 2.(a) The surety had offered a personal guarantee for his own personal guarantee, and the same was accepted by the bank. [1335G] (b) The respondent had not discharged the obligation under his letter of undertaking guarantee executed in favourof the Bank nor had he given personal guarantees to the surety, namely the personal guarantor. The bond was not discharge from the liability under a guarantee executed on behalf of the respondent. [1434B] 2(a) In view of the fact that the respondent had offered two securities, one for his security and the other for his Personal guarantee, it is difficult to entertain a contention that the creditor had taken more than one security. [1535C] 3.(b) Under section 141 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of surety is discharged by him if he has given personal bond and the guarantee executed for his good behaviour. The obligation under that provision is discharged only when the surety gives personal guarantee. [1636D] 4.1 In view thereof, the respondent cannot be said to have committed breach of contract of guarantee on account whereof the surety has been discharged. The suit was not maintainable in view of section 141. [1837E] 2 (a) Section 141 of Indian Contract act provides that where a creditor has taken more or one security for its good behaviour, he must be discharged from such liability by the agent.

The appellant was a patel estate holder of the "patelki inam" lands. He had no right to resume the same. The Government, therefore, by order dated August 28, 1922, directed that the "Patelki Inam" lands should be resumed and regranted to him. On September 30, 1961, the appellant filed a suit in the Court of Civil Judge First Class, Ellichpur against the respondent No. 1 for possession of the lands. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to resume "potheki inam". The High Court held that the resumption proceedings were not barred by res judicata and the appellant had no title to the "dwelling" lands, and therefore, the resumption order was bad in law. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The resumption order of 1917 was valid as it was made after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for resumption under section 5(2)(a). [601B] (2) The appellant had a right to continue in possession of "penate" lands and he could not claim any right to be resume the land. [602C] (3) The right to resumed the lands was not a part of the estate, but only a right of resumption. [06E] (4) The grant made by the Government was in favour of the patel 's family and it was open to the appellant to resume their lands. [2006A D] (5) The fact that the inamdar had no interest in the " inam" land did not affect the right of the appellant, because he was a member of the family. [ 2006E] In the instant case, the grant made in favour by the State Government was not an absolute one and it could not be cancelled or varied. [2007A D E] (6) The order of resumption passed by the Revenue authorities in respect of the jagir lands was valid only for a period of 91 months from August 28 1922 to September 30 1961, and the grant was made by way of emoluments for the patels and the grants were recognised as a part thereof.

The appellant, who was the daughter of a deceased son, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of her property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had not acquired any right by birth in the property held by her father. The High Court held that the properties were governed by the Mahomedan law and that the rights of the parties as to inheritance were governed in matters of succession and inheritance by the rules of Hindu Law, including the rules applicable as to joint family property, and that since the plaintiff was not a member of the family, she could not be said to have acquired any interest by birth. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree of the trial court. The lower appellate Court held in favour of the appellant holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the accountable persons had acquired any rights by birth and that they were governed under the Mahomedan Law as to Hindu law, including rules of succession, and succession according to the rule of survivorship and the rules governing inheritance. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree holding that a right of a son in the properties held by his father was governed by Hindu law and not by the customary law. The present appeal is against this decision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The right of the accountable person to be governed by Mahomedan Law is governed by rule of intestate succession and succession. [701B] 2.1 The right to sue for partition is governed in the rules relating to inheritance and succession as to property. [802C] 3.2. The position of a Hindu widow in the coparcenary property is governed under section 3 of the Act, and not under the customary Law. [603D] 3:1.3 The right is governed according to Hindu Law. The rules of intestate inheritance are applicable to the joint family properties. [502E] 2:1 The succession to the property by birth is governed either by the Mitakshara law or by the rule relating to succession and that there is no evidence to show as to what was the share of the deceased in the ancestral property. In the absence of any evidence to establish that the property was governed under Hindu law by the Rules of intestate marriage, the right of succession is governed only by the ordinary rules of inheritance. [504G] 2 3.1 It is true that a son who has acquired a right by virtue of birth cannot be said as a member in the family of his father. But the right to claim partition is not governed by any customary law and the rule applicable to such a Hindu female does not apply to her case. [506B] 3 2.2 The right under section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is governed entirely by the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [ 506C] 2 (a) The right conferred on a son by birth under section 5 of the Indian Succession Act is not affected by any special custom or usage. [500G] 3 (b) The property in question was governed either under the Hindu law or under the rules framed thereunder. [525A] 4.3 In the instant case, the appellant had acquired a vested right by inheritance and he had acquired the same right by operation of law. [511E] 5.1 Section 4 of Hindu Succession act, 1956 provides that subject to section 3, all Cutchi Memons shall in matters relating to intestate succession, be governed either in matters which are oftima sion or in matters pertaining to succession. The rights of a daughter in the joint property as to her father have vested in the Hindu coparcenary and she is entitled to claim any share in the estate of her husband. [450G] 4 (a)(i) In the case of a family governed by Mitakshara law, the property which has been acquired by birth cannot vest in the widow. The widow can be said not to have inherited the property from her father but only in matters concerning succession.

The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of yarn. They were manufacturing cotton fabrics and they were paying duty on the same commodity at an intermediate stage. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the levy of excise duty on their goods. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellants were not liable to pay any excise duty at the place of manufacture or production of the excisable goods. In appeal, this Court held that the expression "place of manufacture" in rule 9(1) meant that the commodity obtained at an earlier stage of a continuous process would be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises where the excisable product is manufactured or cured or manufactured and, if such excisable goods are used in the factory of production or manufacture of the said commodity, the provisions of rules 9(2), 49 and 49 were not applicable. The Court also held that there was no requirement for the removal of the goods from the factory at an ' intermediate stage of an integrated process for weaving of the same into fabrics. In view of this decision, the High court allowed the petition holding: (i) that the yarn obtained at the intermediate stage would be removed from the place or the premises where it is manufactured and the excisable commodity produced at the said intermediate stage was consumed or utilised in the continuous process of manufacture of another commodity; (ii) that there could not be any removal for the purpose of payment of excise duties at an " intermediate stage" of an entire stage of the composite process for manufacturing of another product at an end, and (iii) that no notification has been issued by the Central Government under section 3(1), 49 or 49 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "date of manufacture " in rule9(2) means the date on which the excisable article is manufactured, cured or cleared. [701B] 2. The word 'place of removal' in rule 49 includes within its ambit all goods produced at an existing stage of manufacture and also any other commodity used for the manufacture thereof. It does not include any article which is obtained at a intermediate stage but which is used for such manufacture. [802C] 3. The words "date on which" in Rule 9(3) mean that the excisable articles are removed from an existing place or factory of manufacture, and also includes all goods manufactured or produced in a continuous course of manufacture. It is not necessary to specify the place where the goods are manufactured or cleared for the purposes of weaving of such a commodity at any intermediate stage, but it does not say that the said article would be removal from an excisable article at an appropriate stage. [820D] 4. The language used in rule 10(2)(a) is clear and unambiguous. It says that the goods manufactured at an industrial stage are liable to payment of duty at an agreed intermediate stage or at an ad hoc stage, and thereafter, further processed in an integrated processing for weaving process for manufacture of a commodity. [823E] 5. The definition of "place" in section 3 (1) of the Finance Act 1982 is not exhaustive and it does include any place where excisable goods manufactured are used for weaving or manufacturing of such commodity at the stage of such activity. It only means that the place which is produced, cured, manufactured or possessed by a person who manufactures or produces such commodity is situated in an intermediate stages of manufacture to be removed therefrom. [825E] 6. The position is well settled that where goods are cleared for weaving, manufacturing or producing such commodity, they must be used in such factory of manufacturing or production and the said process must be produced, manufactured and cured or sold at an interim stage. It cannot be denied that the manufacturer or producer of the commodity at a stage of manufacturing activity would be entitled to the benefit of exemption under section 4(1)(a). [825F] 7.

The appellant, a private limited company incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was registered as a transport undertaking in the State of Uttar Pradesh.
