The Regional Transport Authority, Meerut, by its order dated August 30, 1979, granted permission to the appellant to operate a transport service on the route specified in the scheme. On September 1, 1979 the appellant filed an application before the Hearing Authority under section 68D of the Act for approval of the scheme and for the grant of a permit to it. The respondent contended that the scheme was not published in the official Gazette and that the authority which had the power to publish it had the powers to make such scheme. The High Court, by the impugned order, allowed the writ petition holding that the application filed by the appellant under section68D of Act was not maintainable before the hearing Authority under sections 68 D of the . The High court held that the appellant had no locus standi to file a suit for injunction against the Hearing authority and that it had no jurisdiction to issue an order of injunction restraining the Hearing. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The scheme was published in official Gazette on September 1 1979. It is not open to a party to a dispute that the procedure laid down under section 69D of .the Act has been duly published in its official Gazette. [701 B] 2.2. The power to make an order for the hearing of a case under section 70 D of .The scheme was duly published on September 10, 1979 and it was published on October 1, 1980. It was open to the Hearing Authorities to consider such objections or representations as they may be called upon to consider them. [801 C] 3.3. The right to move for an order under section 67 D of Act is exclusive in character and it is not competent to a civil court to pass any order on the basis thereof. [820 E] 4.4.1 In view of the provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the , the scheme framed by the State Government under section 66D of , the Act, the hearing authority was bound to consider the objections or representation made by the persons interested in the provision of road transport facilities recognised in this behalf by the Central Government and also to consider whether the scheme is approved or not. [821 E] 3:1.2 The scheme framed under section 63 C of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, was published by the Regional Transport Officer on September 9, 1979. The State Transport Undertaking had the jurisdiction to publish the scheme under section 62 D of ,the Act. The Scheme was published under section 72D of ; and it had been published in a Gazette on October 10, 1980, which was published as required by section 68 C of . The scheme had been duly approved by the Hearing Officer under section 71C of the Insurance Act, 1938. [823 E] 2:1 The High Courts have held that since the scheme has been published under sections 69D and 70D of 'the Act, it is open to an aggrieved person to file an appeal before the Appellate Authority under sub section (2) of section 68 D. [825 A B C] 2(a) In view thereof, the High Court was right in refusing to stay the further proceedings in the suit.

The appellant was working as a police officer in the office of the District Magistrate, Delhi. He was prosecuted for offences under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and section 161, Indian Penal Code. The appellant was charged with having committed an offence punishable under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 of the Indian Penal code. The prosecution case was that the appellant had obtained a bribe from Russel Nathaniel on January 29, 1963 for doing or forbearing to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 120B I. P.C., and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had not properly appreciated the evidence and had erred in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court held that the charge framed against the accused was proved beyond reasonable doubts and accordingly acquitted him. In appeal by Special Leave, it was urged on behalf Of the appellant, that the order of sanction under section 6 of the Act was not justified because the prosecution failed to establish the fact that the accused had obtained money from Ruslathan Nathanieiel and his wife and also a gold ring from Ruslu Nathanutty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact that a person has obtained money by giving a bribe or reward for doing any official act, or showing or forbing to show, in the exercising of his office, or forbear to show or forbenearing to give or forbring to show is not sufficient to prove that the offence was committed under section 4(1) (d). [601B] 2. The sanction required by section 6 is a condition precedent for prosecution and it cannot be said that the mere fact of the commission of an offence under section 3(1), Indian Penal Codes, does not make out a case against the person who has obtained the money from him. [602C] 3. The question whether the appellant was guilty of having committed any offence under the Indian penal Code or any other criminal statute is a mixed question of fact and law. It is well settled that in order to establish a charge under section 7, it must be shown that the person concerned had obtained the gratification from him for doing an official act or showing, in his exercise of such office, and that he had obtained it from Rusllathan Nelliel on February 29, 1964. [06E] 4. The fact that there was a gross abuse of his position as public servant within the meaning of section 5[1)(c) of Prevention of corruption Act, 1947] does not mean that the case against him is proved beyond doubt. [2006A D] 5. In view of the provisions contained in section 6(2), it cannot also be said to be a case where the prosecution has failed to discharge its official functions or shown, in their exercise of their official functions. [ 2006E] 6. The facts which have been found by the High court are not sufficient for establishing the fact of commission of any offence charged and obtained by him for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and therefore the charge is established beyond doubt and accordingly the order passed by the trial court convicting the appellant under section5(1A) of 1947 Act was set aside. [2007E] 7. The appeal filed by the State against the judgment of the High Curt was dismissed by this Court on February 17, 1966. In the special leave petition filed by it, it is contended that the conviction and sentence passed by both the courts below were not sustainable in law.

The appellant was prosecuted in a competent court of law for the offences alleged to have been committed by him. He had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The sanction accorded to the prosecution of the appellant was not a valid sanction. The appellant was charged with having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for showing favour to Doraiswamy in respect of the claim cases filed against the Vizianagram Section of the Railway Act, 1947. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 100/- under section 161 I.P.C. and to undergo simple imprisonment for six months. The Special Judge acquitted him but he preferred an appeal to the High Court which was dismissed by the judgment dated November 20, 1953. In this appeal, the appellant contended that the sanction accorded in his favour was not valid as a valid order had been obtained from him and that the prosecution was barred by section 6(c) of the Act. The High Court accepted the contention and held that the sanctioning authority had no jurisdiction to accord the certificate. It was further held that since the sanction was not issued in accordance with section 6 (c), the appellant could not be prosecuted for the offence under section 5(2) of, the Act as he had not complied with the requirements of section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sanctioning authority has no jurisdiction under article 134(1)(c) to grant a certificate. [601B] 2. The mere fact that the appellant had applied his minds and was satisfied that in the interests of justice, he should be put on his trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 6, does not make him liable to be prosecuted in any court of competent Jurisdiction for offences alleged against him. [613C] 3. The grant of certificate is not a mere matter of procedure but it is an administrative act and the sanctioning authorities have no power to accord such sanction. [501D] 4. The authority has to apply his mind and be satisfied that there was sufficient ground for granting the certificate and the sanction applied in this case was not proper. [511E] 5. The prosecution of a person who had accepted illegal bribe is not an offence under article 135(1) (c). It is only when the sanctioning Authority finds that the person has accepted illegal or improper gratification as motive or consideration for reward or reward, that it can be held that he should not accord the sanction. In the instant case, the sanctioning officer had no power under section 197 of the Code to accord sanction to the appellant. [452E] 6. The facts and circumstance of the present case clearly show that the Sanctioning Authority had no competence to accord a certificate in respect thereof. [451F] 7. It is not disputed that the sanctioned authority had applied its mind and was of the opinion that in view of the materials placed before him it had applied their mind and were of the view that in order to give a valid approval, the sanction should be accorded in this matter. [454G H; 452A B] 8. The fact that there is no evidence on record to show that in spite of the sanctioning order the appellant did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office or that he had applied the mind and the circumstances of his case shows that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord him a certificate which was the necessary material upon which he had taken all possible steps. [458A B C] 9. The question whether the sanction granted by the sanctioningauthority is valid or not has to be determined on the evidence adduced before the Court and the facts established are sufficient to justify the grant of a certificate are irrelevant for deciding the issue in this appeal. [459B D] 10.

The appellant, who was the landlord of a building, filed two suits for eviction against the tenants on the ground that he had only a life interest in the premises and that he has only a Life interest in those premises. The Rent Controller dismissed the suits holding that the requirement of the landlords to vacate the premises was not bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. On appeal, the appellate authority confirmed the order of eviction. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that a single petition with regard to two different tenancies could be filed only if there is no possibility or objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The requirement of landlord for reconstruction of the premises is not bona fides required by his wife and children. [901B] 2. The need to vacate a building on the basis that it is a life estate in the hands of the testator or from some other remainder person cannot be defeated by the tenants. [092C] 3. The landlord has only one life interest and he can only have a lifeinterest in those properties. He cannot, therefore, seek eviction of the tenants from the premises on any of the grounds available to him under the Act. [1001D] 4. The High Court was right in holding, that the need to obtain a single application for eviction of tenants from two different tenancyes was not mala fide and that the landlord had only one or more life interest. [1102E] 5. The tenant is entitled to evict the tenants under section 14(1) (b) as he has no right to get possession of the property in question on any other ground available to them under the provisions of the Act, if he is able to prove that there was a life interests in those two premises. [110E] 6. The fact that the tenant had only life interest cannot be denied by the landlords because the tenants have no right or interest in these two premises and they are not entitled to get any protection under section 13(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. [111E] 7. The provisions of section 14 (1) of that Act are not applicable to a case where the landlord has no interest in such premises. It is only when the tenant has no other life interest that he can have a right or claim any protection against eviction under section 12(1). [110G H] 8. In the instant case, the tenants had only two life interest, but they were not entitled for eviction on any ground available under the Tamil Pradesh Buildings (lease and Rent) Act. The landlords had only three life interest which could be protected by the provisions contained in section 14 of that act. [112A C] 9. In view of the above discussion, the High court was right and it was rightly held that the tenants were entitled to eviction on the grounds mentioned in section 13 (1)(a) of Tamil Nadu Act No. XI of 1961. [113B D] 10. The tenants are not the holders of life interest or they have only a right to enjoy the property for their life time subject to certain charges mentioned in the Deed of Settlement. They cannot, however, be denied the right to occupy the premises unless there is an element of necessity. [114E] 11. In this case, it is not disputed that the landlords had no right of occupation of the building on any one or other of them and they were only entitled to retain the property subject to various charges mentioned therein. The rent payable by the tenant was Rs. 1,000/per month. It was also admitted that the rent payable was Rs., 1,500/per months. [115E] 12.

The appellant, who was the intermediary of grove land, had been in possession of certain lands. He was a grove holder and he was entitled to compensation for the entire land. The mortgagee, on the basis of an agreement between him and the mortgagor, executed a sale deed in favour of the appellant. On the basis that the land was part of grove lands, the appellant filed a suit for specific performance of the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to claim compensation for his entire land and that he was not entitled to any compensation for that portion of the land. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the sale deed executed in favour the appellant did not confer any title on him and that the mortgagee could not enforce his right against the mortgage or the grove land. On this view, the suit was dismissed. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that a mortgage is a part of the grove lands. [701B] (2) The expression "intermediary" in section 3(13) of the Act means any person who has been in actual possession of any part of land and includes an intermediary. [802C E] (3) A mortgagee can enforce his rights against the mortgagor or the mortgagee, as the case may be, by enforcing his right to compensation. The expression 'intermediaries ' does not include a grove or grove land but includes a grove land and grove land; it means any grove land which is part of an estate. [901F] (4) A mortgage is an integral part of a grove and the mortgagee can recover his rights by enforcing against the mortgagee. The mortgagor cannot enforce his interest in such grove lands as he could not recover his right from the mortgagee under section 6(a) of Act. [1001G] (5) The word 'interminary' in section 6 (a) does not mean a grove, but includes an intermediate grove land or grove lands; it is only a grove which is included in the whole of the estate and does not cover any part thereof. [1101F G] (6) A mortgagor cannot be asked to enforce his mortgage against the mortgaged property by enforcing the right of redemption. The word "interminaries" in the section means an intermediate plot or grove, as defined in section 2(13), and includes a sub-tenant. [110G] In the instant case, the mortgagee had no interest in the grove properties. He could not be asked by the mortgagor to enforce the mortgage against his right. [111H; 111A] (7) The words "interferemediary ' do not include an intermediary ' and an intermediary.' are only a part thereof and cannot be construed as including an intermediate field. [112B] In this case, it is clear that the mortgagor had no title to the grove or the land in question. He had no rights in the land and he could enforce his claim against the Government. [113A B] (8) The right of a mortgagee to enforce a mortgage under section 3 (13) was not an integral portion of his grove lands but only a subtenant. It was, therefore, not a part which could be enforced by enforcing a mortgage against a mortgagor.

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 326 IPC and Sections 325 read with Section 149 IPC. They pleaded not guilty to the charge of murder but were convicted for the offence under [Section 324] IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of three years and to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000 each. The High Court by its judgment dated 4th September, 1991 acquitted all the accused persons of the offences under Section 325 readwith Section 149 and sentenced them to undergo life imprisonment. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants were guilty for an alleged offence under Sections 302/149 IPC. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of all the appellants for the offences punishable under Section 324 read with 149 IPC is unsustainable and they are liable to be acquitted. [701B] 2. The prosecution failed in proving beyond reasonable doubts that the accused were guilty of an offence punishable under Sections 325/149 and 326 IPC. [802C] 3. The evidence on record clearly shows that the first appellant Subran, who was armed with a chopper, had caused injuries to Suku and Preman. He had also caused injuries by blunt weapons. The medical evidence clearly shows the presence of the first accused Subran in the occurrence. [901D] 4. The fact that Suku died on account of injuries inflicted by him is not in dispute. It was only after the death of Suku, he was convicted for an act under Section 302 IPC and was sentenced to imprisonment for life. [1001E] 5. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the conviction of the accused for the said offence cannot be sustained. [1101F] 6. The sentence recorded by the High court is not sustainable in law. [1202G] 7. The appeal is allowed.

The assessee, a non resident Indian Company, filed its returns for the assessment years 1967 68 and 69, in respect of the said amount on cash basis. The Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee under Section 5(2)(b) of the Act on the ground that it had maintained its accounts on cash and on account of royalty amount received by it in U.K. In regard to the amounts credited to the account of the assessee, the Income Tax officer held that the said amounts were not received by the assessee in UK. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal affirmed the decision of the Income tax Officer and upheld the order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the amount credited to account of income by the Indian Company was not received in U K.K., as it did not receive any royalty amount on its actual receipt. [701B] 2.2 The assessee had maintained a true and correct account of its receipts in U P.K.. The assessee, however, maintained a separate account of all its income from the said royalty amount. It was not disputed that the assessee had made a debit entry in the books of the Indian company on cash. [801C] 3.3 The assessee did not maintain any particular method of accounting regularly in respect thereof and it did so only when it received the royalty amount only when they received the same in U k.K.' [802D] 4.1 In regardto the amounts debited to the accounts of the appellant, the assessee was required to make a true account of their receipts in the Books of the Company. The assessee could not have maintained any particular system of accounting in regard to royalty amount and that it did make an entry in its books of account on cash or in respect thereto. [820E] 4.(a) In regard tothe amounts credited by the Income TAX Officer to the assessee as per its books, the same were credited to his account in Uk.K.; (b) The assessee was not maintaining any particular accounting system on cash; and (c) The amount credited by him to the Bank in UUK. was credited to its account in the Bank. [823E] 5.(a)(i) In respect of amounts credited in UO.K, the High Court had rightly held that it was not open to the Incometax Officer to make an entries in the accounts on Cash and in respect whereof royalty amount was credited by it to the bank. [825F] 6.2 It is true that the High court has not accepted the contention of the Revenue that the method of accountancy adopted by it for all its Income Tax Officers was not correct or that it took the account on Cash basis. But, as pointed out by the High Courts, the method adopted by the appellant in maintaining its accounts was not consistent with the accounting practice followed by it and that the income was credited in the account books of both the companies. [826C] 6.(a). The assessee has maintained a correct and true account on the basis of the figures as per their profit and loss account, but the High Curt did not accept the contention that the amounts were credited in his books of accounts on receipt basis. [827D] (b)(i), (ii) & (iii) In the case of non residentIndian Company, the amount was debited to its accounts in UCO Bank as per the profit and Loss account maintained by it. The High C ourt did accept the submission that the payment of royalty was not a receipt or receipt but only a receipt. It also accepted the submission of the revenue that the payments were credited into the books on cash, but did not take the account in India. [828E] (c)(i).

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 302, Indian Penal Code. He was convicted by the Sessions Judge of Bombay for an offence punishable under section 307 read with section 34, Indian penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence from one year to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the evidence of an accomplice was not reliable because he had made a confessional statement to his brother, and that the Sessions judge had failed to appreciate the evidence against him. HELD: (1) The evidence of the approver is not reliable. It is true that the approver has been able to make a confession to his co accused, but it is equally true that he has made a confession in the presence of two witnesses, one of whom was a witness and another of whom had given a confessional declaration. [601 B] (2) The High court was right in holding the appellant guilty of an offence of murder under section 304, Indian IPC. [702 C] (3) The conviction of the first accused for an offen ce punishable under sections 302, 34 and 201 read with Section 34, I.P.C., is not sustainable on the evidence that he had a motive to commit the crime. [803 D] (4) The fact that the appellant was convicted in the case of murder of one Lahu Vithu Patil on March 17, 1960, does not affect his conviction under section 34 of the Indian Penal code. [820 E] (5) The prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the first appellant had a common intention to commit an offe nce punishable under Section 302, I PC.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 161, Indian Penal code and section 2, Indian penal Code. The Special Judge convicted him of the charge framed against him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) he was not an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation; (2) that he was merely a servant and was employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops and was paid his salary; (3) that the appellant was not a public Servant within the definition of section 2(12), Indian Penal C.P.C., and (4) that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was an officer or servant of the Government. HELD: (1)(a) The High Court has held that the charge against the appellant is proved by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt. [701B] (b) The appellant was an Officer in the Indian Railway Establishment and he was appointed as a "public servant" within the terms of section 81, Indian Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1964 (Act 40 of 1964). He was also a public servants within the scope of that section. [802C E] (c) The expression 'officer in the employment or pay' in the context of section 3(12) of that Act means an officer appointed to any office for the performance of some public duty. [820D] (2)(a). In the present case, the appellant had been working as a Clerk in the Railways Workshops at the time when he was posted as a 'officer' in Railway Carriage workshop. He had been paid his pay and allowances during the period of his service. The appellant had not been able to show any evidence that he had been performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of the Works Manager who were merely auxiliary to them. [823E] (3)(a)(i) The word 'officer" in section 21, Indian Railway C. P.C. has to be construed as a person who was an employee within the term of section 23, Indian Railways C.p.C.. In the instant case, it is not disputed that the word 'Officer' used in section 3 (12) includes an officer who was the lead of the office. [825E] The appellant could not be said to be a public man within the ambit of section 20, Indian C. p.C.; and therefore he was a person performing duties as a public prosecutor within the defined meaning of that word ' Officer in section 2 (12), and therefore a public officer within the purview of that definition would be an officer within that definition. [901F] (ii) The words 'officer " in the case of a public service or a class of Government Companies" in sub section (2), of section 8, are wide enough to include any person who is employed as an officer of the Railway Administration or a Class Iii servant. It would be sufficient if the appellant were not a Public Servant within that term. [1001F G] (iii) The definition of 'public servant " in section 20(9), Indian C, P. C., and the expression 'Officer in the services or pay" in the latter part of the definition are wide and include any officer who is attached to the office of the Executive Engineer who was a Class 1ii servant; but the word "officer" has not been defined in the Act. [1101F H] (iv) The term 'officer ' in section 19(9)(a), Indian Railway Service or a Government Company as defined in section 617 of the I.P., Code, is wide enough and includes any officer attached to such office for performance of certain public duties.

The appellant was prosecuted for contravention of the provisions of the Defence of India Rules and under the Defence Of India Act, 1962. He was convicted by the trial court on a charge framed against him under s. 3(1) (2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the conviction and sentence passed by the lower courts were illegal because they had not been complied with in accordance with r. 141(2) and that the order of the High court was liable to be set aside. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of contravention of r. 140(2). In appeal before this Court, it was urged on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had committed a manifest error in holding that r.141 (2), as amended by the Maharashtra Government, did not contain any provision for proof of judicial proceedings in respect of the seizure and punishment of contraventions of r.. 141(1)(b) of Defence of Indias Act, 1968. Dismissing the appeal, this Court ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of r., 141 (2 ) of the [Police Act] are not inconsistent with any existing law or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any enactment other than this Act. [149E F] 2.1 The words "any person" used in s.3(2)(b), which are in the following terms, must be read as "any officer" and not merely an officer who is authorised to seize or detain a goods under the provisions thereof. [150F] 3.2 The word 's possession' has been defined in section 2 (d) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. It means that any person who is authorized to seize any article or receptacle in which any stocks of jowar are found and who is empowered to seize such articles or receptacle shall be liable to confiscation under the said sections. [151G] 3:1. The word "s possession" has been used in section 3(2), for the purpose of maintaining supplies and services essential to the life of the community. It does not include any provision relating to the maintenance of supplies and Services essential to that life. [152H; 152A B] 2:1 The word possession' is a term which means possession of goods or property in which they are found. In the instant case, the appellant had been convicted by both the courts for contraventions under s 3(3) (a), (b) and (c) of r . 141(4). [152B] 2(i) The word was used in a sense to cover cases where the goods were found. It is not necessary that the person who has been authorised to take possession must be in possession of those articles or property. [153C F] 3(ii) In the present case, it is not disputed that the seized stock of juar was found. The prosecution had also failed to prove that the juar seized from the house of the accused was kept in a separate room and that it was used for maintaining supplies essential to life of community. [155D] 3 (iii) The High court has committed a serious error in setting aside the conviction of the appellants on the ground that the prosecution had failed to establish that the goods seized were not the properties of the jugar or that they were kept in separate room. [156E F; 154A B C] 4.1. In view of the fact that the accused had been acquitted by both courts, it would be open to the State Government to take action under s 5(2); and if the accused is convicted on a finding that the property was not kept in the separate room, he can be prosecuted for violation of r,. 141(3).

The appellant was charged with an offence under Section 302 I.P.C., and he was convicted by the trial court for an offence of murder, punishable under Section 304 Part II, I. P.C. The High Court acquitted him on a charge of murder. He has preferred this appeal to this Court. The prosecution case is that the deceased Kunwar Singh had been murdered in the village Bicycle and he had been killed by some unknown persons. The trial court found that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had committed any offence under section 302 I P. C., and therefore, convicted him of an offence punishable under section 304 PartII, I P C. The State preferred an appeal against the acquittal of the appellant. The learned Judges of the High Court held that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant of an alleged offence under [section 302] I. PC., but on a finding that there had been no evidence at all to show as to what happened to the deceased in the course of the occurrence, convicted the appellant for an act done by him with a gun. The appeal was dismissed. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High court should not have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge and should not be allowed to interfere with the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The evidence of Om Prakash Dubey is cogent and convincing. He had been examined as a witness in the case and he has clearly stated that he was able to identify him. [901B] 2.2. The fact that the accused persons were not known to the witnesses and they were unable to identify them, does not make any difference. It is true that the evidence of the witnesses is cogent, convincing and reliable. But it is equally well settled that the court should be slow in interfering with an order of conviction passed by a Sessions Judge. [1001C] 2:1.3 The High court was not impressed by the evidence adduced by Om Prakash Dwivedi and Ram Chandra. [1101D] 2.(a) There was no material to show, as to why the appellant should have been acquitted on a single charge of conspiracy. [110E] 2(b) The prosecution had failed to establish that the murder of Kunwar Singh was committed in furtherance of the common intention of all the accused and therefore the High ' Court was not justified in interfering therewith. [109G] 2 (c) The High 'Court should not interfere with an acquittal unless it is shown that there has been a substantial error of law or procedure which could have been pointed out by the prosecution. [108A] 3.(a)(i) In the instant case, the evidence on record clearly shows that the occurrence had taken place in the manner alleged by the witnesses. The appellant was not present at the time when he was examined as an accused and he did not know about the presence of Kunwar singh. He was unable to say who had engaged him or who had undertaken him or which had engaged himself or which used to instruct him in the matter. [107A] 4.(a). In view of the fact that there is no evidence on the record to show what happened after the occurrence and the appellant was able not to identify himself, it cannot be said that he had intentionally made an attempt to facilitate the commission of murder of the deceased. [106B] 5.(b) There is nothing in the evidence to suggest that the appellants were aware of the presence or they had gathered there from before the occurrence. The mere fact that some unknown person was present at a particular place cannot be taken as conclusive proof of the existence of an intention on the part of the accused to facilitate commission of the crime.

The appellant was charged under section 302, read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code for having committed the murder of one of the deceased persons. He was also charged under sections 302 and 149, readwith section 34 of the said Code. The learned judges found that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused were not guilty of the offence under section 148, read alongwith section 34. They convicted him under section 304, Part I, read With section 34 and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. He also held that the High Court was right in holding that the said accused did not take part in the commission of the murder. The High Court found that there were no eye witnesses to the occurrence and therefore acquitted all the accused. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1. The evidence is adduced to prove the existence of a common intention with each of the accused persons. [801B] 2.2. The prosecution has failed to establish that the deceased was last seen together in the company of accused 1 and 3. There is no direct evidence to show that they were seen together by the witnesses, or that any other person who was not identified by them, was also present at the time when the incident took place. [901C] 2:1.3 The prosecution failed to discharge its onus to prove beyond reasonable doubt that accused 1, 3 and 4 had a prior concert with each other. [1001D] 2.:1.4. The fact that the appellant was not named in the FIR is not sufficient to establish his involvement in the offence. [1101E] 2.(a) The prosecution had proved that the appellants were seen by the deceased together and they were identified by witnesses, and therefore, there was no question of their participation in the crime. [110G] 2(b) The High court has not committed any error in holding the appellant guilty under section 149, IPC. [108A] 3.(c) The conviction of the appellants under section 307 read with sections 34, read along with section 149 and section 149 is unsustainable. [107B] 4.1 It was contended on behalf of the State that the evidence adduced by the prosecution to prove its case against the accused is not reliable because the witnesses are not eye witnesses. They were not examined in the manner contemplated by section 149 of the Code. [109C] 3(a) In order to establish the guilt of the appellant, it was necessary for the prosecution and the court to have proved that he had a common object with each others. The mere fact that he did not act as an unlawful assembly cannot be held against him merely because he is acquitted by giving benefit of doubt. [106A] 4(b)(i) In the instant case, the evidence was sufficient to prove his involvement and the appellant could not have been convicted under section 34 IPC. He had no intention to commit murder. [105B] 3 (a) It is well settled that when a person is acquitted in respect of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, he cannot be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 149, unless the evidence is corroborated by other evidence. [104C] 4.(b)(ii) The mere presence of the two accused at the scene of occurrence and their participation at the instance of the witnesses in the incident cannot be said to be a material circumstance against them. [103D] 5(c) In view of the fact that there was a common motive for committing the murder, it is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubts. [101E] 6.(a)(i), (ii) and (iii) of section 149 are cases where the evidence of the eye witnesses is not acceptable or cogent.

The petitioner, a registered dealer under the provisions of the Indian Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, applied to the Central Government for grant of licence in respect of certain goods imported by him from the foreign countries. The Central Government granted the licence on 11th May, 1983. On 1st April, 1984, the petitioner filed an application before the Customs authorities under section 15(1)(b) of the Act praying that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date of payment of duty at the time of clearance of the goods from the warehouse. The Customs authorities rejected the application and the petitioner approached this Court by way of a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. This Court, HELD: 1.1. The rate of customs applicable to any imported goods is determined according t o law prevalent in the country on the dates of payment. [601B] 2.1 The rate applicable to all imports of similar goods entered for home con nection under section 46, on the day when the goods are actually removed from the bonded warehouse, would be the rate applicable for the imported Goods. [702C] 3.2. The customs authorities have not applied their mind to the question whether the petitioner was willing to pay duty at that time or not. In view of the fact that the petitioner had no fundamental right to clear the goods on payment of customs duty, the customs authorities were right in taking a decision without any resort to the provisions under section 45(1) (b). [703D] 3.(a) The rate for the import of goods entered into India was not applicable to customs authorities. [777E] 3(b) The petitioner had only sought permission from the Customs Authorities to clear his goods on the basis that he would be entitled to the benefit of section 15 (1)(c). He did not make any application for determination of the question of law and the High Court was in error in holding that the customs authority was right in rejecting the application. [78E] 4.3. The petitioner has, therefore, no case for grant or refusal of permission to clear goods on account of the prohibition contained in section 15 of the Customs Act. [77F] 4.(a)(i) In view thereof, the petition is not maintainable and the same is dismissed.

The father of the appellant died in 1947. He was a minor at the time of his death and he was entitled to a share in the estate of the father. The father of respondent No. 1, who was a member of the joint family, filed a suit for partition of the property and for possession of the properties. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right, title or interest in the properties and therefore the decree passed by the trial Court was not binding on him. On appeal to the High Court it held that the debt was not an avyaharika and therefore was not liable to be sold under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. The High Court reversed the decision of the trial court holding that as the father had no interest in properties, he could not be said to have purchased the property by sale under section 154 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the right, interest and interest of the respondent No 1 were not part of the estate which was sold and therefore there was no question of any partition of his joint family properties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The right, as a result of partition of joint family property is not an absolute right, but only a right to sell the property. [701B] (2) The liability of a father to discharge the debts of the sons is not dependent upon what was the nature of the debt and therefore it cannot be said that whatever the nature thereof was put up for sale as to what passed to the auction purchaser, what the father did was only a part of his estate. [801C] (3) The obligation of a son to discharge his debts of his father which is not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious duty of the members of the family and therefore in view of the express statutory obligation of the brothers, the father alone could not have purchased any property by transfer. [820D] (4) The burden of proving that the father was a part and parcel of his interest in all the properties was upon him. [823E] (5) Where the right of the son to sell his share in all his properties is not disputed, the onus of proving the debt of the deceased father would be on him who has proved the same by leading evidence. [825F] (6) The onus of proof of the debts incurred as a consequence of negligence in the discharge of duties of the parents or the father which does not pass to the family is not discharged by the father and therefore he cannot be held to have acquired any interest in his properties.

The Delhi Administration had issued a notice under section 8 B of the Act on May 27, 1988 to all the police officers and other persons who fall within section 8B of the , but they were not called upon to appear before the Committee. The Committee was also directed to examine the conduct of various police officers in order to be examined at the end of the inquiry. The Delhi Administration issued a show cause notice on May 28, 1988 calling upon all the Police Officers and other police officers to appear for the examination of their witnesses. The petitioners were called upon by the Committee to produce evidence in their defence. They filed their written statement denying the allegations made against them and stated that they had been falsely implicated in the case. The High Court held that the Committee was not justified in issuing a showcause notice under sections 8 B and 8 C of the . It also held that since the petitioners were not parties to the proceedings before the Delhi Administration, they were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 C(2) of the 'Act. The appellants filed an appeal against the order of the Committee dated 29.6.88 before the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the appeal and quashed the orders of the committee and directed the Committee not to examine all the witnesses who were eye witnesses to the incident. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order passed by the High Curt was illegal because it had been issued without jurisdiction in view of section 8 A(2)(a) of 'Act and that the High Courts should not have interfered with the orders passed by them. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Committee has to examine each witness who is cross examined at every stage of the proceedings. [801B] 2.1 In the instant case, the Committee had found that there were a large number of persons who are eye witnesses and others who fall under section 3 B of 'the Act. It was also found that the appellants were not entitled to have been treated as witnesses at every stages of the proceeding. [901C] 2:1 The High Cour t has clearly held that it had to examine only one witness who was cross examined by the prosecution and not by the defence. [1001D] 2(a) In the present case, there is no evidence on record to show that the persons who were witnesses to incidents had been examined at any stage of inquiry. [092E] 2.(b) The Committee had also found in favour of the petitioners and their family members. [103G] 3.1 It was not open to the Committee either to examine or to call for a report from the police officer concerned. [104H; 104A] 3(a). In the circumstances, it is not possible to hold that the petitioners are entitled to any relief under section 9 B of . The Committee could have examined only one person who was examined at each stage of enquiry and not the other persons. [105G] 4.2 It is true that the report of the Delhi Police has been submitted by the Inspector General of Police, Delhi Administration on May 29, 1988. But it is clear from the record that the said report was not produced before the Court. [106H; 107A] 5.1 Section 8B(2), which deals with the procedure for holding an inquiry and the procedure to be followed in holding such inquiry has been provided in section 9D of . It is well settled that the procedure prescribed by section 9 D of . A.P. Act is not a mandatory provision but it is a mandatory requirement. [107A] 4.(a) The procedure prescribed under section 10D of 'The , and the manner of holding an enquiry has been laid down in section 8D of the A. P. Act.

The appellant, a registered firm, filed a return of its turnover for the quarter ending on 30th June, 1959, showing the total amount of tax payable by it. The assessing authority assessed the lump sum of Rs. 1,12,000/- as per the provisions of section 3 and the appellant was liable to pay the tax on the basis that the said amount was not a part of the lump amount of the tax. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who confirmed the order of assessment. The State Government appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The proviso to sub section (3) of section 4 is ultra vires, and it does not make any difference in the tax payable on fares and freights. [801B] (2) The word "tax" used in the proviso to subsection (3), as it stood at the relevant time, means a tax on passengers and goods carried by road or inland waterways. It is not confined to a tax which is levied under the Act. The words "tax on passengers or goods carried" are wide enough to include taxes on passengers, goods and goods transported by road, or inland watersways. [901C] (3)(a) The expression "tax payable" in section 3(1) of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959 is not defined in the Act, but it is a tax levied under section 7 of the said Act. [1001D] (b) The words 'tax on goods carried or inland Waterways' are wide and they include taxes which are levied under sections 7 and 8A of the Act; and the word "fee" in the context of the proviso cannot be read as a tax, because it is not a tax. [1101E] (4) The power to levy a lump sum payment is not an inherent or extra ordinary power. It does not extend to a fee which is charged on passengers carried by roads and inland waterway. [110G] (5) The language of the notification clearly shows that it is only a tax and not a fee. [111H; 111A] (6) The notification issued under section 3 of the Punjab Passengers and goods Taxation Act does not impose any restriction on the right to collect lump sum from passengers or passengers carried in the vehicle, but merely lays down what the amount of lump sum should be, if lump sum is paid by him immediately upon such cessation.

The appellant was employed as a casual worker in the respondent company. He was terminated by the management on 1st August, 1974 and he was paid full back wages for the period from 1 st August, 1975 to 31st August 1974. The management filed an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act before the Labour Court claiming that the appellant should be reinstated in service with full backwages. The Labour Court held that the termination of services of the workmen was bad and directed their reinstatement. On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The order of the Labour court is vitiated because it has become final. [601B] 2.2. The appellant was not entitled to any back wages as he had been deprived of his job for no fault of his. He could not be paid full wages for a long period since he was already in service. [702C] 3.3. The award of the labour court is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Labour Judge for fresh disposal according to law. [803D] 4.1 The appellant should pay full back salary for the entire period from January, 1974 to 31 st August 1974 within a period of two months from today. If he has not been paid full compensation for any period during which he was out of employment, he would be entitled to full back benefits. [903E] 4.(a) The appellant is entitled to all the back wages in addition to the amount already paid as retrenchment compensation. [1001F] (b) The award is setaside and the case is remitted back to the labour Court for fresh consideration of this question whether the appellant is justified in awarding full back wage or not. [1103G] 4(c) In the present case, the appellant was working as a daily wager in the office of the respondent Company. He had been retrenched by the respondent on 1 st September, 1974. He has been paid retrenchment compensation for the said period. The respondent company is entitled only to full wages and not any amount less than 75% of the back wage. [110G] 5.(a)(i) In view of the fact that the workmen concerned had been terminated by way of retrenchment, the question whether they should be paid any back salary or not does not arise. [111A D] (ii) The respondent Company was entitled to get full back the wages from 1st September, 1975 till the date of reinstatement and the relief of reinstatement with continuity of service is granted. [112E] 6.(a).

The deceased was married to Churi on August 18, 1958. The accused had gone to the house of Shri Mahajan and after the death of the deceased, he left for Kotkbai in the house. He was also present at the time when the incident took place. On September 3, 1958, the accused went to the residence of the father of the boy and informed him that his son had been murdered by Churi. The deceased was taken to the hospital where she died on August 19, 1958 and the report was lodged by Shri Mahajan (PW 10) at the police post. The prosecution case is that the accused left for the village and after he returned from the village, he went to Kotkabai in the morning of September 3. 1958 and met with an accident. He also informed the police about the death. On October 5, 1958 the deceased was sent to the police station at Kotkhai where she was found dead. The police recorded the statement of the accused under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Sessions Judge held that the evidence of the witnesses was not reliable and that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the deceased had committed the murder of Churi and that he had been falsely implicated in the case. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court should have accepted the evidence given by the police and convicted him under section 302 Indian Penal Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that there is no reliable evidence to prove the guilt of the appellants beyond any doubt. [701B] 2. The fact that the dead body was found in a well situated at Kotkibai and that it was not possible for the prosecution to prove that the death was due to the injuries sustained by Chururi on account of the assault on the deceased is not established. [802C] 3. The evidence of PW 10, who had seen the dead bodies from the house, clearly establishes beyond any shadow of doubt that he saw the accused and the deceased in a wet condition at the house where they were residing. He further deposed that when he was informed about the murder by Chura on August 20, 1958 he went there to see film at Kotakibai and after seeing the film, he found that the body was lying near the dead of the deadbody. The medical evidence also establishes beyond a shadow of doubts that the injuries were caused by the accused. [902D] 4. The mere fact that Churi had been admitted in the hospital does not mean that the appellant could have been convicted under section 304 Part I or section 302 IPC. [1001E] 5. The conviction of the two appellants under section 201 read with section 34 Indian Penal Cods is based on the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the High court has rightly come to the conclusion that the appellants had committed murder of the victim. [092F G] 6. The facts in this case are not similar to those of the present case. It is true that the two accused were acquitted by the Sessions Judge but the fact that they were convicted under sections 302 and 201 readwith section 34 IPC does not make them liable for any punishment. [1101E C] 7. In view of the above discussion, the appeal must fail and it is dismissed.

The plaintiff 's father, the defendant, purchased a property from one of his brothers, who was the owner of the properties. The plaintiff claimed that he had purchased the properties in the year 1939 and that he was entitled to a mortgage decree for sale on the basis of the provisions of section 82 of the Contract Act. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff ' s father was liable to contribute in equal shares to the extent of Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 20,000 respectively. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court held that the mortgage decree was not a mortgage debt within the meaning of section 43 of the Indian Contract Act and that the suit was not maintainable. The High Court also held that there was no contract to the contrary in the document, nor did it give a right to the plaintiff to redeem the whole of the balance of the property to the sum payable by him on the date of the mortgage. On further appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The provisions of the Transfer of Property Act are not applicable to the facts of this case and the High court was in error in holding that there is no contract between the parties to the effect that the amount payable by the plaintiff should be reduced to Rs. 40,000. [601 C] (2) The right to redeem is a matter of law and it is for the judges to apply the law to the fact of this liability to the amount rateably due on it under section 82. [061 D] (3) The plaintiff ' must be able to establish that he has not made out any case in his plaint or set up a case which would entitle him to a decree for redemption. [63 F] (4) The suit was barred by limitation and the plaintiff could not have been permitted to take advantage of section 54 of the Evidence Act. [64 G] (5) The High court had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit under section 43, C.P.C., because the plaintiff had failed to establish his case on the facts.

The appellants were appointed as Asstt. Engineers (Civil) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka on the post of Asstt. Engineer (Civil). They applied for the posts of Civil Engineers and 110 Mechanical Engineers in all 450 Civil Engineers. The appellants were selected by the Public Health Engineering Department for the post and they were given appointments under the impugned Rules. The selection was made according to the rules. The 2nd appellant was appointed as Assistant Engineer (C) on the basis of marks secured by them in the qualifying examination and 66.40 marks out of 150. The 1st appellant was selected by Public Health Engg. Department for appointment under the said Rules. He was also given appointments on the posts which were advertised and he was selected on the ground that he had secured much higher marks than the appellants in the written test. The 3rd appellant was not selected as Assistant Engineers (C). In view of the fact that the 1st respondent was selected for appointment by Public Works department, Government had already taken a decision to appoint him under the Rules and the selection was also made according ly to the Rules, he cannot be said to have been discriminated against. The State Government has now framed new rules on 4th April, 1985 which are in violation of the judgment of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors.. In view thereof we do not consider it necessary to quash the selections on the above ground. The appeals are accordingly allowed.

The State of Bihar, through its Inspector of Police, Ramgarh, submitted a report to the Superintendent of Police on 11.4.1983 stating that the deceased was murdered by the appellant and his brother. The police investigated the case and found that there were no incriminating circumstances against the accused persons. The prosecution relied upon the evidence of Sadanand and P.W.62, who were also members of the Indian Administrative Service. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish that the murder was committed by the accused. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court should not have accepted the evidence adduced by the prosecution and convicted the appellant under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Code. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellant is based upon circumstantial evidence and the High court has rightly held him guilty of the offence. [601B] 2. The circumstances relied upon by the High are not sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. [613C] 3. The fact that the appellant was a Member of theIndian Administrative Service, is also not in dispute. It is true that the evidence on record does not show that the accused had any motive or knowledge to kill the deceased. But it is difficult to accept the criticism of counsel for the appellant that the circumstances relied on by the trial court are not enough to establish his complicity with the crime. [501C] 4. The facts in this case do not indicate that the conspiracy was hatched at the time when the murder took place and the appellant had no motive or any knowledge to murder the deceased, nor is there any evidence to show that he had any intention to kill. [511E] 5. The mere fact that some persons were present at the scene of crime does not establish the complicity of the appellants in the commission of the crime by circumstantial evidence. [504D] 6. The circumstance relied upon for convicting the appellant, Sadanand, is not sufficient and it cannot be held that he was a member of the service. [506E] 7. In this case there is no direct evidence to establish any conspiracy between the two persons. There is no evidence to prove that the crime was committed in the manner alleged by the appellants. The circumstantial evidence does not indicate any connection with the commission or motive for the murder of the deceased nor is it sufficient to show any link between the accused and the crime, as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the charge against the appellant cannot be said to have been established. [500G] 8. The case of Sadananda Yadav vs State of Rajasthan, ; , followed.

The appellant company was a factory in the State of Maharashtra. The respondent was employed as a casual labour in the factory of the appellant company and was receiving wages at Rs. 2,000 per month. On January 1, 1961, the appellant Company made an application to the Tribunal for fixing the minimum wages payable to its workmen under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and the Tribunal by its order dated June 3, 1960 fixed the minimum wage packet of comparable concerns at Rs 2,500 per month and fixed the dearness allowance at Rs 1,000. The Tribunal held that the total wages were not on the basis of the average wage packet fixed by it but on the assumption that the maximum was 15 months as the maximum. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal has committed an error in fixing the maximum wages at 15 months and fixing the same rate of dearness allowance for factory workmen as in the case of clerical staff. [701 A] (2) The minimum wage packets of comparable concern were not available on the date of the application but on that day, it was fixed at Rs 5,000 by the Tribunal. The maximum was about 15 months. The minimum wages fixed by the tribunal is about 15 days and therefore the total wage packet for clerical staff and subordinate staff should be taken into account as the average wages for clerical employees. [801 B] (3) The maximum is about the fixation of 20 months as in case of other comparable concerns. It would be open to the appellant to fix the same rates of dearness allowances for factory workers as in that case, but on its basis it should have done so the total Wage packet of similar concerns at the rate of 15 months or 15 days as the minimum Wages fixed by this Court is about 14 months and therefore it should be open for the Tribunal to fix a higher than 15 months wages. [901 C] (4) The fixation of minimum wage was not on account of any interference with adjustments as to call for any interference in adjustment as to calls for any intervention or adjustments. [1001 D] (5) The increase in the maximum is over 15 months, which is a reasonable figure and thus arrived at a just figure for basic wages. It cannot be said that the minimum Wage packet fixed was less than 15 days. [1101 E] (6) The rate of wages fixed under the Act is not on any higher side as compared to the total price of comparable industries.

The Rajinama was granted by the Rajinarama in favour of one Shiddappa, who had executed a mortgage deed on November 1, 1937. The Rajinamama was given by him to Annappa 's son and his son. The plaintiffs 1 and 2 were also the legal representatives of Annaappa. The appellants filed an application under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code for cancellation of the mortgage deed dated November 1 , 1937. In the said application, it was alleged that the Raj inama had not been executed by Shiddannappa and Annaiah. The trial Court held that the plaintiffs 1 to 6 were entitled to redeem the mortgages on the basis of their interest in the mortgaged property. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellants could not claim redemption of the mortgages as they had not acquired any right to the mortgagees. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The High court was wrong in holding that there were no pleadings and cogent proof that the mortgage was subsisting on November1 , 1937 when the Rajasama executed by him was the registered occupant. [701B] (2) The plaintiffs had not claimed redemption of their interests in the property. They could not have filed a suit for redemption of mortgages against them. [802C] (3) The appellants were entitled only to redeem their mortgages on their own account and not on the mortgage. [820D] (4) The right to redeem was not merely of the mortgagor but also of the mortgagee. [823E] (5) The rights of both the brothers Shiddaiah and Anappa were governed by the provisions of section 74(1)(b) of the Code. [825F] (6) The mortgage deed executed by the appellants in their favour was not a valid one, but only of an absolute right to convey the title in the suit property to the mortgagors. [826A D] (7) The mortgagee had not created any interest in his share in the mortgage property and, therefore, he could not acquire any interest therein.

The respondent, a registered dealer under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, was assessed to sales tax at the rate of 5 per cent on the turnover of carbon paper. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who confirmed the order of assessment and dismissed the appeal. On further appeal by the respondent, the Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur, set aside the order passed by the Sales tax Officer, and confirmed the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 6%. The respondent challenged the validity of the levy by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the word 'paper' in entry 18 of the Second Schedule to the Act was not used in the sense in which it has been understood in common parlance as understood in the popular sense and therefore, the word "paper" in entry 22 of the First Schedule to that Act would be construed according to the strict or technical meaning of the language contained in the word. The appellant filed a writ appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The word ' paper' is not defined in the Act and the Rules. [801B] 2.2. The expression 'paper ' has not been defined in any technical sense but it has to be understood in commercial parlance. It does not mean that the typewriter in the ordinary sense is to be considered in the light of what is meant by a typewriter. [901C] 3.3. The words 'paper " have not been used in any commercial sense and they are, therefore, not part of a typewriters. They are, however, not parts of a motor car or a vehicle. It cannot be said that the expression ' paper ' has been used for printing, writing or printing or for drawing on or for preparing or for packing or for making on or to prepare or for any other purpose without it. [1001D] 3:1.2 The word " paper" in Entry 22 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to, the Constitution of India is not used as a verbatim reproduction of the word and therefore the word has been interpreted in the commercial sense. [1102E] 2:1 The word has not be understood according to its popular sense but has to mean that it has also to be construed in the common parlance or in the trade parlance. [110G] 3;2.3 It is not necessary for a typewMAN to have been used as an essen tial part of the typewriting sense and it has no commercial meaning. [109H; 110A] 2(a) The word used in entry 23 of List I of the Constitution means that it is understood in trade parlance or by the use of the expression "paper ' in common legal parlance or otherwise" in the same sense as understood by the ordinary dictionary. It has to bear in mind the meaning which it had to be interpreted according to their popular sense. The term 'paper" has not to be read in a technical sense and that it does not have any commercial meaning, but it is used for drawing or for printing on or making on, or for preparation or for filling on, any other form of paper. [111A D] 2.(a) In the instant case, the expression used in Entry 23 of the Schedule to The Notification issued by the State Government under the first proviso to section 5(1) 'of the Orissa General Sales Tax Ordinance, 1948, was not specifically mentioned in the notification. [112E H; 110B] 3.(b) The expression "for printing" has been defined under entry 18 in the First schedule to the Notification issued under the second proviso to Section 5(2). It is clear that the words 'for printing' have not to refer to any other forms of paper and therefore it cannot be construed as a part of any other kind of paper or any other article.

The appellant was employed in a factory at Amroha and he had the right to transfer his employees from one concern to another. He was transferred to another concern on February 2, 1955. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the owners of the Mills at Amroha. On March 19, 1955, the appellant filed an application under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, for setting aside the order of transfer and for a direction that the respondents 1 and 4 should be transferred to any other concern in the same line. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant had no right to continue to transfer him from one factory to another and that he was not entitled to transfer the respondents I to any of his concerns at Amroha, and that the order passed by the State Industrial Tribunal was illegal. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the finding of the State industrial Tribunal holding that the transfer of respondents 1, 4 to 5 to a new concern was valid and amounted to alteration in the conditions of service of the appellant and that they were not entitled, as there was no express or implied condition of service. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order of the High court setting aside that order is illegal and void. [701B] (2) The transfer of respondent 1 to another concerns at Moradabad was valid in law and could not be set aside by the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution. [802C] (3) The appellant had a right to be transferred from one industrial concern to one concern, but he had no such right. [601D] (4) The question whether the transfer was valid or amounted to an implied condition to transfer respondent 1 from one concerns to another was not open to the Labour Appellate Tribunals under section 10 of the Act and therefore the order dismissing the respondents 's application for setting it aside was illegal and invalid. [783F] (5) The High Court had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding of fact, as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the . In this case, the order was passed by an Industrial Tribunal on February 6, 1956, and therefore, the question whether respondent 1 was entitled to be posted to another industrial concern at Amroha was not a substantial question. [784H] (6) The right to go back to one concerns at Rampur was implicit in the contract of service or under any statutory provisions. [780F] In this connection it is necessary to refer to the observations of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India vs K.S. Jagannathan, ; , followed. (7) The mere fact that the employer had the option to transfer an employee at Amroha to another factory at Moradabad would not make any difference because the right of an employer to transfer a workman at Amroha is implicit in his contract of employment or under some statutory provisions and therefore he was bound by the terms of the contract.

The appellant company was incorporated under the provisions of the Act and its members were governed by the provisions contained in Chapter V A of the Insurance Act, 1948. The appellant company had been registered as a 'State Insurance Corporation ' under the Act on April 30, 1969. It had been carrying on business in various places in the State of Gujarat. On March 26, 1969, it was registered as an 'State insurance Corporation ' and its employees were governed under Chapter VA of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The respondent company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions relating to the payment of special contribution by the appellant company. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions in Chapter IV A of Chapter V-A of Chapter VI were not applicable to the appellant Company and that the levy was not a fee but a fee. In appeal to this Court, it contended: (1) that the Act did not contemplate any payment of contribution under Chapter IVA of Part V A; (2) that there was no provision in Chapter VI for payment of contributions by employers under Chapter VI or for payment thereof and (3) that section 28 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which provided for payment by an employer to his employees, did not make any provision for payment to his employee as a fee; (4) that it had been made clear in the case of factories or establishments situate in areas in which the provisions were to be made applicable to them and that section 22 of the principal Act was not attracted to such cases. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The expression 'appropriate' in Chapter III A of Part VI of the insurance Act is a word of wide import and includes all employees in factories or establishment situate in any area in which provisions are made by the Legislature of any State. [601B] 2. The words "appropriate" in Chapter IIA of that Act do not contemplate payment of any contribution to be paid under Chapter IIIA of this Act. It is only when the whole Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would be necessary for the Parliament or the Legislature to decide whether the provisions are applicable to such factories or other establishments situate within the State. The word 'appropriate" has been used in a wide sense and includes any scheme framed by the Government under Chapter VIIA of it. [701C] 3. The definition of 'appropriate authority' in section 2(a) of the Central Act is not confined to an establishment or establishment which is owned by the Central Government or the State Government. It does not contemplate that the Central or the Government, as the case may be, will be borne from the general revenues of the State and that it would also be borne entirely from the aforesaid fund only. [801D] 4. The object of Chapter IV-A is to provide for payment out of the contribution payable under Chapter II A of this Chapter. It provides for payment in addition to the contribution which shall be paid by an employee under Chapter X A of that Chapter. [820E] 5. The scheme of Chapter III-A makes it clear that the contribution to the fund must be paid out of any other fund, whether it is a tax or fee or a fee or not. It also provides for the manner in which such contribution is to be levied and the manner of insurance. [823G] 6. In view of the fact that the scheme of Chapters IVA and VA makes no provision for the payment by any employer to its employees, it cannot be said that the amount payable under section 28(1) of Chapter II-A was not an 'appropriate amount' within the meaning of section 2 (a) or section 23 of the Indian Contract Act. [825G] 7. The provisions contained therein are not applicable in respect of the payment to employees under Chapter I A of Schedule V of the said Act.

The petitioners were appointed as daily rated workmen in the establishment of respondent No. 2 on a consolidated pay of Rs. 10,29,40,583. The services of the petitioners were regularised by respondent No 2 on the basis of an order dated 31st March, 1988 issued by the State Government. The petitioners were absorbed in the said establishment on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workmen and there being no work available for them, they cannot be regularised. The management filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of absorption and also praying for a direction to regularise their services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners are not entitled to regularisation on the grounds that they were not working as regular workmen in spite of there being a vacancy in the Establishment. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The order of the High court is unsustainable and it is set aside. The writ petition filed by the petitioners is allowed. The impugned judgment of the Division Bench is set side. The appeal is allowed to that extent. [701B] 2.2. The appellants are entitled to get their regularisation on a permanent basis in view of the order dated 30th March, 1987 passed by this Court in Writ Petition No. 3308 of 1985. [771C] 3.3. In view of this position, the impugned judgment is set at naught and the appeal is dismissed. The respondents are directed to regularise the services of all the petitioners on a regular basis in accordance with law. [78D] 4.4. The direction given by the High C ourt to regularise services of these petitioners is quashed and set aside and the matter is remitted back to the High cour t for fresh consideration after giving due opportunity to the parties concerned. [79G] 3:1.2 It is not necessary that all the persons who are appointed on a temporary basis should be regularised in service. The regularisation of such persons should be made only on humanitarian grounds and not on humanitarian ground. [80H; 80A] 2:1 The High Curt has rightly held that the appellants were not entitled for regularisation of their services as they were working as daily wagers since January, 1988. [81G] 2.(a) In view thereof, the appellants are not eligible to be regularised and their services should be treated on humanitarian considerations. [85A] 3.(b) The High court has rightly dismissed the petition filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. [86B] 4.(c) The impugned order is set-aside and the writ petitions filed by respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are allowed.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for partition of the property in question on the ground that Pir Baksh was the sole proprietor and owner of the Azamabad Tea Estate. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the sale under exhibit 12(i) was not valid and accordingly dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and held that the plaintiffs were entitled to a declaration that the mortgage in favour of Pir Aaksh was void and the sale was not legal. The High Court also held that since the mortgage was not executed by Ismail, the sale could not be set aside as the sale deed exhibit 12 (i) did not affect the title of Ismail. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiffs' suit for a declaration of their right to the extent of 2/2 as owners of the entire interest effected by him under exhibit 13(i), was barred by res judicata. [601 A] 2. The sale deed Exhibit 12(ii) is not conclusive and it does not affect any title except to the share of Ismail in the Azambad Tea Estate, which represented the interest of Ismail, as a result of the sale. [702 B] 3. The right to pass title to Pir Caksh was not affected by the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained by Ismail and the subsequent sale in favour thereof. [803 E] 4. The suit for declaration of his right to receive 8 pies share of the properties sold under exhibit12(i)(a) was barred, because the sale did not take place during the pendency of the suit and the plaintiffs' claim to have purchased the entire property from Ismail was based on the sale deeds Exhibit 12 (ii). [703 B] 5.
