The plaintiff 's right to get a decree for partition in respect of the remaining properties was not extinguished by reason of the provisions of the Crown Grants Act and hence, the suit for recovery of possession of the mortgaged property was barred. [777 C] 6. The appellant 's contention that the transaction was void as being contrary to the sale having been made out of the title to the property conveyed under exhibit 14(i). The High court held that there had been no mutation in the revenue records when this sale was effected and therefore, the mortgage by Ismail was not correct. [77 D] 7. The fact that the appellant ' s right to obtain a decree of partition in regard to the remaining property conveyed by exhibit 12 is not inconsistent with the sale being made out under exhibit 9(i); nor does it affect any right to have a share in the property sold under Exhibit 12. [78 E] 8. In view of the fact that there was no mutation of the revenue record when this transaction was made out, the appellant could not claim any relief against the mortgage which he had obtained under exhibit 11(i)." The High Courts held that as the mortgage had been executed by the appellant in favour Of Ismail and Pir, the entire estate was not liable to be sold. [76 F] 9. In the instant case, the property was purchased by Ismail from Ismail and his co-sharers who were not the sole owners of Pirs. The mortgage was executed by him in favour o the appellant as full owner of Pus. No title was conferred on him by exhibit 13 (i). [77 G] 10. The burden of proving that the mortgagee had consented to the execution of a mortgage decree is upon the plaintiff who has failed to discharge his onus and the burden of proof lay on him to prove that he had consented for the execution. [79 H] 11. In this case, there was nothing to show that the property which was conveyed under Exhibit 13(ii), was not intended to pass in lieu of the whole interest effected thereby.

The appellant, who was charged with an offence under section 173 of the Code, was tried by the learned Sessions Judge for offences punishable under sections 173 and 207A of the Indian Penal Code. The learned Sessions judge convicted him of the aforesaid offences and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 500/- and in default of payment of fine he was directed to suffer simple imprisonment for six months. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant but reduced the sentence from imprisonment for two years to three months. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 173(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code are mandatory in character and they have not been complied with. [701B] 2.2. In order to appreciate the point raised by the appellant it is necessary to set out the relevant provisions of the said Code, which read as follows: (1) The provisions contained in sections 173(3), 207A and 207-A of Criminal Procedure code are mandatory, and that they have been complied therewith. [801C] 2.(2) The provision of section 207A is mandatory, but it does not affect the inherent right of the accused to have his defence taken before the court of sessions. [820E] 3.3.1 The provisions relating to the trial before a Sessions Judge are mandatory and they do not apply to cases before him. [823G] 2(a) In the instant case, the appellant was charged under section 207 A of the old Code for offences under sections 174 and 207 A and Section 207A, and he was convicted by the trial court. He was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for three months and a further fine of rupees 500/- under section 209A of Indian Penal code. [825G] 3(b) The appellant had been charged under sections 172 and 207B of the new Code for an offence punishable under section 174 of the Act, and the trial had not been vitiated by the failure to comply with the provisions of sections 173, 207A or 207A. [822E] 4.2 In view of the fact that the appellant had failed to show that he got the necessary copies of depositions before the courts concerned, it was not open to him to have the documents referred to in section 173 and the statements recorded under section 164 and the statement recorded under Section 164 and other relevant documents or extracts therefrom, on which the prosecution proposes to examine as its witnesses. [821G] 4(a). The provisions regarding the trial of an offence are mandatory. It is not open for a person to have any defence taken by him before the magistrate before whom the committal proceedings were pending that he had no opportunity to show cause against his conviction. [824E] 5.3 In view, however, of the provisions relating, to the examination and statements recorded in section 164 or other relevant document or extracts thereof, on behalf of the prosecution, it is not possible for a Court to hold that the provisions regarding examination and statement recorded by the police officers before whom such proceedings were brought to, 293 see that all the documents, or extracts thereto, on their part, are furnished. [826E] 6.4 The provisions in section 207B have been incorporated in the Code with retrospective effect from 1st April, 1956. It does not appear that the legislature intended to make a departure from the provisions contained therein, and it has also made no such departure. [828F] 5.(a) The language of section 209(3) is clear and unambiguous. The provision regarding examination of witnesses before whom an offence was committed is in the nature of a procedural law. It cannot be said that the Legislature intended to give retrospective effect to the provisions in sections 207A to Section 173, and Section 208A. The legislature has not used the words "shall" or "may" in section 209 (3)

The respondent Municipality had issued a notice under section 153A of the Act to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in question. The appellant filed his reply to the notice and contended that the nuisance was one which ought to have been found by the Special Officer. The Special Officer rejected the contention on the ground that the respondent Municipality did not comply with the requisition. The respondent Municipality challenged the order of the Special officer before the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove that a nuisance was created in question and that the notice issued by the Municipality was invalid. In appeal, this Court held that the provisions of section 153 A were not attracted because the nuisance which was alleged by the respondent was one of the matters for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality. The order of Special Officer was upheld by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of sections 153A and 153A are not applicable to a case where the nuisance is created in respect of a public health or fertility of the soil. [801B] 2.2. The word 'reasonable' has been used in section 153-A(1) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. It does not require any judicial officer to be present at the time when the notice was issued under sub section (1) or subsection (2). The word reasonable is not defined in the Act. [901C] 3.3. The expression 'reasonable restriction' has not been used either in the statute or in the rules framed thereunder. It is a matter of discretion to be exercised by the authorities concerned and it cannot be said that the legislature intended to confer any arbitrary power on them. [1001D] 4.1 In the instant case, the respondent had issued notice under sub Section (1), which was served on the appellant on July 21, 1958. The notice was not accompanied with a copy of the application for discharge. It was only after the appellant received the notice that he could be asked to comply with it. [1101E] 4(2) The respondent had no authority to issue any notice under subsection (1). The notice issued under section153A is not an empty formality. The procedure prescribed by sub section(1), therefore, must be followed in this case. [110G] 3.(3) In the present case, it was not disputed that the Municipality did comply with requisition in respect to a nuisance which had arisen in the manner specified by the notice. It could not be said on behalf of the respondent that the action taken by the appellant was one such as would amount to an encroachment upon the public health and fertility. [111G] 4.(4) The provisions contained in section153 A are not attracted when a nuisance is caused by the use of water or any other substance. It cannot be denied that the act of the municipality was not in accordance with law. [112A B] 5.1 The word "reasonable" has been defined in section 3(3)(a) of Chapter III of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 and it is clear that the word ' reasonable restriction' must be read as a reasonable restriction on the exercise of the right conferred by sub Section(1). [112B] 5.(4A) The expression "reasonable restriction" has not necessarily to be construed in its strict sense. It may mean a reasonable restrictions which are imposed by law and which are not imposed by any competent authority. [113C] 5(5)(a)(b) In order that the State Government should take immediate action, it must be satisfied that there is a nuisance or likely to arise from the use or consumption of water in the surrounding areas. The question whether the nuisance has been created in the area or not depends upon the nature of the nuisance and the circumstances in which the nuisance had arisen.

The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or both. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles in question were not meant for the purpose of construction, operation or maintenance of railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The prosecution has established that the goods were being used by a railway administration and that they belonged to any particular railway administration. [901 A] 2. The fact that the article in question was not meant to be used for construction or operation of railway administration does not make it clear that the property belonging to the railway administration was intended to be kept within the definition of railway store. [0902 B] 3. The word 'in' in section 2(1) means any property which is used or intended to have been used by the railway Administration for construction, maintenance or operation or maintaining a railway stores. [1001 C] 4. The words 'any property belonging' in the definition are not meant only to be construed as including all articles of the nature specified in section 3(1). It does not mean any property belonging exclusively to a railway department. [1101 D] 5. The expression 'in" in section 1(2) means property which has been used or is intended to use for the construction, or operation and maintenance of a railway store within the defined meaning of that word. [110 A B] 6. In the instant case, the appellant had purchased the goods from one of its employees in open market where they were being carried on the business of railway receipts. The goods were not intended to come into existence at all because they were used or meant to have taken place in the construction or maintenance operation of a Railway store within that meaning. [111 A B C] 7. In view of section 3 (1) of the Railways Act, it is clear that when the railway stores are purchased by a person other than the railway servant, he must be shown to have purchased them from one or more persons in open markets and not merely from others. [112 D E] 8. The definition of 'in 's case does not require the prosecution to prove any of the articles which were being actually used or were intended to take place in construction or Maintenance operation of Railway stores within that definition. [113 A B H] 9. In this case, it was not shown that the railway store had been purchased by the appellant from one person in open auction and that the appellant was not in possession of any railway stores at all. The evidence showed that the Railway stores were being sold to the appellant for a price which was less than the cost of the goods. [114 A B D] 9: The prosecution failed to establish that the items in question belonged to a particular railway department and that it had been used and intended to operate or maintenance operations of a railways store within its meaning. The burden of proof is on the prosecution, if it fails to prove the same, then the burden shifts to the accused to account for his possession of the same.

The appellants were tenants in the demised premises. They filed a suit for ejectment of the tenant on the ground that they had been inducted into possession by Smt. Anandi, who was a statutory tenant on behalf of the appellants and that the tenancy rights were heritable and the heirs of the tenants were entitled to remain in possession even after determination of their tenancy right. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellants are not entitled to continue in occupation of the demised shop as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants. On appeal, the appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there is no provision in the Act which excludes the heirs from the tenancy and the legal position of the tenancy. [901B] 2.1 Section 13(1)(a) to (k) of the Act does not apply to the facts of this case. It only provides for a contractual tenancy on the death of the landlord or his heirs as the case may be, but does not have the effect of divesting their rights in the tenanted premises governed by the Act. [0901C] 2:1 The legal position is that the heirs are entitled to enjoy the protection under the Act and also subject to the right in favour of the landlords. [1001D] 2(a) In the instant case, the appellants were not tenants in respect of the tenanted shop but were tenants on the demise of the statutory tenant. They continued to remain as on their death till the date the tenancy was determined by a decree for eviction against them. [1101E] 2.(b) The legal heirs of statutory tenant are entitled only to remain and to be governed by Act, 1963. [110G] 3.2 Section 13 (1)(c) of Act does apply to such tenants who were not in possession of the premises on the appointed day. It is clear that the relationship between the landlord and the tenant was that of a contractual tenant and they continued to be in possession till the appointed date. The legal representatives of statutory tenancy are entitled, as held by the High Court, to continue to have an estate or interest in the premises governed under the provisions of the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land. [111G] 2 (a) The relationship between landlord and tenant was not that of contractual tenancy but that of tenancy rights on the basis of which the appellants had been conferred with the right to continue as tenants in their own property. [112A D] 3.(b)(i) In view of the provisions contained in section 13(2) of Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 1958, the relationship of landlord and tenants is not that OF contractual tenancy. The relationship of tenant and tenant are governed by section 13 (2) (a). [111B C] 4.1 The relationship is not a contractual one. It does not include contractual tenancy or any other right in respect thereof. The contractual tenancy is not an absolute one. The terms of the contract are not inconsistent with each other. [113A D; 113E] 3(b) In order to constitute a contractual relationship, it must be established that the tenant had been carrying on business during the life time of the contractual tenancy and continued to carry on business till the death or retirement of the deceased tenant. The contract is not inconsistent With each other and the relationship is governed by Section 13 of the Rajasthan Rent Act. The provisions contained therein are not applicable to the present case. [114E] 4(c) In a suit filed for eviction, the landlord had sought for possession of premises on behalf or part thereof. It was contended that the contractual tenant had no right to remain with the landlord as he had been in possession during the period when the tenancy commenced and continued till the demise.

The appellant Board was established in the year 1966. The appellant Board had been functioning as a managing agent of the Board and had been receiving grants from the State Government. On or about January, 1967, the appellant Board issued a notice to the workmen of the appellant company asking them to show cause why they should not be directed to pay interest on the amount of principal and interest payable to them under section 64 of the Act. The workmen filed their reply to the said notice denying the claim made by the appellant. The Industrial Tribunal held that the interest was payable to the Board as a result of the provisions of the Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme framed thereunder. The management contended before the Tribunal that the employees of the company were not entitled to any benefit under section 66 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 because they had been paid interest on loans advanced by the Board. The Tribunal held against the appellant and directed the management to pay the interest on such loans. On appeal, the High Court set aside the award holding that the workmen were not covered by the provisions contained in the Provident Funds Scheme and as such the question of payment of interest did not arise. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The employees of a company are entitled to the benefits under section 65 of the Contract Act. [701B] 2. The Board is entitled to take into account the financial capacity of the Company and to have taken credit for any subventions from the Government. [602C] 3. The interest payable by the company to its employees cannot be deducted in order to ascertain the financial capability of the employer. [613D] 4. The position of the State is that the Board has been receiving grant from the Central Government and it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to take credit for such loans, if it is not able to account for any loss to the Government or to have incurred a loss. [502E] 5. The question whether the interest payable under section 63 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 can be taken into account in calculating the profits does not arise because the Board had not been receiving the grant from its State Government and therefore the provisions relating to the payment of principal or interest could not apply. [511G H; 516A] 6. The fact that the appellant was receiving grants on behalf of the Central Board is a clear indication that the amount payable under Section 63 of that Act cannot be taken as dividend to any sub loan. [504B] 7. In view of the fact that there was no financial capacity to implement the Provident fund scheme and the amount to be paid to the State, the question whether there should be a further loss to Government or not does not result in loss to it is irrelevant. [506C] 8. The High Court has rightly held that there could be no dispute that the Provident funds scheme was framed by the Central and the appellant had been paying interest on those loans. [525D] 9. In the instant case, the Board was a statutory obligation and therefore it was not bound to grant any benefit to the employees under section 55 of the Employees' Provident Fund Act, 1952. The appellants were not liable to pay any interest on these loans. Therefore, the provisions regarding payment of dividend to the appellant are not applicable. [500G] 9 A. In this case, there is no dispute as to the financial position of either the Board or the State. It was only a statutory liability and therefore there could not be any question of giving any benefit in respect of the loans advanced to the appellants. [600H; 516B] 10. The scheme framed by Central Government under section 59 of the Factories Act, 1953 is a welfare scheme for the welfare of workers. Therefore it cannot be said that the provisions are applicable to all workmen. [110C] 11.

The appellant husband filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of 1973 for maintenance from her husband. The learned Judge of the High Court, after hearing both sides, dismissed the application and confirmed the order of the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 was not a just ground for refusing to live with the wife because she refused to live in her husband's house and hence the second Proviso to sub rule (3), which was inserted with the clear object of preventing the wife from living with her husband, was not applicable. The High Court held that the appellant husband had failed to prove that he was impotent and was unable to live together with her. In this connection it was observed by the High court "that the second explanation to sub clause (3)(b) of sub section 2 of section 488 of the code of 1973 was not attracted because the wife refused to reside with her, as there was no intention on the part of the husband to refuse to live and hence she was entitled to maintenance from the appellant. The appellant husband contended that the first proviso to subsection (3A) of Section 125 of Code of 1898 was not available to him because he had failed in proving that he is impotence and was not able to live along with her." In this Court, it was also observed by this Court that the question whether a wife could refuse to living with the husband or not did not arise because she declined to live separately from her. The Court further held that if the husband refused to keep his wife in a situation where her husband had contracted marriage with another woman and the wife refuses to live, then the second Explanation to sub Section (3B) of [Section 125] of Code was inapplicable. In view of this finding it is not necessary for the appellant to prove the fact that she refused or neglected to live at her husband because she did not refuse to keep her husband in a position to live. The second proviso which was added with the specific object of enabling the wife to live without any intention on her part to refuse, was also inapplicable. It is true that the proviso to Section 125(3) was introduced with the express object of punishing the husband for cruelty but it does not mean that the husband should be able to maintain his wife. The proviso to section 125(1) of Code is a very wide and comprehensive one and it cannot be extended to cases where the husband has contracted marriage without any desire on her own, as in this case there was neither any intention nor any intention at all on her. It would not be just ground to refuse the wife 's refusal to live or live with her unless she refused, for which reason she could have been compelled to live independently. The object of enacting section 125 is to prevent the wife who has contracted a marriage without anything more and it does appear that the wife was unable or unwilling to live as husband. It may be that the marriage between the parties was not bona fide but was not bonafide. In such a case, the Court may have to consider whether there was just ground on which the husband could have refused to living in a place where he had contracted a second marriage without his desire to live for her husband or for any other reason. The fact that the spouse refused to stay with him would not make it clear that the spouses were unable or willing to live independent of their own, and that they were unable to maintain themselves. In the present case, there was nothing on record to show that the parties had refused to continue living together as husband and wife. It was also not proved that the two spouses were unwilling to reside in a particular place where they had contracted another marriage without their desire to reside. The evidence of the witnesses clearly shows that the relationship between the spouses was not cordial. In these circumstances, it is difficult to hold that there was any intention or intention on their part to live separate from each other.

The plaintiff was the owner of the land in question. The Municipal Board of Bhavnagar had been given a notice under Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for possession of the lands and other properties which were in occupation of the Municipality. The defendant No. 1, the State Government, on receipt of the said notice, filed an application before the City Civil Court at Bhavnagar praying that the suit be dismissed as barred by limitation. The City Civil Judge rejected the application holding that the plaintiff had not shown possession of any land and that the land was vested in the Municipality under Resolution 37 dated 19th January, 1948. The plaintiff preferred a second appeal to the High Court against this judgment and decree of the Trial Court. The High Court held that the Municipal Board had been conferred with the right to sell the land as well as other properties and that it was not necessary for the Municipality to have informed the State of Saurashtra that the lands were vested in Bhavnagar Municipality. On appeal by special leave, the High court reversed the judgment and order of the City civil Court holding that there was no evidence to show that the possession of these lands had been taken over by the Municipal board. The appellant has filed this appeal against the judgment of the High tions. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The suit is not barred by time. It is well settled that a person who claims title to the property as owner of an estate or other property cannot claim any right over it unless he is shown to have been in possession thereof. [701B] 2.2. The burden of proving that the property was not vested in a Municipality is on the plaintiff and the burden of proof is upon him to show how his possession was with the Municipal Boards. [802C] 3.1 The burden is on him to prove that he had been in occupation as owner thereof. In this case, the Municipal Committee has not produced any evidence to establish that the defendant No 1 was in possession of Government of India. [901D] 2:1.2 The High court was right in holding that since the plaintiff failed to show his possession, the suit was liable to be dismissed. [1002E] 3:1:1.(a) In view of the fact that the State had not produced evidence to prove the ownership of the property by the Municipality, the plaintiff could not claim any title over the land. [1101F] 2(b) The High Curt was right, in holding, that the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for possession based on title to them as owners of the properties. [110G] 3.(a)(i) In the instant case, it is not disputed that the Government of Saurashtra had granted permission under Resolution No. 77 dated 29th February, 1948 to the Municipality for sale of the suit lands. The Municipality was in occupation and possession of those lands. It was only on 7th July, 1952 that the Municipality applied for permission under resolution No.77 dated 29 th February,1948 to the State government for sale thereof. The State Government had granted sanction under Resolution 77 dated 19 th January, 1950 to the Municipal Corporation for sale and the Municipality had also granted permission to the municipal corporation for sale. [111H; 111A] 3(a)(ii) In this view of things, the Municipality was not entitled to claim any relief from the Court. [112B] 4.1.(b) Under the Resolution No 77 dated 30th February 1948, the Government had given permission to all the municipalities of Bhavnad and the Municipal Council for sale to the appellant. The Government of Gujarat had also given permission under Section 70(2)(a) of the Bombay Town Planning Act to the municipality to sell these lands. [113B] 3 (b) In any event, the appellant was not in possession as a tenant of the State.

The appellant was appointed as a "officer in the service of the Government" by the Government. He was, however, not performing any public duty within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was, therefore, not an officer within the definition of a public servant within the scope of section 2(9), and therefore he was not a public servants within the terms of section 3(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. He, however held that he was a public man within the ambit of section 5(1) (d) and therefore, he was also a public officer within section 21 (9). The appellant challenged the conviction under section 5 (1) of 'the Prevention of Corruption Act II Of 1947 before the High Court of Bombay. The High Court held that the appellant was not an "officer" within the purview of section 20(9)(d), and that he had no authority or jurisdiction to perform public duty entrusted to him by the government. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word 'officer in' used in section 21 of the Act II must be construed as a public person within the expression "officer". Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word 'Officer" in section 20 (9) means an officer appointed to perform a public duty and includes an officer in the Government service of a department or pay of the government and is performing a public duties entrusted to such a public office. [701 A] 2. The expression "officers" in the definition must be understood in the sense in which it is used in the Act. It is not necessary that a person should be in the pay of an officer or a public service paid by Government to do public duty. [602 B] 3. The words 'officer' and 'pay of the State Government" are defined in section 2 (9), Indian Penal code, which means "a public servant". It is clear that the expression 'officer" in this definition must mean an officer who is appointed to discharge a public function entrusted to it by the State or is performing some public duty which he was performing. [802 C] 4. The definition of public servant contained in section 3 (1)(b) of Prevention of corruption Act IIof 1947, does not include any person who is employed to exercise, to perform, to discharge, to keep an account of its forest revenue and to pay a certain proportion to the Government, keeping an account thereof, and to discharge duties which he is performing. The term 'officer ' in section 19(9)] means "any person who was employed to perform any public duties" and therefore a public Officer within the defined meaning of that expression in section 22 (9)(b), Indian penal Code, would be a public Servant within the definitions of section 23(9). [803 D] 5. The object of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is to provide for the prevention of adulteration of food articles and to prevent adulteration of such articles. It does not make any distinction between public servants and persons employed in connection with the discharge of duties entrusted by the Act to them. [820 E] 6. In the instant case, the appellant had been appointed as an officer of the Department of Food and Civil Supplies, Government of India, and he was, thus, a public functionary within the contemplation of section 19 (9A) of The appellant could not be said to be a "Officer" within section 20 of the Code. [823 E] 7.

The Respondent filed a suit against the Appellants for recovery of Rs. 1,00,000/= from the Appellants on account of arrears of rent and interest due to them under section 60(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code") in respect of the portion of the building in which the Respondent was residing. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the Respondent 's half share in the said property was exempt from attachment and sale in revenue recovery proceedings under the said Act. The Appellants filed an appeal against the decree of the trial court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no provision in the Code for attachment and sell in revenue Recovery proceedings adopted by the Sub Judge, Patiala, C.P., Patiala, in Civil Appeal No. 554 of 5.9.79 and the decree passed by the Addition District Judge, Sangrur, in C.M.A. No. 2944 of 1980 was not liable to attachment and sold in revenue recover proceedings under section 59 of the said Code. The Respondent filed an application for stay of the execution of the decree against him. The learned Single Judge dismissed the said application holding that since the Respondent had failed to pay the arrears of rents due from him, he could not be evicted from the property attached and sold by the Appellants in revenue proceedings under sections 60(2) and 60(3) of Code. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 60 of the code are applicable to attachment of property and sale of revenue recovery proceeding under the Act. [601B] 2. The expression "such attachment and selling in revenue recoverable" used in section 60 (1) is a word of wide import and has no meaning in law. It does not include any other kind of movable or immovable property. The words "such property" are not defined in the Act but they have been given the meanings which are given in the proviso to sub section (1). [602C] 3. The word 'property' is used in a restricted sense and it includes any movable or immoveable property. It is not confined to immovable property, but it does not mean anything other than movable or moveable property. Therefore, the expression "any other movable or movable property" has no significance in law as it does cover only movable or Immovable properties. [062D] 4. The phrase 'such property' in section 61(1)(c) of C. P. C. is used to denote immovable property and not any movable property. [20063E] 5. The definition of "property" in section 2(d) of Act, which defines the expression 'property" as including any immovable property other than immovable property specified in the schedule. It includes any immovable or movable properties other than moveable or immovable properties specified in Schedule I. Therefore the word 'any other immovable property' has no relevance to movable or movables specified in schedule I. [ 20063E H] 6. The term "property", as defined in section 3(d), means immovable property which is exempt from attached and sale under any of the provisions of the Act, but does not cover any movable immovable property or immovable assets. Therefore it cannot be said that the word "any movable or other immovable" has any relevance to immovable properties. The Explanation to sub Section (1)(a) of section 61 clearly shows that the expression movable or tangible property shall include all immovable and movable properties specified therein. [63F] 7. In the instant case, the Respondent is a co-operative society registered under the provisionsof the Punjab Co operative Societies Act, 1961 and the Appellant 's share in that property was not exempt from the attachment and sales in revenue recovered. The respondent had no right to sell the property in question. [64G] 8.

The respondent was the owner of the lands in question. He had purchased the same from one Smt. Natha and the value of the land on the date of the original assessment was Rs.1,000/and the value was fixed at Rs.2,000/- per acre. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the acquired lands were not liable to be assessed as the correct market value of those lands. The trial Court decreed the suit and granted compensation at the rate of Rs.3,000/-. On appeal by the State Government the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the Civil Court and held that the respondent was entitled to receive compensation at a higher rate than what he had actually adopted. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court has committed an error in holding that the enhanced compensation awarded by the Land Acquisition Officer was not correct or that the same had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and that the value fixed by the Special Deputy Collector was not a correct valuation of the acquired land on that date. [701B] 2. The order passed by this Court in C.A. No. 1053/72 dated January 9, 1970 is clearly erroneous and is liable to set aside. [602C] 3. The enhanced compensation fixed by this court was not proper or that it was a mistake apparent from the record of the case and as such it was not liable for assessment. [063D] 4. The correct valuation was made by the Collector on January 9/2, 1970 and the same was rightly assessed at Rs..2,500/- per acres. [2006E] 5. In view of the fact that the original assessments were made after the expiry of three years from the date on which the enhanced amount had been paid by the Government, the High court was in error in setting aside the order passed under section 61 of the Act and restoring the enhanced amounts to be included in the assessment record. [ 2006E] 6. The view taken by the High Courts that the enhancement of compensation awarded is not correct and that it is a mistake discovered by reference to such other evidence is not a mistake which could be regarded as proper evaluation of the right to receive the compensation as on the previous occasion, is erroneous in view of its true valuation. [2007E] 7. The question whether the enhanced value of acquired lands on the basis of their estimated value was correct or not has been decided by this judgment and it is not necessary for us to go into that question at this stage. [ 2007E] 8. In the instant case, the original notification under section 4(1) of the Land acquisition Act had been issued on January 10, 1970. The Collector had assessed the value at Rs.,2,250/and after deducting therefrom the extra compensation awarded for the lands acquired by the respondent, the enhanced land value was determined by the competent authority at Rs... per acre and the market value was accordingly fixed at a sum of Rs..3,500/-. [2006F] 9. The notification under s.4(1)(a) of Act had not been issued in pursuance thereof. It is only on the ground that the Collector had no jurisdiction to issue the impugned notice under section 59 of the Ac tion Act. [2008E] 10. In this case, it was the duty of the respondent to have taken all reasonable steps for challenging the validity of the notice issued under s..59(a) and (b). The High court has not committed any error in interfering with the impugned notices issued under section 60(a), and (c). [2006G] 11. In a case where the original order passed in the proceedings under section 63 A of the . the Act had already been quashed by this very Court, it would be open to the respondent either to challenge the validity thereof or to seek further relief in accordance with law. [2009E] 12.

The appellant 's election to the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank, Chandrapur was held on 18.8.1986 and he was elected as Director of the said Bank on 18th August 1986. The appellant filed an application under section 78(1) of the Act before the Deputy Registrar for setting aside the election of the appellant. The Deputy Registrar by his order dated 7.12.1987 dismissed the appellant ' s appeal against that order. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of the Assistant Registrar on various grounds including the ground that the appellant had ceased to be a Director and his seat already fell vacant. The High Court held that the election was not valid as no notice under section 73FF(1), was issued by the Deputy Inspector General, who was competent to take action under section 74FF(2) of Maharashtra State Cooperation and Textile Department Act, 1960. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 73FF of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act, 1961 provides that no person shall be disqualified for being a Director or any other office bearer of the society unless he has been given an opportunity to show cause against his disqualification. The provision is not mandatory but directory and it is only in case where the notice is issued by an officer who is competent to issue such notice that the Deputy Commissioner can act under section 76FF(i)(b) of that Act. [701B] 2. Section 74FF of Bombay Cooperative Society Act, 1959 provides for disqualification on account of his having ceased to hold office as Director or a member of the committee and his holding office as such. The word 's' in the section is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the context of the provisions contained in section 73F(1). [702C] 3. Section 78(2)(b), which provides for setting up of a Committee, reads as under: "Section 78(3) "The Committee shall consist of three members and two other members to be appointed by the State Government from amongst its members who are not less than twenty five years of age on the date of the meeting. The term 's" is defined in section 2(d) which means a person who has been elected as a Director of a society or a person having been disqualified for continuing as such under section 77FF(ii)(b). [602D] 4. Section 75FF(a), which deals with the disqualification on the ground of default, provides that if a member fails to show sufficient cause within the time specified in sub section (1) or where he has not given an option to show good and sufficient cause for his failure to show satisfactory explanation, he shall be deemed to have been disqualified from continuing as Director. [603E] 5. The expression 's having been elected" is a term of art and it must be construed in the light of the context in which it occurs. It does not mean that if the person who had been elected has already ceased to have any right to continue as such, he would cease to be Director or member of committee. [613G] 6. The words 's holding office' are used in section 78FF(b) and it cannot be said that the disqualification continued after the election is set aside by the impugned order. [643A D] 7. In view of the fact that the notice under Section 78 (1), which was issued on 18/8/1986, was not a valid notice under sections 73FF (2) and 73FF, it cannot, therefore, be said to have lapsed in law. [503E C] 8. The contention that the order removing the appellant from the Committee of Directors is without jurisdiction is also devoid of merit because the appellant has ceased to become Director or Member of the Committee on account thereof and his name was removed from the committee of Directors. [511G H; 516A D B] 9.

The respondent was serving as a Supply Inspector in the State of Maharashtra. He retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for which he was chargesheeted. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the pension to the extent of 50 per cent. The order of reduction of pension by 50 percent was made by the State Government after the retirement from service. The appellant challenged the validity of the Government 's order dated December 4/1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to him by 50% in view of the fact that the respondent had already retired from the service on reaching the ageof superannuation on October 16. 1978 and he was also awarded a penalty of reduction by 50 percent in his pension. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State government had no authority to initiate any proceedings against the respondent for determining the pension payable by 50per cent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of reducing the 50 per centum pension by 100 per cent was not in accordance with rules and therefore the reduction of 50 percent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The impugned order of the High Court enhancing the pension by 60 per cent is unsustainable. [901B] 2. The Government had power to reduce the pension from 50 per Cent to 50 per day. It was not open to the State to impose any punishment on the respondent. [1001C] 3. The power to enhance the pension was vested in the Government under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules and therefore it was not necessary for the State Legislature to take a decision whether to reduce or reduce the amount to 50 percent. [091D] 4. The provisions of Rule 189 of the Rules were enacted to provide that before any order is passed, the State Govt. shall take into consideration the fact whether the respondent has already retired or not and if so, what was the quantum of pension which he would have drawn if he had been retired from Government service. [992E] 5. The language used in Rule 189(1) of the rules is clear and unambiguous that the power to increase the pension is vested in Government under rule 188 of Rules. It is not necessary that the Government should take into account the fact, whether the Government has power to impose a punishment on an employee for misconduct or negligence or financial irregularities which he may have committed during the period of his service or after the completion of his services. [982E F] 6. The expression "shall" in Rule 188(1)(a) is not defined in the Rules but it is used in the context of the case. It does not mean that the rules are to be construed as they are intended to be interpreted and applied to all cases where the Government servant has already been retired or discharged from service, and the reduction in pension is made by 50%. [993E] 7. The word "shall ' in Rule 187(1), is used for the purpose of the enquiry contemplated under Rule 189. It must be construed strictly. It cannot mean that it is not mandatory to take into consider the question whether the reduction was excessive or not. [19992F H] 8. In the instant case, the respondent was retired from his service on superannuation and he had already been paid pension by the Government. The fact that he had retired from services on reaching age of retirement on attaining age of 58 years on reaching 60 years on attaining superannuation on March 31, 1977 is not in dispute. [20002G] 9. In view of this position, the High court was right in quashing the order reducing the respondent 's pension by Rs 50 per month. [19982E H] 10.

The appellant, who was the landlord of a building situate in village Kherra, District Kanpur Dehat, filed an application under section 3(3) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, for eviction of the tenant from the premises on the ground that he had committed certain irregularities in the construction of a house. The District Magistrate by his order dated January 7, 1964 rejected the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to get permission under section 4(3). The appellant filed an appeal before the Commissioner and the Commissioner allowed the appeal. In the revision petition filed by the appellant against the order passed by the District Magistrate, the Commissioner held that the District Collector had no jurisdiction to entertain the application made by the landlord for permission under Section 3(4) of Act No. III of 1947. The High Court set aside the order of the District Judge and dismissed the revision application. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the Act did not intend to confer jurisdiction on the Commissioner to deal with the applications made by landlord for eviction under section 2(3), (4) and (5). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on the District magistrate under section 5(1) is a plenary one and it does not extend to the exercise of that power in relation to orders passed under the relevant provisions of Act III of 1948. [601B] 2. The Commissioner has no jurisdiction over the matter. He has no authority to deal in any application made under sub section (2), as he can only decide the question whether a particular case is or not within his jurisdiction. [702C] 3. The powers conferred on him by section 3 (3) are limited to the extent that it does so expressly or impliedly, and that the Commissioner has jurisdiction over matters in respect of which an order under the Act has been made by him. [803D] 4. The word 'jurisdiction' is not defined in the Code but it is a general one. It is well settled that the power conferred upon the Commissioner under section 6(3)(a) is to be exercised only when there is a failure of justice or illegality in the order made by an authority subordinate to him. In other words, the jurisdiction conferred on a civil court has no application to the facts of the case. [777E] 5. The expression 'jurisdiction" in section 3 of the Code does not mean that the powers conferred upon a civil Court are limited only to the question as to whether a plea can be raised before a civil or criminal court in relation thereto. [78F] 6. In view of the provisions contained in section 2 (3), the Commissioner is empowered to deal only with the legality, propriety and correctness of the order which may be passed by him, alter or reverse his order. The jurisdiction conferred upon an authority under section 7(1)(a), therefore, does not include the power to grant permission under that section. [77F] 7. In a case where there is no illegality in exercise of the powers vested in a civil courts, it is open to the Commissioner, to deal either with the correctness, legality or propriety of the orders passed by an officer subordinate to it, alter, or reverse the order. [76G] 8. The words 'jurisdiction ' are not defined either in the Act or in any other enactment. It does not refer to the jurisdiction of a civil and criminal court. The term 'jurisdiction', therefore, refers to the power of a Civil Court to deal even with the merits, legality and propriety of an order passed under section 8(1). [77G] 9. In cases where there are no illegality or irregularity in exercise thereof, it would be open to a civil suit to deal as if it is not a case of irregularity or illegality. [79F] 10.

The appellant, a Member of the Punjab Public Service Commission was appointed as a Member by the President on the recommendation of the High Court. He was removed from his office by the order dated March 10, 1983. The appellant filed an application before the High court for review of the order of removal of the Member of Haryana Public Service commission. The High Court dismissed the review petition and confirmed the order passed by the Chief Justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain a reference under article 317(1) of the Constitution because the President had not taken into consideration the facts found by the Supreme Court in respect of the charge of assault and he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the Secretary, Government of India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "in any case" used in article 317 (1) is a word of wide import and it must be construed strictly. It does not mean that the Judge should have taken into account all the facts which he has to consider before making his order. [849B] 2. The words "in such a case" are not intended to cover cases where the evidence is recorded by the learned Judge. In other words, the evidence must be recorded by him in accordance with the procedure prescribed in article 318(1). [850C] 3. The word "in" in article 316(1), is used in contradistinction to "in the case of a person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court". It does mean that if the Judge takes into account the facts, which he had taken into possession, he should have obtained the opinion of a body or authority. [950E] 4. The learned Judges of the Delhi High Court were right in holding that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and that he was guilty by a criminal court of law. [1052F] 5. In view of the fact that the charge against the appellant is not proved, the question whether the appellant should be removed from office on the ground of misbehaviour or otherwise does not arise for consideration in this case. [1153G] 6. The order of the President dated March 11, 1983 was passed by him after the full satisfaction of the charges and the report of the Commission. It is not disputed that the report was submitted to the President. The report was sent to the Chief Secretary on August 10, 1982. The Chief Secretary had no authority to make a reference to this court under article 316 (1). The High court was right in rejecting the review application filed by the appellant. [1253G H] 7. In the present case, the appellant has been convicted for an offence of murder and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He is entitled to be reinstated in service with full back wages. [1354F] 8. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant, who was the founder of the temple, had a right to worship in the temple. He had a private temple and he had a fundamental right to perform all the duties of worship in it. The appellant had a statutory right to be worship in a public temple. The respondent claimed that the endowment was a private one and was not a public endowment. The trial court held that the dedication was a public trust and, therefore, the endowment could not be inferred from the evidence adduced by the parties. On appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had no right to the temple or to worship at the shrine in question. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The endowment is a public religious endowment. It does not make any stipulation for taking offerings from members of the public or in the hands of the strangers or members of their descendants or members. [833G] 2. The dedication was of a public nature and the intention to instal a family deity in the place of worship was merely to endowed a private property belonging to a particular community which also shows that the temple was of an ordinary nature. [934A C] 3. The fact that the founder had a personal interest in the endowment does not show that there was any stipulation to take offerings from the members of his family or in their favour. [1035B] 4. The mere fact that some persons belonging to the community were also dedicated for the purpose of maintenance of the Temple is not sufficient to indicate that there were no such stipulation for take offerings. [1134C] 5. The question whether a public institution was of any kind and whether it was a religious endowment or not has to be determined by the evidence led in each case. [1235D] 6. The position is well settled that a private trust is a private nature and if there is no such condition, the same would be an essential ingredient for taking the offerings from its members of public. [1334E] 7. In the instant case, the respondent was not able to establish that the endowments were of a private character or of a religious denomination. The evidence led by the appellant clearly shows that there is nothing to show that any contribution was called for from members and they chose only a particular person belonging to such community which clearly shows the intention of the founder to endowed the temple with the use of the idol in the Temple.

The appellant Bank was a registered firm under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The respondent was appointed as an agent of the appellant Bank by the appellant and he was authorised to act as his agent for the purpose of carrying out contracts with the Government. On July 19, 1948, the appellant issued a bill in favour of the respondent for the monies due to him and also endorsed on it the endorsement on the bill dated July 19. 1948. The appellant Bank filed an appeal against the decree passed by the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no equitable assignment of the funds in favour the appellant. On a proper construction of the document the High Court held that there is no equitable assignmen of the fund and that the debt due to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund in favour. The Bank filed a suit for recovery of money against it under the provisions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to attach the money due to it under a bill dated June 19, 1949 and that there were no equitable assignments of the moneys due to them. On appeal by special leave the High court held that the amount due to Takhatmal was a specific Fund in favour and that it was irrevocable. The appeal against this decision was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Bank that the High Courts were wrong in holding that no equitable transfer of the money was made by the lender to the appellant bank and that as the loan was advanced to the borrower, the debt owing to the lenders was not a specific amount payable under the bill. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The liability of the borrower to pay the amounts due to his agent is a statutory assignment of a definite fund in his favour. [601B] 2.1 The High Courts have committed an error in holding otherwise that there has been no equitable assigning of the monies in favour or under a contract with the Bank. [613C] 3.2 The High court was wrong in not holding that it had no equitable title to attach and that since the debt was not specifically assigned, the amount payable by the borrower would be credited to his account. [501D] 2:1.1.2 In the present case, there is a clear distinction between a loan advanced to a creditor and a specific endowment. The loan was a loan granted to the Bank and it was a simple assignment of its funds. It was not an equitable assignment. The debt due under the contract was not in respect of any specific fund but was a general one. [511E] 2(a) The High courts were wrong on the ground that there had been no such equitable assignment by the Bank to the creditor. [452B] 3.(b) The liability to pay money due under a bills is a contractual obligation and not an implied right of the lender. [451C] 2 (c) The plaintiff could not have claimed any equitable assignment in his plaint for the amount which was due to be paid by him to the defendant. [454E] 3(a). In the instant case, the High courts had committed an illegality in holding the appellant to be a creditor of the loan advanced by him and imposing a liability on it. [453F] 4.1 It is true that the liability of a debtor to pay his debts is a specific obligation and the debt is not a definite amount payable in respect thereof. But, as the Highcourt had committed a manifest error in finding that there could be no equitable assigned by the plaintiff, the suit was liable to be dismissed. [401F] 3 (b) In the case of a loan which was advanced by the defendant to the plaintiff for the money borrowed by him from the Bank, it is not necessary that the defendant should have been authorised to execute a decree in favour thereof.

The respondent was employed as a Manager of the Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthers and Co. Ltd., Assam, in the year 1963. He was appointed as an Assistant Manager of M. I.T.D. on June 30, 1964. On July 1, 1966 he was transferred to the Assam State Sugar Corporation Limited. The respondent was paid a salary of Rs. 27948/ representing the interest on such contributions. In the assessment proceedings for the year 1964 it was contended that the receipt in question being an income from other sources, the same was exempt from tax under section 17(3) (ii). The tribunal held that the respondent was not entitled to any deduction under section 56(I) of the Act and accordingly allowed the appeal. In appeal by certificate the High Court held that since the receipt was not in respect of salary or wages, it could not be considered as salary. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "profits in lieu of salary" is a word used in section 17 (3) and not in an approved superannuation fund. It does not mean that the said receipt was exempt under section 2(24). [401B] 2. The words "in addition to any salary or wage" are not defined in section 2 (24) of Income tax Act, 1961. The word "profits" is used in a wide sense and it has to be understood in its ordinary meaning. It must mean the salary which is earned by an assessee from other source. [402C] 3. The receipt in respect thereof was not exempt under any of the heads specified in section 56 (I) but was exempt therefrom. [301D] 4. The said expression "in lieu of salaries" means the salary or salary which has been earned by the assessee from a provident fund, his own contributions to the fund or any interest on that amount. It is not necessary for the purpose of this case to refer to section 17 of the Income tax act, 1961 as it stood before its amendment in 1964. [219F] 5. The definition of "profits and gains" in section 4(1) (iv) of Act No. 43 of 1961 was amended by the Finance Act, 1966 with effect from April 1, 1965. The explanation to that section provided that the income derived from other assets shall be chargeable to tax under any head specified in [218F] 6. The assessee had not been able to show that he was receiving any salary as defined in clause (b) of section 2 of the said Act. He had not produced any evidence to show his source of income. [519G] 7. The Tribunal was right in holding that the receipts in question were not income. The High Court was wrong in holding, on a proper appreciation of the evidence, that the assessee was receiving salary as per the provisions of section 17 and therefore the same could not have been treated as salary under section 4 (1) of 'the said Act; [520H] 8. In view of the above discussion, the appeal is allowed and the order passed by the High court is set aside. The matter is remitted to the High Income tax Tribunal for fresh disposal in accordance with law. There will be no order as to costs.

The petitioner who was a cow and calves of cows, male and calve of buffaloes and cales of cows and calf of all ages of calves and calims of cows was entitled to be registered as a slaughter house under the provisions of the Bihar Act. The petitioner claims that he is a cow, buffalo and caluse of cows. He has also claimed that he has been in possession of the slaughter house for more than six months since the date of his detention. The High Court held that the slaughter of cows by the petitioner was not valid as it was violative of article 19 (1) (g) and is, therefore, void in so far as it prohibits the slaughter or breeding of bulls and working bullocks without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The slaughter of buffaloes by the petitioners was not a valid slaughter house. [601B] 2. The provisions of section 3(1) of the Act are not violative of Article 19 (2) (a) and (b). The slaughter is not a mere animal but a breeding of cows for human consumption. It is only a breeding and working bulls and bullocks which are useful as well as usefulness, without prescribing a test or requirements as to its age or calves or requirement. [701C] 3. The banning the slaughter by the State Government in so many words cannot be said to be unreasonable. [802D] 4. The restrictions imposed by section 3 (1)(g) are not reasonable and valid in so much as they are not arbitrary, but only reasonable and rational. [820E] 5. The restriction is not reasonable or rational. It does not violate the rights of the petitioners under article 19(1)(f). [803F] 6. The impugned Acts do not violate any fundamental right of the petitioner under article 21 (1). The restrictions are not unreasonable, but are merely reasonable and fair in so long as they prohibit slaughter of bulls or bullocks without prescribed test or standard or requirement for their age and usefulness and usefulability. [823E] 7. In view of the provisions contained in section 3 of the impugned Acts, it is not possible to hold that the petitioners were entitled to continue to be slaughter of all cows, calves, bulls and Working bullocks without any test as to whether they are fit for slaughter or not. [825F] 8. The State Government has not been able to show that the cattle of the Petitioners were unfit for slaughter. [826A D] 9. In the instant case, the slaughter was not in accordance with the provisions laid down in section 2(1). It is a matter of common knowledge that the animals are slaughtered and calrated. The petitioners have been in occupation of cows without prescribing the test or prescribed any test. [827B C] 10. The cattle of bulls, bulls, and working bullock were not fit for human habitation. They were not so fit for consumption as to be capable of yielding milk or calve.

The respondent was appointed as a Manager of the Company on June 30, 1956. He was promoted to the post of Manager on July 31, 1957 and he was confirmed in that post on August 1, 1958. On September 26, 1956, the respondent was transferred from Nagpur to Nagpur. The Company was subsequently dissolved by an order dated October 25, 1956 and the respondent continued to work as Manager till March 31, 1959. In the meantime, the Company terminated the services of the respondent on June 29, 1960. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Standing Orders applied to the respondent and his service was terminated in accordance with Standing Order Nos. (f) and (g). Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The Standing Orders apply to the Company only if it is shown that the Company has committed a breach of any Standing Order or Standing Order. [701B] 2.2. The word 'employee' in Standing Order no. (g) of standing orders means an employee who was employed in the Office, Mains Department, eta., of the company at Nagpur and Wardha. The expression 'employee ' has been defined under Standing Orders as meaning a person appointed in the office, Main's Department, or the Company at Nagpur, or Wardha, or Nagpur, to whom tickets had not been issued. [601C] 2.(a) The word "employee" in Standing Orders does not mean an employee employed in any department, but includes an employee in the Department, and the expression 'employer ' has not been defined in Standing orders. [613D] 3.3. In view of the definition of an employee under Standing Order, it is clear that the respondent had no ticket to whom he was appointed in accordancewith Standing Orders and, therefore, his services were terminated in contravention of Standing order No. 5. [501E] (b) The Standing orders do not apply to employees who are employed in a department but only those who are working in the same Department. [511G] 4.4. In respect of the Standing Order which is applicable to the case, it has been held that the word ' employee' in the Standing order no. 5 does not include an employee within the meaning of the Central Act and, as such, the Standing orders apply to all employees only if they are employed by a department, and, accordingly, the High court was right in holding that there is no question of applying Standing Orders in respect of employees who were employed in different departments. [504D] (c) The respondent had been appointed in contraventions of Standing orders and, thus, he was not entitled to any relief under the Standing Rules. [506E] 5.1 In view, however, of the fact that the High Courts have held that there was no violation of Standing Regulations, the question whether the Standing Regulations apply or not does not arise for consideration in this appeal. [500G] (d) The High court has committed an error in holding otherwise. [525E] 3.(a). In view thereof, the impugned order is set aside and the writ application is allowed. No costs.

The appellant, Hindustan Steel Ltd., was a part of the establishment of the Hindustan Steel Limited. The Company was established by it and it had to be treated as a separate establishment for purposes of computation of bonus under the Act. The workmen of this undertaking were treated as separate establishments for purposes for computation of the bonus under section 16(1) of the Act, but the Tribunal held that the entire paid up capital of all the units on the basis of consolidated accounts was not a part or branch of an establishment and, therefore, the question of computation did not arise. The appellant, Bharat Steel Ltd. filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the correctness of the decision of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the entire payment of bonus was made by the Head Office or branch thereof and, as such, the provisions of section 16 (1) were not applicable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant, that the High court had erred in holding that alloy Steel Project was a separate unit for purposes set up in the year 1961 and, consequently, the Tribunal was wrong in holding, that alloys steel projects were treated separately for computation under section 15(1). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "any other establishment" used in section 16 of the Payment of Bonus Act is not confined to a separate industrial establishment. It does not include any other establishment which is owned, controlled and managed by one single Company. [601B] 2. The word "any "any" has been defined in section 3(d) of that Act as including alloy steel projects. Therefore, the entire amount of bonus payable to the workmen of the Head office was treated as part of their establishment for computation purposes of bonus. [702C] 3. The words "any such other establishment", used in the proviso to sub section (2) of section 3 are not applicable to a case where the whole of the paid up equity share capital is held by one company and, accordingly, the amount of Bonus payable to each unit on the foundation of consolidated account was treated separately as part and loss accounts were prepared and maintained. [802D] 4. The Tribunal had erred, in holding the entire claim of bonus for the year 1965 66 as a part and branch of the other units of Hindustan Steel. [820E] 5. The question whether any bonus was payable to alloy Steels Project or other units on account of consolidated profits of all such units is not a matter which can be decided by the Tribunal in view of the provisions contained in section 6(d). [803F G] 6. The proviso to section 3 (2), therefore, does not apply to a company which is an establishment owned, managed and controlled by one or more companies. [823A D] 7. The definition of "any 'establishment" in section 2(d)(i) of Act No. 21 of 1965 clearly shows that all such establishments are treated as constituting one establishment for the purpose of computation under the provisions relating to computation of compensation under the Payment Of Bonus Act, 1965. [825E] 8. In view of this position, it is not possible to hold that all these units are separate establishments and they are treated separately from other units. [826A D; 882F G H] 9. The fact that all the employees of Hindustan steel Ltd., who were treated in the same establishment as a distinct establishment for purpose of computing bonus under Section 16(2) were treated to be part of such establishment does not mean that all those employees of the said company are treated together as separate units for purposes relating to calculation of bonus on the ground that they are separate units. The mere fact that some of them are treated in one establishment cannot make any difference because the entire share capital of the company is held separately from others.

The appellant company was manufacturing sugar from molasses and it had obtained a licence for the manufacture of rayon grade pulp. The appellant company obtained a certificate from the Director of Industries, Haryana State Agricultural Marketing Board, New Delhi that the said industry is an industry within the meaning of Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act and that it has been used in its business. The Company was manufacturing rayons from molasses. It had obtained licence for manufacture of royon Grade pulp from molasses which was granted by the Director. The company was also manufacturing raedon grade napulp from sugarcane. The factory was registered under the [Karnataka Agricultural Produce Market Act, 1961]. On April 1, 1976, the appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification and prayed for a declaration that the sugar manufacturing industry is not an industry covered by Entry 15 as it is not a notified item. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the notification was ultra vires the Cess act and the cess Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The word 'veable' in Entry 15 is used in the sense of 'vegetable product'. It does not mean 'vetable' product. [701B] 2.2 The word "vetral" has been defined in Entry 14 as meaning 'vets and vegetables which are grown in a farm and are used for the purposes specified in the Schedule I. In order to bring an industry outside any of the entires in Schedule I, it must be understood that the word 'vestipure' is used for both the purposes. [801C] 3.3 The word `vetative' has been interpreted by this Court in several decisions including State of West Bengal vs Union of India & Ors., ; , and State of Maharashtra vs Union Of India & Anr., ; ; , referred to. 4.1 In view of the above, it is clear that the term 'vetonable' has not been used for any other purpose. [820E] 3,4A] 2: The word ''vetation" in Entry15 of Schedule 1 means any industry specified in Schedule II to the Act and includes any industry which is engaged in the manufacture or production of raedons from sugarcane and also includes any other industry specified therein. [823B] 4.2 In view thereof, it cannot be said that the expression 'vellable' is not used in Entry 16 of Schedule II. The term 'vessels' has to be understood as meaning "vets" or 'vellerised". [823C] 5.3 It is clear from the above that the words 'veltative" have been interpreted in different senses and it cannot mean 'use of a product. In the context of Entry15, the word ''vesti pulp' has also to be construed as meaning any industry for certain purposes. The expression 'vesiti pulp', therefore, must be construed in common parlance and it must not be given its popular sense or it must have been understood in common legal parlance. [825D] 4:1.2 It is well settled that the meaning given by the word "vesti Pulp" in the Act cannot be read as 'veliable' because it has to bear the same meaning as assigned to it in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. The words 'vesati pulp" have to be interpreted in the light of the definition of 'veswari pulp'. [825E] 4;2.3 In the instant case, the term "vellables" has not only been used but has also been used as a synonym for the word and it is used as an expression 'repair of products'. The word has to have been used with reference to the product itself.

The appellant, a tenant in the premises in question, filed an application under Section 10(3)(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondent on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on a business. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the practice of law was not a 'business within the meaning of Section 10 (3)(b) (i) of that Act. The High Court held that the use of the word 'business ' in the context of the Madhya Pradesh Act, is not decisive and that it did not include any profession or trade. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'business' has been defined in Section 10 of the Act as meaning "any profession". It does not mean any profession. [701A] 2.2 The word 'trade ' has been used in a wide sense so as to include any trade or business within the definition of that term in Section 3(a) of Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act. [802B] 1.3 The expression "business" is defined in section 10(1)(b)(iii) as meaning 'any profession'. It does include any practice of a profession. It does also include any business or trade within the scope of that definition. [901C D] 2.(a) The word "business " has been interpreted by this Court in several decisions including [State of Madhya Bharat vs P.N.A.T.M.S.E.B. ; , referred to. (b) The expression used in the Madhya Bharat Act is capable of including the practice ' profession or business'. It is not necessary that the word " trade" should be given a wide meaning so as not to include such practices of a particular type as to exclude any profession, trade or businesses. [1001E] 2(a). The word used in Section 5(3) (a) means that it includes any profession which is carrying on business and the word used is capable ' in relation to that profession.

The respondent was a firm of the appellant and the appellant had entered into an agreement with Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills on 30 September, 1942 for payment of Rs. 4,00,000 to the appellant. The respondent agreed to pay the amount in instalments. The appellant paid the amount on demand and the respondent agreed that he would deposit the same in the account of Lakshmi Ratan Jute Mills. On the basis of this agreement the appellant was entitled to withdraw the amount deposited by the respondent with the traders. The suit was filed on 16 May, 1953. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant could not be said to have paid the sum of Rs 4,000 in the year 1943 and therefore limitation would start from that date. On appeal the High Court held that there was a demand for a part of the amount which was deposited by Lakshmi Ratan Mills and that the respondent had no other source of income except the amount of Rs 3,00000 which was not deposited in the bank account of the respondent. The High Court also held that the suit was barred by time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the trial court was wrong in holding that there were no demand for payment in the month of October 1943 and that there had been a demand in the months of 1943 and 1944 for a sum of money which was paid in the usual course. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The deposit by Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills was not a loan but a loan given to Lakshmi Ratan Textile Mills. [701B] 2. The amount of the loan advanced by Lakshmiars Cotton Mills to Lakshmi Rattan Spinning Mills was Rs. 3,000 and therefore it could not have been said that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can start from the time of October, 1943. [802C] 3. The payment of the money in instalments was made on demand by Lakshmi Rantan Cotton Mills and the amount was paid on demand. The fact that the entire amount was deposited with the trader does not make any difference to the question whether there was an unqualified requirement for a full sum before limitation can be said that the whole amount was not payable on demand or on demand but on demand which was made in the ordinary course.
