[820D] 4. The mere fact that there is a demand of Rs 2,000 by Lakshmi Government does not mean that there should be an unconditional demand for part of that amount. [823E] 5. The word 'deposit' in the agreement between Lakshmi Ratan Spinning Mills and Lakshmi Rattan Textile Mills clearly shows that it was a case where money was advanced by the partners of India Supplies on the one hand and Lakshmi Ratan Textiles Mills on the other hand and the payment was made to them and they were paid in usual course, and therefore there was no need for a substantial part of amount. The condition imposed by the agreement is not an unqualified one but it must be a case of deposit. [825E] 6. In the present case, the appellant did not pay any amount on account of interest or on the ground that the amount had been deposited in his usual course and therefore the question of limitation would not arise. [826F] 7. The expression 'deposit ' in the context of section 5(2) of the Limitation Act means deposit of money by a person who has paid the principal or any part thereof, whether as principal or as principal, but does not include interest on such amount. It is clear that there can be no question of law arising out of an unqualified obligation to pay any sum in instalments and therefore section 5 (2) would apply. [827G] 8. The words 'deposit " in the manner provided by section 5 are wide enough to cover all kinds of deposits which may be made by a firm or a company or a firm, as the case may be, for a period not exceeding one year from the date on which it is due and payable.

The petitioner was detained under the National Security Act on the ground that he had already been in custody and yet he was not in jail. The grounds of detention were served upon him on the basis of which the order of detention was made. He was informed that his detention was necessary for preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The detaining authority, however, did not choose to file an appeal against the order. In the writ petition filed by the petitioner it was contended that the grounds of arrest were vague and indefinite and that the detenu had been in jail since the date of his detention and that he was already in custody when the order was made and that there was no warrant for passing the order under section 3(1)(a) of the National P rocedure Act. The High Court rejected the writ petitions holding that the order passed by the detaining authority was not justified because it was based on a wrong assumption that the petitioner had been already in jail when the detention order was passed and he was still in custody at the time the order is made. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court cannot be sustained as it was passed after the appellant had been acquitted by the trial court. [701B] 2. The mere fact that the appellant was already under detention for a period of one year and that his release on bail was pending in re spect of which he could not be granted bail, does not mean that the detaining authorities were justified in passing the impugned order of preventive detention. [802C] 3. The detenu had already served with the order and he had been remanded to judicial custody on the 27th February, 1986. He had been detained under section 108 of the Customs Act for a long period of time and he could be released only after the expiry of one month from the date when the impugned detention order came to be passed. [902D] 4. The fact that there is no warrant of arrest in respect of the detenu by the Central Government does not affect his right to get bail, if he is already in prison. [1001E] 5. In view of the above discussion, the petition must fail and it is accordingly dismissed.

The petitioners were engaged as casual labourers in the Department of Posts and Telegraphs, Government of India. They were appointed on daily wages basis for a period of one year from 1st April, 1986 to 5th February, 1986. The respondents issued an order dated 30th May, 1986 terminating their services with effect from 5th March, 1986 on the ground that they had not completed 240 days in a periodof three years and more as on 1st June, 1986 and that they were entitled to be absorbed as regular employees of the Posts and telegraphs Department. The petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 958 of 1987 before the High Court challenging the order terminating their service with effect on 5th May 1986. During the pendency of the writ petition, the respondents issued a notification dated 30 th May,1986 terminating their employment with effectfrom 5th June,1986. The appellants challenged the said order by filing Writ Petition Nos. 959 and 960 of 1987 in the High court. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners were not entitled to get the benefit of the enhanced rates of daily wages as they had been continuously working for more than six months since 1st January, 1986 when they were appointed as casual labour on daily wage basis. The State Government issued a circular dated 30/5th June 1986 terminating the services of the petitioners with effect form 5th April,1986 and that the respondents were not bound to absorb them regularly in their service. The writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the said orders were dismissed by the High Courts. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1.1 The State of Punjab has framed a scheme on a rational basis for absorbing as regular workmen in the Posts & Telegraphs Department at the rate of Rs.210 and Rs.260 respectively. It is not disputed that the appellants were appointed by the Union of India as casual workers in the Postal and Telegraph Department at a rate equivalent to the minimum pay in the scale of semi skilled/skilled labour. The said scheme was framed on a basis for absorption as regular labourers in Posts & telegraphs department at a rates equivalent to Rs. 210 and Rs,260 respectively, but without prejudice to absorb the casual labourers who had been working for less than six month since 1 st January,1986 when they had completed 720 days in 3/5 years. [901B] 2.2 The appellants were not appointed by way of direct recruitment as regular workers in Posts and telephone departments at a fixed rate equivalent thereto. They are not entitled for the same benefits as are being paid to the regular employees in Posts or Telegraphs department, at a uniform rate equivalent thereof. [1001C] 3.3 The State has framed an order on 30th June 1987 terminating their appointments with effect retrospectively from 5 th February,1986 which is now impugned before this Court. The order of termination was passed on 30 th June 1987 and the appellants had been paid salary and allowances as are paid to regular employees at a higher rate than the minimum of the pay in scale of Rs 210 and that there should not be any variation in the respective job content of corresponding cadres but without any increments with effect. [1101D] 3:1.2 It is true that the State Government has framed the scheme on an equitable basis for absorb the appellants as regular labour in Posts/ Telegraphs Departments at a lower rate than minimum of pay in scales of Rs210 and Rupees260 respectively but without anything more. The Scheme was framed by the Central Government on 30/6th June 1988 and the same was published on 6th July, 1989. [110E] 3;2.3 It is well settled that the employees who are employed as casual labourer in Posts / Telegraphs departments at the rates equivalent thereto can be absorbed in the posts or telegraphs departments of the Central Govt. and the State Govt.

The appellant, a registered dealer under the provisions of the Act, filed a return showing an income at Rs. 22,000 per annum, and claimed that he had not paid any duty in respect of the assessment year 1950, but filed a declaration under section 24(3) on January 5, 1950, stating that he was liable to pay tax under section 23(4). The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the return filed by the appellant was not correct. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer and held that the returns were not in accordance with the provisions contained in section 24 (3) of the. Act. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the assessment proceedings commenced by the Department under section 22(1) of that Act, after a notice under section 34(2), had been served on the assessee and therefore he could not be treated as a return filed under section 25(3). HELD: (i) The returns were in accordance to the provisions relating to the assessment years 1950, 1951, 1953 and 1954. [701B] (ii) The return was filed after a period of one year from the date of the notice under Section 22(2) and therefore it could not have been treated as an income chargeable to tax under the Act. [802C] (iii) The assessee had not disclosed in his return that he did not file a return under section 30 or section 24A of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, on January 4, 1950. He was not entitled to claim any exemption from payment of tax under sections 23(1), 23(2). [803D] (iv) The assessment proceedings were started by the department under section 26(3)(a) and section 24 of the Incometax Act, 1961, after the expiry of one month from the service of the notices. [820E] (v) The notice was not served on him within the time allowed by section 22 (1). [820G] (vi) The assessing officer had no jurisdiction to proceed under section 27(3), because he had no power to issue a notice for assessment under section 28(2); and that the notice was issued after a proper enquiry.

The respondent, a registered society, was constituted under the provisions of the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (for short 'the Act') for the purpose of providing for election to its members. The respondent, who is a registered Society, filed an application before the Central Government on 29.8.1985, praying that the Scheme should be amended and the same be amended so as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to elect their representatives. The Central Government by notification dated 23.8,1982 (Annexure A), published a scheme for the election of its members in the State of Haryana. The appellant, who was a registered association of non workmen, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Scheme on various grounds including that it had been framed under Section 9(1) of the Act and that the Central Govern ment had no jurisdiction to make any amendment in the Scheme. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the scheme was not only defective but also invalid, as it did not provide for election or nomination of its employees. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 9 of the Punjab Co operative Societies Act, 1961 (for brevity 'the Punjab Cooperative Societies Act') provides that no amendment shall be made in the scheme unless the Central Govt. is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient to do so for the ends of justice. [701B] 2.2 The Central Govt., by notification No. F.1(3) FD/Gr.II/78 dated 23rd August, 1982 (Annexure R), published in the official Gazette, Part I, dated 24th September, 1982, was amended and substituted by the following clause: "The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, amend the Scheme so as not to restrict the choice of appointment to the three persons specified on the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of workmen, as the case may be, for election of their representatives." [702C] 2.(a) The Central Governmen t has no jurisdiction in respect of the choice to appoint the true representatives of the employees or Association or non workmen. [601D] 3.(b) The Scheme is not a mere camouflage but it is intended to give an artificial meaning and, therefore, the Central government had no power to amend the scheme so as only to restrict its choice in the manner provided by the Act. [802E] 4.(c) The object of the scheme is to provide for elections to the employees of the nationalised bank, who are not workmen, to be appointed by the Central Gov ernment of India and, if necessary, to amend such a Scheme in such a way as to restrict their choice in such manner as to reduce their choice. [820G] 4(d) The scheme is not an artificial one but it merely provides for election and nomination of representatives of employees or associations of workmen. It does not provide any other method of appointment which may be adopted by the State Government. [823E] 5.(a)(i) The power to make a scheme in such circumstances as to regulate the conduct of elections is not conferred on the Central or the State Govt. under Section 8(1). The scheme, therefore cannot be said to be an artificial provision and, consequently, it would be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [825E] (ii) The powers of the Central and the State Governments are not limited in their scope to make rules for regulating the conduct o f elections. It is only with a view to ensure that the election process is not abused or misused, the power can be exercised by the appropriate authority. [826C] 6.(a). In the instant case, the scheme does not contain any provision for regulating conduct of election in such cases as to control the conduct and the manner of conduct of an appropriate election.

The respondent assessee, a registered dealer under the provisions of the Act, was assessed to tax on the sale of certain goods. The respondent assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of assessment and the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the demand for recovery of penalty. The High Court held that the Appellate Authority had no power to stay the recovery proceedings pending before it and that the Tribunal could not have given any such direction as was necessary in a routine way or as a matter of course in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. In appeal by special leave, the assessee contended that the order passed by the Appellate Commissioner was without jurisdiction inasmuch as he had no jurisdiction to stay recovery proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of stay is not an inherent power but it is a discretionary power conferred on the Tribunal and the Tribunal has no power under section 254(6) to grant any interim relief in favour of the assessee. [701B] 2. The Appellate Assistant commissioner had no authority to stay any recovery proceedings or to pass any order for staying recovery of tax or penalty payable by or imposed on the assessee as a result of pendency of an appeal. He could not exercise his power under sections 254(5) and 255(6). [702C E] 3. The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in holding that the appellate authority had no powers to stay proceedings pending disposal of an application for staying the recovery proceeding or to grant a stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate power. [801D G] 4. The order passed under section 45 of the Income tax Act is not a final order and it does not give any such power. It merely gives the necessary relief to the assessee in exercise thereof. [820E] 5. The appeal was, accordingly, dismissed.

The respondent was posted as a Station Officer in the Police Station, Intiathok, in his charge sheet dated July 28, 1953. He was charged under section 7 of the Police Act (1) for defalcation of public money by the respondent and also for taking bribe from him. The respondent was charged with having committed offences punishable under sections 7 and 13(2) read with section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He pleaded that he had been guilty of misconduct in respect of which a departmental inquiry was held at an earlier stage and that the order of dismissal was passed by the Superintendent of Police on November 17, 1952. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the departmental inquiry against the respondent was not vitiated by any serious irregularities or misbehaviour in regard to the charges levelled against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in quashing the order passed by Superintendent of police and that since the respondent had been charged with a grave misconduct, the departmental proceedings should be quashed. HELD: (1)(a) The High court was not right in holding that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect to the misconduct alleged against the appellant. [701B] (b) The order of suspension passed by an Inspector General of Police is not a punishment and therefore, it could not be said that the respondent has been charged for any grave misconduct or misbehaviour. [802C] (c) The departmental proceedings were held in accordance with the provisions of para 486 of the police Regulations. The order was passed on November 18, 1952, and the appellant was placed under suspension by an order dated November 17. 1952. He had been charge sheeted under section 13 of the P.C. Act for defalcating public money. [902D] (d) The respondent had not been given a reasonable opportunity to defend himself against the charges leveled against him, and therefore he was entitled to be heard in person. [1001E] (2) The impugned order of punishment is illegal and void. [093G] (3) The appellant was not afforded an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses on behalf Of the respondent. He did not have a reasonable chance to defend his case. [1102F] (4) The disciplinary authority had no jurisdiction to proceed with the departmental enquiry against the delinquent officer. [110H; 1101A B] (5) The power of the Superintendent to dismiss an employee is not an administrative power and therefore it cannot be said to be a judicial power.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialists ' grade II on September 9, 1966. He was promoted to supertime grade I on February 8, 1971 and he was posted in the Specialists grade ' grade I. On October 1, 1971, he was promoted as Director of Health Services, Manipur. The post of Director of health Services, was converted into a specified post by virtue of an amendment made in the rules. He joined the post on November 9, 1971. He had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists grade and was appointed to super time grade II. On January 10, 1971 he was transferred to the post vacated by him which was converted to a specified Post with a specified number of Specialists Grade ' posts. The appellant was promoted on February 9, 1972 as Director. He filed an application for being considered for promotion from the date on which Dr. Sen and his junior were promoted as Specialists. The Tribunal held that the promotion of the appellant was not qualified because he had put in a specified category post. On appeal to this Court it was contended by the appellant that the promotions of the aforesaid four respondents could only be made after they were promoted from the rank of Director. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The promotion of Dr. P. Sen is not a promotion but a substantive appointment and he cannot be considered for the post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 because he was appointed on February 10, 1972. [801B] 2.2. In view of the fact that the appellant had put his name at par with Dr. S. Sen, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the Promotion of the four respondents was not a condition precedent for promotion to super Time grade II because he did not put his names at par in the speciality in which the post was converted from a specifiedpost to a particular post. [901C] 3.3 The appellant had been promoted as a specialists ' Grade ' on February 7, 1971 when he was offered promotion to the said post. He could only have been considered for such post by promotion and he would continue to be in supertime scale II because his name was not recommended for promotion by the Selection Committee. [1001D] 3:1.2 The appellant cannot claim that he should be considered as a member of the specialists Grade because he has put in less than 8 years service in class I. [1101E] 2:1 The appellant is entitled to be considered under rule 8 (3) for promotion on the basis of his performance during the period when he had not completed 8 years' service in Class I. He cannot claim seniority over the appellant because he would have been senior to Dr. L.C. Jain who was promoted earlier than him. [110G] 2 3:2.1 The promotion to Supertime grade II is governed by rule 8(3) and, therefore, the promotion to that post must be made on the date when he has not put a specified percentage of specialization in the specialties. [111A D] 2;2.2 In view thereof, the appellant cannot be denied seniority over Dr. Jain because he is senior to the Specialist ' grade. [112E] 3;2:1: The promotion was made on February 6, 1971 whereas the appellant could not have been promoted earlier on February 5, 1971 because of his failure to put in 7 years of his service in that grade. Therefore, the promotions were not qualified for the posts which were converted into specified posts. [113A D; 113B] 3 :2.3 In view Of the fact whether the promotion was qualified or not, the question whether the appellant should be treated as a person who is eligible for promotion does not arise because he cannot claim any seniority over his junior.

The appellants, who were tenants in the land of the first respondent, purchased the same from one Smt. Ram Sarup and obtained a declaration under section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) on April 15, 1953. The first respondent filed an application before the Collector for determination of his surplus area under section 10 A(a) of the Act. The Collector rejected the said application by his order dated March 5, 1953 and held that the lands were not surplus land but were not part of the surplus area. On appeal to the Collector, the State Government confirmed the order of the Collector. In revision, the High Court set aside the order passed by the Collector and remanded the case for fresh consideration. The appellants challenged the said order before this Court in Civil Appeal No. 1348 of 1953. This Court allowed the appeal and held: "The question whether a person who has purchased the land under section 20A(a), is entitled to retain the surplus land or not, was left open by the High court for consideration. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of section 19 B were not applicable in the case of lands acquired by the State and as such the provisions were not attracted. The High Court held that section 19A(4) was inapplicable to the facts of this case and, therefore, the provisions could not be applied to the land acquired by a person under section 5 A of the Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1952. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The expression 'reserved area' in section 19(4)(a) is used in relation to lands acquired for public purposes and it does not mean that the entire land held by a tenant or owner is liable to be excluded from the permissible area of his holding. [701B] 2.2. In the instant case, the appellants had purchased the surplus areas of their holdings under section 18A(1) of Act X of 1952. The lands were acquired by them for public purpose and they were not in possession of any land. They were not acquired by way of gift or bequest from the tenants. [801C] 2:1.3 In view of the provisions contained in section 20B, the surplus lands held by the appellants could not have been excluded from their holding. The provisions of sections 19B and 20B are applicable to the case where the land is acquired by any person under a law for the time being in force or by an heir or tenant. [820E] 2.(a) In view, of the language used in section 10A(b), the surplus properties held by them could not form part of their holding and they could not acquire any lands by way thereof. [823G] (b) The provisions contained therein are applicable only to cases where the lands acquired under a statute for public use and not to cases which are covered by the provisions relating to acquisition of land by the Government or by the persons who have purchased the lands under section 3A(2). [820H; 801F] 2(a)(i) The words 'reserved areas ' in section 18B(1), " reserved areas ' and "shall be at the disposal of the State government or any officer emed by it in this behalf shall furnish to the Government a return in the prescribed form and giving particulars of all lands which were held by him within a period prescribed. [822E] 3.(a)(ii) The word 'reserved' in clause (i) of section 10(a). 'reservation area ' means the total permissible area which is not covered by any law for time being In force or save in the cases where it is not so covered, the entire area which was not covered within a prescribed period.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the will set up by them was genuine and valid. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were entitled to compensation in respect of Malguzari lands as devisees under their will setup by the defendants. The High Court held that the suit was not barred by the decision of the Compensation Officer, but by the operation of section 3 of the Act 1 of 1951 and that the decree for payment of mesne profits was not binding on the plaintiffs. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to determine the competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the estate devised in favour of Dayaram and that since the will did not set up any right or title upon the land, the suit could not be filed within two months from the date of the order. Held, that section 14 of Act 1of 1951 was extinguished by the notification issued under section 3(1) of the Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 Of 1951 and the High court was in error in holding that section 3 did not extinguish the rights of the plaintiffs to receive compensation in accordance with the provisions of the said Act. The suit was barred by section 14(2) of Act I of 1951. Section 14(1)(a) of this Act provided for a period of two months and if no suit was filed within one month from that date, the Compensation officer would proceed to decide the competing claim of persons who had claimed proprietary rights in respect thereof. The proviso to section 14 (2) did not apply to the case of Dayaram. The plaintiffs were not entitled to any compensation in view of the provisions contained in section 3. The appellants filed a writ petition in the HighCourt challenging that decision on the ground that the decision was not final and conclusive. Held:(i) Section 14 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (Act 1 of 1894), which provided for payment by way of compensation to persons claiming right or interest in respect thereto, did not confer any right on them to receive the compensation in question. The right to receive a compensation under section 14 was not extinguished by an order made by the Compensation Officers under sub section (1) and therefore the decision could not operate to deprive the plaintiffs of their right to claim compensation in a summary inquiry held by the Collector. [701B] (ii) Section 3 of Act 2 of 1951 did not create any right in favour or title on the land. The rights of persons claimed under section 4 were extinguished by virtue of the notification dated December 8, 1950. The provisions of section 14 were not applicable to the facts of this case and therefore it was open to the plaintiffs ' to file a suit against the defendants for setting aside that decision. [801C] (iii) Section 2 of Act 3 of 1951 does not confer upon the State Government any right to recover compensation in any summary inquiry conducted by the Land Compensation Officer under sub Section (1). The right of persons to receive interest in the land is extinguished by a notification issued by the Government under section 2 of the Acquisition Act. [901D] (iv) Section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not create a right or an absolute right in respect to any property vesting in the State. It only provides that where there is a dispute as to title, the decision shall be binding on both the parties and if the decision is not final, the order would be binding upon both the persons claiming interest in such land. [1001E] (v) The right conferred by section 3 is extinguished because the rights conferred by the Act are extinguished by notification issued in exercise of the power conferred by sub section 1 of section 4 of Act l of 1951, and therefore, the right to compensation under that section cannot be taken away by a subsequent notification.

The appellant was a tenant in respect of the premises in question. The respondent filed an application under section 12(3) (a) of the Act for fixation of standard rent and for recovery of possession of the property. The Rent Controller rejected the application on the ground that the dispute raised by the appellant was not covered by section 12 (3)(a) and the notice terminating the tenancy was illegal. The appellant filed an appeal to the Appellate Authority under section 11(4) of Act. The Appellate Authority held that the respondent had failed to prove that the standard rent fixed by the order dated January 30, 1969 was excessive or inadequate and that the tenant had not made any application within one month of service of notice under section 13(3)(b) of 'the Act. On appeal the Appellate Court upheld the decision of the Rent Controller and dismissed the suit. The High Court held that since the respondent did not raise a dispute as to standard rent, the question of standard Rent was not raised by him and it was open to the appellant to raise a contention before the Rent Control Tribunal under section 10(3). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The provisions contained in sections 12 (2) (b) and 12(4)(a), are as follows: (i) that the notice issued under section 9(3), is not limited to a dispute raised within one year of the service of the notice; (ii) that it is only if the tenant makes an application within two months of the date of service, that he can be deemed to have accepted the amount of standard rents or permitted increases specified in the order made by the Court. [801F] 1.2. The expression "shall" used in section 12 of the Bombay Rent Act means that the rent is excessive or insufficient and that it includes not only a dispute but also a dispute. [902B] 2.1 The words "shall be determined by the court" are very wide enough to include any dispute as regards standard rent. It does not mean that the court has no jurisdiction to determine the standard Rent. [1001F G] 1.(a) In the instant case, the appellant had made an application for fixation and payment of standard charges in regard to the standard rents. The tenant had made a demand for arrears of rent and the same was accepted by the landlord. [1102G] 2.(b) The respondent had not raised any dispute before the court as to the amount payable by him under section 8(3); nor did he make an application to the Court under sub section (3). [1003A B] 3.2 In view of the provisions contained therein, the dispute as raised by a tenant is not confined to a question of Standard rent and it is open to him to raise such a dispute in regard thereto as to Standard Rent. The dispute as framed by the Rent Tribunal is not restricted to a disputed standard rent or permitted increase specified in order made under section 3(a) (i). [1103B] 3.(c) In view, of the provision contained in section 11 (3), the dispute in respect thereof as to rate of standard rental or permitted increased or permitted does not fall within the ambit of section 12. [110C D] 3(d) The question whether the respondent is entitled to recover possession of any premises from the appellant under section 14(1)(a)(b)(c) of Bombay Rent Control Act, 1958, is a mixed question of law and fact which has to be decided in the facts and circumstances of each case. [111G] 3 (e) The dispute raised in the present suit was not confined only to a claim for possession of premises but also to a demand of rent or permit increases specified therein. [112A B C] 4.1 In view thereof, the respondent cannot be said to have made an appeal under section 116B of the Representation of People Act, 1951.

The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1939 and it had a controlling interest in the shares held by it. The respondent company, as its directors, was appointed to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. in respect of the shares which, under the articles of association of the company, were entered into with the appellant before the Tribunal. On the question whether the respondent company is a director or not, the High Court answered that question in favour of the appellant holding that the directors of the respondent Company are not having any controlling interest and, therefore, they cannot be said to have a controlling interests in the company. The High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to vote at the meetings of the shareholders of the Company since the shares were held by them in the respondentcompany and were entered in the share register as holders of the majority of the shareholding of the companies. In appeal to this court, it is contended on behalf Of the appellant that the High court had erred in holding that there was no room for doubt that the shareholders holding the majority were not having a controlling Interest in the Company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The shares held in the Respondent company are not "a controlling interest" within the meaning of section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 and, as such, they must be regarded as having a control interest in that company. [701 A] 2. The expression "any other person" used in section 2(21) means any person who holds the majority shares of the equity capital of the Respondent Company. [802 B] 3. The word "any person" is not defined in the articles but it has been used in a wide sense. It does not include any person holding the minority shares of a company. In the case of directors, who hold the majority shareholding of a shareholder, they are to be regarded by them as having no beneficial interest in their shares. [901 C] 4. The words "any member" in section 25(1) of Income Tax Act do not mean any person other than the person holding majority shares. It is only those persons who hold majority shares which are entitled to cast their votes according to the directions of his principals. [1001 D] 5. The directors of a Company may well be regarded, as having "a control interest" in that Company. But they cannot claim any beneficial interest on their shares because they hold majority of their shares and have no beneficial interests in their share. [1101 E] 6. The Directors of the Appellant company are neither the shareholders nor the shareholders. They are not directors of that company, but only those who hold minority shares. Therefore, the directors cannot be regarded to have any beneficial interests on their respective shares. In this case, the Directors of that Company were not holding majority of its shares and had no beneficial or beneficial interest. [110 F] 7. The shareholders of thatCompany are not members of thatcompany. They cannot be treated as having any beneficial or interest in them. [111 H; 111 A B] 8. In view of the fact that the Directors have no interest in these shares, they could not be regarded under section 25 (1) as having only a controlling or interest which is vested in them and, consequently, the shareholders cannot be described as having an interest in those shares. The Company was not holding any beneficial, interest in its shares. There was no need for the Directors to have such a controlling, interest. Therefore the directors could not have been treated as holding majority in their respective shareholding. [112 A B C] 9. In order that the shares of that COMPANY should be held by the shareholders, it must be shown that they hold the same or similar position as those who held majority shares and that they are entitled for vote at general meetings of that companies. [113 D E] 10.

The respondent was appointed as Accounts Superintendent on a temporary basis in the year 1966. He was promoted to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents on a permanent basis and he was confirmed in that post with effect from 1st October, 1956. The respondent filed an appeal before the Karnataka Appellate Tribunal against his promotion to the post of Accounts Superintendent. The Division Bench of the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the respondent was not entitled to be promoted as Accounts Superintendents because he had passed the S.A.S. Examination in the years 1966 and 1968. The appellant challenged the order of the Division Bench before this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no justification for not passing the Departmental Examination and Kannada language test for the purpose of earning increments and for promotion to Accounts Superintendents. [701B] 2.2. The order of promotion passed by the Board under section 79(c) of the Act is not liable to be set aside as it is contrary to the provisions of the Regulations framed by the State Government under section 9(c). [702C E] 3.1 The respondent was promoted on a substantive basis and his case for promotion was considered by the board in its meeting held on 19th May, 1969. He had passed Part I and II of the S otice Examination in which he was denied promotion to that post. [601F G] 2.(a) The respondent could not have been promoted as a Accounts Superintendent because he did not pass the Departmental examination and Kannadada language tests for the purposes of earning increment and for promoting him to that cadre of accounts Superintendents. He could not be promoted to that grade because he passed the departmental examination and passing of the Part I & II of S oce Examination in view of the subsequent Resolution dated 19thMay, 1969 and 5th January, 1970. [76G] 3.(b) The High court was right when it held that the Resolution dated 20th May 1969 and 05th January 1970 were not applicable to the allottees. [77H; 77A B] 4.2 In view of this finding, the respondent could have been denied promotion as Accounts superintendent on a regular basis. [78B] 3(a) It is well settled that the right of an allottee to be considered for promotion is a statutory right and it cannot be taken away by any subsequent Resolution. The right of the allottee to get promotion is not a statutory one. [79C F] 4.(b)(i) In view thereof, the High court rightly held that there is no justification in not passing of Departmental Examination. [80D] 3 (a) There was no reason for not allowing the respondent to pass the departmental examinations and Kannadi language test. [81E] 5.3 The High Cour t has committed a serious error by holding that since the respondent had passed both the examinations and the Kannada languages test, he could not get promotion as an allottee. [82F] 4(b) In the instant case, the appellant was promoted as an Accounts Superintendent in the cadre on a purely temporary basis and the respondent did not possess the requisite qualification for being promoted to this post. The promotion of Accounts superintendent was made by the Government after consultation with the Board. [83G] 5.(c) The order dated 19 th May, 1970 was passed by way of supersession of the earlier Resolution dated 18th May 1970. The said order was challenged before the High C ourt in a writ petition filed by the respondent. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that it was not open to the Board to pass an order of supersession after consultation and consultation with th e Board. It was further held that since there was a clear cut violation of the principles of natural justice, the order passed by t he Board could not stand.

The appellant, a minor, who was the victim of an accident on 1.12.1987, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Orissa under Article 32 of the Constitution for quashing the award of compensation made by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Berhampur, in favour of the appellant and against the respondents. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief as prayed for. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the claim made by her was a case of custodial death and the appellant had no right to the compensation claimed under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not entitled for any relief in exercise of the power under Article 226 of the constitution. [601B] 2.1 The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain a writ petitions under Article 227 of the Constitution of India and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable only in respect of claims made by persons aggrieved by an award of monetary compensation in proceedings under Article 14 or 226 of Constitution of India. [701C] 2:1 The appellant was entitled to compensation in a proceeding under Article 323A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, as a result of the alleged breach of its public duty and the right of the citizen to protect his fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution of the country. [802D] 2(a) The appellant had not challenged the award made by it on the ground that the compensation awarded was in excess of the amount claimed by her. [820E] 3.2 The High court has committed an error in holding that there was no infringement of fundamental rights of the petitioner under Article 21 of theConstitution of India, as the appellant did not challenge the award passed by the Tribunal on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. [823G H] 2.(b) The High courts have jurisdiction under Article 136 to entertain writ petitions against an order of the Tribunal in exercise its power under Articles 32 and 226 of a civil suit or criminal proceedings, based on tort. [825E] 4.1 In view of the above discussion, the appellant is entitled to the relief claimed by him in the petition. [826A D] 2 (a) There was no violation of fundamental right guaranteed by Article 21. The award made under Article 31(2) of the Articles 14 and 16 of the Act was not enforceable against it. The appeal is accordingly allowed, but without costs.

The petitioner was convicted by the trial court for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed a petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging his conviction and sentence on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to interview the prisoners as also to the interviewing the prisoners. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to be interviewed only under section 161(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, but it did not order him to be heard at the time of the execution of the death sentence. In appeal by special leave, this Court held that the right to interviews could not be denied merely because the prisoners were willing to be interviewing their relatives, friends and legal advisers as also the newspapers Today, India Today, the Press Trust of India Today was directed to consider the question whether the petitioner should be allowed to interview only under sections 161(3) and 162(2). The Court, HELD: (1) The right to interviewed is not a matter for us to decide. It does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, India today. [701B] (2) The freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of Constitution is not an absolute right, nor does it confer any right to express any particular view or opinion but it does confer no right to give an interview under section 162(3). [702C E] (3) The Court should be slow in granting the relief sought for by the petitioner. [601D] (4) The object of article 19 is not to provide that every prisoner shall have a freedom of expression and that every person who wants to interview a prisoner must have an unrestricted right to speak or write on his behalf. [76G] (5) The Constitution does not confer any rights on the petitioner to interview any prisoner. It merely confers no right on him to interview anyone. [77A B] (6) The expression "any person" in article 19 (1)(b) of constitution means a person who has been sentenced to death and includes a person whose sentence is confirmed by the Supreme Court or the High Courts. [78C E F] (7) It is not necessary that every citizen should have an opportunity to interview every prisoner. The right conferred under article 19 cannot be denied only because he has been deprived from interview.

The appellant was the owner of a tea garden and he had been put in possession of the same. The Receiver, after the sale of the tea garden, took possession of it on August 26, 1950. On October 4, 1961 the appellant filed an application for delivery of the property to the Receiver. The Subordinate Judge allowed the application and directed that the sale be made absolute. The appellant appealed against the order of the Subordinate Judge. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had committed a serious error in holding that the Receiver was not liable for the loss caused to the tea gardens by fire and that the appellant was entitled to recover damages from the Receiver as well as from the receiver. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of attachment passed by the District Judge is not sustainable under section 145(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [701B] 2. The sale of tea garden in favour of the Receiver is not a valid sale and the appellant cannot be made liable for any loss caused by the fire. [602C] 3. The suit was not maintainable because the Receiver had taken possession of his property on August 25, 1950 and that he had sold it to the appellant. [613D] 4. The auction purchaser was entitled under section 146(c), of the Civil Procedure Code to recover the amount due from him as a surety for the fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of court in any suit or in any proceeding in any civil or criminal proceedings. [502E] 5. The liability of the auction purchaser is not disputed by the appellant and it is not open to the High court to direct that the amount payable by him be recovered from the appellant as a security for the performance of his duties under section 144(c). [603F G] 6. The obligation in relation to the sale is not discharged by the Receiver but only on account of the loss occasioned to the Tea garden by fire. It is not necessary that the property should be sold or otherwise disposed of as a result of the fire which may have been caused by fire, and that it must be shown to the Court that the said property was being used for the purpose of the business of tea cultivation. [403G] 7. The fact that the auction sale was made in favour o the appellant does not mean that the respondent could not be held liable for loss occasioned by the Fire. [544A D] 8. The respondent had failed to prove that the damage caused to his tea garden by the said fire was due to the fire and he was put in charge of the management of the factory. He was, therefore, entitled to get damages from him. [543B] 9. In view of the fact that there is no evidence on record to show that the loss suffered by the respondent was due from the fire, the High Courts were not justified in holding otherwise. [542C D] 10. The appeal must accordingly be allowed and the judgment and decree passed by both the courts below are set aside. The appeals are allowed. There will be no order as to costs.

The State of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification under section 3 of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1959, on April 11, 1960, for the sale of wheat to the Controller of the State Government at the controlled price. The State Government by its order dated May 11, 1961, declared the goods as "sale" within the meaning of the said provision. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification before the High Court. The High Court held that the sales were not liable to tax under the U P. Sales tax Act and the sale was not taxable. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transactions of supply of wheat were not exigible to tax as they were not goods within the definition of the word 'sale' in section 2(h) of the Act; that the High court had erred in holding that the sale did not result in sales and was not liable for payment of sales tax under section 2 (h) read with section 4 of the Central Sales Tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'sale ' has a wide meaning and it is not necessary to refer to any other provision of the statute or to define the word "sale". [601B] 2. The words "sale ' in relation to the goods" have a wide connotation and they are not restricted to only sale of goods but also includes sales which are on account of the goods being sold within the State. [602C] 3. The word "goods" has a wider meaning and its meaning is that it includes all kinds of movable property, including immovable property. It does not include any kind of movable or immovable property; it does not mean anything else but includes any kind which is used in connection with the business of the assessee. [063D] 4. The definition of 'sale" in section 3(h), as amended by U. P. Act No. 1 of 1962, clearly shows that the transaction of supply must be one for sale of the wheat purchased or purchased by the dealer and not for sale within the ambit of the definition. [63G] 5. The transactions of purchase of wheat are not exigible under section 4(h). The goods were supplied to the State of U.p. at the time when the Order was made, and the order was passed on May 11/1961. [64A B] 6. The sale of rice is not a sale within meaning of section 2 of the Sale of Goods Act. It is only a sale which is exigible to sales tax. [65E] 7. The goods are supplied by the State to the dealer. The order was made under cl. 5 of the Order and the supply of goods was not subject to restrictions, the transaction could be regarded as a sale. [66F] 8. The power conferred on the State is not an absolute power but only an administrative power. It can be exercised by the authority concerned in accordance with the provisions of the law. [68A B C] 9. In the instant case, the transactions were not subjected to sales Tax and the goods were not sold within that time. The orders were made under s. 3(i) readwith cl. (e), (f). The order did not amount to a sale in the sense that it was an administrative order. [67A B D] 9: The transactions were of supply and purchase of goods, but the transactions could be treated as sales within the scope of the expression 'Sale ' in section 4 (h). [68B C] 10: The transaction of supplying wheat to State Government is not exigible on such transactions. It was a sale by the manufacturer to the purchaser. The transaction was not an administrative one and it did not involve any transfer of goods from the seller to the buyer. The contract between the parties, therefore, amounted to a 'sale within the purview of section 4.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 (hereinafter referred to as 'the PASA) on the ground that he had committed a breach of the provisions contained in section 3(1)(a) of the PASA. The grounds of detention were served on him and his report was received by the Advisory Board on August 7, 1986. He submitted his representation to the State Government on June 23, 1986 and the State government rejected the same on July 24, 1986 on the basis that there was no Advisory Board in existence to which a reference could be made under section 11 of the Act. The petitioner filed an appeal before the State Govt. against the order of detention. The State Govt., by its order dated August 7/24, 1986 dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order passed by the State Gov ernment on July 25, 1986 rejecting his representation. The present petition has been filed by the petitioner challenging the validity of the order dated May 26, 1986 passed by respondent No. 1. The learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the detention order was bad in law as it was not made within three months from the date of the second order of the Advisory board and since the report of the advisory Board was received on August 07, 1986, the detention was valid. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions contained therein are mandatory in nature and they have to be strictly construed. If the report is not obtained within three weeks from the day of its receipt or within three days from the said date, it cannot be said that there is sufficient cause for detention of the person beyond the period of three months after the date on which its report was obtained before the hearing of the case. [801B] 1.2 The order of preventive detention has to be made within a period of two months from its receipt and the report must be obtained within one month from the time when it is received by it. If there is no Advisory board in existence, it can be said to have been satisfied before the date when it was received. [901C] 1.(a) The order passed under section 3 of the COFEPOSA Act has to specify the period for which a person may be detained and the period within which such person may not be detained. If he is not satisfied with the report, he can make an application to the Advisory authority for extension of time. [1001D] 1(b) The provisions of section 3 have to apply to the order made under sub section (1) of section 4 of the said Act and if there is a reference to an Advisory Board, it has to refer to an advisory board in place to which the Advisory Boards have to submit its report. [1101E] 1 (c) The proviso to section 3 makes it clear that the Advisory boards are required to be constituted within three years from the receipt of the report and if they are not so satisfied, they can make a reference under section 4(1). [1002F] 2.(a)(i) In the instant case, the Advisory Advisory Board had reported about the existence of the grounds on which it was passed. The Advisory Board did not have any such record as required by section 3. It was only after the expiry of three weeks that the petitioner could make a representation to that authority for extending the jurisdiction of the State Govern ment to that Authority. [110G] 1[(ii) In view of the proviso to sub section 2(1), the Advisory Committee is not bound to forward the report to the Government and if it does not submit its recommendations within three month from its receiving, it would be open to the Central Govt., to make a fresh reference under Section 4(2).

The respondent, who was the original claimant before it, filed a claim for compensation under section 17 of the Act. The appellant claimed that he had given an award dated 20th January, 1977 in respect of the subject matter of the dispute and that he was entitled to file the same on the ground that the award was not made within the period of limitation. The respondent contended that the reference was barred by time as he had filed a suit against the appellant because the award had been signed by both the parties and that the respondent had given a notice under section 16(5) of the . The Civil Court, after hearing the parties, held that the arbitration agreement between them was not valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the arbitrator had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the award and that since the respondent did not dispute the fact that the subject-matter of the suit or over the parties to it, he had no right to challenge the award. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The arbitration agreement was not a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of Act. [801B] 2. The expression "arbitration agreement" is defined in section 2 (a) as meaning any agreement which is in writing signed by either party to the contract or by his agent, or by any other person on his behalf and which contains a statement that the parties have agreed to refer their disputes to arbitration. [901C] 3. The word "arbitrator" has been defined in clause (d) of section 3 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940. It is not necessary for the purpose of this case to decide whether the arbitration clause contained in the agreement was a proper and valid arbitration agreement or not. [1001D] 4.1 The expression 'arbitration clause' is defined by section 2 of the Contract Act as meaning "any agreement which contains an arbitration agreement which contain an arbitration clause". It does not include any agreement containing an arbitration Clause. [1101E] 3(a). In the present case, the respondent was entitled only to challenge an award on the grounds that it could not have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect thereof. [110G] 4.(b) The expression used in section 17(5)(d) is "any arbitration agreement" which contains any arbitration clause. It does include any arbitration agreement containing a arbitration clause." [110H; 110A] 5.2 In the instant case, it was not disputed that the appellant had given notice under Section 16(4) of The respondent had taken the responsibility of solving the dispute in terms thereof and had agreed to submit the award to the arbitrator. It was only after the filing of the application for setting aside the award that the same was made. [111A H; 110B] 5.(c) In view of the fact, that the agreement between the parties was not an arbitration one, it could be said that the dispute raised by the respondent in the present civil revision application was a valid arbitration clause and the appellant could not challenge the Award on the basis that the disputes raised by it were not arbitrable. [112A H] 5(a)(i) The High Court was right in holding, that there was no valid arbitration Clause in the contract between the appellant and the respondent. [113B C] 6.1 In the facts of this appeal, the High court was right when it held that there had been an arbitration Agreement between the respondent and the petitioner. [114E] 5 (a)(ii) The question whether the respondent could have the consequence of rendering a court entirely lacked jurisdiction in the sense that it did not give notice under sections 16(1) and 17(4), was a matter which could be decided by the civil court. [115F H; 115A B] 6.(b)(i).

The respondent 's mortgage was a mortgage by conditional sale of the mortgaged property. The mortgagor sold the mortgaged properties to the mortgagee on January 30, 1937. The respondent filed a suit in the Court of the Sub Judge, Asansol for recovery of the debt and for recovery thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent ' s mortgage was not an absolute interest but only a statutory right to recover the debt from the mortgagor. The High Court held that the mortgage was in the form of an English mortgage and that the right to recovery of debt was not a vested right to be transferred to a submortgage under section 28, sub section (1) of section 28. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. A mortgage is a transfer of a right to redeem the property and it is only a mortgage which is in the nature of an assignment of the mortgage debt. The right to receive the amount of the loan is not an interest in the mortgaged. [675 C] 2.1. The expression "all the rights" used by section 28 means that the mortgagee still retains a legal interest in property and the mortgagor continues to retain a legal title in the property. [76 D] 3.2. In view of the provisions contained in section 28(1) (a), the right of the mortgagee to recover from the mortgaged is not a statutory one, but an absolute right to get the amount recovered by sale of mortgage. The word "all" used in section 29(1)(b) is wide enough to include a mortgage and it does not include a sub mortgage. [77 D] 2:1. In the present case, the respondent was a mortgagee with possession of the property on January 1, 1939. He had no right to sell the mortgaged assets. The mortgage was created by conditional transfer of the right in favour of the mortgagor and the respondent had no interest in that property. Therefore, the right was not transferred to the submortga gee. [775 E] 2(i) The right of a mortgagee to get his mortgage money under section 29 (1)(c) is an absolute one and it cannot be transferred or extinguished by sale. [78 D] (ii) A mortgage which has been created by a conditional transfer in favour the mortgagor, does not create any interest in immovable property but only creates a right of redemption. The mortgagee continues to remain in possession of such property till the date of the suit. [79 E] 3(i)(a) The respondent ' was a sub mortgagee and he had no legal interest therein. [80 F] (b) The mortgage deed was not executed by the mortgagor but only an absolute estate. It was a conditional sale. Therefore the right which was transferred to him under section 30 of the Act could not be transferred. [81 G] 4(ii)(a). In view thereof, the mortgage deed is not one in terms of section 29 of the Indian Contract Act and the right conferred on the mortgagor by section 30 is an assignable interest. [82 H] (iii) The proviso to sub section 1 of section 36 of the Transfer of Property Act applies only to a transfer or mortgage which takes place after the commencement of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [83 G] 5(ii) The expression 'all the right" in section 30 means that right which is transferred to another person and not to any other person. [85 H] 6(iii) A mortgagee who has no interest therein cannot transfer or alienate his rights unless he has received notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section 2 of section 30. The proviso does not apply to a mortgage executed by a mortgagor but merely an absolute owner.

The appellant and his wife were brothers. The properties gifted under exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2 were joint family properties. They were partitioned by a registered deed dated April 15, 1946. The appellant was the son of Venkatacharyulu. He died on February 22, 1949 leaving behind him his widow and two sons. On March 31, 1950, he filed O.S. No. 63 of 1954 against the respondents for recovery of possession of the properties covered by exhibit A1 and exhibit B2. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 6(h) of the Andhra Pradesh Hindu Succession Act, 1956. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no valid gift under exhibit B1 and Exhibit A2. [801B] 2. The question whether the properties gifted to Venkatachariulu were ancestral or not did not arise for consideration of this Court. [902C] 3. The fact that the properties were purchased by Venkatacwarulu in his individual capacity was not disputed before the trial courts and it was only after the partition, he sold the properties under exhibitA1 and A2 to his sons. He had no power to make a gift of his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his brothers. [1001D] 4. The mere fact that Venkatacuttulu had no right to make any gift of the property covered by Exhibit 187, does not affect the validity of the transfer under exhibit 1 and A 2. [092E] 5. The transfers were made without consideration of past cohabitation between Venkatacharharyulu and his sons and they were free to make an assignment. The transfer was valid and legal. [1101F] 6. The gift under Exhibit 187 is not a valid gift. It is a gift by way of gifts. The property gifted under Exhibit 186 is not the subject matter of any gift. The entire properties are ancestral or joint family property. The gifts were made in consideration of the past cohabitations and there was a disruption of the joint family in 1947. [110G] 7. The right to alienate the coparcenary property was not affected by the partition. The alienations were invalid. The alienation was void under section 2(d) of Act 1 of 1956. [111A D] 8. The power to sell the properties was not a mere matter of fact and it could not be exercised in any manner. [112E] 9. In the present case, the properties are not ancestral or Joint family property but were only ancestral properties. The sale deeds executed by Venkatachaharyulu in favour of his sons were invalid as they were not hit by section 6 (h) Of the Andhra State Law.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was carrying on business in the name and style of "M/s. M/s Kamalabai G. Ranade". The assessee had filed an application for revocation of the notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 before the I.T.O. on 5.12.75. The L.I.C., after considering the material placed before it by the IIC.L.C. and after hearing the parties, passed an order dated 5.1.76 revoking the notice issued under section 227(3)(vi) of Income Tax act, 1961. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the delay in making the requisite statement was not due to any deliberate inaction or negligence on the part of the L. I.C.'s officer and, therefore, the delay was attributable to the LI.I.,C. as well as to the assignee of the policies to whom the payment thereunder had to be made by the LIA. The assessee filed a special leave petition in this Court against the said judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that there was no delay on the basis of the registered assignment and, consequently, the application for revoking the notices under section 11(3), (vi) and 226(4) of 'the Income Tax ACT, 1961 was not maintainable. [701B] 2.2 The High Courts were wrong in holding otherwise. The impugned judgment of a learned Single Judge is liable to be set aside. [802C] 3.1 In the present case, the LOI issued by the appellant under section 22(3A) of Act, 1962 was not revoked on 5th December,75 and, as such, the appellant could not have been made to pay interest for the period after inordinate delay in payment thereof. [820G] 2:1 The appellant had filed a suit against the LOC for recovery of the amount due under the policies which were held by it to be payable only to the assignor. The claim was barred by limitation. [823C] 2 3.2 In the instant case, there is no dispute that the LCO had made the requisite statements on oath under section 21(3). It is not disputed that the appellant had made a statement on oath on oath before the LAC on 5 th December, 75 and, in fact, he had made such a statement only after the LC. had made it on oath. [825D] 3:1.2 Under section 226 of the Act, the assessee is entitled to make the requisite declaration on oath within six months from the date of service of notice under clause (vi). The LAC has not made any such declaration in terms of section 226. [826E] 2;3.3 In the facts and circumstances of this case, it cannot be said that the High Courts have committed any error in holding the appellant to be entitled to interest for payment by theLIA. [827A D] 3;4:1 It is well settled that a person who has made a false statement on his oath before a court or authority cannot be held liable to pay the interest unless he proves that the statement was false. [828E] 3,5A] 2(a) The LIA is not an instrument of trust. It is a document which is required to be registered under section 12 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The document must be in terms thereof and must be accompanied by a declaration on affidavit.

The respondent was a candidate for election to the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly from the State of Madhya Pradesh. He filed an application under section 29(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 before the High Court of Madhya Bharat, Jabalpur, contending that he had not made any application under the First Schedule to the Limitation Act and that the period prescribed for such an appeal was not a period of limitation prescribed therefor by the First schedule. The High Court dismissed the said application holding that the provisions of section 29 (2) were applicable to proceedings under special or local law for which a period prescribed therefor had been prescribed in the First and Second Schedule. On appeal, the High court held that the words "any special or other law prescribing for any suit, appeal or application by any special orlocal law" used in sub section (2), of section 3 of the Limitation act, 1963 were applicable only to proceedings which are not of a type for which period prescribed therein by the first Schedule. The respondent filed an appeal under section 116 A of the Act before the Madhya Bharat High Court against the order of the Tribunal, and the High appellate court held in favour of the respondent holding that it was not necessary to make any application for the purpose of determining any period of time prescribed therefor in the Second Schedule because it was sufficient if the special or such local law prescribes for such a suit, Appeal or application. The appellant filed an objection under section 30(2)(a) of that Act before this Court contending that the appeal was barred by limitation and that since the provisions contained in the first schedule were not applicable to any proceeding under special law, the provisions thereof would apply to proceedings relating to special or general law for the time being prescribed therefor. The Madhya Bharat Legislature enacted the [Madhya Pradesh Legislative Council (Amendment) Act, 1963] (No. 20 of 1963). Section 29(1) of this Act provided that "the provisions contained therein shall apply only in so far as they are not expressly excluded by such special or special law". The appellant contended that the first proviso to section 29 was not applicable because it did not prescribe a period for which an appeal or an application could be filed under a particular local law. Held, further, that the language of sub section(2), subsection (1) and sub section 2 of section 30 of the Indian Limitation Act is identical with that prescribed in First Schedule and that there was no express provision in the said Act to prescribe a limitation for such appeal or the application. In the instant case, the appellant had made an application before the Tribunal under section29(2). The High court was right in holding that sub section 1 of section29 of the [Indian Limitation Act] applied only to suits and appeals which were not of any kind for which the period of Limitation prescribed therefor was prescribed by the Second schedule. In view of the provisions relating to limitation prescribed for an appeal, it is clear that the application under sub section 3(2)] of the First or Second Schedule must be made before the period specified therein. The proviso to sub section 4 of section 28 of the Madhya Land Revenue Code provides that "if such period are prescribed therefor" by the Central Government, the provision contained in section 29 shall apply to such appeal and application as if such period were prescribed therefor under a special or specific law for any case. It is not necessary for the purposes of this case to refer to sub sections (2)(b) and (3) of section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The language of subsection (2)] is clear enough that it provides a period within which an application may be made under a general or special laws for any appeal, appeal, or application, by any other special or particular law for such case. The words "if any special" in sub sections(2)" are not to be construed as including the provisions regarding limitation prescribed therein.

The appellant, a private operator of the respondent-State Transport Authority, Mathura, was running a bus stand at the relevant time. The State Transport Authority issued a notification fixing a bus stands under section 76 of the Act and that was challenged by the appellant before the High Court in a writ petition filed by him. The High Court allowed the said writ petition holding that the Regional Transport Authority had no power to fix a bus Stand under section 68(2)(r) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. It also held that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction over the area and that the order passed by the District Magis trate was not a valid order. The appellant filed Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 958 of 1986 in this Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court holding that section 76(2) (r) had no application to a bus depot and that it was open to the Regional transport Authority to determine any convenient place or places within the Town Area of Baldev (Mathura). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 68(1)(r), as amended by the Act, confers power on the State Government to fix the number of vehicles to be used in a public service vehicle and to issue a notification determining the area in question. The Regional Transport authority has no power under section 70(2). [601B] 1.2 Section 68 (1)(s) of Motor Vehicles act, 1939, which is in Chapter IV of the , provides for fixation of a bus standing at the bus stand and to start from there to be a bus Depot. The District Magistrate has no jurisdiction to fix or alter any bus stand under section76 of the . [602C] 1.(r) The Regional transport authority had power to determine a bus place or halting places which are not the same as bus stands. [603D] 2.1 The Regional Government had power under Section 68 to fix and fix a number of bus stand in the area of Baldev and to stop its buses at the Bus Stand. It was open for the Regional Government to take action for determining any convenient places or places beyond the Town area of the Baldev (xviii) as a bus stood. [613E] 2.(r). The District Magistrate had no authority under section 69(2), to fix, or alter, a busstand and to grant permission to the President of the Mathura Township to stop their buses at that bus stand. [503F] 2(i) The State Government had no competence to fix any bus stands in the areas of Baldev, Baldev and Baldev. [511E] 3.(ii) The District Judge was not right in holding that there was a valid notification fixing the number or places of bus stands at the time of issuing the impugned order. [504G] 4.(iii) The High court had no powers under section 67(2)[503C] 5.(iv) The power to issue an order fixing a Bus stand under Section 76 of Act is not confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places but it was only in respect of a public bus stand which was a sort of radiating centre of all the bus stands and that too was a matter relating to traffic. [506D] 4(i)(ii) In view of the provisions contained in section 68 (2), the District Judge had no other power under sub section (1) of section 76 to fix parking places or halting place at any time. [500E] 5(iii) Sub section (3) of Section 68 of the U.P. Act confers power upon the State Transport authority to fix such number or place as may be necessary for the purpose of carrying out the functions under sub sections (1), (2) and (4). The power conferred on the Regional Authority by sub section(1) is not limited to fixing a vehicle stand and halting place.

The appellants were prosecuted for offences under Sections 7 and 7 of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The trial Magistrate convicted them on a charge under Section 7 of that Act. The High Court set aside their conviction and sentence. On appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellants under Section7 of the Act was not justified. [601B] 2. The prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants were guilty of an offence punishable under Section 8 of the said Act. [613C] 3. The burden of proving that the accused persons committed an offence under Section 9 of the aforesaid Act lies on the prosecution and the prosecution has not proved that they were guilty, was not discharged by the trial Magistrate. [501D] 4. The onus to prove the guilt of the accused is on him. It is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of the presence of the offender at the time of commission of the offence. [511E] 5. The fact that the appellant Malkiat Singh was not in possession of any paddy or truck, does not make it an attempt to commit the offence of export. [504D] 6. The mere fact that a person is in possession would not make him an attempt on the part of the prosecution to commit an offence of Export. [506E] 7. The appellant Malicat Singh had been convicted under Section 13(1)(d) read with Section 14(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay fine of Rs. 5,000/-. He was also convicted under Sections 13(2), 13(3) and 13(4) of that act. [500F] 8. The facts found by the High Court are not in dispute. It was only a preparation on the basis of which the offence was committed. [525G H] 9. The evidence on record clearly shows that the prosecution had not proved the commission of an attempt at export. The accused were charged under Section 5(1) readwith Section 13 (2). They were convicted for offences punishable under Sections 8 and 7 read with Sections 13 (3), 13 (4) and 14(5) of this Act. They were sentenced to imprisonment for one year, and a fine of rupees five thousand. [450G] 9 A. The sentence of imprisonment was not excessive or harsh. It could be imposed only on the person who committed an attempt. [452H; 452A H] 10. In view of the fact that there was no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of Punjab Padways (Exports Control) order, 1959 and as a matter of fact the prosecution failed to establish that the goods were exported within the definition of 'export ' under Section 2(b), the High court was not right in setting aside the conviction.

The appellant, a firm called the E.G.M.T.L., was incorporated in the Managing Agency Agreement on January 1, 1956 and the terms of the Managing Agent were to be treated as one entity and the remuneration for the entire year 's work was to be paid by way of remuneration for each year of the year. The appellant, who is a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, applied to the High Court for a direction that the remuneration payable to the appellant should be determined in accordance with the terms and conditions of the agreement entered into between the parties. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Managing Agents were not liable to pay any remuneration for their services as they had been appointed by the appellant, but on the facts of the case, held that the appellant was entitled to the remuneration from the date of his appointment and that the respondent was entitled only to the entire amount of remuneration. The appeal preferred by the appellants against the said judgment of the High court was dismissed by this Court. In the present appeals, it is contended that the High Courts were right in holding that there was no express or implied term between the assignor and the assignee as regards the remuneration and that since the assignment had been expressly excluded from the scope of the terms, the remuneration could not be said to have accrued to the respondent.
