Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 's remuneration' in clause 10 of the Agreement is an indivisible contract for a whole year ' s work which has been assigned and the assignee was entitled either as part of the deed of transfer or independent thereof. [601B] 2.2 The term 's salary' in the agreement between the appellant and the respondent, as appearing in clause 3 of the managing Agency Agreement, is an inseparable contract for whole year "s work which took place with it a right to the whole income that fell due after the date when the commission for the year was incorporated into the Managing agency Agreement. [701C] 2:1 The term "s remuneration" in the present case does not include any remuneration or remuneration for services rendered by the assignee and the assignment is only an indivisible one. [802D] 2(a) The expression "s salary" in clause (b) of the Agency Agreement means the remuneration which is payable to a person who is entitled to receive the entire income that falls due after his appointment as a whole day 's employee. [820E] 2.(b) The term includes any remuneration, not being remuneration for service rendered by a person other than the assignors. [823A D] 3.2 In the instant case, the respondent had been performing the functions of a Managing Agent and he was also discharging the duties of a managing agent. He was also performing the duties as a part of his agency. The respondent was not entitled to any remuneration from that date. [825E] 3.(c) The respondent is not entitled under clause 10(a)(i) of Part I of the General Conditions of Service of the appellant. [826A D E] 4.1 In the case of a firm, it may be stated that the managing agency was only an inseparable one and the appointment of the assign or the assignee was only a part and not merely an indivisible part. The remuneration for such services could not therefore be said as to be a remuneration for any purpose. [822E] 4.(a) In the circumstances, the HighCourt was right in dismissing the writ petitions. [828B D] (b)(i), (ii) & (iii) of Article 226 of the Constitution of India. [829A D; 882F] 3(a). The respondent had not been performing any part of its functions and it could not have been said that he was not performing any work which was incidental to his employment as a Managing Agency.

The appellant was married to the deceased Sunderpatti on August 13, 1963. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker, and Badri Shanker, who were living in the house of the accused. The prosecution case is that after the marriage, the accused went out of the house and came out at about 6 a.m. on August 12, 1963 and started quarrelling with him. On August 13. 1963, he was sleeping in his house and when he opened the door of the room, he found that he had "finished Sunderpatti" and thereby finished the daily quarrels. The accused went to the house where he saw the deceased and the deceased were sleeping. He then took out a knife from his pocket and gave him a blow with an iron rod on the head of the deceased. The deceased was taken to the hospital at about 7 p.m., but he succumbed to the injuries. The trial court found that the accused had committed the murder of Sunderpatti, and convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the extra judicial confession made by the accused was not voluntary and could not be relied upon as a piece of evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The extra judicial confessions are admissible against an accused person. It is well settled that the evidence adduced in the case of an extra judicial confessional statement can be used only as a corroborative piece of proof. [601B] 2.1 The extrajudicial confession made to the police officer cannot be relied on as a substantive piece of fact, unless it is corroborated by other evidence. [702C] 3.2 The extra Judicial confessions are not admissible in evidence. It can be acted upon if it is shown that the deceased had "previously quarrelled with him". [703D] 2:1.3 The extra-judicial confession is a weak piece of substantive evidence and cannot be used as a substitute for the substantive piece. [802E] 3:2.4 The extra -judicial confessions are inadmissible in evidence, unless the same are corroborated by some other evidence or by other independent evidence. The courts below have rightly held that the prosecution has failed to prove the extrajudicial confessions. [903G] 2.(a) The extra niceties of the evidence do not lend any support to the case made out by the prosecution. [1001E] (b) The High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had "involving" the deceased to his house when he entered into the room and brought out a pistol from his house. [1103G H] 3.(a)(i) The evidence of P.W. 1, P. W. 2 and P. Ws. 3 and 4 clearly establish that the appellants had "convolving". [1002E C] (ii)The extra judicial statement made by P.Ws. 3 & 4 is not a substantive evidence. There was no reason for the High court to hold that the said extra judicial statements were inadmissible in law. [110G H; 1103A] (iii)The High Court has rightly held the extra neces of the extra Judicial confession as inadmissible in the circumstances of this case. [107F] 4.(a). The extra ficeties and assumptions are not inconsistent with each other. It cannot be said that the courts below were wrong in holding the extra fen tions to be inadmissible in view of section 157 of the Evidence Act. [108A B] (iv)The evidence of the witnesses is not consistent with each others. The High court has rightly pointed out that the circumstances relied upon by the trial court are inconsistent with the hypothesis of guilt and the accused must have been able to establish his innocence.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the respondent 's Branch Office on May 1, 1976. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Manager on June 30, 1977 and he was confirmed in that post on July 31, 1977. On August 5, 1977, he was transferred from the office of the Regional Transport Authority, Cuttack to the office at Cuttack. The appellant was posted as a Clerk in the Office of the respondent. He continued to work till September 7, 1977 when he was relieved from his duties. In the meantime, on October 9, 1977 he was again transferred to the Office at Cuttack and he joined the service on November 30, 1978. On December 5, 1979, he filed an application for being appointed as an Assistant Manager in the office. The respondent contended that he had been working as a Manager since May 1 1976 and he had not completed his 55th year of service. He also contended that the Board of Management did not have any power to terminate the services of the appellant on account of his failure to give him notice or pay in lieu thereof. On September 7/9, 1977 the respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority against the order of termination. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order passed by the Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the appellant had not been given any opportunity to show cause why he should not be terminated from service, the order terminating his services was illegal and void. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The power of termination is a discretionary power vested in the Board under Article 311(2) of the Constitution. It is a well settled principle that the power of dismissal or removal is an arbitrary power which can be exercised only if there has been some material before the Board to come to its conclusion. [601B] 1.2. The order terminating the services is not in accordance with the provisions of law and the rules framed under the Act. It does not contain any reasons for terminating the service of an employee or officer. The Board has no power to dispense with the services on account thereof. [702C] 1.(a) In the instant case, the respondent was appointed on May 31, 1976 as a permanent employee and he continued to be in employment until his appointment was terminated by tendering one month 's notice or salary in lieu of notice. He had been appointed on June 29, 1977 but he was not in need of any employee 's services of a particular employee. [802D] 1(b) The respondent was not entitled to any compensation under the provisions contained in Rule 5 and 6 of the Rules of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules, 1976 which came into force on May 29, 1976 when he had already been appointed as Assistant Manager. [820E] 2.(a)(i) In view of the fact that the respondent had not made any request for being absorbed in service by giving one month's notice or wages in lieu whereof he was required to be absorbed in his place, the Board could not have dispensed with the service by issuing a direction to pay him one month' salary including allowances upto the termination of his services. [823E] 3.(a). The respondent had been terminated by the appellant 's order terminating her services on May 30, 1976 and she was relieved on June 31, 1978 from her office at the time when she was appointed. The termination of her services is illegal and invalid. [825F] 4.(b) In any event, the termination is not a dismissal or discharge simpliciter but it is a punishment inflicted by way of penalty. [822E] 5.(c) The order of removal is not an order of dismissal. It merely provides for payment of compensation to the employee in lieu Of notice. The payment of such compensation does not amount to any reduction in rank.

The appellant, who was the highest bidder for a right or privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor in the State of Orissa, filed an application under section 22 of the Orissa Excise Act, 1915 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') before the Collector of Excise, Cuttack praying that the auction held by him be set aside. The Collector of excise, Cuttack rejected the said application on the ground that the appellant had no right or licence for manufacturing and sale liquor in Orissa State and that the Collector was not concerned with the question whether the appellant was a licensee under section 6(a) of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court against the order of the Collector dated April 16, 1971. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the bid submitted by the appellant for the grant of a right to hold a public auction for the granting of such a right was illegal and that it had been rightly rejected by the State Government. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has committed an error in holding that section 6 (a) was not retrospective in operation. [901B] 2.2 The High Courts have held that the right to auction for grant of such right or privileges and privilege under section 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 was not a matter of procedure but a matter which had been expressly provided by the Amending Ordinance, 1970. [1025C] 3.1 In view of the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case (supra) and the decision of this Court in Jaiswal 's Case (supra), the High court was right in holding the auction to be illegal and void. [1126D] 2:1 The State Government had no authority to issue a public notice for purposes of sub section (1) of section 22, as the power of the Legislature to hold public auction was not limited by the provisions contained in sections 2 to 5 of Amending Act, 1970, and that such a direction could be issued only if the Collector had no jurisdiction to make an order under section 23(2). [1026E] 3:1.2 In view thereof, the High Courts were right in quashing the impugned judgment of the High 'Court holding that it was not necessary for the State Legislature to issue any public notice to auction the grant or privilege and to accept payment therefor. [110G] 2.(a) The High ' Court had no power under section 19(1)(c) of Orissa Excise (Amendment) Act, 1971 to direct the Collector to cancel the auction in question. [109A B] 3.(b) The State Legislature has the exclusive right and privilege of selling liquor within the State. It is not necessary that the State should hold a private auction for granting such a privilege or privilege. [108E] 4.1.3 In view, however, of the fact that the High' Court had held that it could not be said that the Government had exclusive right to grant such a licence, the appellant cannot claim any right or benefit under section 20(1) (c). [110H; 110A B C] 3(a)(i) The power conferred on the State by section 19 of the Amendment Act of 1971 is not retrospective. It has been expressly made retrospective in effect. [111B D] 4.(b)(ii) The right to sell liquor within a State cannot be said to have accrued to the appellant because the State had no competence to issue such a notice under section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. [112E] (c) The appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 11(1). [111D] 4(a). In view that the question as to whether the auction conducted by the Collector is illegal or void, does not arise for consideration in this case. [113A B D] 5.(b).

The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence i.e. on 19 December, 1967 accused No. 2 and 3 were found in the godown of Takalkar. The evidence of Dinkar and Dinkar was that they had kept the articles in the gunny bag which he had seen in the factory of Takkar. Accused No. 3 was found in his godown at about 5 p.m. on 20 December, 1966. Accused Nos. 1 and 2 were found to be in possession of the articles. The prosecution case is that accused No 1 and 3 went together for the sale of cycle to Rupvate. Accused no. 3 asked Dinkar to produce the gunny bags which he did not. Accused nos. 1 & 2 were also found in their godown at 5 p, 6 p. m. on 21 December, 1968. The trial court convicted all the accused under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. In appeal by the State it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that there was no evidence to connect accused No 3 with the murder of Narendra. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles were kept in the godowns of Takkalkar and that the same were not recovered from the house of accused No 2. In regard to the recovery of the incriminating articles, the High court observed: "The evidence of the witnesses clearly shows that there is no evidence on record to connect the accused No 4 with the crime. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution are not sufficient to establish the guilt of accused Nos. 3 and 3. It was also contended that there were other circumstances which would indicate that the deceased Narendra had left his house at about 6 p,6 p. M. on 22 December, 1964 and that he had gone along with accused No 5 for the purpose of sale of the cycle to him. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the evidence of PW 2 is not reliable because there was a clear corroboration from the evidence on the record to show that the accused Nos 1 & 3 were present at the time when the deceased was found dead in the house. It is also contended by the learned counsel that the circumstances relied on by the High Courts are not enough to establish their guilt. The fact that the appellant had kept his cycle with him and gave the key of the godown to accused No, 2 and the articles recovered from his possession does not indicate that he was present at 5 a.m., when the dead body was found. It may be noted that the recovery is not of any incriminating article but it is of no use to the prosecution case because the evidence shows that the said articles were given by accused No2. 3. The conviction of the appellant under section 304B read with sections 34 and 302 read by the Sessions Judge is based on the circumstantial evidence. The facts are clearly established from the record. The circumstantial evidence was sufficient to connect him with the offence. The circumstance relied upon against him is not sufficient in view of the fact that he did so at 5. p.M. on 23 December, 1963 and that his dead body had been identified by Dr. Nanavati. The recovery of articles from the godown at Takalkerkar was also proved by the evidence adduced by the witnesses. The accused No1 and 3 are not guilty of any offence under section 120B readwith section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. They were convicted for an offence under sections 302/34 and 302/120B read together with section 120 B read with Section 34 of I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment of life. The appeal by special leave was dismissed. In this Court, it is contended that in view ofs. 34 of Indian Penal code, the prosecution has failed to establish that the death of Narendra was homicidal or that he died of murder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.2.

The appellant was allotted a plot of land at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per sq. yard and he paid the amount of compensation to the owner of the original plots. The Town Planning Officer made an award on the basis of the market value of the plot at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions of section 71 were not attracted and the compensation was payable on the ground that the land included in the final scheme, the value of which was estimated at its market value at the time of the declaration of the intention to made by the Town Planning officer under section 32 (1) (iii). The High court held that the appellant had no right to obtain compensation from the local authority and partly from the Local Authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was in error in holding that section 71 of the Act was not attracted because the land comprised in the original plot included in a final scheme. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 71 and 64 of the Bombay Town Planning Act are applicable to the acquisition of the land under section 68 of the said Act. [801B] 2. The expression "land" has been defined in section 2(d) of the Land Acquisition Act as follows: "(d) 'land' means any land which is not included in an original plot but is not acquired by the local authorities for public purpose or for a public purpose, and includes lands which are not acquired under section 66." [802C] 3. The word "land", in relation to a town planning scheme has been used in section 71(1) of that Act and it is clear from the definition that the expression "Land" has not been defined either in the Bombay Land Acquisition Rules or in any other law. [820G] 4. The words "land which is injuriously affected by the making of a town Planning scheme" have to be read as "land". It is well settled that the word "compensation" means compensation payable on each plot included within the final Scheme, and not the final plot. [823C] 5. In determining the amount payable to an owner for loss of land it has to be determined whether an owner of an original Plot is given a reconstituted plot or not. The scheme as provided in section 64 (1)(iii) of Bombay Land Development Act is applicable to acquisition of land under that Act. It is clear that the compensation payable to the appellant was assessed at its full market value and it was therefore, not open to the Town planning Officer to determine the amount to be paid by the appellant to the local Authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. [825D] 6. The fact that the scheme is framed under section 71 (1), does not mean that the Town Development Officer has a duty under section 64(1)(iv) of Act to determine compensation payable in respect thereof from the public authority or partly from such person as may been agreed upon between the parties, and partly by the Local Authorities in cash. [826E] 7.

The testator was to select the house of his daughter for the daughters and he had a number of properties. The testator intended that each daughter would be selected by the legatee who was the guardian of the three children. The object of the testator was clearly to select his son for the daughter and to make the selection. The intention of the executant was also clear that each son would be given the right of selection to the daughters. The proviso to section 89(1) of the Act provided that if the testator intended to select a person for the children, he should give to the legatee the right to select such person for his daughter and the mother. The provision contained in section 89 was not complied with by the testator. The High Court has held that the testator had no power to select any one of the daughters who was his guardian and that the bequest was void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the will did not give the right in respect of the properties to which the legatee belonged but only a small portion of the property which he had given to the children. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The testator had intended that the daughters should get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. [701B] (2) The intention was clear that the legatee would select his sons for the two daughters and give them the right. [802C] (3) The will did contain a provision that each child would be allotted to the daughter. It is not necessary that the children should get the area of land devised to take them out of the vattam. [901F] (4) The object was to provide for the appointment of the legatee and the procedure for selection of his son in the matter of selection of the sons. [1002G] (5) The language used in section 90(1)(a) is clear that if a testator intended the bequest to be given by him, he would select the children to the mother and then make it clear that he intended that all the daughters would get their properties after taking them into account. [1101F G] (6) The words "the right of appointment" in section 91(1), are not capable of any precise interpretation. It does not mean that the Will should be read as a whole and if it is clear, it must in the circumstances be held that each minor would have to get his properties after giving him the right, but only small portion thereof which he intended to give to his daughters. [110G] The testator was required to select one of his sons who was entitled to the property. He had a right to choose the children for the purposes of section 91 (1). [110H; 110A B] (7) The word "may" in the proviso to Section 89(2) is not capable either of precise interpretation or of precise construction. It must be construed as meaning that the words "shall give to each daughter" are different in the case of widow and children who were entitled to select their sons for her daughters and if they were entitled then to select them for the properties. [111A B C] (8) The expression "may ' in the will shall mean that every son would have the right given to his daughter or children as and when they become major. [112B D] (9) In the instant case, the testator did not choose to select either of his daughters or of his mother. He was not entitled to make any selection. [113A B E] (10) The proviso does not say that if there is no words in the Will which can be construed to have been used in the Act, it will be presumed that every child would have right given for selection and if he is not so entitled then his son would get his property. [114B D; 115E] (11) The phrase "

The appellant was the owner of a plot No. 201 and he had purchased it from one Mohd. Bashir, who was the co-sharers in the same village. The respondents were the owners of the plots in dispute. On the basis of a registered sale deed dated 1357 Fasli, the appellant became the coowners of the land in dispute and the respondents were recorded as co-sharer in the revenue records. The appellant filed an application under section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 for restoration of his possession over the plots. The District Judge dismissed the said application on the ground that the appellant had failed to prove that he was not a co-owner of the plot No 201 and, therefore, the respondents could not be evicted from the land. The High Court held that the respondents had proved that they were in joint possession of the lands and plots in question. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 49 of the Act are mandatory in character and it is not necessary that the person who has acquired a right to be heard should have been given an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken against him. [901F] 2.2. The procedure prescribed under section 49(1) of the Land Reforms and Land Reform Act, 1953 is mandatory in nature and it cannot be held that a person who had acquired a vested right to remain in possession of a part of his land can be evicted only by the Collector. [1001B] 3.3. The right of the appellant to get the plots from the consolidation authorities was not affected by the abolition of zamindari. It was not open to the respondents to prove the factum of their ouster from possession, unless a clear ouster was pleaded or proved. [1101C] 4.1 The High court has rightly held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had practised a fraud on the consolidation authority and was assured by the defendants who were in exclusive occupation of the entire land. [110G] 3:1.2 In view of the clear admission of the respondents' case that they had practised fraud on consolidation authorities, it is difficult to hold that there could be no evidence for establishing that the plaintiff was not at all aware about the consolidation proceedings and was told about the partition proceedings. [109H; 110A] 3 3.1 It is well settled that a mere statement of facts cannot be taken as conclusive proof of a fact which has been admitted by the parties to the litigation. The burden of proving the existence of fraud on a particular date is upon the party who asserts the existence and it can be rebutted by evidence adduced by the other side. [111A] 4:1 It was open to a person, who had created a fraudulent transaction in order to gain advantage from the same transaction, to take advantage of his own wrong. [112B C] 3; 2.3 The High Courts have rightly held against the appellant. [113D] 3 & 2.4 In view thereof, the appeal is allowed and the judgment of the District Judge is set aside. The suit filed by the respondents for partition of plots Nos. 201 to 274 is dismissed.

The petitioner was elected as a Prime Minister of India in the year 1951. He was elected to the Council of Ministers on the basis of the oath register maintained by him. The petitioner filed an election petition challenging the election of respondent No. 1 and his other members of the Council. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had not been able to establish that he is a Minister for the Union or that he has been described as Prime Minister. In appeal, this Court held that the oath was not a constitutional document and it was not necessary that the person who took the oath should be a Minister of the State. The Court also held that there was no evidence on record to show that the respondent No 1 was a Minister or that the nomination paper of the petitioner as Prime Ministers was not signed by him as Prime Secretary but by the incumbent himself. In view of this finding, the petition er filed an application for review of the order dated January 9, 1989. The petition was dismissed by the High Court on February 10, 1990. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has not been given any oath in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and the rules framed thereunder. He is a person who is entitled to be appointed as Prime Minis ter for the State and he cannot be said to have been elected as Prime minister. [701B] 2.2 The petitioner was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister by the President of India on January 9/9, 1951. His appointment was not in accordance therewith. He had been described in the petition as a Minister. He has been defined in Section 2(d) of the Government of India Act, 1935 as an officer of the Union and he is entitled for the post of Deputy Prime Mini ter. [801C] 3.3 The petitioner had been appointed as a Deputy Prime Ministers by the Council on January 10, 1951 and his appointment was also described in that petition as an MLA. He did not have any constitutional sanction for the posts of Deputy Chief Minister. [820G] 4.4 The petitioner is entitled only to the post which he held as a member of the Legislative Assembly. [823C] 5.1 In view thereof, the petitioner cannot be denied the right to hold the post as a Member of the House of the People. [825D] 3(i) The petitioner could not have been appointed by the Union Government as Prime Cabinet Minister because he was not an MLA and he had been designated as Prime President of the Assembly. He could not be said as a person holding the office of Deputy Speaker. [822E] 5.(ii) The petition is misconceived and it is liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [821F] 6.2 In view, however, of the fact that the petition was filed in the High court after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for filing an election appeal against the order of dismissal passed by the Election Tribunal, the High Cou rt should not have entertained the petition on the ground that it was barred by time. [826E] 6.(iii) The High Cou rity has no jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 226 of the Consti tution of India. [827A D] 7.3 In view o f the above, the writ petition is dismissed.

The appellant, a factory, was engaged in the manufacture of "strike" and the workers were paid holidays with pay under section 49 A of the Factories Act. The appellant was appointed as a "Strike" on 1st November, 1948. On 1st December, 1948, the appellant was given a holiday for work on 1 st November, 1949. On 2nd January, 1950, the workers who had been working in their own factory were allowed to leave the night shift without any notice and they were not entitled to annual holidays with them. The management issued a notice under section 48A of the Act calling upon the appellant to show cause why the provisions of sections 49 A and 49 B should not be extended to them. On 3rd January, 1951, the management called for a report from the Inspector of Factories, Madras, who submitted his report. The Inspector of Factory, Madras sent a reply on behalf of the appellant stating that the workers had been allowed to work on the night of 1st October, 1948 and that they were entitled to pay holidays with their workmen on that day. On 4th January, 1952, the Inspector issued a show cause notice under sections 49A and 49B of the Factory Act calling for a explanation from the appellant as to why the workers should not get the benefit of holidays under section 50 A of Factories Act and the provisions relating thereto should not apply to them and that the appellant should be directed to pay off the holidays under sections 48A and49 B. The respondent, who was working in his own factory, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued by the Inspector on behalf the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the action of the management was illegal and void. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that the High court had committed an error in holding that section 49A of Factories act did not apply because the workers themselves were entitled under the rules to annual holiday with them and, therefore, they should be treated as deprived of their right to annual hours of work on that night. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the new Act are not applicable to the case of the workmen who had participated in the strike. [701 A] 2. The workers were entitled only to annual days of continuous service in their respective factory and they would have been entitled to the annual holidays at full rates as provided for in section 49 B. [802 C] 3. The workmen were entitled not only to the weekly holidays but also to the hours of rest on that date. [820 D] 4. The employees were entitled, under the provisions contained in sections 49B and 49 A, to annual leave without pay and they had been paid holidays at half rates as prescribed for in sections 48 B and 49 C. [823 E] 5. The work of stoppage of work was not a strike but a break in service. It was an illegal strike which resulted in the interruption of service. [825 F] 6. The workman was entitled to a annual holiday on 1St November, 1947, when he had been engaged in his factory for a period of twelve months ' continuous service. He was entitled only for annual holidays and not to any other weekly holidays. [826 A B] 7. The worker was entitled for annual holiday at half rate as provided in section 48B of Factories. [827 C] 8. The employee had been given a notice by the management to work in his personal capacity on 1.11. 1948, which was not complied with. He had been permitted to work only for a week and that he would have completed a periodof twelve months' continuous service if he had not completed a specified period of 12 months ' continuously. [828 E] 9.

The appellant, who was working as a driver of a vehicle bearing registration No. MP-01-A-905, had been convicted by the trial court under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He was also convicted under section 5A(1) of the Act and sentenced under section 79 I. P.C., but he was acquitted. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed his appeal. In the appeal, the High court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and consequently dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal of the appellant, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 79 I..P. C. provides for a certificate of fitness in respect of a film which is a film. The certificate issued under section 4A(2) of Chapter II of the Penal Code is conclusive evidence that the film has been certified by the Central Board of Film Censors, acting within their jurisdiction and on an application made and pursued in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason which of a mistaken belief, believes itself to be reasonable by law. [601B] 1.2 The certificate under section 3(1A) of Act is conclusive proof that the certificate has been granted by it in good practice. It is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the certification has been obtained by mistake of law or that the Certificate has been duly certified by it. [702C D] 1.(a) The certificate is conclusive and does not affect the validity of the prosecution. [803D] 1(b) The prosecution must be proved beyond reasonable doubts that the appellant had committed an offence under section 293 I.p.C.; and that he was guilty of having committed an act which constitutes the offence under sections 292 I,P.c., and that the conviction of the accused is based upon a valid certificate issued by it under section 80 I.

The appellant, a Government Pleader, Madras, was appointed as an Advocate of the High Court of Patna by the Chief Justice. He was also appointed as a Government pleader for the State of Bihar. On his appointment as an advocate of the Patna High Court, he was appointed to represent the Government in all the civil cases. The Government Pleader was appointed by the High court and he was also designated as an Additional Advocate General. In the year 1979, the appellant filed a writ petition in the Patna high Court challenging the appointment of a Government Advocate for the Patna District, but the same was dismissed on the ground that the appellant had no locus standi to file the writ petition. The appellant then filed a Writ Petition in the High Courts which was allowed by the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench held that the appointment was made by the Government Pleader and the appointment made by him was not legal. In appeal, the Division bench of the Calcutta High Court reversed the decision of the learned single judge and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of an Advocate for Patna District is a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. It is not a judicial function or duty to be performed by him in the due exercise of that office. [701B] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the Government pleader had no power to appoint a Government advocate for the Bihar State. [802C] 3. The power to make appointment of Advocate for Bihar State is not an independent and responsible character, but a judicial duty. It must be exercised by him only in the manner prescribed by law. [601D] 4. The Court cannot interfere with the discretion of the Government or its subordinate officers. The Courts are not expected to interfere with their discretion unless they have shown that they have acted on extraneous considerations or have acted in a manner which is unbecoming of a public servant. [76G] 5. The State Government has no power under any statute to appoint an Advocate or a Government Counsel for the High judiciary. [77A B] 6. In view of the fact that the High Judiciary is not only a judicial office but also a judicial officer, it cannot be said that the Court has no jurisdiction to interfere in the matter. [78C] 7. The petitioner 's claim that he was entitled to get a decree for possession of the property from the State Government and that he had a right to get possession of his property from Bihar State Government is not correct. [79D] 8. In this case, the High Powered Committee has made an enquiry into the question whether the petitioner ' s claim to be in possession of any part of the land of the government Pleader. The report of the Committee was accepted by the State and the Collector. [80E] 9. The fact that a Government Pleader is only an agent of the Court, does not mean that he has a right or authority to make an enquiry as to whether the Government Pleaders are responsible for the conduct of litigation. [81F] 10. In order to appreciate the question raised by the petitioner it is necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Rules framed thereunder. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Code') provides that every person who is a party to any proceeding shall be personally liable for prosecution if he proves that the proceedings were not conducted in accordance with law or that he did not have due regard to the circumstances of the case. [82G] 8A F] 9: The High Power Committee has clearly stated in its report that the petitioner was entitled only to get compensation for his property and that the State had no right to claim any compensation for the property.

The appellants were the shareholders of the Mills. The shares of the Bank of India were sold by the Bank to its nominees on May 6, 1948. On June 30, 1949, the Bank issued a notice under section 66(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') calling upon the appellants to sell the right to the Bank Of India shares in the Bank. The appellants filed an application for the issue of a share certificate and the High Court held that the distribution of the right was not a dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act, but it had no jurisdiction to grant the certificate. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The right to apply for the shares of Bank of Baroda in favour of the appellants was not an "dividend" within the definition of the expression 'dividends". [701A B] (2) The word 'divend' in section 2 (6A), as it stood before its amendment by Act No. 11 of 1956, did not include dividend but only a right to sell shares of bank of India. It was therefore not an 'dicend'. [702C D] (3) The expression "divorce" in the definition did not take within the extended meaning of that expression in section2(6AA). [703B] (4) The words "dive share certificate" in section 3(6) of Act were not confined to a right of distribution of dividend. It could not be said that the right of the bank of Baroda to sell its shares was an "sale" within section 2A(6), as the sale of the shares by the appellants amounted to distribution of dividends within the ordinary meaning of the word 'sale". [802C E] (5) The question whether the right under section 2B of the Act was a dividend or not did not arise for consideration in this case. [704G] (6) Section 2(2A) does not take into account any other provision of the Income Tax, and it merely takes within its ambit the right conferred on the Bank by section 2D of the said Act to sell or transfer the shares held by the shareholders. The right under that section is not an absolute one but only an absolute right to transfer the right in favour thereof. [805C] (7) Section 3(2B) does take within its fold the right which has been conferred on a Bank of the Baroda to exercise the option to purchase the shares. It does not, therefore, mean that the rights under section 3A were not an exclusive right to exercise any option in favour or otherwise. [605D] (8) The power to sell and transfer the share certificate is not confined only to the sale by the bank to its shareholders but also to the right given to them to exercise such option. [820E] (9) Section 4 of the Registration Act does not confer any power on the Registrar to sell, transfer or otherwise deal with the shares in question. The power of the Registrar under section 5A is not limited to the distribution by the Board of Directors of the Company.

The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court challenging the order of the learned Single Judge refusing to examine the witness who was present in the court. The learned Single judge allowed the petition and directed that the appellant should be examined by the Court on the ground that the witnesses were not present when the evidence of the appellant was recorded and, therefore, the appellant could not be cross examined by a witness who is present in Court. The Division Bench of the High court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had failed to produce the witnesses who are called for the examination of the witnesses and, consequently, the petition was allowed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the order passed by the learned single Judge is illegal and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has committed an error in holding that a party who is not present in court cannot be cross examine by a person whose name is not mentioned in the list filed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1A. [801B] 2. The order passed under Rule 1 A is not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. It was not open to the Court to refuse to examine such witness who are present when evidence of such witness was recorded. [901C] 3. The power conferred upon the High Courts under Article 227 of the constitution is a discretionary power and it cannot be exercised in a routine manner. The discretion has to be exercised judicially i.e. on the basis of sound principles of law, justice and fair play. [1001D] 4.1 The High Courts have no jurisdiction to refuse the examination or to examine any witness who may be present when such witness is not available at the time of recording his evidence. [1101E] 5.2 The power under Article 136 of theConstitution is a very wide and discretionary power. It cannot be used in a casual manner. It can be exercised only if there are compelling reasons for which the Court would not extend its assistance to procure the presence of witnesses or to procure their attendance by the court, but if it is shown that the witness was present when he was called for his examination by the High Power Committee, the power under Rule IA cannot be invoked.

The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College on April 27, 1981. He was appointed by the Committee of Management in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Scheme of Administration. The appellant was selected for appointment as Head of Institution on April 28, 1981 and he was appointed on April 29, 1981 on which appointment was made on April 30, 1981 under the order dated April 7, 1981 issued by the Director. On April 27.1981 the appellant was promoted as Principal in the College. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of appointment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order contained in radiogram had no effect on the validity and the appointment of the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The power to make appointment is conferred by the statute and the scheme of Administration envisages making of an order consistent with the provision of the statute. [901 A] 2.2. The appointment of a Principal or teacher in a private college is not a matter of right but it is made on behalf of the management. It is only when the appointment is otherwise valid, that the power to appoint is conferred on the Committee and the Director has no power to do so. [0901 B] 2:1.2 The power of appointment is given by the Regulations to make appointments in contravention of the provisions contained in the Act. The order of the High court does not show that it was made in violation of the provision contained in section 980(3) of the Code. [1026 C] 2 3.2 In view of the fact that the appointment was otherwise valid and the power conferred on a Committee to make the appointment had no force, the order passed by the High Powered Committee cannot be sustained. [1127 D] 3.3 The power conferred upon the Committee under section 9(3)(a) is not an absolute power but it has been given to the State Government in exercise of its power under section 4(1). It is a well settled principle that the powers conferred on an authority by statute are subject to the provisions made in the statute itself. [1227 E] 3:1 The power under sections 9(2) and (3)(b) is an absolute one and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [1328 F] 2;2.3 In the instant case, the appointment order was issued by a Committee of management in accordance therewith and the appellant had no right to challenge the same before making any further order. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellant, a textile mill, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the validity of the Sales tax levied on it under section 5(1) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the goods were not "goods" within the meaning of item 22 of the first schedule to the Central Excise Act, 1941, as they were not 'end product' within the definition of "textile". In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High court had erred in holding that there was no material before it to come to a conclusion that the product for which the Delhi Cloth Mills was entitled to exemption was an "dryon" fabric. The learned Single Judge held that the word "fabric" used in item 22 did not include any other kind of fabric and, therefore, the goods could not be said to be covered by item 22. On appeal by Special Leave, the Division Bench reversed the judgment of the High 'Court holding that it was not a case of "deyon" fabrics. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word "woven fabric" in item 19 of the First Schedule to the Act means any fabric which is capable of being described as a textile fabric. [801B] 2. The expression "fregnation" in article 22 of Part I of the Constitution includes all goods which are capable of be described as an "textiles". It does not include "dwaron" or "woollen fabrics". The word 'woollen fabric" is used in a sense and it means any other form of fabric. Therefore, the word 'fabric' in article 19(1)(g) must be construed to mean "a textile fabric which has been capable of producing or producing or manufacturing goods at all stages of production." [802C] 3. The words "wine fabrics" are not defined in the Act. It is a textile fabrics. Therefore the word used in article 20(1), in its ordinary sense, means "any other form whatever it may be called". [803D] 4. The definition of 'textiles' in item 21 of the Schedule to that Act does not exclude any other forms of fabric which are entitled to the exemption. It does cover all goods manufactured at a stage of production. Therefore it cannot be said that the impugned goods "fould be treated as textile fabrics" within item 22, because they were neither processed nor sold in the market. [820E] 5. The term "wines" is not defined anywhere in the Central Act. The meaning of the word is clear and unambiguous. It must be given its ordinary meaning. Therefore there can be no doubt that the said expression would include all goods produced or manufactured at any stage of manufacture at a time when they are sold in market. But it does not mean that the same thing should be left to the discretion of the taxing authorities. [823E] 6. The question whether the impugned product is an "winery fabric" within Item 22 of Schedule to Central Excise Tariff Act, 1940, was considered by this Court in the case of [805D] 7. In the instant case, the High Courts have held that there is no material on record to come at a conclusion as to what appeared to the High Curt to be a textile Fabric. The impugned goods were neither manufactured nor sold at any time when it was sold in markets. Therefore they cannot be treated to be "wis" or 'wis". [823F] 8. In view of the above, the impugned order is set aside and that of the Commercial Tax Officer is restored. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The respondent was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. On September 8, 1988, the Government of Bihar issued an order of transfer of the case from the Labour Court, Dhanbad to the Labour court, Dhanbad. The appellant company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order of the Government and praying for the transfer of its case from one Labour Court to another Labour Court at Dhanbad on the ground that the respondent was not entitled to be transferred to another Tribunal at Dhanbad because he had been residing in the colony quarter at Dhanbad since he had already been residing at Dhanbad, and therefore, the transfer was illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the transfer order of a workman could not be interfered with by the Government unless it was shown that there was a violation of section 33 B of the (14 of 1947) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The transfer order is vitiated for non-compliance of section 34B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [901F] 2.2 The transfer is not in accordance with the provisions of section 5(7A) of 1947 Act and therefore the High court was right in holding that there is no violation of Section 33 B. [1001G] 3.3 The transfer of a case from Labour Court Dhanbad to another labour court at Dhanbad is an administrative order which can be interfered by the High Courts only if it is shown that the Government had not been misled by the representation of the workman in making the order of transfers. [0901F G] 4.1 In the instant case, the respondent had been working as a Senior Assistant Electrical Engineer in the appellant company at Dhanbad and he was transferred to a Labour Court for disposal. The transfer was made on September 8/1988 and the respondent filed an application before the Labour Judge, Dhanbad for transfer of his case from Dhanbad to any other Labour Court. The Labour Judge by its order dated October 7, 1988 allowed the application and directed that the case be transferred back to the labour court, Patna. The State Government preferred a writ appeal against the said judgment of the High Cou rt which was dismissed on November 5, 1988. In the meantime, the appellant filed an appeal before this Court which was also dismissed by this Court. [1101F H] 4(a) The transfer orders were quashed and set aside by this court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [1202B] (b) The High Cou nt has no power to interfere with the order passed by the Labour C ourt. [110G] 5.(c) In view of the fact that the appellant had been staying at Dhanbad for a long time, it was not open to the High C ommissioner to transfer the case at Dhanbad to one Labour court at Patna. [111A D] (d) The order of transferring the case is vitiated because the respondent has been residing outside the colony quarters at Dhanbad when he had applied for leave and he has been staying in the Colony quarter at Ranchi since he was residing outside that colony. [112E] 6.(a) In the present case, it is not disputed that the petitioner was residing in a colony quarter of Dhanbad where he was living outside the said colony. He was also residing outside his colony quarters when he applied for permission to leave and the appellant has been working there since he has already been staying outside the Colony quarters at Ranchi. [113G] (c) The respondent had not produced any evidence to show that the employees of the company were residing in Dhanbad where they were living outside his Colony quarter. It was only on the basis of the materials available before the labour Court, that the order was quashed and the matter was remanded back to it for fresh consideration.

The appellant company was incorporated under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The management of the hotel was taken over by the Government of India and a notification was issued on October 7, 1955, under section 10(1) of the Act, for the purpose of making a reference to the Industrial Tribunal. The appellant company filed an application before the Tribunal for referring the dispute to a tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal after hearing the parties passed an order on October 9, 1955. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the reference made by the Commissioner of Labour and the award made by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the reference was incompetent because it was not made under section 12 (4) of Act, as the dispute was not referred to the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The reference was bad for mis-joinder of parties and the question whether the appellant company is a workman or not has been raised in the present case. [801B] 2.2. The expression "any person" used in section 10 (1) means any person who is employed to do any skilled, unskilled, manual, supervisory, technical, professional or clerical work for hire or reward and includes any such person as may be notified by the appropriate Government from time to time. [901C] 3.3 The expression 'any person' used in the definition of "workman" in section 2 (k) means a person who has been employed to perform any skilled or unskilled, supervisory or technical work for remuneration or reward. [1001D] 4.1 The word "workmen" is not defined in the Act. It does not include any person employed to carry on any skilled and unskilled manual, clerical or technical duties for hire of a workman. The definition of 'workman' in section 3(k) of Industrial Disputes act, 1947, clearly indicates that it is an industrial dispute within the meaning of the said Act. [1101E] 4.(a) In the present cases, the appellant Company was not a party to the reference and therefore the reference could not be made under the Act as the workmen were responsible for the dispute. [110G] (b) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 11 of the ID Act. The question whether an industrial disputes exists or is apprehended to be connected with the employment or non employment or not was raised in this form and the Tribunal had therefore power under section 8(1)(a) of that Act to make such a reference. [111G] 4(c) In view of the fact that the dispute between the management of Hotel Workers ' Union, Delhi and its workmen was referred for adjudication to the tribunal for making a Reference under section 9 of the I.D. Act, it is not open to the appellant to contend that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction in reference to such an industrial matter. [112G] 5.(a)(i) The question as to whether the dispute is an Industrial Dispute within the definition or not is a question of fact which can be determined by the Tribunal under section 3 (k). [111H; 111A C] 6.1 In view, however, of the facts and circumstances of this case, it would be open to both the parties to raise their respective contentions before the Industrial tribunal for referring them to a Tribunal for adjudication under section 2(k), if so advised. [113G H; 112B] (ii) The dispute between employer and employees is not an industrial Dispute within section 2A of the . In view thereof, it cannot be said that the appellant was not an industry or that the workmen concerned were responsible to the dispute for the reason that they were employed in the hotel.

The appellant imported a rod bushes and camshaft bushes, which were imported by the appellant, from its parts. The Customs authorities, however, refused to grant exemption under Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 1st March, 1976, on the ground that the bushes, in question, were parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading No. 84.06. The appellant filed an appeal before the Collector of Customs (Appeals), who allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Appellate Tribunal and dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The exemption granted to parts of the engines mentioned under Heading 84.6 is only for the purposes of Heading No 84. 06. [801 E] 2.2 The exemption is not in respect of parts of such engines, which are specifically included under Heading Nos. 8406. 8409. 8405. [908 A B] 3.3 The exemption cannot be denied to parts imported by a manufacturer, who has already been included under Chapter No. 85. [1001 E F] 4.1 In the instant case, the appellant had imported a rods bushes and had also imported them by the bushes which have been imported by him. Therefore, the goods imported by it are parts of a engines, falling under Chapter 84. The exemption does not apply to parts thereof. [1102 A B C] 3:1 The Notification does not contain any provision for the exemption in respect thereof. It only says that parts of engines, mentioned under heading No.84.06, shall be all the parts of engine, which must be all parts of those engines, except those parts of which are included under a Heading No 85.06 or 84.04. [1202 E] 3;2 The Notification also does not say that parts thereof will get the benefit of exemption from payment of duty in respect thereto. It merely says that the parts imported would be parts of motor vehicles falling under heading 84.05. The Notification only says so. [1301 F] 2:1 In view of the language used in the Notification, it is clear that parts which are not specifically included in the engines, as mentioned under Chapter 85, will get exemption from duty in terms of Heading 8406 and 84.07. [1402 G H] 3 :2 The notification does not state that parts imported shall be parts thereof, but only those parts which have already been excluded from the benefit. Therefore the parts which were specifically included within the scope of the Notification are parts which will get exempted from payment duty in view of Heading Nos 84.01.06 and 85.04, as they do not contain a provision for exemption from levy of duty under the Notification. [1502 A C] 2 3:2 The goods imported are parts thereof and not any other parts of that engines, but also those parts, which have now been included in Heading No 8.01 or 8406, as the case may be, as provided by the Notification itself. Therefore there is no material or evidence to hold that the appellant is entitled to the benefit under the notification. [1602 A D] 3 & 2:2:1 Section 130E of the Customs Act, 1962 provides for exemption in certain circumstances. The goods are parts and not parts of any engine. The condition precedent for claiming the exemption is that they must be parts which do not include parts of an engine. Therefore it cannot be said that the goods are part of a engine. [1802 A] 2;3:2 Section 130A of the Act provides for grant of exemption in case of parts imported from duty. The conditions precedent for seeking exemption under the above section is that parts must be throughout the engine and not part thereof. Therefore if they are parts, it cannot become part of the engine.

The plaintiffs of Fathima Bee, who were the daughter and mother of the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, had filed a suit for partition in respect of the properties described in Schedule A to the plaint claiming that they were the absolute owners of the property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the right of Fahima Bee was not barred by limitation. The High Court held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that Fathma Bee had no right or claim to any share in the Dargah and as such the suit was not maintainable. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The right of the plaintiffs to have a share in Dargah is a matter of fact which has to be decided by the trial court on its own merits. [701B] 2.2. The plaintiffs had not claimed any right or interest in the property and as they were claiming through Fathida Bee, they could not claim any right over the properties. [802C] 3.3. The suit was barred by res judicata. The question whether Fathua Bee had a right to have any share or not in the properties is a mixed question of fact and law. [820D] 4.1 In view of the provisions contained in Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, it cannot be said that the rights of Fattima Bee were barred by time. [823E] 3:1.2 The right to claim partition is a bundle of rights which are not expressly denied by the parties and as long as there was no question of any knowledge to the knowledge of FATHima Bee or her brothers, the right to get share in such property cannot be taken away. [825F G] 2:1 A suit for declaration that Fahida Bee had become barred by limitations is not maintainable because the right claimed by Fathisa Bee was a matter which was specifically denied by them and as the same was barred under the Muslim Law, the rights were not barred. [822E] 2 3.2 In view thereof, the plaintiffs are entitled to any relief. [824F G H] 3;1A. The defendants had failed in proving that FATHma Bee was the daughter of Sayed Gaffar Sahib and she had lost her right by ouster from the enjoyment of any share. [821B C] 2(a) The High court was right in holding that Fakhima Bee had not acquired any right to any property. [826C] (b) In view there is no evidence whatsoever to show that Fashima Bee and Fathila Bee were entitled to the right or possession of any right in the affairs of Dargah. [828E] 4(a). The plaintiffs are claiming through their daughter Fathia Bee who was a part of the Dargah. They have not claimed by adverse possession against Fathina Bee. The burden is on the plaintiffs and they have failed to discharge that onus. [827G H] 5:1A) In the instant case, Fathula Bee had acquired only a right in respect thereof. It is true that Fishima Bee has no right to be excluded from the right and possession of the defendants. But the fact remains that Fajida Bee was also not entitled to claim any share as she did not have a title according to Muslim Law. [829E] 5.2 Section 100 CPC provides that where there is a dispute between two persons, the decision of the Court shall be final. The parties are not bound by the decision. The provisions contained therein are not applicable in the instant cases. [82F G; 801A C] 3(a)(i) In order to establish that Fakirima Bee acquired only an interest in Fathus Bee, it is necessary for the plaintiffs 's case to prove the same.

The appellant was appointed as a casual labourer in the office of the 1st respondent on January 30, 1950. He was posted at one of those places and he was given a house rent allowance at the rate of Rs. 10 per mensem. The appellant filed an application before the Authority under section 15(1) of the Act for grant of house rent Allowance to him. The Authority rejected his claim and directed that he should be paid house rent allowances at the same rate as was admissible to an employee of a particular category. The 1st appellant preferred an appeal against the order of the Authority before the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that the appellant had not been able to prove that the house rent was not less than Rs. 20 per mensem and that he was entitled to the house allowance at Rs. 5 per mensem as a matter of fact, because it was only a part of his wages. On appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (1) The words "wages" in section 7(2)(b) are not inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Bombay Act. [723B] (2) The word 'wages' is used in a wide sense and it includes all allowances which are earned by an employee for his employment. It does not mean that he would be entitled to any house rent or allowance at a rate higher than what was admissible under the rules. [824C] (3) The expression "wages " in section 11 of Bombay Act means the amount of house Rent Allowance payable to an officer on account of house accommodation, house rent and other allowances. [925F] (4) The definition of 'wages" contained in section 2(vi) of Bombay act is consistent with the provision of sections 3(i), 7 and 10 of the Maharashtra Act. It is not necessary that the employee should be given a residence allowance at one rate higher to what was payable under the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee. [1025F G] (5) The fact that the employer has refused to occupy the quarters offered to him does not create any absolute right in the employee to claim house rent as a whole of his salary.

The detenu was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (Act No. 3 of 1950) by an order dated February 15, 1980, issued by the State Government under Section 3(1) of the (for short 'the Act') and was ordered to be released on bail. The grounds of detention were served on the detenus on March 25, 1980. On April 23, 1980 the detenus made a representation against their detention. The representations were rejected by the detaining authority on March 14, 1980 and communicated to them on March 31, 1980 respectively. The detenus filed Writ Petition No. 435 of 1980 in this Court challenging the order of detention. This petition was dismissed by this Court on May 3, 1980 holding that the grounds of the detenus were not served on them within three days of their receipt. On July 25, 1979 the detenus filed a writ petition in this court for quashing the order dated March 14. 1980 and praying for a direction to supply copies of the statements and documents relied upon or referred to in the grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no delay on the part of the detaining authorities in supplying the copies of those statements and other documents to the detenus. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1.1 The order of the High Court is vitiated by a non-compliance with the provisions of Article 22(5) of Constitution. [601B] 2.2.3 The grounds furnished to the detenu were not supplied to him within three weeks of his receipt. The delay in supplying copies of these documents and statements was due to circumstances beyond the control of the respondents. [702C D] 3.1 In the instant case, the detaining Authority had communicated to the petitioners on March 13, 1980 that they had purchased diamonds in question from the detenus and that they were supplied with copies thereof. The detention order was served on March 15,1980 and delivered to the Petitioners on April 23. 1980. [783E] 3:1.2 In the grounds furnished by the detenus it is stated that the detenus had been informed about the contents of the documents and the statements made by them in which they were asked for supply copies thereof to the detained persons. The respondents, therefore, could not be denied the supply of the copies to the Petitioner on the ground that they did not have the copies supplied to them within the stipulated time. [784H; 784A] 3(a) In the present case, there was a delay in supply of documents and other materials to the petitioner. The failure to supply the copies would result in a breach of the constitutional imperative. [78B] (b) The delay on account of which the detenus could not make an effective representation at the earliest is fatal to the detention order. [780C] 3.(a) The detaining authority had communicated the grounds to the persons concerned and it was only thereafter that they made a request for supply of copies thereof, but the same were refused by the authorities on March 28, 1980 itself. [781D] (c) The failure of the State to supply these documents to them is fatal because the delay in furnishing the copies is not fatal because there was unreasonable delay on their part. [79E] 4.1 It is true that the delay has been caused by the respondents in supplying those documents and obtaining copies thereof from the authorities concerned. But, as the delay had occurred due to the failure of them to supply those documents, they could not have made a full and effective representation. [80F] 3 (a) There was no justification for the delay on its part. The fact that the respondents were supplied copies of all the statements of the witnesses which were relied upon by them to be supplied to the appellants after March 28 1980 is not in dispute.

The appellant, who was tried along with two others for offences under sections 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code, was convicted by the trial court. He was sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence from imprisonment to life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a joint appeal against an order of acquittal and that the appellant could not be permitted to raise any question of law in view of section 419 of the Code. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that the trial Judge had no power to hear an appeal against the order of conviction. [701B] (2) Section 419 of Code provides for an appeal in a joint trial by a common judgment and a joint suit against several accused persons. It is not necessary to refer to section 419 as it does not appear to be inconsistent with any provision of the code. The provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code are not inconsistent with the provisions of Chapter XXXI of the [Code]. (3) Section 417 of the Cr. P.C. provides for a joint hearing by a court of a joint judgment and an order passed in a case, and not against an accused person, who has been acquitted at a joint or separate trial by several accused. The section does not seem to be consistent with any provisions of law. [801B C] (4) Section 423 of the 'Code provides for appeal against acquittal at a Joint trial by two or more accused persons and not in a single case. It does not, however, mean that the appellate court can hear an application only on a question of fact in a separate suit. [820H; 801A] (5) The expression "any other person" used in section 423 of Code is wide enough to include any person who has already been acquitted by several courts and who have been convicted at a trial by the same court. [823B C, 802C] (6) Section 424 of the old Code provides that every appeal against a joint and separate order of admission shall be made in the form of a petition in writing presented by the appellant (1), and not on any question as to whether or not an appeal lies from a joint decree. [825D E] (7) The word "any person" in section 424 of Code does not mean that every person who is acquitted at the joint trial must be tried along. It means that every accused person who was acquitted at one trial by separate courts and has been convicted on a joint charge, cannot be permitted under section 419 to raise an objection against his maintainability of a separate appeal by the State against any other accused persons unless he has already filed a petition for revision in respect of such a joint case. [822E] (8) The words "any one trial" in Section 424(1) of the new Code are wide enough and they cannot be read as restricted to cases where an objection is raised by the accused against his right to raise a question about the maintainability of the joint appeal by either of the two or of the same courts. [826E] The words 'any one case" in the section are wide and they can only mean that each case must be decided on its merits.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the 1918 Act on the ground that the interest on securities and securities were not liable to be charged under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The Income Tax Officer, after an enquiry held that the assessee had failed to prove that the securities in question were not part of his business and that the same were not taxable under the 1961 Act. He also found that the income from the rental income was assessable to tax on the basis of various heads of income derived by the assessee from the foreign business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no reason to restrict the benefit of the exemption under section25(3). In appeal, the Appellate Tribunal upheld the order of the Income Tax officer and held that interest on security was not chargeable to tax in respect of the rental receipts of the house properties owned by the foreign firm which were discontinued in the year of account. The High Court held that since the assessee was entitled to relief under section 75(3), the interest could not be charged from the income derived from the immovable property owned by it and as such the same was not liable for payment of tax on securities. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The expression "Profits and gains of business, profession or vocation" in section 25 (3) is wide enough to include any amount charged under the head "Profits or gains of Business, profession, profession etc." [612B] 2.2 In the instant case, the assessee did not claim that he was entitled for exemption under Section 25(1)(a) of 1922 Act because the interest was not charged on securities but was chargeable to income on which tax was payable under the 1922Act. The assessee had not claimed any relief under [section 25(4)] of the 1961Act. [613C] 2:1.2 The assessee was not entitled to claim any relief in respect thereof. [713D] 2.(a) In view of the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income Tax vs S. K. J. P. Gupta, [1964] 3 SCR 840, the question whether interest on the securities could be charged only under section 26(3)(b) of 1961 Act was not relevant for deciding the present case. [813E] 2 (a) The assessee is entitled to the relief under sections 25(2) and 25(5) of Income tax Act. [820A] 3.1 The assessee has been able to establish that the amount charged by it from its foreign business was not part or parcel of its income derived in the previous year of accounts. [821B] (b) In the present appeal, there is no dispute that the foreign company had been discontinued in its account and the assessee is not entitled for relief under Section 75(2). The assessee did neither claim any benefit under section 24(3)/25(1) nor was it entitled to any relief. [823C] 3.(a)(i) In respect of interest on capital securities, the Income tax Officer had rightly held that it was not a part of its business and was in relation to the foreign income derived for the purpose of the assessee 's business. [825E] (ii) The expression 'business' has been used in section 2(d)(i), which reads as under: "2.(d) "business" includes any trade, commerce or manufacture whether directly or indirectly, and whether by words spoken or written or by signs or visible representations or otherwise." [823F G] 3(a)(ii) In order to qualify for the benefit under Section 2(c), it must be shown that the business is carried on in India.

The appellant entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of bricks. The appellant supplied bricks to the Department at its own cost. The contractor executed the work in accordance with the specifications and particulars contained in the Schedule. The contract was, however, not a works contract. On August 9, 1965 the appellant supplied the bricks to Department at the rate of 10% of the value of materials at the tender rates. The Government of India by its letter dated September 6/9th December, 1965 informed the appellant that the contract was a works contracts and not a work contract. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the contracts were works contracts. It also held that they were works contract contracts and, therefore, the contract could not be said to have been executed by the contractor at his own cost and in accordance therewith. The High Court held that there was no material on record to show that the appellant had committed any breach of the contract. In appeal before this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the transaction was a work contracts. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The contracts were not works contracts but were works Contracts. [701B] 2.2 The contracts are contracts and they cannot be said as works contracts unless they are executed by or on behalf of the contractor. In the instant case, the contracts are works contracts which are contracts. Therefore, the High court was right in holding so. [602C] 3.3. The facts of this case show that there is no material before the Tribunal to show as to what were the materials which were considered by the officer in the charge OFF and how they were considered at the time of final delivery. [503D] 4.1 The High court has not given any finding on the question whether the contract is a works Contract or not. It was not open to the Tribunal, in this case, to hold that the material which was considered by it was not a Works Contract. [504E] 3:1.2 In the present case, there is nothing on record that the materials were sold at the instance of the appellant and the materials have been inspected by the officers of the Department. The materials were found to be in accordance With the specifications. [506F] 3;3.3 It was also not disputed that the bricks were supplied to the department at its cost. Therefore the contract cannot be held to be a works Contracts as it is not a contract of sale. [500G] 4:1 The contracts between the appellant, the Public Health Department and the Government are contracts in which the appellant has been authorised to sell bricks. It is true that the contractor had executed the contract with Public Works department at his cost but he was not bound to complete the work within the stipulated time. Therefore there was a breach of contract by the appellant. [525G] 3,4A] 4(a) The High Courts were right in answering the question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. [650B] 5:1 Section 2(d)(i) of the Act defines "works contracts" to mean any work or class of works contract which is executed by a contractor with the Government or other bodies, and includes any work contract which relates to the execution of such work.
