The word 'works contract' has been defined in section 2(j) as meaning any work which is completed by the Government, or other body, and include any work contracts which relates only to the completion of such works contract, but does not include any such work contracts as are executed either by the Contractor himself or by some person on behalf or by any person on his behalf. [600G] 5.2 Section 2 (j) defines "work" to include any kind of work done by a person on the premises of a contractor.

The petitioner who was a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution in the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir challenging the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on March 25, 1975. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the two Proclamations were not valid as they had been duly approved by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Speaker. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Proclamation dated March 25/26, 1975 was invalid because the Legislative Council of Jammu had not been constituted in accordance with the provisions of the Act 30 of 1976. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The validity of a Proclamation of emergency issued on the 3rd day of December, 1971 and the Proclamation issued on 26th June, 1975 cannot be questioned in this Court under Article 136 of the constitution. [601B] 2. The Proclamation of General Assembly dated March 26, 1975 is valid only if it was published in the official Gazette. It does not say that the Legislative assembly of Jammu State had been constituted by virtue of the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament and the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976. [701C] 3. The two Acts of 1976 and 30 of1976 were duly approved on March 26/26th June 1975 and they were duly published in official Gazette and therefore the Proclamation was valid only when it was issued by the Houses of both the Houses. [802D] 4. The Legislative Assembly had not yet been constituted. It is true that the Speaker had no power to issue a Proclamation under Article 356 of the Parliament. But the fact that he had been authorised to issue the Proclamation on March 27, 1975 does not mean that the said Proclamsations were duly authenticated by the House and the Houses were duly notified in the Official Gazette. [820E] 5. The fact that the Proclemations of Emergency were kept in force at the expiration of two months from the date of the resolution of the House would be sufficient to prove that the resolutions had been validly passed by the Parliament until they were approved by both the Speaker and the Chairman acting as President of India in the year 1977. [823E] 6. The question whether a Proclamation issued under Article 174(2) of the Government of Jammu And Kashmir could be held to be valid only on the expiry of two years from the day when the resolutions were passed by either House of Parliament or the Houses thereof, would not arise for consideration in this case because the two Acts had been approved by all the three Houses of the Legislature. [825E] 7. The second question is whether a proclamation issued under article 174(1) of Constitution could be validly issued when the Legislative Assemblies of Jammu& Kashmir and Ladakh were duly constituted. [826A D] 8. The power to make a Proclamation is not an inherent power but it is an inherent powers which can be exercised only if the resolutions are duly approved. [822E] 9. In the instant case, the two acts of emergency had been passed by all of them on March 28, 1975 and the two resolutions were duly passed by each of the Houses and they had not ceased to be in force thereafter at the end of the period for which the resolutions of both Houses were issued. [828B] 9 A. The first part of article 174 is a general power conferred on the House to make an order under that article. It cannot be said that the second part of the article is a special power conferred by the Constitution on the Houses concerned. [829C D] 10. The third question is, whether the two statutes of 1976 were duly sanctioned by both House of People ( Extension of Duration Act,1976) and 25th June 1978 when the Parliament passed the Proclamation under that section. [827E] 11.

The appellant was the owner of a public temple situated in the City of Madurai. The respondents were the owners of the said property and the appellant 's case was that the property belonged to the family of the appellant and therefore capable of valuation. The Trial Court held that the appellant had not proved that the private properties were the private property of the family and that it was not a public religious or charitable temple within the meaning of section 2(b) of Madras Act 19 of 195 1. The High Court, however, held that since the property was not an immovable property, the question whether the property is a public or a private temple would not arise at all. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that the properties were not private properties and that the respondents were not entitled to any relief under article 133(1)(a) and (b). [601 B] (2) The question whether a public trust is a private property or a public one does not arise for determination in this appeal. [602 C] (3) Under section 2 of Madras Public Trust Act, 195 1, the property shall be deemed to be an immovable properties within the definition of that term in section 2 (b), and if it is a trust created by a person who is not a member of a Hindu family, he would be entitled to the benefit of exemption from payment of fees. [063 C] The expression 'public trust' has been defined under section 2 sub section (1). It means a public charitable or religious institution which is a body corporate and includes a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. [63 D] (4) Under the Madras Public Trusts Act, it was open to the State Government to declare that any property of a private trust created for public purpose by a private person would be exempt from payment thereof if such property was an immovable or public temple within that term. The word 'public' has not been defined in the Madras Act, 19 of 1951. [64 E] (5) Under Section 2(c), it is open to a public institution to declare its property as a private one and the property which is capable of being valued would be exempted from payment. [65 F] (6) The word "public trust" has not necessarily been defined either in the Act or in the Trust Act. It is not necessary that the public trust should be a private or a religious institution. [66 G] (7) Under clause (a), it was permissible for a public authority to declare any property as an immovable and public temple, if such a declaration was made by him in his plaint and the case of the respondents was accepted by the Trial Court. [68 F] The High Courts were right in not holding that there was no question of valuation of the property under 0. 1,000 6126 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The question as to whether a private religious or public trust created under section 3(b), could be treated as an "public temple" within the ambit of section 3 (c) of the Tamil Nadu Public Trusts (Amendment) Act, 1955 was not open to challenge in this Court.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent 's factory at Calcutta. He was paid a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month and he was given cash allowance for the period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1957. The appellant claimed that he had been working as a Clerk in the establishment of the respondent on a monthly salary of about Rs. 5,000/-. The appellant contended that the re employment of the workmen was not proper and that the said payment was made by way of cash allowance. The Tribunal held that the appellant was entitled to cash allowance at the rate of Rs.. 10,500/- per annum for the entire period from March 31 1957 to March 30, 1958. The respondent ' s case was that the aforesaid amount had been paid in lieu of cash allowances and that it was not a cash allowance but a cash payment of Rs., 10,250/-. The Tribunal found that the respondent was entitled only to cash allowances at the rates prescribed by the Factories Act and that he was not entitled to any cash allowance as he was employed for the whole period from May 1, 1957 to June 31, 1958, and so, the Tribunal held in favour of the appellant. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance which was less than the wage structure devised for the employees of the company. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether a particular amount is payable by way o f cash allowance or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [701B] 2. The word 's pay' in the definition of wages means the basic pay which is paid to the employees for the work done by them. It does not include any other kind of remuneration. The definition of "wages" in the Factories act clearly shows that the payment of cash was made on the basis of a salary or allowance and so it was an implied condition of service. [801C] 3. The expression 's salary' is defined in the Act as follows: (i) " wages" means the pay which has been paid to an employee for the day he worked for the employer; (ii) "wages", in relation to a work done under a contract, includes all remuneration payable to an officer of the establishment or to any other person employed by him; and (iii) "s salary" is defined as follows : (i). " wages " means the amount paid to a workman for the labour of his employer; and "wages " in relation thereto", in the case of a work which is not performed under a written contract, the wages payable to such officer shall be the same as that paid to him by way Of cash allowance; (iii)(a) " Wages" means all remuneration paid to any workman for labour of the employer who has been employed for work done on a day or part thereof in accordance with the terms of the contract and includes all allowances which are payable to him under a decree or order of a Court or Tribunal or other authority. [820B] 4. The payment of salary is not a matter of right but it is a matter relating to employment. It is a question of fact whether the employer has made an express condition of his service and if so, whether he was bound to make such a provision for the benefit of the employee. [823C] 5. In the present case, the appellant had been making provision for payment of the salary in lieu thereof. The claim for cash allowance was not pressed by the appellant before the Tribunal nor was it urged that the same was an express provision for grant of cash Allowance. [825D] 6. The fact that the employer had made a provision to provide some cash allowance is not disputed.

The respondent, the Union of India, the Railway Administration, was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund Account in which he had obtained a money decree against Browne. The respondent, who was an employee of the Indian Railway Administration and was entitled to receive the amount standing to his credit in a Provident Fund account in a provident fund account in sterling. He was also entitled to interest on the amount lying with the Reserve Bank of India as the agent of the railway administration. On August 26, 1947, the respondent filed a suit against Brownere for recovery of money from him and for recovery thereof. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondent had not authorised the Reserve bank to receive payment of the amount in sterling and that the money remained with the Bank as the agents of the Railway administration. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondent was entitled under section 3 of the , Indian Contract Act to recover money from Browne on his behalf. [601B] (2) The High Court was right in holding that the amount which was due to the respondent as an agent of Browne had not been paid out of the Fund and that it was a security deposit. [702C] (3) The fact that the appellant had not made any payment to the ReserveBank of India for conversion of the money into sterling did not make any difference in this case because the respondent was not the agent or the Bank. [803D] (4) The liability of the respondent to pay the amount on his own behalf was not disputed by the appellant and, therefore, the High court was right that the attachment was not legal tender. [820E] (5) The order passed by the High 'Court directing attachment of the amounts standing to the credit in the Provident Fund Accounts in a pension account in which it was found that the Bank had failed to pay out of its fund and that there was no legal tender, is bad in law. [821F] (6) The Bank could not be said to have been authorised by the Reserve Banks to receive payments from Browner. [823A] (7) The payment of money on behalf of the appellant was not a legal tender but was made out of his fund and was liable to be returned to him. [825B] In the present case, the Bank did not send the amount to the Westminster Bank as an Agent of Browner for payment at the place where payment was required either under the law or under the rules. The Bank had no authority to receive any payment from Brownee.

The appellant, a workman, was appointed as a driver by the management of the respondent company on June 30, 1971. He was found guilty of misconduct and was dismissed from service with effect from July 1, 1972. The employer filed an appeal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal which allowed the appeal and set aside the order of dismissal. The appellant challenged the said order of the Tribunal in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the order passed by the Tribunal was not vitiated on account of any error apparent on the face of the record, because it had been made without jurisdiction and without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The order of termination is a colourable exercise of power vested in the management. It does not affect the merits of the case. [701B] 2.2. The Tribunal was right in holding that the termination was a colourable piece of victimisation or unfair labour practice and that it had lost confidence in the employee. [802C] 3.3. The question whether the order is mala fide or an act of victimisation, or an unfair labour practices, does not arise for consideration before this Court. [820D] 4.1 The Tribunal has held that there was no evidence to show that the employer had lost faith in the workman and that the same was a mere camouflage. [823E] 3:2. In view of the fact that the management had lost the confidence in its employee, it could not be said that the finding recorded by the Labour Court on this point is based on no evidence. [822F] 4:1.2 The Tribunal had rightly held that since the employer was efficient and had lost his confidence in him, it was not open to the management to proceed against the workman for misconducts or on othergrounds. [821E] 2:1 The order passed is a result of victimisation and unfair labour Practice. [825F] 3;2.3 In view thereof, the Tribunal has rightly held the termination as invalid. [824G] 4;2A] 2(a) The High court was right, in holding, that the appellant had lost its confidence in it. [826B] 3(b) The order is a mere device to cover up what was really an order of discharge simpliciter and the Tribunal could not go behind the form of the order because it was merely an order which did not amount to one of the grounds on which the order was based. [828C] 4(c) In the instant case, the appellant was appointed by the Management as a Cleaner in the respondent Company. He had been working as a cleaner in the factory and he was also employed as a helper. The management had not challenged the termination of his services on any ground whatsoever. [829E] 5:1 It is true that the Tribunal had held that it was a case of victimisation but the question whether or not the order terminating the service was a camouflage to coverup what was being done by the respondent, does no longer arise for determination in this appeal. [827A D] 2.(a) In view Of the fact, the termination is not a colourable act of management and it amounts to an unfair Labour practice. [853B] (b) It is well settled that the question as to whether or whether the termination has been a colourable device to take away the confidence of the employee in the company must be determined by the tribunal on its own merits. [852A D; 854 E] 3.(a)(i) The Tribunal, therefore, was right when it held that though the termination had been a motive for victimisation or an attempt to take advantage of the situation, it did not come within the purview of the definition of unfair labour ' as contained in s. 2(d). [853C D; 954 E F] 4.(a).

The State of Uttar Pradesh, through its Secretary, Medical Council of India, issued a notification dated 9.2.1988 under section 3(1) of the U.P. Re-organisation Act, 1986 (U.P., Act No. 1 of 1986), for the establishment of a new medical college in the State of U. P. and for the purpose of providing facilities to the victims of medical negligence. The notification was published on 9.3.1988. In the said notification, it was stated that the State Government had been pleased to establish a new Medical College at Moradabad Camp in Uttar Pradesh. It was further stated that there were no other medical colleges in U.S.P.; and that the facilities for such treatment were not available in the rural areas of U P. The State Government issued a Notification dated 9th March, 1988 under section 4(1)(a) of UPP Act No 1 of 1987. The petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 1148 of 1988 before the High Court challenging the notification and praying that the said writ petition be dismissed on the ground that the petitioners were not acting pursuant to and under the 255 authority of Government and that they had been deprived of their vision in theysis of the vision in their hospital. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the impugned notification was ultra vires the Constitution and directed the State to take appropriate action against those responsible for such mishap and illegal acts of the doctors who were not duly qualified by the Medical Council at the time of surgery. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State has been empowered under section 2(2) of Uttar pradesh Act No 3 of 1987 to establish an institution in a medical college for treatment of any disease or injury which may be caused by such mis-hap or illegal acts. [601B] 1.2 The State is not bound to take action against the persons who are responsible for the misha portition of the patients at the hospital. It is only if the State has taken a decision that the person who was in charge of the mis-home and the vision of the people at the Hospital should be restored to his position in the mortuary. [701C] 1.(a) The State cannot take action under section 5(1), (2) or (3) of Act No 2 of 1987 against persons who were responsible for mishacat ion of the patient at the hospitals. [802D] 1(b) The Medical Council, in its report dated 9 th March,1988, had recommended that the patients should be admitted to the hospital and that there was no other person who could be associated with the mishome or the destitute. [820E] 2.(a)(i) In view of the fact that the medical colleges at Moradabad were not functioning pursuant to the recommendations made by the sub committee of the Indian Medical Council and that it had been found that the health of the victims was not satisfactory, the State could not have taken action against them for such breach. [823E] 3.(a). The State can take action only if there is a violation of the provisions of section 5 (1) or section 5 of Act no 2 of1987. [825F] 4.(b) In the instant case, the Medical College was established in the year 1988 and the facilities were available to the patients who had operated upon at Moradabad camp for cataract on account of the disease. The medical colleges were not functional in the month of June, 1988. The Medical College could not be located in Lucknow because of the ill health of its employees. [822F] 5.(c) In order to establish that the doctors at Moradabad had operated at Moradabad and that their vision was about 380 and the eye camps for catastrophoric disorders were not in existence, the medical college at Moradabad was required to be located at Lucknow.

The appellant, a member of the Samiti, was elected to the Samiti by the then Chief Minister of Assam and he was appointed as a Byabasthapika and byabasthapanika. The appellant was elected as a member and by his election in 1984 he was elected by the Samiti from the Samiti. On the basis of the resolution passed by the Board under Section 3 of the Ordinance, the appellant filed an application before the Chief Minister praying for a direction to restore the Society back to its original position and to take over the management of the Rashtrabhas Prachar Samiti. The Chief Minister by his order dated 30.10.1984 declared that the appellant was entitled to continue as a part of the Committee and he would be restored back to the Society with effect from 1.10, 1984. The State Government by its order dated 15.12.1984 appointed the appellant as a full time member of Samiti and by virtue of the provisions of Section 3(ii) of the Act as it stood then in 1984. On 30.9.1984 the appellant submitted an application to the Chief Secretary for restoration of the Society to its place of management. The Government rejected the said application on the ground that the same was not maintainable because the appellant had no locus standi to file the writ petition and the same could not be entertained by the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution. On appeal, this Court held that the State Government had no right to continue the Society as a whole and it was only if the State was intending to restore its assets and properties of the society to its new place of administration that the Samiti should restore back to it. The Court also held that since the appellant did not challenge the constitutional validity of the ordinance, the writ Petition was not competent. In appeal by special leave, this court has directed that the Society be restored to its position and the State shall take over management of its affairs from the Board or the State as the case may be. The appellants have filed this Writ Petition challenging the legality of the notification issued under Section3 of the Assam Rashtrabh Prachar Samhi Adika and Karyapalika and the subsequent order dated 28.10..1984 passed by this Court in a writ petition filed by the appellant against the respondent No. 1, the State of Assam, the Board and the appellant respectively. The High Court has held that as the appellant is not a member or a member, the question of his locus standi does not arise. It was further held that if the appellant has any locus standi in the matter, he cannot be heard to say that he had no interest in the affairs of the said Samiti and therefore he cannot challenge the validity of this Act. The appeal by Special Leave is against the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The notification issued by the Government under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is a piece of legislation enacted by the Parliament and it is not open to the State Legislature to make any provision in that behalf. [701B] 2.2 The power conferred on the State Legislatures under Article 246(3) of Constitution is plenary in nature and has been given wide powers to legislate on matters enumerated in List I of Seventh Schedule. It is a well settled principle of law that the power of legislation can be exercised by the Legislature only if it is found that there is an apparent abuse of power or there is a manifest abuse of the power. [801C] 3.3 The power under Article 254(2) cannot be exercised in a manner which would amount to an abuse of powers. It must be exercised with great caution and circumspection. [820E] 4.1 In the instant case, the power conferred by the Act is not only arbitrary but also manifestly arbitrary. The power has been exercised in violation of the principles of natural justice.

The appellant, who was the daughter of Kamala Devi, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of her properties in the court of Subordinate Judge at Asansol. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the gift made by her was not valid and legal. The High Court held that the gifts were not valid as they were not made at the time of the marriage but were only a part of the estate of Ram Kishori Lal, and that the properties given to her by Sumitra Devi were not the properties of Kamala, and therefore, she could not get any larger estate than what she was entitled to. The appeal filed by the appellants against the decree of the trial court was dismissed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had committed a serious error in holding that there was no consideration whether Sumitra Devi was competent to make a gift at the date of the final settlement of the family negotiations at Deoghar, and since the gift was made long after the marriage, the same was not competent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The gift made in favour of Kamala is valid and valid in Hindu law. [801B] 2. The mere fact that the property given to Sumitra Devi by her husband at the marriage ceremony was a part and parcel of the joint family property for the benefit of the daughter and the son in law, does not make any difference whether she made a gift or not. [902C] 3. The fact that Kamala Devi had executed a deed of gift in favour on March 10, 1940, does no change because the gift is binding on her husband and the daughter. [1001D] 4. The property given by Sumitra to her husband was a Hindu widow governed by the Mitakshara law. It was not necessary for her to make any gift at that time. [092E] 5. The properties given by Kamala Devi were in fulfilment of the pre nuptial promise made by the daughter, and the gift in question was a valid one. [1101F] 6. The gifts were made after the death of Kamala. It is not necessary to make an express provision for giving any kind of gifts at that point of time. The deed of gifts does not contain any stipulation as to the payment of any sum by Sumitra, and it only says that the donee shall be entitled to a sum of Rs. 1,000/- per month from the date on which the gift becomes effective. [110G] 7. In view of the fact that there is no consideration, the gift could not have been made at that stage. [109H; 110A] 8. The position in law is well settled that a gift made after a marriage cannot be said to be valid unless it is made by a Hindu woman who has given a gift in fulfilment or fulfillment of the promise. [107B] 9. In the instant case, the gifts are not valid at the relevant time and they were only part of her estate. The condition that she would make a valid gift at any time cannot be held to be invalid unless it was made by an Hindu woman. [108A B] 10. The provisions of section 14 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which are in pari materia with section 14(1) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, have been substantially complied with.

The appellant, who was the candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) to the Haryana Legislative Assembly, filed an election petition in the Punjab and Haryana Legislative Council on the ground that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency wherein he had been elected. The appellant Bhagat Singh was also a candidate who had been nominated by the first respondent (Tej Singh). The appellant, however, contested the election petition contending that the allegations made against him were false and fabricated. He further contended that the election of the first Respondent (Teji Singh) was not in accordance with law and the High Court should have allowed his appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 is a special provision which provides for an appeal from an order of the Tribunal to the Supreme Court. The provisions of section 123(3) are not intended to prevent any person who has been nominated as a candidate at the election to any seat in Parliament or Legislative Assembly of a constituency where he has been elected as such. [701B] 1.2 Section 123 (4) provides that no person shall be qualified for election as a member of the Legislature of a Constituency unless he is, by virtue of his religion, a Hindu undivided family and has held office in any other State or Union Territory. The language of section 124(3)(a) is clear enough to indicate that the disqualification under section 123 (2) is not intended merely to prevent a person who had himself been nominated at the elections to any other seat in the Legislature. [801C] 1:1.3 In view of the provisions of Section 123, it is clear that the corrupt practices mentioned in the election petitions are not made out and the allegations against the appellant Bhagat singh were false. [820G] 2.1 The High Court was right in holding that the allegation against the first appellant Bhagat Ram was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [823B] 2:2.1 In view thereof, the High court was right to set aside the election on the sole ground of corrupt practices as contemplated by section 123. [825G] 1.(a) The High court had rightly held that the charges against the second appellant Bhagatram Singh were not proved and the Tribunal was right, in holding so, to hold that the charge against him was not established beyond reasonable doubts. [822A B] 2.(b) In view whereof, the election petitioner Bhagat Singh could not be declared as a duly elected candidate at any other place. [821B] 3.2 The High Courts were wrong in holding otherwise. [824E] 3.(a)(i) The allegations against Tej Singh and his supporters were vague and did not disclose any corrupt practice. [826A B C] (b) The allegation that the posters were circulated by the voters to the voters was false and manipulated. [828B C] 3(c) The charge of corrupt practice under section 100(2)(a)(ii) is also not proved. [827C] 4.(a). In view, therefore, the allegations are vague and do not disclose a corrupt practice as contemplated in section 123 of the Act. [829E] (d) The election petition was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [982F] 5.(a), (b)(i), (c) & (ii) In the instant case, the appellant had been duly elected as a Member of the Legislative Assembly and he had also been duly nominated by him. [976G] 6(a). The allegations made in the petition are vague. It is not necessary for the petitioner to prove that the poster were circulated to the electors.

The respondent was appointed as a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, who was then the Chief Minister. He was also the Chief Justice of the High Court. The respondent was the Chief Secretary of the State Government. On the basis of an order passed by the High court, he was transferred to the Punjab & Haryana High Court and he was posted as a Deputy Chief Minister in terms of section 19(1) of the Act. He filed a writ petition before the High Judge of the Punjab and Haryana High court challenging his transfer from Punjab &Haryana High Court to Punjab & Nagaland High Court on the ground that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to punish for contempt under Article 215 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under section 19 (1) as there was no exercise of jurisdiction by the high court in exercise of its jurisdiction to punishing for contempt. In appeal, the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court held that the order passed in exercise jurisdiction by a single judge of the Court was not correct and it did not exercise jurisdiction under Article 129 of the constitution. The Division Bench also held that there was nothing wrong in the High Curt holding that no writ could be issued against the respondent for contempt of court. In the appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that the impugned order passed on the basis that the Chief Ministers headed the Chief minister headed by him were not competent to punish the contemnor is erroneous and illegal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power under section 20(1)(a) of Act has been conferred on the High Power Committee constituted for the purpose. It does not confer any right of appeal on the appellant against any decision or order passed under section 18 of the act. [775B] 2. The jurisdiction to try a contempt is conferred on a court only if there are two parties, namely, the Chief Secretaries and the Chief Justices of the States concerned. In other words, the High power Committee constituted by it has no jurisdiction over the contempt proceedings. [77C D] 3.1. It is true that the power under Article 216 of the Code to punish a contemnor for contempt is not conferred on any court but it must be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only two parties and one party, namely the ChiefSecretary and the Secretary. The exercise of such jurisdiction by either the High Commission or the Chief Election Commissioner does not involve any exercise of power or jurisdiction by any other authority. [78E] 3:1. In view of the provisions contained in section 19 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, it is clear that the jurisdiction to deal with contempt is vested only when there are both parties and if there is no exercise or jurisdiction of the court, the same cannot be exercised by any person other than the Chief secretary. [79F] 3(ii) The power conferred on High Court under section 21 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not an absolute one but it is a discretionary power which can be exercised only in exceptional circumstances and for good reasons. It may also be exercised in exceptional cases where there are no exercise and jurisdiction of any other court. [80F] 4.2 The power to punish contempt is given to the High Commissioner under section 22 of the Indian Penal Code. The same cannot, therefore, be exercised either by a person other then the State or by any officer subordinate to him. [81G] 3.(ii) In view thereof, the appeal is incompetent and it is not maintainable. [82A D] 4(iii) The High court has committed an error in holding that there were circumstances to indicate that the appellant was guilty of contempt of Court. [85E] 5.3.1 The High Power committee constituted for this purpose had no power or authority to punish any contemnor under section 23 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. He filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that he had not paid or tendered to the lessor at the hearing of the suit, as required by section 111(g) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') as required under section 111 (g) and (h) of that Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to protection against forfeiture for non payment of rent under section 112(g). On appeal by the respondent, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions as to notice in writing as to a lease were not applicable in all cases but were only procedural and technical rule introduced in 1929 and therefore the principle of equity is applicable in such cases. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language used in section 111 of the Act is clear and unambiguous. It does not mean that the legislature intended to confer a right on the lessor to terminate the lease by giving notice in advance of the intention to determine the lease. [723C] 2. The words "shall be given" are very wide and they do not mean merely a formal or informal one. In the case of a tenant, he is bound to give notice in the prescribed form to the landlord for determination of the lease and it does not imply that the lessor has no discretion in the matter. [823D] 3. The word "shall" used in the section means "may". It does mean that if the intention of the legislature was clear, the court would have jurisdiction to grant relief against forfeiture. [924F] 4. The expression "shall 'shall ' is not defined in the Act but it is a rule of law and equity. In England, the word "may" has been used in a sense which means that the intention must be expressed by the legislature. It is well settled that the words "may ' are to be given effect to" have been used to convey the meaning of the word 'shall'. [925F] 5. The rule enunciated in section 112 (g), as amended by the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947, is not based upon any principle of justice, equity and good conscience. It only means that if there was a forfeiture for breach of landlord 's title, a notice in regard to the intention should be given. [1025F G] 6. The phrase "shall "may "shall have" has no meaning in section 114(g), and it is not necessary that the rule enunciated by the Privy Council in the case before it was amended by this Court in the year 1929, should be held to govern even agricultural leases made prior to 1st April, 1930, when the legislature had enacted the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act. [1125F H] 7. The principle of law is applicable to a tenancy which is not governed by the English law but it has no application in India. [1226A C] 8. In view of the provisions contained in section 113(g)(i) of Bombay Rent Act, the lease was determined under section III (g). The lease was thus determined on 1st May, 1930 and the lease had been determined on that date. [1325F D] 9. The lease is not a lease but it was a statutory recognition of principle of fairness and equity in justice, good conscience and good mind. [1426E] 10. In order to be entitled to the protection against eviction under section 114 (g)(ii) of Act, it must be shown that the tenant had been given notice in accordance with section 111 and had not complied with the provisions of section 111. The landlord ' has a right to terminate his tenancy by giving him one month's notice or pay rent for three months.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent No.2 in the year 1969 and he was dismissed from service on 30th June, 1970. He filed an appeal against his dismissal before the High Court which was allowed by the learned Single Judge of the High court. The Division Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court held that the order of dismissal passed by the Arbitrator was illegal and void and set aside the same. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of guilt recorded against him was not based on any evidence and therefore, the learned single Judge had no jurisdiction to interfere with the punishment imposed upon him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the learned Arbitrator is vitiated by mis-appreciation of fact and law. [901B] 2. The High Court has rightly held that there was no justification for interfering with the findings recorded against the appellant. [093C] 3. The finding of misconduct against the respondent was based on surmises and conjectures and therefore it was not open to the learned Judge to interfere in the matter. [1026F] 4. The learned single judge had rightly held the respondent guilty of misconduct and dismissed the writ petition. [1125G] 5. The question whether the findings of guilt were perverse or not is a pure question of fact which has to be determined on the evidence adduced before the Arbitrator. [1105B] 6. The award passed by him was based upon the finding that the respondent had committed misconduct and therefore he was guilty of mis-conduct. [109G] 7. The findings recorded by the arbitrator were based on conjectures and surmises and, therefore, it was rightly set aside by the High Curt. [108A] 8. The fact that the appellant was dismissed in respect of a charge which had been proved against him is not a ground for setting aside the order passed by an Arbitrator. It is well settled that if the findings are based on no evidence and the same are perverse or contrary to law, the High Courts would not interfere with such finding. [107C] 9. The respondent was dismissed on the ground of misconduct. He had been found guilty of the misconduct and he had been awarded a punishment of dismissal from service. [111D] 10. In view of the fact that there is no evidence to show that the findings were perverse, the only ground on which the inquiry was held to be invalid by the respondent is that the enquiry was not vitiated by any mis-reading or inciting the strike and all the respondents were found guilty.

The appellant, who was a tenant holding land less than the ceiling area, had executed a deed surrendering his leasehold right to the landlord on or after the 11th day of April, 1957. The appellant, being a tenant in respect of the land held by him, had filed an application under section 6 of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 for restoration of possession of the said land to the tenant. The application was rejected by the Assistant Collector on the ground that the landlord had not surrendered his leasehold rights to the appellant before the commencement of the Act and therefore, he could not be deemed to be a tenant under section 5(2)(a) of the Amendment Act, 1968. The appeal filed by the appellant against the order of the Assistant Commissioner was dismissed by the Appellate Authority on the same ground. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 6 were not applicable to the case and that the appellant had no right over the land as he had already surrendered his lease hold rights in respect thereof. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Transfer of Property Act are applicable to cases where a person has been in occupation of any land on or before the 11 th day of May, 1957 and was cultivating it at the nilam after the 10th day Of April, 1956. [601B] 2. The expression 'tenant' in section 6(2) of Kerala Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1970 is not defined in that Act but has been defined in section 3(1)(a). The definition of 'tenant" in section 2(i) of that Act includes a person who was in occupation on or prior the 11 day of 4th April, 1955. [701C] 3. The word 'tenant " in section 5 (2)(b) of Act is not used in any law and it does not include a tenant who has been cultivating land on the 11 nd day of4th April 1957. [802D] 4. The words 'landlord ' in section 7(2), are not applicable in the case where a landlord had already transferred possession of his leasehold interest to the Government before the 10 th day Of May, 1956 and was in possession of such land on that date. [820E] 5. In view of the provisions contained in section 4(1) (a) read with section 6 (2), the landlord could not have been deemed to have surrendered his tenancy right to him under section 7 (2). [801F] 6. The tenant holding the land less in extent than ceiling area was entitled to continue in possession even after the commencement Of the Act. [823A D] 7. The proviso to section 6 is applicable only if the landlord has already transferred the leasehold rights of the landlord before the date of publication of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms(Amendment) Bill, 1968, in respect whereof a notice had been issued by the court and the tenant holding such land was in arrears of rent. [825E] 8. The language used in section 9(2A) is not applicable where a tenant has already surrendered the leasehold right in respect thereto. [826F] 9. In order to appreciate the contention that the proviso to Section 6(1), which is applicable to a case where the landlord was in actual possession of any part of the property on or from the 11 date of commencement of this Act, it would be necessary for the court to consider whether the tenant had surrendered his right to such landlord before 1st April, 1958. [827G] 9 A. The Explanation to section 7 is applicable where the tenant has not surrendered the lease hold right in any part on or thereafter. [828B] 10.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21st October, 1968. He had been convicted under Section 135(1)(ii) of the Act and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000/. The appellant appealed to the Collector of Central Excise, Bombay, who confirmed the order of confiscation but dismissed his appeal. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the goods were not smuggled goods and, therefore, the appellant was liable to be penalised under Section 112(a) of Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had been falsely implicated in the case because he had no knowledge about the goods being smuggled into India. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 111(d) of Customs Act are not applicable to cases where the goods have been seized under the Act. [701B] 2. The burden of proving that the person from whom the goods are seized had a knowledge about their origin and recent import was on the appellant is on him. He has failed to discharge his onus. [602C] 3. The onus of proof is on the prosecution to prove that the articles were smuggled into the country without any reasonable excuse. In the instant case, the burden of proof was not discharged by the prosecution. [613D] 4. The goods in question were admittedly seized from the appellant and the appellant could not establish that he had knowledge about them when they came from or when the goods came from. [502E] 5. The fact that the gold was recovered from the possession of a person who is found to be in possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually were, would not make the prosecution case bad. [511G] 6. In view of the provisions of section 112(b) of act, it must be held that there was no evidence to show that the seized articles were not imported into India and that they were smuggled goods. [452H; 452A] 7. The mere possession by the accused of such articles at the time when they were found in unopened boxes on which they were seized from his custody would not enable the prosecution, if it was proved that the same were smuggled or imported into the Country without any excuse. [451B] 8. In this case, there is no evidence that the appellants had been in possession for a long time when the articles came from and after the goods had been brought into India by them. The prosecution has not established that the article was actually imported or brought into the State of Bombay. [454A B] 9. The facts are not similar to those in the present case. It is true that the contraband goods were seized under a valid licence issued by the Central Government and the same had been used for the purpose of carrying out the business of manufacture and sale of gold. But, it cannot be said that the prosecution has failed in proving that they had been guilty of any offence punishable under Section 111 (d) or 112(e). [452B] 9 A.

The appellant, a registered firm, was formed in pursuance of a Charter from the Durbar. The Association was constituted on June 26, 1946 and it was registered as a Company under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The appellants were members of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for accounts of a dissolved firm. The appellant filed a suit against the Association for accounts and for accounts. The suits were dismissed by the trial court on June 27, 1946. The appeal to this Court was allowed by the High Court on July 11, 1947. In the meantime, the appellants applied to the High court for an order that the accounts of the dissolved firm be made available to them. The application was rejected by the Trial Court and the suit was dismissed. On appeal to the Supreme Court, HELD: (1) The provisions of section 69(3)(a) of the Rewa States Companies Act are not applicable to the present case. [601B] (2) The High Court has erred in holding that the appellants were entitled to a decree for accounts under section 69 of the said Act. [702C F] (3) The suit was not maintainable because the appellants had not filed any suit against them and, therefore, the suits were not maintainable. [803G] (4) The mere fact that the suits had been filed by one member of an unlawful association which is a legal Association does not make the suits maintainable. The question whether the suits are barred by section 69 (3)(b) of that Act or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In this case, the suit for accounts was not filed by the appellants before the Trial court but was filed by another member of the association which had been dissolved in February 1948. [903G H] (5) The suits are not barred by sections 69(2)(a), 69(1)(b). The question is whether the suit is maintainable because section 69 does not provide for a decree to be passed on the basis of the allegations made in the plaint or it is a suit which is not barred under section 4(2) of Act 1935. [1003G; 1004A] (6) The cause of action for filing suits against the appellants was the same as that of the earlier firm and, consequently, the trial Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. [1105B] In the present appeal, the question whether a suit is barred by limitation has been raised on the ground of violation of section 4 (2). The High court has erred, in holding, that the suit filed by respondent No. 1 was not barred from the date of registration as a company under the Bhopal State Companies act and, accordingly, the plaint was liable to be dismissed.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under sections 120B, 420 and 468 of the Indian Penal Code. The learned Magistrate took cognizance of the offence on the basis that the complaint was not filed within the period prescribed by section 210(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court quashed the proceedings on the ground that the allegations made in the complaint were not sufficient to constitute an offence under section 9(1). In appeal, this Court held that the provisions of sections 210(2), 420 and 471 of the Penal Code did not apply to the case as it was a case where the acts alleged to have been committed by the respondents were punishable as contempt under the Indian penal Code. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The complaint filed by the respondent against the appellants was not maintainable in law. [901 A] 2.1 Section 210(3) of Cr.P.C. provides that no Court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under the Act except upon a report in writing made by an officer mentioned in sub section (2). The complaint is to be filed within six months from the date on which the offence was alleged to constitute such offence. [1001 B] 2:1 Section 209(3)(a) of Code of Civil Procedure provides that where any act alleged to constitutes a contempt of court is an offence punishable as aforesaid, it shall not be competent for any Court to take cognizance thereof if it is committed in respect of the same offence. The expression "any offence" used in section 210 (1) read with section 50(l) of Criminal P.C., does not mean that the offences mentioned therein are not part of the offences specified in the said sub section. [1101 C] 2.(a) In view of the provisions contained in sections 210 and 471, it is clear that the offence under the Penal code is an act which constitutes a criminal contempt of Court. [110 D] 3.1 The expression 'any offence' used in sec. 210(l)(a), as interpreted by this Court in Bathina Ramakrishna Reddy vs State of Madras, AIR 1964 SC 1026, would mean that there must be an offence mentioned therein and not merely the same. [111 A B] (b) In the instant case, the complaint filed against the respondents was not a complaint under section 210 of the Cr. P. C. The Magistrate took into consideration all the relevant facts and circumstances and came to the conclusion that the ingredients of an offence were not made out in the present case. [112 A B D] (c) In regard to the second ground on which cognizance of an offences is taken by a Magistrate taking cognizance of a complaint, it was open to the High Court to exercise its powers under section 482 of the Criminal P C.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court for offences under Sec. 441(1) of the Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He filed an appeal before the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the appellant had not been released on bail, but he was in confinement. In appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) The appellant was a poor person and was convicted under Secs. 441 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence punishable under Sec.(1)(b) of that Act; (ii) the appellant was not released on his own bond without sureties, and (iii) the magistrate had no jurisdiction to release him on his personal bond without surety. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of the court to release a person on bail is not limited to cases where the accused has been convicted by a competent court for an offence under Sec(1)(a) or (b) or Sec.(2) of Sec.(3) of Chapter IV of the Penal Code. [419C] 2. The discretion to release on his bond is not confined to cases in which the conviction is based and the power of release on bail does not flee justice, but extends to cases of imprisonment for a term which may be less than two years. [520E] 3. The Court has no jurisdiction under Sec.- 389(1), to release an accused on his private bond without any sureties. [621F] 4. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 437(3) and (4) of Cr.P.C. [722G] 5. In view of the fact that the High court has no power under Sec- 389(2), it cannot be said that the discretion to grant bail is confined only to cases which are not relevant considerations, but only to those cases where a person is in confinement and that he is in custody. [321B] 6. The object of granting bail is to enable the accused to secure his release on such bond as may be reasonable. It cannot be denied that the accused is entitled for bail under Sectiss. 441 (1) and(2). [322C] 7. In the instant case, the appellant has been in confinement since he was not in custody at the time of commission of the offence. He was released on probation by the court after his release from jail. The order of the High Judge is set aside. The appeal is allowed.

The assessee, a registered firm, was carrying on business in the name of 'Castle Mills' at Bombay. The assessee had been assessed to income tax under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not liable to be included in the assessment of the assessee for the year 1951 52, 'Cessle Mills ' and that the Appellate Assistant commissioner had erred in holding that the business of the firm was not a separate entity. The High Court on appeal by special leave reversed the order of the Tribunal and held that it was not open to the Appellate Tribunal to call upon the Tribunal to state its case and refer it to the High Court for a decision. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court had erred both in holding the business as 'Cartle Mills'. [701B] 2.2 The High Courts have committed an error of law in not considering the question whether the business was separate entity or not. In the present case, the Appellate Commissioner has held that there was no material on which it could be said that the two businesses were separate entities and that they were separate. [702C] 2:1 The Appellate Tribunal had erred by holding that there is a double presumption in favour of the view taken by the Appellate Authority that the firm 's name was not included in its assessment of income at Bombay but was only assessed at Bombay in the status of a registered company. [601D] 2.(a) The High Income tax Officer, Special Circle, Amritsar, had jurisdiction to call for and examine the record of any proceeding under section 66(1) of the Act. [802E] (b) The Appellate Authority had no jurisdiction to direct the Tribunal or to state a case on the basis of any other material on the record. [820G] 2(a) In the instant case, there was nothing on which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner could have come to the conclusion that the 'Captle Mills were separate entity and that it had earned income. The finding of the Appellate Asst. Commissioner that the "Castles" were separate is not correct. [823A] 3.(b) In view of the fact that the Income tax officer had jurisdiction under section 16C(1)(a), the Appellate Deputy Commissioner was justified in holding against the assessee. [825E] 4.2 It is well settled that the High court has no power to direct a Tribunal or the Tribunal, as the case may be, to state 's finding of fact on any other relevant matters. [826C] 3(a)(i) The expression "any other material" in section 16B(1), must be construed in the context of the facts and circumstances of each case. [827A] (ii) The word "any" in the section must be interpreted in the light of other relevant factors on which its conclusion is founded and ignores other relevant materials on which such a conclusion is based. [828C] 4(a). In the context, it would not be open to an Appellate Assistant Commission to call the assessee 's case for a reference under section 26A(1). [826D] (iii) The words "any material" used in section 15B(2) are very wide and they must be read as comprehending only such material which is relevant for the purpose of determining whether or not it is relevant. [829E] 5.(a)(b) It is true that the word 'any' in section 14B(3) has to be construed strictly, but it cannot be so interpreted as to mean that the Tribunal must have jurisdiction to decide all questions of fact which are relevant for determining whether a question of law does or does not arise out of the order. [822E] 6.(a).

The appellant, a Minister in the Irrigation Department of Punjab Government, was appointed as a Secretary of the Department of Irrigation on January 29, 1974. He was also appointed as an Engineer on probation for a period of two years. On February 18, 1975, he was confirmed in the service by the Secretary of Irrigation Department. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Minister dated February 18 1975 and praying that the Minister be impleaded as a party to the petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on March 19, 1975. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions because the Minister concerned had been appointed as the Minister in charge of Irrigation department of Punjab. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The Minister is a person who has been appointed by the Government and he is not a party in the petition filed by him. He is an officer of the Government. [801B] 2.2. In view of the fact that the appellant had been working as an Executive Engineer in the Department, it was not open to him to file his personal affidavit in regard to the allegations made against the Minister. [902C] 3.1 The High court was right in holding that the allegation made by the Minister against the appellant was not a part of the petition and that the Secretary had acted as an agent of the State Government. He could not have filed his personal affidavits in regard thereto. [1001D] 2:1.2 In view thereof, the High Curt was right to dismiss the writ appeal. [1102E] 3:1 The Minister concerned was a party and he was bound by the directions given by the High cate General for the State of Punjab in regard t o the allegations contained in the amended petition. [110G] 2.(a) In view, of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not possible to hold that the allegations in the writ peti tion were not correct or false. [100H; 101A B] (b) The Minister was a necessary party and as such he could not file his affidavit in respect thereof. [101B C] 2(a) The High Cate General of Punjab had filed an affidavit in reply to the writ application. He had also filed an additional affidavit in support of his personal counter affidavit. In the reply to this additional affidavit, it has been stated that the Ministers were not necessary party. [102G] 3.(b) It is true that the Governor was a statutory authority and he could have exercised his powers under Article 166(4) of the Constitution of India. But in view of Section 5 of the Punjab Public Services (Reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes) Act, 1976, it cannot be said that the State had any right to make an application to the Minister for making a representation against the order made by him on February 18. 1975.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. He filed an application under section 259 of the Act for recovery of arrears of rent and other payments due to him on account of arrears payable by him in respect of the land or buildings upon the ground that it was not liable to be recovered under any express provision of the Punjab Municipal Act (III of 1911) which authorised the Board to recover all arrears of taxes, water rate, fee or any other amount. The respondent filed a suit for recovery against the appellant on the ground inter alia that he had been paying rent and for the time being in arrears of land and buildings on the basis of the lease in his favour. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was not entitled to recover the arrears of tax, water rates, rent or any amount recoverable under any other provisions of the act. The High Court held that the appellant had been able to prove that he was liable to pay the arrears and that the Board was not bound by the terms of the contract between him and the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High Court had no jurisdiction to direct recovery of the amount due under any specific provision of law. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the Magistrate directing recovery of rent is not a decree within the meaning of section 259(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to get the arrears from the Board as rent or other payment. [701B] 2. The words "claimable" in section 259 have been used in the sense that it is only an amount which can be recovered by a committee under the Act or the rules made thereunder. [802C] 3. The word 'claimable' has not been defined in the Act and, as such, the liability of the Board is not confined to the rent payable on account thereof. [820D] 4. The expression "claimsable" means any amount which is due to the Board under the provisions of this Act or rules made there under. [823E] 5. In the instant case, the respondent had been in arrears from January 7, 1960 till February 7, 1961 and, thereafter, he was paying rent for the period from January 9, 1960 to March 31, 1962. The appellant had not claimed any amount as arrears of water rate or other payments. [825E] 6. In view of the provisions contained in section 260(1)(a) of Punjab Municipal Corporation Act (IV of 1911), the respondent could not recover the rent due on account whereof he was required to pay rent for a period from February 7. 1960 till March 31. 1962. [826B] 7. The payment of arrears and other amounts by the Board in respect thereof is not an amount recoverable as arrears under any general provisions of law but only under the rules framed thereunder. It is, therefore. clear that the liability to pay rents on land and building was not a claimable under the act or the Rules made thereunder and, consequently, the High court had no power to direct the recovery of such rent. [827E] 8. The fact that the rent was payable by the respondent in respect whereof the appellant claimed arrears of electricity tax is not disputed. It cannot be said that the amount recoverable from the appellant under any special provisions of section 260 of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 was not payable by it to the respondent as rent. The question whether the respondent is entitled to recovery of any amount from the owner or the occupier of the property as rent is a matter which can only be recovered on an application to summary proceeding as provided in the rules and the Land Administration Rules, 1937. [828E] 9. In this case, it was admitted that the arrears were payable by respondent under the Punjab Public Premises (Eviction) Act, 1950. The amount recoverable was not disputed but was claimed by the appellant as arrears.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman in the area of his business situated at Bikaner. He was appointed for the purpose of canvassing and promoting the sale of the product of the company in any particular area or in the areas of his operations. The appellant was employed for canvassing and promotion in the said area. On the basis of this appointment he was transferred to the place of his work. In the year 1973, the appellant was engaged as a Section salesman for the purposes of procuring orders for sale of his product. He had been appointed for certain number of districts and in the meantime, he was also employed for selling the products of the Company in any other area or for purchasing the same from the various dealers appointed by the company. The management after considering the evidence produced before it found that the appellant had been working for canvassing salesmen for the company and that he was required to supervise the work of the local salesmen. On these facts, the Labour Court held that the termination of the appellant from service was illegal and directed his reinstatement with full back wages. The appeal filed by the appellant against this order was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the management that the finding recorded by the Labour court that the services of the respondent company were not employees under the Act was erroneous and that the Labour Judge had committed an error in holding that the respondent was a workman. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding, that the order of termination of service was bad as it was contrary to the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act. [701B] 2.1 The appellant is not a "workman" within the meaning of the expression 's employment under the Industrial Dispute Act. He is not an employee under the company but is a "employee". [702C] 2:1.2 It is true that the word "employment" in Section 2(9) of the Act means any employment which is made available to an employee for wages, whether paid or not, and includes any employment on behalf or for remuneration. But it does not mean that the employment must be for remuneration or otherwise. [602D] 3.2 The word "wages" in the context of Section 2 (9) means any remuneration which is paid by way of salary to an officer or servant employed for wages. It does not include remuneration for work done by a person other than his employer. [76E] 3:1 The word 'wages' in the definition of workman under the [Industrial Disputes Act, 1947], includes remuneration for services rendered by a contractor for doing any work which is incidental to his main work of canvassing or promoting the salesmen employed for sale and also includes remuneration paid for work performed by a servant other than himself. [77F] 3;2.3 The word used in Section II(9)(a) of Industrial Disputes Ac t, 1947 means that the person employed for the production of goods for sale is an employee within the definition. It is not necessary to refer to the definition under the said Act because it does cover remuneration paid by a workman for work which was incidental to the main work. [78F] 4.1.4 The word employed in SectionII(9), as it stood in the year 1898, means that person employed in any industry or business of manufacture or sale of goods and also include remuneration paid to an agent for work in his establishment. It includes remuneration payable to a contractor who is engaged in the production or manufacture of goods. [79F] 2(a) The word must be given its ordinary meaning. It must mean that person who is employed for carrying on any industry, business or trade of manufacture and also the word must include remuneration which are paid by him for work incidental to such industry, trade of manufacturing or sale.

The appellant Company was a Government lessee in respect of the land in question. The State Government had granted the lease to the Company for a period of five years commencing from 1.10.1977 and ending with 31.3.1978. The Company had been holding the land as a lessee under section 181 of the Madhya Bharat Act No. 66 of 1950. On or about 7.4.1979, the State Government issued an order for eviction of the Company from the land on which the Company was holding the same in terms of the original lease granted by the State. The appellant Company filed an application before the Additional Collector under section 182 of the Code praying that the Additional Commissioner be directed to decide the application within a period specified therein. The Additional Collector, however, rejected the application and confirmed the order of eviction. On appeal, the High Court held that the Company had not become an ordinary tenant in respect thereof and, therefore, the Additional Collectors were justified in holding that the land was not an ordinary lease. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has committed a serious error in holding the order passed by the Additional collector as illegal and without jurisdiction. [701B] 2.2 The High court had erred in holding against the Company that the appellant Company had become an ' ordinary tenant under section 183 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No.66 of 1950) and that the order for ejectment passed by Additional Collector was not correct. [801C] 3.1 In view of the provisions contained in section 182(2)(i), the Company is entitled to hold land as an ordinary lessee under Section 181 of M. P. Land revenue and Tenancy act, Sampat 2007 (Rules No. 1) and the Company cannot be held to be a Government tenant within the meaning of the said Act. [820H] 3:1 The Company was not a Government lessees within the definition of the word 'land" in section 2(i) of the Act No 66 of 1956. [823B] 3,2A] 3.(a) In view thereof, the Company has been holding land as lessee under the original Lease granted by State Government or to whom a right to occupy land as per the original leased out to it. [822C] (b) The Company is not a 'State Government lessee within the defined meaning of section 2 (i) and therefore, it had never become an " ordinary tenant" in respect whereof the Company could be held under the old lease granted to it by State government or to which a right was granted by that Government. [821B] 4.2 In view Of the provisions of section 182, the company is not entitled to continue as a Government Lessee within the term of the lease granted in its favour. [825C] 5.3 The Company has no right to hold the land under the new lease granted on the basis of the fresh terms agreed upon between the parties. [824D] 4.(a)(i) The company was not entitled for any protection under section 197 of the Cr.Pc. as it had not been holding over under the erstwhile lease granted under section 178 of the code.

The State Government of the United State of Travancore, by notification dated July 1, 1949, declared that the provisions of Ch. IV of the principal Act were applicable to the holders of land comprised therein and to vest in the Government under any law for the time being in force, subject to the provisions relating to acquisition of such land. The appellant was a holder of land in an estate in an Estate in an Indian State. On July 1. 1949, the appellant filed a suit against the State Government for a declaration that the Act was not applicable to him under any other law for time being In the suit, the plaintiff prayed for a decree for possession of the land comprised in his holding and also for mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant was entitled to compensation at a rate which could be determined and given as a measure of compensation. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The provisions of the Act were not applicable in respect of acquisition of land under any existing law for a period prior to July 1., 1949. [701 A] (2) The power to acquire land under section 1(3) of the Travancore Act was exercisable only if the law relating to the acquisition of the said land was not enacted by a notification under section 45 of the Indian Land Reforms Act, 1950. [802 B] (3) The words "any person" in section 1 (3), which are not applicable, would mean that the State has no power to make any provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land is held by a person under his personal cultivation of the holder, compensation shall not be less than the market value thereof. [820 C] (4) The word "any" in the section means "any land held by an individual or body corporate or association or body of individuals whether incorporated or not". It would mean "any other land held jointly by a company or body or individuals, whether incorporated and not, which is owned or controlled by the Government." [820 D] (5) The expression "person" in article 31(2) means any person who has been in continuous possession of any land comprised within the ceiling limit applicable to them under any such law for that time being. [821 E] (6) The notification issued under section I(3), by the Central Government, was not a law in force at the time when the Act came into force and the power to bring into force the provisions thereof was not conferred on the State.

The widow of her husband 's estate was in possession of the limited interest of a Hindu widow. The widow had acquired by a gift from her husband, the widow and she was not under any legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. In view of the provisions of section 5(1)(a) of the Madras Estates Land (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, the right of a widow to receive the property on the death of her father was extinguished by her subsequent alienations made by her. The Hindu widow had no legal or valid obligation to pay the full value of the estate in lieu of her maintenance. She was not entitled to any protection under section 5 (1)(b) of that Act, and she could not have claimed any right on the basis of a surrender made by the widow. In the present case, the question whether the widow had become absolute owner of the property after the death or whether she was under no legal obligation to give her consent to the surrender was a matter which was decided in favour of the widow by the Madras High Court. The Full Bench held that the widow could not claim any right to receive any compensation on the ground that she was a widow and, therefore, she had acquired a limited interest in the property during the life time of her deceased husband. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision in [Sreeramu vs Devaraya] (1) was not applicable to the facts of the present cases because the widow was not a widow but had acquired an absolute interest in her estate and, as such, she could only claim any protection against her death. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The right of the Hindu widow to get the property by surrender is a right which has accrued to her husband on the date of surrender. [901F] 2.1 The right to get compensation on account of surrender is not an incident of surrender but an act of self effacement by the wife. It is only when she becomes entitled to receive such compensation that the right to recover possession of property during her life time can be extinguished and, in the absence of any legal obligation under which she could have obtained the properties. [1001F G] 2:1. The position of a person who has acquired an interest by adverse possession is not a matter of law but an incident or fraud or collusion that might arise, when the widow herself is not capable of disputing her own grant and thereby claiming any right in respect of the enhanced property. [1101G] 2(a) In the instant case, there was no legal and valid obligation on the part of the deceased to surrender the estate. The fact that the appellant had acquired the limited interests of a woman who has been acquired by her from her father does not affect her right to claim any benefit under section 4 of the Act. [110H] 2 (b) In view, of the clear language of section 4(1), it is not possible for the court to hold that the surrender made on behalf by the appellant was a voluntary act on the parts of the body of the person who had acquired such interest. [111A D] 3.1. It cannot be said that the legislature intended to confer a right on a widow in respect only of her own property and not merely on the personal knowledge or possession of a female Hindu widow, as the case may be. The word 's name is not defined in the Act but it has been used in section 4 (1). [111B D] 2.(a) The expression 's names' in section 3(2)(b), means that the person whose name is entered in the record of rights and who is entitled to get possession of any property on behalf or for the benefit of which he is entitled. [112E H] (b).

The appellant, a cotton mill company, had been registered under the provisions of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (U.P., for short) and its shares in question were pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The appellant was appointed as a Receiver by the Collector of Kanpur on February 1, 1985. On March 31, 1985, the appellant filed an application under section 169 of the Act before the High Court of Allahabad praying that the order passed by the Board of Directors dated February 1.1985 be set aside and that the appellant be declared to be the owner of the Cotton Mills Company. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice issued under section 170 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956 was not valid as it had been issued in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 169 and 171 of the said Act. On appeal by special leave, the High court held that the company had ceased to be a member of the Polytex Company because of the appointment of a Receiver under section 18AA (1) (a) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed in favour by the High. Court is not valid since it had not been issued under sections 169 or 171 of that Act. [701B] 2. The company was a registered owner of cotton mill and the appellant was entitled to be declared as the owner thereof. [802C] 3. The right to vote at the meeting of the company was vested in the Cotton Corporation, which had been appointed in respect of the shares pledged in its favour by it. [601D] 4. The rights of the appellant were not affected by the appointment or transfer of the management of the cotton mill. [820E] 5. The position that emerges from the facts of this case is that the Cotton Mill Company had been given a part of them and that they had also been pledged in their favour. [823G] 6. The shares in the Polymer Company were pledged by the appellant in favour thereof. The sale proceeds of the goods were credited to the account of the Central Government. The amount due to the Central Govt. was not paid to the Cotton Company. [825E] 7. The fact that the sale proceeds had been deposited in the Bank of India and that it had also vested in it under section 17AA (2) (b) of that act, is not disputed by the respondents. [826G] 8.
