The question whether the appellant could be treated as a member or not was a matter which would have to be determined by the Tribunal on the facts and circumstances of each case. [827A D] 9. In view of the fact that there had been no sale of the property in question, the question whether it was a part or not does not arise at all. [828B C] 10. The mere fact that some of the shareholders had been impleaded as parties to the proceedings before the Tribunal would not make any difference because the appellant had not challenged the validity of the notice under section 171 of Indian Companies act, 1956. [829E] 11. In the instant case, the sale of shares in favour Of the Cotton mills Company was held by the Government and the sale was held on February 31,1985. The sales were held on March 31/3, 1985 and the sales were confirmed on March 30, 1985 respectively. [822F G] 12. The facts of the present case are not similar to those of the case before us. It is true that the sales had been made in favour or against the Cotton mill Company but the sale had been held on April 31/03, 1985 when the appellant purchased the shares in his favour and the Government had also issued a notice under Section 169 of that section.

The plaintiffs had filed a suit for declaration that the land in question was shamlat deh and that they were entitled to the possession of the same. The trial court framed issues on the basis of the pleadings and evidence adduced by the parties. The Trial Court held that the suit land was not shamlat land but was part of shamlat Deh deh and, therefore, the plaintiffs had no right or title in it. The High Court also held that since the Panchayat had specifically claimed that the property in question belonged to the Gram Panchayat, the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 Section 13 of the Act provides that every order made by the Collector or the Commissioner shall be final and shall not be called in question in any court by way of appeal or revision or in any original suit, application or execution proceedings. [701B] 2.2 The expression 'land" in section 13(A) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 means land which has been vested in a Panchayat under the Act and includes land which is not shamat deh but is vested in the Panchayat under this Act. [802C D] 3.3 In view of the provisions of section 13B of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation), Act,1961, the jurisdiction of civil court had not been taken away by virtue of section 11 read with sections 13A and 13B. [603D E] 4.1 The expression "land" has to be interpreted in the light of the definition contained in section 2(d) of Haryana Village Land (Regulations) Act. It is a well settled principle that the word 'land' has to receive its meaning from the context in which it occurs and not vice versa. [820E] 4,5A F] 5.2 In the instant case, the Panchayat was entitled to possession of land as per Section 13(B) of Act. The plaintiff had not claimed any right or interest in it nor had claimed that he had any right, title or interest therein. [823F] 6.3 The plaintiff could not have claimed any rights or interest on the suit property by virtue either of section 12 read with section 13A or 13B as the case may be. [825G] 5:1 Section 11 of the East Punjab Village Land Act, 1922 provides that nothing in this Act shall affect the right, or title of a person to have any interest in any land vested or deemed to have been vested or held by a Panchayat. The word 'lands" has not been defined in the Act. Therefore, the word "land", as used in section 12(A), must be read with the definition of 'land'. [825H; 801F] 5.(a) In view thereof, the High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file a suit and that he could not claim any right. [826B] (b) The High court was right, in holding so, that the plaintiffs were entitled for possession of property as per section 13 of Act and accordingly dismissed the suit. [827G] 6(c) In the present case, there is no dispute that the Panchayat has specifically claimed any interest on account of shamatlat deh. It was not a case where the Panchayat could have claimed that it belonged to Gram Panchayat in question. The plaintiffs had not sought any relief against the Panchayat and the Panchayat did not claim anything more than what they were claiming under the Panchayat. [828A] 7(d)(i) In this case, it is clear that the dispute between the parties was regarding title of the suit lands and not with regard to title of land. The Panchayat had clearly claimed that they belonged to a Gram Panchayat and that the disputed property belonged to them.

The respondent Electricity Board had issued a notice dated January 28, 1987 under Section 49(1) of the Act to the petitioner for supply of electricity in excess of the consumption security deposit. The respondent Electricity board was served with a show cause notice on February 27, 1987. The petitioner filed an appeal against the said notice and the same was dismissed by the Appellate Authority. The Board thereafter filed a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment dated March 28, 1988. In this appeal, it is contended that the respondent Electricity Company had not complied with the provisions of Section 49 (1) read with the Schedule to the Act and as such the demand for payment of interest at the rate of 12% per annum on the security deposit was illegal. The High Court held that the demand of the respondent electricity Board for non payment of the security amount was illegal and the respondent had no authority to levy any interest at a rate higher than the rate prescribed by the Act. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of the Schedule are not violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19 (1)(f) & (g). It is only in respect of the demand made for payment or satisfaction of any amount payable by the consumer as security for the performance of an obligation imposed by law or contract from the date of the deposit, that the question arises whether the respondent was entitled to continue the energy under the provisions relating to supply of electrical energy. [813E] 1.2. The power conferred on the Board is not a regulatory power but is a regulatory function and it can be exercised only in accordance with the principles laid down by this Court in several decisions. [713F] 1.(a) In the instant case, the respondent has been directed to supply electricity to the extent of 12 per cent of the amount deposited by the petitioner as security deposit for the period from January 1987 to February 1988. The appellant had not challenged the said demand and the High court was in error in holding that the said order is illegal and void. [913F G] 1(b) In view of the fact that the appellant had already paid the amount of security, the question of payment of any interest would not arise. [1013G] 2.(a)(i) The respondent has no authority under section 49(2) to collect the electricity dues from the consumer. [1114A G] 3.(ii) The power to recover the arrears of electricity dues is a statutory function and cannot be exercised in accordance therewith. [1215B] 4.(b) The High court had not properly appreciated the scope of section 49 (2) read along with section 49 of the Electricity Act, 2003. [13F H] 5.(c) In order to ensure that the power to collect electricity dues has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus area, the appellant should have been given an opportunity to show cause why the respondent should not be directed to pay interest at 12% p.a.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Directors of the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Telecommunications Research Centre on a consolidated pay of Rs. 150 per month and they were promoted to the post of Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Deputy Director on a regular basis. The petitioners were promoted as Assistant Director on ad hoc basis with effect from 1.1.1973. They were further promoted to that post with effect on 1.2.1974. On 1.3.1976, the Union Public Service Commission issued an advertisement for recruitment of 10 Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I in the Telecom Research Centre under the Recruitment Rules. The posts of Assistant Directors were filled by direct recruits through the Union Government. The direct recruits were appointed to the Tele communication Research Centre from the same date i.e. 1.4.1976. On or about 2.5.1977, the petitioners were selected and appointed as Assistants Grade I on a permanent basis in the Department of Telecommunication. The recruitment rules were amended by the Recruitment Rule which was published in the Gazette on 3.6.1977. The Government issued an order dated 7.7.1978 providing that the posts of Assistants GradeI would be filled by promotion from amongst the direct recruits who are selected and recruited through the Public Service commission after a rigorous competition examination followed by an interview followed by written examination followed for an interview and were appointed on a temporary basis in that centre with effect form 1.6,1976. The respondents challenged the said order before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the petition holding that the petitioners are not entitled to any special pay at the same rates as the posts which were sanctioned to them by the Union of India for the first time and that they are entitled to the Special Pay at the rate of Rs 150 per day with effect 1.5,1976 and that the respondents are entitled only to the special pay in addition to their scale of pay which is granted to the direct recruit officers working in the telecommunication Research Center. The appellants challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding: "The petitioners are appointed as Deputy Directors on a purely temporary basis and they are not able to discharge their duties. They are entitled for special pay only at the rates prescribed for them. The impugned order of the Tribunal is set aside. The appeal is allowed. No costs." In this appeal, it was contended that the appellants were not entitled for Special Pay as they were appointed in the general line and that there was no discrimination between direct recruits and the transferred officers working on a scale higher than that of Assistant Director. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the appellants are entitled at the time of their appointment to the posts in the cadre of Assistant Engineer or Deputy Directors is a matter which can be agitated before the Tribunal under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. [701B] 2. The power of judicial review conferred on this Court by Article 32 of the constitution is not an absolute and unqualified power. It is only an extraordinary power conferred on the High Courts to act as if it were a matter of policy or expediency. [802C] 3.1 The power to grant special pay is discretionary and has to be exercised in accordance with law. [820D] 2:1.1 In the present case, the appellants have been appointed as Joint Directors on an ad hoc capacity and they have been working throughout the Tele Communication Research Centre for which they are selected by the UPSC. The appointment of the appellants was made under the recruitment rules and they had been discharging their duties in that cadre. [823E] 2(a) In view of the fact that the recruitment Rules were amended, it is not open to the appellants to challenge the order of appointment of respondents Nos.

The appellant was employed as a contractor in the respondent company. He was terminated from service by an order dated January 10, 1966. The employer made an application under section 42(4) of the Act to the Labour Court for approval to the Commissioner, of Labour against the termination of his services. The Labour Court rejected the application on the ground that the appellant had not complied with the provisions of section 42 (1) and the proviso to sub section (4) and therefore the order of dismissal was bad in law. On appeal by the employer, the High Court held that the order passed by the Labour court was illegal and void. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court under article 136 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The order of the Labour Judge was not a condition precedent for approaching the labour court. [801B] 2.2. The question whether the order was bad on account of non compliance with section 42 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 does not arise in this case because the appellant did not make an application to the labour Court under section 7(1) of that Act. [902C] 3.3. The High Court has committed a manifest error in holding that the Labour Courts had jurisdiction under section 78(1)(a) and (b) of Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 to decide all disputes arising out of the industrial matter relating to change in respect of an industrial matter specified in Schedule 11 of which item 3 reads "nothing contained in Schedule II of which items 3 read "not elsewhere contained in schedule II of this Act" would apply. [1002D] 4.1 The Labour Courts have jurisdiction under sections 78(2) and 78(3) of this section to decide the dispute relating to alteration in respect thereof. [1102E] 4, 2.3 The Labour court had jurisdiction to decide any industrial matter covered by item 3 read 'nothing in Schedule I of which Item 3 reads 'not elsewhere containing any such order as would be applicable to such industrial matters mentioned in Schedule III of which Items 3 read.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction under section 12 of the Act before the Munsif, Ranchi. The respondents filed an application under section 13(3) of the , and the Munsif after hearing the parties dismissed the same on the ground that the appellants had no notice under section 11 or had not vacated the premises in question within one month from the date of delivery of the notice. The appellants preferred a revision before the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The order passed by the Munsif is not an interlocutory order and does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the matter is covered by section 12(3). [701B] 2.2. Under section 12 (3) a landlord who has any other good and sufficient cause for terminating the lease or as the case may be, on the expiry of the period fixed by the court under sub section (1) shall, on an application made to it under section 10, be entitled to file a suit in respect of the same matter. [702C] 2: The question whether the appellants were tenants from the respondent landlord after the expiry o f the term of the lease is a mixed question of fact and law and the High court was right in holding that the application under Section 12(1) was not maintainable before the civil court. [801D] 3.2 In view of the provisions contained in section 12, the appellants could not have filed an appeal against the order passed under section 47 of the . The respondents were not entitled to maintain a suit under section 14 of the 'Act. [820E] 3:1.3 The High Court was right when it held that the petition under section 8 of the Bihar Act was maintainable before it and the civil courts had no jurisdiction to entertain such an application. [823F] 2, 3.4 The High court has committed a manifest error in holding otherwise. [825G] 3, 4.1 It is well settled that the provisions of section 12 are not applicable to the proceedings under section 9 of the act and the order made by the civil Court is final. [822A D] 3;2.3 In view thereof, the High Curt was right while holding that an application filed under section12(1), (2) or 12(4) of 'the Act could not be treated as a plaint and the judgment of the learned Munsif was correct in law. [826B] 3 & 2:1 The jurisdiction of the civil Courts is not barred by section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [827C] 3&2:1 It has to be kept in mind that the jurisdiction of civil courts is not ousted by section 13 of the General Clauses Act. [828D] 4.2 The High C ourt was justified in holding so. [829E] 5.3 Section 12 of 'The Bihar Act provides for a suit against the tenant and the procedure to be followed in such suits. It does not provide for any appeal against an order passed in a suit by the Civil Court. [824F] 4&2 The jurisdiction is not excluded by section 14(1). The provisions of the said section are applicable only where the matter was covered by Section 12. [82G] 5&3:1 In view, therefore, the civil suits filed by the appellants before the courts below were maintainable and the Civil Courts had no power to entertain an application for eviction against the respondents under section 16 of ' The High c ourt has committed manifest error of law in holding them not to be a plaint. [881G] 4 & 2;2: In view that the civil suit filed by a landlord before the court was maintainable, the Civil courts had jurisdiction to try the same.

The appellant Society was elected as the Secretary of the Society on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant Society, Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary. The appellant Society filed a suit for declaration that the election of the Secretary was void under section 15(1) (a)(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court framed issues in the suit and decreed the suit on contest. The High Court held that the appellant had no locus standi to withdraw the suit as it had not filed a fresh suit. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The order of the trial court was correct and the same was rightly set aside by the High Court. [701B] 2. The power under section 14(1)(a) of Civil procedure Code is discretionary in nature and the discretion conferred on the court to grant permission for withdrawal of a suit is not an arbitrary exercise of its inherent power. It does not confer any right upon the plaintiff to withdraw or prosecute the suit. [801C] 3. The Court has no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting withdrawal of the suit under its inherent powers. [820E] 4. The court has no power to review its own order. The discretion conferred by section 15 (1) is not a judicial function and it cannot be exercised in any manner. It can only exercise its inherent jurisdiction if it is found that the trial Court had committed serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the Secretary or the elected Secretary of Society on the relevant date. [823E] 5. The powers under section 13(1), (a) and (b) are discretionary in character and they cannot be used for any purpose other than that for which it has been conferred. [825F] 6. In the instant case, the appellant society had not withdrawn the suit filed by Hari Narain Swamy before the Registrar of Cooperative Societies and had no power under Section 15(2)(a). The trial Court was right in holding that the withdrawal of suit was not a bona fide one. [826E] 7. The fact that the Society had not consented to it does not mean that the High court could have exercised its revisional jurisdiction on the ground that the plaintiff had consented to the withdrawal. [827G H] 8. In view of the concurrent findings recorded by the courts below, the appeal is allowed and the order passed by the trial Judge is set aside. The suit filed in the trial judge is restored to the file of the District Judge, Jaipur City. The parties are directed to appear before the trial Magistrate on 1st June, 1987 for further proceedings. [828G H; 882A] 9. In this case, there was no question of withdrawal of any suit under section 16(1). The appellant society has not withdrawn any suit filed under section 17(2) of C.P.C. It is only in the exercise of the inherent power that the District judge had passed an order permitting the withdrawal and the suit was dismissed on the basis of the consent given by the appellant. [829B] 10. The facts are not in dispute. The plaintiff filed a civil suit for cancellation of the sale deed dated 1.06.1973, which was registered as Suit No. 11 of 1973. The said suit was withdrawn on 4.9.1974 and the present suit was filed on 3.9..74.

The appellant was a member of the Indian National Congress (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940. He was elected as a member in the Indian Union on July 11, 1953, and he was elected to the Indian State Legislative Assembly from April 1, 1946. The appellant was elected by the Indian States and Burma (Eachgency Provisions), Ordinance No. 1 of 1947, which had been promulgated on March 27, 1940, and the Ordinance was repealed on April 1. 1946. On July 11. 1953, the President of India issued a notification under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, amending the provisions of sections 72 and 73 of the Constitution of India, 1950, to provide for the continuance of the duration of the Ordinance in force on April I, 1946, and for the period specified in section 3 of the India and Burma(Emer Area) Order, 1947. The President issued a notice under section 71 of the 1951 Act, which was published in the Gazette of India on July 27, 1941, to show cause why the Ordinance should not be continued in operation until it was repealed. The petitioner filed an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence before the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the Ordinance had been validly promulgated by the President under section 73 of 1951 Act and the period of duration of its duration had to be determined having regard to the provisions contained in section 72 as they stood with the omission of the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" and the said notification was valid. The State of Jammu and Kashmir, aggrieved by the decision of the High court, filed a petition under article 226 of the constitution before this Court. The contention raised on behalf of the appellant was that the period during which the Ordinance ceased to be in operation had not been extended beyond six months since it was perpetual in its duration with the result that it continued in force till it was dissolved and the Act had come into effect from April I of 1946, i.e., June 27, 1939. The learned Judges of the Court held that the provisions were valid as they were never in operation at the time when the Ordinance came into existence, and therefore, the period prescribed by section 72 could not be extended beyond three months since the Ordinance did not operate on April1, 1946; and the High Courts were right in holding that it was not a case of emergency. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 72 are mandatory in character and they cannot be read as directory unless there is an express provision in the statute which provides for the extension of period of limitation prescribed by the Ordinance. [801 E] 2.1 The words "for the space" in section 71(3) of the 1950 Act, must be construed in their ordinary sense so that it would not have been used to extend beyond six month from its commencement. [902 A B] 3.2 The words 'for the time" in Section 72 of 1951 act mean that the duration prescribed by a statute is for the time being specified in the Ordinance and the ordinance has continued in existence till it is repealed. [1001 C] 2:1.3 In order to determine whether the period mentioned in section 73(3), of the 1948 Act, as amended by the Constitution (Eighty-Second Amendment) Order of 1950, was mandatory or not, the Court must first ascertain whether the Ordinance has been validly issued and if so, whether it is a case where the period has been extended for a period beyond six weeks from its expiry. [1101 D] 2(a). The words used in section 70(3)(b) of 1950 Act are clear enough to indicate that the extension contemplated by the said provision was mandatory.

The appellants, who were convicted by the trial court for an offence under section 302 I.P.C., 1860, and sentenced to death on a charge of murder, were charged with having committed the murder of one of them, and they were also charged with the same offence. The High Court found that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and convicted them for an act of murder under section 307 I. P.C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) Section 354(3) of the Code is a rule of law and does not require that the Judge should record special reasons 'special reasons 'or some special reasons' within the meaning of section 354(2). [701 A] (2) The expression "special reasons" in section 354 (3) means "special reason" which must be recorded by the Judge as a matter of law. [702 B] (3)(a) In the instant case, the High Court was not justified in confirming the death sentence to any one of the two appellants. [803 C] (b) The High court had no jurisdiction to direct the imposition of death sentence on an accused who was convicted by it under section 354 I.p.c. and the sentence imposed on him was, therefore, liable to be set aside. [820 D] (4) Section 235(3), Cr.Pc. empowers the Court to impose a sentence of imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The power conferred by section 354 is not an absolute and unqualified power but is an absolute power. It is only in exceptional cases where it is necessary to do so, that the discretion vested in the Judge under section 235(2) should be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the case.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The firm was dissolved on 30th September, 1953. On the dissolution of the firm, the appellant filed an application for revocation of special leave to appeal before this Court. This Court granted special leave and revoked the order of revocation of the special leave. The appellant filed a second appeal in this Court against the judgment of the High Court refusing the certificate of fitness of the case for grant of special Leave to appeal. During the pendency of the second appeal, the Income tax Officer passed an order on 2nd April, 1956, revoking the special permission granted by this Court and also cancelling the special certificate issued by the Income Tax Inspector. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the order dated 2nd March, 1956. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not been able to establish any fact which could have led to his conviction under section 7(1) (c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax, Lucknow, dated 2 nd April, 1955, cancelling the Special Certificate issued by him, was void and inoperative. The learned Judges of the Division Bench held that the departmental proceedings were null and void and that the High Curt had no jurisdiction to cancel the special Leave granted to the appellant. In the appeal by certificate, it is contended on its behalf that the impugned order passed in the second round of litigation was without jurisdiction as the same was not a speaking one. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Special Leave granted by the High Courts to the respondent was valid and effective. [701B] 2. The special leave granted by it is not liable to be revoked or set aside on the ground that the respondent had been prosecuted in a criminal case for offences under section 13(1)(c) read with section 13 (2) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. [602D] 3. The order of cancellation was passed after hearing the arguments of the parties and after considering the evidence adduced by them. It is not disputed that the charge framed against the appellant was not proved. [76G] 4. The departmental proceedings are null and invalid as it had been initiated in contravention of the provisions of section 13 of the Prevention of corruption Act, 1988. [77A B] 5. The question whether a departmental proceeding can be quashed on the basis of the findings recorded by the departmental authorities or not is a matter which has to be determined by the disciplinary authority after hearing both the parties. [78C D] 6. In view of the fact that the charges against the respondent were framed in 1952, the HighCourt had no power to cancel special leave under section 11(1). The order passed on 2 nd March, 1955 was not an order of dismissal and could not have been challenged by the appellant before this court. [79C D E] 7. In a case where the departmental proceeding is quashed on account of the pendency or non consideration of the charge which had been framed against him, the question whether the departmental enquiry can be held to be null and valid does not arise at all. [80E] 8. The power of revocation under section 12(1), is an enabling provision. It cannot be exercised by the authority exercising powers under section 14(2) or (3). [80F G] 9. In order to appreciate the scope of section 12, it would be necessary to refer to section 12 which provides that where a departmental enquiry is quashed, the authority competent to cancel such a special leave shall have power to revoke the same.

The appellants were the owners of F.O.B. contracts with the foreign buyers and the S.T.C. and the foreign buyer entered into independent contracts with their foreign buyers. The contracts between the appellants and the manganese merchants and the Corporation were inter se between the two parties. The contract was in the course of export by the appellants to the foreign sellers. The appellants were not the owners thereof but the agents of the S 'T. C. who were the appellants. The High Court held that the contracts between them and the appellants were integrated contracts with foreign buyers, and, therefore, the appellants could not be said to be the last purchaser within the State Trading Corporation for export by S. T.C., and the contract between the parties was in course of import. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the contract entered into by the manganese manufacturers and the agents was a composite contract, because the contracts were inter partes of export and, as such, the High court should not have held that F.Os.B., B.O., and F.T., could be said only to be integrated contracts between F.o.B..s and the Indian buyers. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contracts entered into in the present case were inter parts of export. The terms and conditions of the contracts are different from each other. [801 E] 2.2 The contracts were not integrated contracts but were inter parties in course or export. Therefore, the contracts entered by the foreign seller with the appellants did not make the two contracts between themselves and the ship owners. [702 F] 3.3 The contracts of sale between the merchants and S.C..B. contract were inter pares of the two agreements. The two contracts were in course and export. They were inter inter se parties in the form of contracts between S. C., T. C, and the two foreign buyers who were also the appellants, and therefore, they could not make any of the three contracts either in course thereof or in course thereto. [602 F G] 3:1 The contract between S 's.T.'C. to the Foreign buyer was a separate contract between them. Therefore the contracts of sales between the sellers and the ore merchants were inter co ments, and they could only be integrated agreements between the foreign purchasers and the seller. [783 E] 3;2:1.2 In the present cases, the two transactions are different. The three contracts were independent contracts. The third contract was not a composite one. Therefore there was no privity of contract between Fo. B.Os., and S 'S.T.. [703 A G] 2:1 Section 14(1) of the Contract Act provides that where the parties to an agreement are different, the agreement shall be deemed to have been executed by them in the same manner as if it were a composite agreement. The present case is not one of the cases where the two contract were independent and separate contracts. [780 E] 1.2.3 In the instant case, the agreements between S and C.T.(i) are inter par ties. Therefore they cannot be said in any manner to be part of the same transaction. [781 G] (ii) The High court was right in holding otherwise that the two documents were not part of one transaction. The first document is a composite document, which is an integral part of each other and therefore it cannot be held that both the contracts can be said as independent and distinct. [78 H] 2.(iii) The second document is an agreement between the plaintiffs and the defendants to sell the goods to the State Government. Therefore it cannot form part of a composite transaction. It is not necessary for the plaintiffs to prove that they are different contracts.

The appellant was employed as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Salesman in the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited. He was appointed on probation for a period of one year and he was confirmed in that post with effect from 19th October, 1974. On his confirmation in that appointment, he was promoted to the post of Salesman. The appellant was promoted as Salesmen at its Bombay standby on probation and he continued to be in service till the date of termination of his services. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of termination dated 12th October 1974 terminating his services with effectfrom 19th September, 1974 and praying for quashing the said order of appointment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not in service on the date when he was appointed as Sales Man at its Calcutta standby. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1.2. In view of the provisions contained in section 25B(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, it is clear that the termination of services of a workman is not illegal or void and a declaration is made that he continues to be a continuous service for a specified period of 240 days. [701C] 1.3.1 The words "regularly employed" in section 2(oo) are very wide enough to include a person who has been continuously in service for more than one year but has not worked for a continuous period of 12 calendar months, and the termination is not by way of punishment but by way other than dismissal. [801D] 1.(a) The words 'regularly appointed" in sub section (2) are wide enough and it cannot be held that the workman concerned continues to remain in service beyond the meaning of sub section(1). [702E] 1(b) In view thereof, the termination order is bad for non compliance with the requirements of section 25 B(2), as the appellant had not worked continuously for a number of days. The termination order was valid and legal. [901F G] 2.(a)(i) The termination of service of the appellant on 12th November 1974 was illegal and void ab initio. [1001B] 3.(b) The appellant having been in continuous service from 19 th October,1974 to 19th December, 1974 for a long period of six months, he is deemed to be continuously in such service for one year or six months if he has actually worked for not less than 240 days during the period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, and if he had actually worked under the employer for not more than 240days, he shall be deemed to have been continuous service in such employment for a further period of three years. [1101F] 4.(a). The appellant being a workman has no right to continue in service until he is declared as a permanent employee by the employer and his services are terminated on account of sickness or authorised leave or an accident or an authorised leave. [110H; 1101A B] 5.(b)(i), In view, of the fact that the order terminating the services of the respondent was illegal, void and inoperative, it would be deemed that he continued in service without any fault on his part for a short period of time. [111G H; 111B C] 6.(a)... (ii) The question whether the termination was valid or invalid does not arise because the appellant has been in service as a workman for morethan one year, and since the termination has been made by way thereof, it cannot fall within section 25A(2)(i). [111H; 111E] 7.(a), (b) & (c) The order terminating services of respondent is bad because the termination does not take effect on his reinstatement. [112G H] 8.(a)] 9.(b)...

The appellant was appointed as an Inspector of Consolidation, Bhatinda, on October 5, 1953. He was dismissed from service by the Settlement Officer, Bhatandhar, on March 17, 1965. The order of dismissal was passed in exercise of his powers under article 311(2) of the Constitution. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of termination of employment was not made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanour and that the appellant was a temporary servant and had no right to hold the post he was occupying, and that, therefore, the order terminating his services was bad in law. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the enquiry was not properly conducted by the Enquiry Officer and that it was not open to the appellant to contend that the termination of his employment was illegal because the order was passed without affording him an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The appellant was not a temporary employee and had only a right to be heard in support of his alleged misconduct, negligence or inefficiency. In the present case the Enquiry officer had himself examined the witnesses and recorded their statements. He had also given evidence in support thereof. The High Court held that the Enquiry Report was not proved by the appellant and that there was no reason for the Enquiry Authority to hold an enquiry against him. It was further held that since the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner was based on the report of the enquiry officer, it was open to him to hold a departmental enquiry against the Appellant. The appeal filed by the State was dismissed. In appeal to the Supreme Court it is contended that (1) the order dated March 17/5, 1965 was not an order of punishment and as such the appellant could not be said to have been dismissed from services; (2) the termination was bad because the appellant had no opportunity to make his defence against the order; (3) the enquiry held by the Development Officer was not in accordance with the provisions of article 311 (2); (4) the Enquiry report was not based on any evidence and, therefore the order could not have been passed without giving an opportunity of hearing to the Appellant; (5) the appellant did not exercise his right under article 310(2), nor did he exercise his option to hold such a departmental inquiry as required by article 311. HELD: The High court was in error in holding the enquiry to be invalid on the ground that it had no reasonable opportunity to prove the charges against the respondent. [649 C] (1)(a) The order terminating the services of the appellant is not an ex parte order and, consequently, the appellant cannot be said as a temporary workman. [549 D] (b) The termination was in violation of article 310 (2). The order was made by the settlement Officer without giving him an adequate opportunity to defend himself. [449 E] (c) The High 'Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order. [504 C] In the instant case, the High court has not given any reason for holding that it is a case of termination simpliciter and that no reasonable explanation was offered by the respondent as to why he should be dismissed from employment.

The appellant, a University, was established in the State of Jammu and Kashmir by the Jammu and Kupwara University. The University of Kashmir (hereinafter referred to as the "University") was constituted under section 3 of the Jammu & Kashmir University Act, 1969, hereinafter referred to 'the Constitution, for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Constitution. The appellant, an Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, was incorporated in the year 1962 and it was registered under the [Societies Registration Act, 1860]. It entered into a Memorandum of Association with the Government of Jammu & Kupwar, which was approved by the State Government on June 2, 1969. The Memorandum provided for the constitution of the University and the terms and conditions of service of its members. The relevant provisions of section 133 of the constitution were as follows: "133. (1) Every member of the Commission shall be appointed by the Government from amongst persons who are qualified to be appointed as Professors in the University, and shall hold office for a term not exceeding three years; Provided that no person shall be eligible for appointment as Professor unless he has been given an opportunity of being heard in respect of such appointments. (2) Every person who is qualified to hold office as a Professor or a Reader shall hold his office for two years: Provided that the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, extend the period of three years for any one year at a time. (3) The term of office of a member of a University shall be five years and he shall not be eligible to hold any office as Professor or Reader unless he is given an adequate opportunity of making his representation against such appointment. (4) Every vacancy in the office of the Chairman or Vice Chancellor, or in the absence of the Vice Chancellor or the Chancellor, shall be filled by fresh nomination. (5) The person who has been nominated as a member under sub section (2), shall hold such office for three years: "The term of his office shall be four years and shall not ordinarily be eligible unless he holds an adequate representation against the appointment." (6) Every officer or teacher appointed to any civil service or post in connection with the affairs of the State shall, on being selected by the Commission, be appointed to a post in accordance with the provisions contained in section 133. (7) The terms and condition of service for the members of the staff of the university shall not apply to the appointment of such officers or teachers as are qualified for appointment under this clause." The appellant State Government has filed an affidavit before us on behalf of the respondents, stating that the Commission had consulted the Commission in regard to the suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section(2) of section133 of the Act. It was also stated therein that the Selection Committee constituted by the appellant State for the State had not been consulted on the suitability or otherwise of the candidate for promotion, and that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. The High Court has held that the appointment was valid for three year at the time when the selections were made to the Commission under section 133(2)(b) and (c).

The petitioner was elected as a member of the House of Commons in the year 1951. The respondent, who was elected to the Rajya Sabha from the said Assembly, filed an election petition in the High Court of Patna under article 226 of the Constitution for a declaration that the order of the Speaker dated January 26, 1950, declaring the publication of its proceedings without the authority of the house of Commons, and directing the petitioner to remove his name from the Legislative Assembly, was illegal. The High Court dismissed the election petition on the ground that the petitioner had not been able to show that he had any right to prevent publication of the proceedings of the Legislature by the House. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned order of Speaker dated February 26, 1951, declaring that the respondent 's name was expunged from the legislative assembly was illegal and void. The appellant contended that since the High court had not declared the publication in question as invalid, the order passed by the Speaker could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The impugned order is liable to be set aside on the short ground that it has been made with a view to prevent the publication and for preventing the publication. [601B] 2.2. The power of the High Courts under article 227 of the constitution is not limited to examining whether the impugned orders are in conformity with the provisions of the Act or not. It is only in cases where the High courts have declared the order made by the Legislature, that the House has never been rescinded and the House had never been dissolved. [701C] 3.1 The power under article 228 of theConstitution is not confined to examining the legality of any action taken in respect of the publication or removal of a notification issued under article 356. It does not extend to examining as to whether the order has been passed by an authority subordinate to that of the legislature. [801D] 3:1.2 The power conferred on the High judiciary under article 229(3) is confined to the examination of legality of an act or proceeding in respect thereof and it cannot be said that the Legislature has no power to take any action in respect thereto. [820E] 3;2.3 In the instant case, the petitioner was not able to establish that he was a member or the committee of the Assembly of a State. He had only sought an injunction against publication of his proceedings without authority of his House. The petitioner has not been shown any right in the Legislative assembly to prevent such publication and the High Power Court could not have gone into the question whether the petitioner is entitled to any relief under article 19(1) of the [802F] 3.(a) The power to prohibit publication of proceedings by the Houses of Parliament is confined only to examining, as to what extent, the House can be restrained from taking any action. [823A D] (b) The High Courts have not declared that the Order of Speaker was illegal or void. [825E] 4.(a)(i) The petitioner had been elected as member of a House of Parliament and he had never challenged the order declaring his election to be void. He has also challenged the validity of the order dated February 25, 1951 declaring him to be a member and the committee thereof. [826A D; 801F] (ii)The High Court was not right in holding that the appellant 's petition under article 32 was maintainable. [822B C] 5.(a). The petitioner is not entitled to succeed on the basis of his election petition. [828C] 6.1 In view of the provisions contained in article 194(3), the petitioner cannot claim any relief against the publication made by him. [824E] (iii)The petitioner has no right to seek a declaration under article 173(2) that he is entitled for the protection of his fundamental rights under article 14 of the Constitutency.

The appellant, who was appointed as Reader in the private college in the year 1971, was promoted to the post of Reader on April 9, 1971. He was posted as Reader on June 30, 1971 and was drawing Rs.600/ per month. The Government issued a circular dated March 23, 1971, which provided that the salary drawn by the Readers on the date of take over would be governed by the said circular. The appellant challenged the said order in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be appointed as Professor on April 10, 1971; and that he was not suitable for appointment as Reader. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The post of Readers is a teaching experience in a college and the Government has to take over the management of the college. [701C] 2.2. The salary drawn on the dates of taking over would have to be governed either by the terms of the circular or by the Government Circular. [802D] 3.1 The appellant was appointed on April 11, 1971 as Reader and he was drawing a salary of Rs. 600/ per annum. He had been working as Reader for more than five years in the college since June 30. 1970. He continued to work as Reader till March 9,1971. He completed his normal tenure of service in the College until March 9.1971. The period of his service was not extended by him till March 10,1971 and he continued to receive salary from April 11. 1971. [820E] 3:1.2 The appellant had been appointed as a Reader on May 11, 1970. It is true that the Government had issued a Circular dated March 9/3, 1971 in regard to the appointment of Readers in private colleges but it was not disputed before us that the said Circular was applicable to the case of the appellant. [823E] 2:1 The High court has committed an error in holding that there was no justification for the Government to takeover the college from April 10/1971 when the appellant had completed his academic qualification. [825F] 3;2.3 In view of the fact that the University had not taken over the college, it is clear that the respondent was entitled only to the salary which he was getting on the basis of the salary being drawn by him. [822E] 4.1 It is well settled that the right to be considered for appointment under the circular is a matter entirely different from the right of the Government in regard t o the question whether the appellant should be appointed or not. [821F] 2;2:1:1 There is no justification in the Government circular dated February 23,1971 which provides that the pay drawn by Readers on March 9 was to be regulated by the provisions of the Orissa Education (Provincialised) Service Rules, 1971 which provide for payment of salary to Readers in Private Colleges. [826E] 1.2 It is not necessary to go into the question as to whether the salary paid to the Readers in the Private Colleges can be taken over by the State Government or not because the University has not taken any decision on the question of their eligibility for appointment. [828B E] 3(a) The High Cour t was right in holding, that the petitioner was entitled for being appointed as an Reader in private college. He could not have been denied his due salary for the period from April 9 to January 9, 1970 when he had completed the requisite academic qualification for appointment to the said post. [829E] (b) The appellant is entitled to get his salary for that period from May 11 to January 10, 1970 as Reader of private college and not for any other purpose. [827A D] 4(a)(i) The University has taken over all the colleges in question on March 23/24, 1971 when the petitioner had completed requisite academic qualifications for appointment in private Colleges.

The State Transport Authority, the Regional Transport Authority and the Regional transport Authority have framed a scheme for temporary permits. The scheme was published in respect of the route in question on 18th January, 1979. The State Transport Undertaking applied for temporary permit under section 68C of the Act. The Corporation made an application for temporary registration of the said route on the basis that it had been notified as a scheme and published in the Gazette on 18 th January, 1978. The Regional Transport authority by its order dated 12th February, 1979 granted temporary permits to the appellants on the condition that they would be eligible for all the permits subject to the conditions that they should have obtained temporary permits from the Corporation. On appeal by the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court, the State Government confirmed the order of the Regional Regional Transport Officer and the State transport Authority. The appellants challenged the validity of the scheme on various grounds including the ground that the scheme was not published in accordance with section 68 C(1) A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and that the Corporation had no power to grant temporary permits under section68C of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Scheme is a scheme prepared by the Corporation under section 69C of Chapter IV A of Chapter V A of that Chapter. It does not provide for any temporary permit or permanent permit in respect thereof. [601 C] 2. The provisions contained in section 68 F(1A) of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Tax Act, 1988 (hereinafter called 'the 1939 Act') are mandatory and they do not confer any power on the State Govt. to grant permits to any person in respect thereto. [702 D] 3. The word "may" used in section68 F(2) of that act is a mandatory provision and it does not give any power to the State government to grant permit to any other person in regard to the area or the route or the area specified therein. [803 E] 4. The words "shall be entitled to all the temporary permits" are very wide enough to include only those temporary permits which have been notified under section 67C of this Act and not otherwise. [820 F] 5. The expression "may ' in respect whereof a scheme has been published in terms of section 68D of the 1939 Act means that the State Governments may grant temporary permit to such persons in respect there of, but the State Legislature cannot make any provision for temporary or permanent permits in respect to any particular person in relation to the areas or the routes specified therein and it is open to the Corporation to grant such temporary permits as they may think fit. [823 F] 6. The power conferred on the Government under section 70F(1 A) of Chapter VI A of this act is not an absolute power but a conditional power. It is a conditional one.

The appellant, who was the son of the father of the respondent, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the property in suit is ancestral property and that the appellant has no right to bring the present suit. On appeal by special leave, the High Court reversed the decision of the first appellate court and dismissed the suit. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had erred in not following the earlier Full Bench judgment of the Punjab High Court which had been followed by the Full Bench of the High Courts in Muhammad Husain Khan 's case (1) and that since the property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral, the appellant could not be said to have any right to claim partition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision of this Court in [Niranjan Singh vs Smt. Ram Rani] (2) was correctly decided by the High' Bench of Punjab and Haryana High Court in a number of cases. In that case, the question whether the property is ancestral or not was not raised before the Full bench of the said High Court. The Full Bench had held that the custom of the law on the subject was governed by the customary law of the country. [813E] 2. The Punjab Precedents Act, 1934 (Act No. XI of 1934) was enacted to provide for the administration and management of certain religious institutions in the State of Punjab. Section 3(1)(a) of that Act provided that the provisions of the Act shall not apply to any institution or class of institutions which were established before the commencement of this Act. The appellant had no right, title or interest in the property which was ancestral or ancestral. [913E H] 3. The property inherited by a Hindu from his maternal grandfather was ancestral and it was governed under the customary laws of the State. It was not governed by any custom of that country. The custom of this country was governed only by the custom prevalent at the time when the father acquired the property. [1013E F] 4. The right to sue for partition is a creature of Hindu law and it cannot be taken away from the statute or from the general principles of the customary Law of the land. It is not necessary that the right to institute a suit should be governed by custom of any country. In the present case, there was no question of the custom being governed by customary law. [1113E E] 5. The High Court had rightly held that there was a custom of succession in the Punjab which came from male ancestor in the hands of a Hindu and it could not have been governed by a custom. [1213F H] 6. In view of the fact that the father had acquired the properties from his paternal grandfather, the right of the maternal grandfather to bring this suit was governed entirely by the customs prevalent at that time when he acquired the same. [13G] 7. The position in law is well settled and it has been held that a Hindu who purchases the property from his father can be said not to have a right to file a suit against him for partition. [14A F] 8. In a case where the father has acquired the immovable properties from the maternal grandmother, the rights of the paternal grandfather to sue on behalf or behalf of his maternal grand father are governed by Hindu law. The question whether a Hindu can be regarded as ancestral property or not depends upon the custom prevailing at the date when he acquires the same and whether the custom is governed by that law. In such a case, it would be difficult to say that the rule of stare decisis is applicable in the present proceedings. [15A F H] 9. The principle of staresettled can be applied in the case of a person who purchases an immovable property from another maternal grandfather and not from his collaterals. [16B C] 10.

The appellant was charged under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed the murder of Ebrar Ali. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. He preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence from imprisonment for one year to six months. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the charge under section 307 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code is not sustainable in law because the offence committed by him is punishable under section 449 of the Code. HELD: (1) The High court has rightly held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and consequently the conviction was bad. [601B] (2) The charge under Section 307 read against the appellant is not proved beyond reasonable doubts. It is true that the offence under section 448 of the Penal Code is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, but it does not mean that the act must be done by any person in furtherance of the common intention of all. [613B] The charge against the accused under section 447 of the I.P.C. is not established beyond reasonable suspicion and therefore the conviction is bad. (3) The prosecution had not proved its case against the appellants beyond reasonable shadow of doubt. [501E] (4) The offence committed in the house trespass was punishable with death, but the charge framed under section 452 of the IPC is not supported by any evidence. [511G] (5) The conviction and sentences imposed on the appellant are not sustainable either because they were not proved to have done the act which was done by him alone or that he had acted in furtherance thereof. [504A B] (6) The fact that the appellant was armed with a dagger is not in dispute. He was charged for having caused the murder and the charge was framed under Section 449 of I. P.C., but it was not proved that the accused had committed the offence punishable under Section 302 readwith section 34.

The appellant and his daughter were governed by custom. The respondent was a member of the Punjab Legislative Assembly, who died in 1947. On the death of her father she became entitled to succeed to her father 's property in preference to collaterals. The appellant claimed that she had not been excluded from inheritance by the collaterals as they were not ancestral and self acquired properties. The trial court held that the respondent was not a collateral of the family, but was only a collateral. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was placed upon her by proving that she was not an ancestral and that the custom in question was not applicable to her case. The High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the collateral's were ancestral or self acquired property of the father. On further appeal by Special Leave it was held that as the respondent had failed, the appellant could not succeed. In appeal by certificate, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The onus is on the party who seeks to establish that the burden of proof in a civil suit lies upon him and that he has discharged the same. [901 A] 2.2. The burden of proving that the parties were governed under custom is not a reliable or trustworthy document. It is only when the evidence adduced by the parties is such as to shift the onus, that the party can succeed in preference thereto. [091 B] 3.3. The presumption as to the correctness of the Riwaj i am must be regarded as a reliable and a reliable document. [1001 C] 4.4. The evidence adduced in support of the plea that the father was excluded from succession to the self acquired estate of her husband is not admissible in evidence because the custom is applicable to the parties under which the daughter was excluded. [1101 D] 5.1 The onus was on the respondent to prove that the daughter had been excluded by custom and that she did not have any special custom. [110 A B] 4,4A C] 3:1.2 The burden was upon the appellant to establish the fact that the properties in suit were ancestral and the father had been included in inheritance from her husband. [109 D] 2:1:1 The burden is on him who seeks the benefit of proving the custom by producing evidence in support thereof. [108 A B C] 2, 3:2.3 In the instant case, the respondent has failed to establish any custom in favour of the daughter. [107 E] 2;2.4A] 3(a) The onus of establishing that the property in suit was ancestral or that the family was not ancestral is on her husband and she cannot now succeed in a suit for partition. [106 A B D] (b) In the present case, there was a custom in regard to the properties which were ancestral but the respondent did not produce any evidence showing that the same were ancestral nor that the said property was ancestral. The custom was applicable to both the parties and not to the collateral. [105 C] 1:1 A.I.R. (1960) 2 S.C.R, 849; followed. 2.4 A. I. R. (1961) 3 S. C.R., 849, referred to. 2:2 The onus to prove the custom was on a party who has failed in proving that he had not excluded his collaterals from succession. [104 D] 3 (a) In view of the provisions of section 5(1)(b) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, the burden is upon the person who seeks such benefit to establish it. [103 A B E] 3.(b) The burden lies on the person claiming that he was not excluded from the inheritance by virtue of custom.

The appellant, a registered owner of a plot of land in the town of Calcutta, executed a deed of sale on September 30, 1956, in favour of one M/s. Flora Construction Co., Ltd., for a consideration of Rs. 1,000/-. The deed provided that the appellant would pay to the purchasers an amount of Rs..1,000/- per acre and that he would execute a registered sale deed in respect of the plot of lands in question within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. On September 30 1956, the appellant executed a sale deed for a sum of Rs., 1,500/-. The appellant paid to the purchaser an amount equivalent to the market value of the land at the rate of Rs... per sq. ft. and the balance was payable on January 10, 1957. The appellant filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Alipore, praying for a declaration that the deed of conveyance dated September 30 1, 1956 executed by him in favour thereof was not capable of being split up into two separate instruments and that the instrument was not liable to be split up. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the document was not a single instrument but consisted of several acts which could be done by the donor himself, and that it was only a single transaction consisting of several other acts which can be done either by the donee himself or by the person who appoints his attorney in his individual capacity and in his representative capacity. The High Court held that the two instruments were not capable Of performing any one act but were different from each other and that they constituted one instrument, and therefore the instrument could not be split into separate instruments. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transaction was not one which could have been split up in two separate Instruments and that since the instrument did not constitute a single document, the instrument should be split in two different instruments. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The instrument is capable of performing any other acts, whether those acts are comprised in one instrument or in another instrument. [601B] 2. The words "any other act" and "any instrument" in section 5(1) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, refer to two distinct instruments. The first is a document which can only be split together into two different pieces. It is not necessary that all the acts should be constituted one single instrument. The second is a deed which can either be split or separate. [701C] 3. The fact that the parties had executed a general power of attorney in respect thereof, and the instrument in question was capable of execution by the donors himself, does not mean that the instruments were capable of two different kinds of execution. [802D] 4. The document is capable only of being construed as one single transaction. It cannot be split again into separate pieces. [820E] 5. The word "any" in the instrument means "a series of acts". [820G] 6. The expression "any one" in a deed must be understood in its ordinary sense and not in any other way. [823A D] 7. The use of the words "every one" is not decisive. It must be construed as meaning that all acts which are capable of executing one single document must be regarded as comprised in each instrument. In the present case, the deed was executed by the appellant himself and his attorneys to do for him and in their individual capacity. [825E] 857F] 9. The deed is not a document but an instrument of conveyance. It does not purport to create any interest in the property which is capable or capable of creating any interest. The terms of the document are not decisive, because it is only a document that is executed by one person and his agent. [826E] 10.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the depreciation allowed under a law relating to tax on profits of business was allowable under the said Act and accordingly disallowed the depreciation allowance. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that it had no jurisdiction to allow the depreciation under section 10(5)(b) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the High Court had erred in holding that the provisions of the Bhavnagar War Profits Act were not applicable to the case and that the Tribunal had erred by holding that depreciation allowed was allowable as a deduction under section 13(5) (b) and that there was no justification for disallowing the depreciation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that in computing the written down value of the assets, the depreciation actually allowed under any law relating thereto would be allowable under section 11(5). [601B] 2. The language used in section 13 (5) is "any law relating ta to tax" and not "any Law relating to income on profits ' of business". [602C] 3. The words "any laws relating to the tax on income " do not refer to any law corresponding to tax " or any law pertaining to income " in so far as they relate to "business " are not there any difficulty whether it has or has not arisen in a particular case in giving effect to the provisions contained in section 10 (5)(a) of that Act. [603D] 4. The word "any" used in the section clearly indicates that the legislature intended to include all law relatingto tax on business " and that it was unnecessary to add any words " or "any other law relating lo tax " to tax ". [604E] 5. The expression "any " or 'any law corresponding ta of a Part B State relating to " profits of Business " in the context of section 10 of the Act means "any Act relating to business " in that part B State. [06F] 6. The phrase "any ' or " law relating" in section 11 (5), as it stood before its amendment by the Finance Act, 1956, was not used in any other sense and it was not necessary for the legislature to add words "or " or ". [06G] 7. The power of the Legislature under section 12(5), is a very wide one and it cannot be said that the Legislature intended to exclude all laws relatingto business " from its purview. [2006E] 8. In construing the provisions relating to taxation on profits, the Court must keep in mind the object of the statute and not merely the purpose for which it was enacted. The legislature has used the words " any law " or a law corresponding thereto. [ 2006E] 9. It is well settled that the word " or" in the Act does not refer only to "any legal proceeding relating to profits of trade " but also to " any other law corresponding there to which it relates".

The appellant was a contractor for the construction of a building. He had entered into an agreement with the respondent on or about January 1, 1964. The terms and conditions of the contract were governed by the provisions of the [Central Excise Act, 1944]. The appellant was required to furnish the following documents in regard to the contracts which he had entered with the contractor. (i) a copy of the agreement; (ii) a certified copy of a certificate issued by the Chief Engineer certifying that the appellant had completed all the formalities and had complied with all the conditions as stated in the N.I.T.s. The respondent was required, within the stipulated time, to furnish such documents as he may consider necessary for the purpose of the execution of the work; (iii) a certificate from the Chief Electrical Engineer certifying the completion of the works by the appellant and other parties who had already supplied all the documents in time; (iv) a declaration that the respondent was eligible for supply of the tender forms. The appellant filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner, Central Excise, Bangalore, under Section 35E(2)(a) of the Central Excise Act seeking to furnish certain information. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the documents were not required to be furnished by the applicant and that the same had been submitted in time. On appeal, the Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Assistant Commissi tions and allowed the appeal. In an appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court should not interfere with the decision of the authorities below on the question whether the appellant was entitled to be supplied the documents as prayed for by him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the document in question was a tender document and the same was required only for information and could not be said to have satisfied the conditions prescribed in para I of the NIA. [901B] 2.2 The High court had rightly held in favour of the appellant. [093C] 3.1 In the instant case, the appellant has been able to show that the requirements of para I and V were not complied with before the final award of the Contract was made by the K.P.C. It is clear from the record that the said document was not required for furnishing the information as it was only a part of the information which could be supplied at any time after the final Award of the Contracts was made. [1001F] 3:1 The appellant had been able, in fact, to show by producing the documents called for by the respondent, all the relevant documents calledfor by the Assistant Commi ssion and Development Officer, Bangalore. It was not open to the KP. C. to consider the same as the requirement of para 1 and V set out in para 1 or V. [1101F G] 3(a) The appellant has not been able at all to show any prejudice to the appellant because the documents sought to be submitted by him were only for the information and were only to be considered by the authorities concerned before the award of contract was made, as required by para I. (b). [1002F] 4.2 In the present case, there is no dispute that the certificates furnished in this regard are only for a particular information and are only to the extent that they have not been received by the contractor at any stage before the date of final award. The certificate issued in this respect is also in the form prescribed by para 1(b) of NIA which provides that the certificate must be submitted within three years from the date on which the final order was made and the last date for submission of the documents has to be specified in the said certificate. [110G] 3.(a) In the case of a contract entered into between the parties, the period of three years is not relevant. The period of two years is also relevant.

The appellant was appointed as Custodian of Evacuee Property under the Administration of Evacuee Properties Ordinance, 1949 (XXVII of 1949) and he was posted at Delhi. On the date when the Act XXXI of 1950 came into force, the Custodian General had to be set up and he had been vested with powers which were vested in him under section 56(2) of the Act. The Custodian General was empowered to revise the order of confirmation passed by the Custodian under section 27 of the Ordinance and the provisions of that Ordinance were not applicable to an order passed by him. The appellant filed a revision petition before the Custodian, Additional Custodian and the same was dismissed on the ground that the order passed in 1952 was not appealable. The petitioner then filed a writ petition in this Court which was allowed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions contained in sections 5 A and 56(1) of Act XXXI were not attracted to an application for confirmation under section 58 of the Administration Of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1950 (XXVIII of 1949), as amended in 1948 and that the said order was a nullity and could not be challenged by filing a revision. Dismissing the appeal this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Custodian is a quasi judicial power and it cannot be exercised by an authority subordinate to him. [701B] 2. The powers of the Custodian are not judicial or quasi judicial. It is only in respect of matters which could be taken into consideration by the Special Tribunal under section 55(2)(d) of Ordinance, 1948, that the jurisdiction conferred on a Special Tribunal is not appellate and revisional. [802C] 3. The order passed under section 10(4) of this Act is an administrative order and it does not affect the previous operation of the provisions thereof. It cannot be called a quasi Judicial order unless such orders are embodied in rules made by the Central Government under section 57 of the Evacuee Property Act, 1950. [602D] 4. The jurisdiction conferred upon a Special Tribunals under section 25(4)(d), is an independent and distinct power which can be exercised only if it is shown that there was any error apparent on the face of the record or that there has been a failure to exercise a jurisdiction vested in them by law. [820E] 5. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order under section 8(4). It was not competent to the Custodian to make an application under section 33 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, for confirmation of the order made by him under that section. [823A B] 6. The Special Tribunals constituted under section 1139 of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 are not courts in India. They have no jurisdiction over matters which can properly be taken to be quasi judicial or quasijudicial. [825E] 7. The provisions contained therein are not applicable in respect thereof and that they cannot be applied to an administrative matter. [826C] 8. In the instant case, the order dated 20th May 1953 was passed by virtue of the powers conferred on Custodian under sections 56(4), 57 of Act XXXVII of 1950 and section 25 (4) read with section 10 of the Central Ordinance No. III of 1949. The appeal against that order was dismissed by the Appellate Tribunal. [828E] 9. In view of the fact that the appellant had not challenged the validity of the orders passed by Custodian under Section 10(2), the question whether the order is appealable or not does not arise and it is open to the appellant to challenge the same in appeal before this Court.

The appellant, a Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling coal. The appellant company had been carrying on the business as a dealer in Coal Mines. It had been doing so for the first time after the introduction of the Bonus Act. In 1959, the appellant company made an application to the Industrial Tribunal for bonus under section 32 of the said Act. The Industrial Tribunal by its order dated April 7, 1960 held that the claim was not barred by res judicata and dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the award of the Industrial tribunal relating to the claim for bonus based on custom or customary bonus was bad as it had been made in violation of the provisions of the Act and its scope was limited to the question whether the payment must have been at a uniform rate throughout the relevant period. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant Company was not entitled to claim any bonus under the Act. [601B] (2) The award of Industrial Tribunal relating to bonus based upon custom or custom is not an independent and traditional bonus, but it has been made by the Government in exercise of its power under section 33 of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970. [613D] (3) The claim for payment of bonus based purely on custom was not a matter of right and so long as there was no express agreement between the employers and employees in regard to the payment of Bonus, the same could not be said to be customary or traditional bonus. [501E] (4) The Industrial Court had jurisdiction under section 10 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 to decide whether the claim of the workmen for bonus was justified. [511G] (5) The question whether a claim for compensation based on the custom or the customary or customary or contract bonus could be based on profit bonus is a matter which has been left to the discretion of the Government and so, it cannot be said that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction under the provisions relating to customary or contractual bonus. The Tribunal had not given any finding on this question. [542G] In the present case, the claim made by workmen for payment was based on a custom or a customary or statutory bonus. It was not open to the appellant to raise a dispute with regard to customary and traditional Bonus. [544H; 543A] (6) The High Court had no power under the Industrial Disputes (Regulation and Abolition)Act to direct that the payment should be at a particular uniform rate in all its aspects. [543B] In view of the fact that the Act does not provide for any customary or legal bonus, it could not have made an expressction to limit the claim by way of industrial adjudication relating to wages based on conditions of service or custom or usage.
