[547C] (7) The appellant had no right to claim bonus under a different guise and the question of profit bonus based only on the terms of contract or customary, or contractual wage was not raised in any manner. [549D] In this case, there is no dispute as to whether the appellant is entitled to get any bonus. There is no evidence that the workmen had any right to get bonus under any other enactment. [546E] The Tribunal has held that it was open to a party to claim a higher amount of bonus than what was claimed by him in his application for bonus. In view, however, of the admitted position that the bonus based thereon was not an ordinary or customary one and so the question raised by the appellant was not decided against the appellant, the Tribunal held that there was nothing wrong with it. [550F] (8) The decision of the High Court is clearly erroneous because the claim in this case was based upon a custom which had been prevalent in the establishments before 1965.

The respondents were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab on a substantive basis in accordance with the Haryana Superior Judicial Services Rules, 1963. The High Court by its order dated April 1, 1970 directed that the seniority list be drawn up and the names of the respondents and others who were appointed as direct recruits to the Higher Judicial Service prior to December 31, 1976 should be drawn from the date of their confirmation in accordance therewith. The appellants challenged the aforesaid direction by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the impugned directions issued by the Governor of Punjab and Haryana were not binding on the High court and the High Courts had no jurisdiction to issue any direction for the fixation of seniority of the direct recruits and direct recruits. In appeal, the Division Bench of the HighCourt held that the appellants could not be placed in the seniority lists prepared by the High Power Committee and as such they could not claim seniority over respondents and other persons who were promoted or appointed to a post prior to January 31, 1970. The State Government preferred an appeal against the aforesaid order before the Division bench. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that there was no question of seniority in the Superior judicial service and the appellants were entitled to seniority over the respondents. In the Letters Patent Appeal filed by the State of Haryana, the High Judge held that there had been a violation of Article 233 of the Constitution inasmuch as the rules framed under the Haryana Higher Judicial Services (Amendment) Act, 1976 did not provide for any retrospective effect to the rules made under the aforesaid provisions and in accordance thereof. The appeal was allowed holding that Rule 8 of the Superior Civil Service Rules,1963 did not apply to the case of direct recruits who were promotees prior to the date on which they were promoted and appointed to such of them as were promoted prior to their confirmation. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Power Committees constituted under the rules have been empowered to make appointments to the posts in the service after December 31 1976. [832E] 2.2 The High power Committee has been empowered by Rule 8 to frame rules for recruitment and promotion to the higher judicial service.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, who were appointed as Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants in the State of Andhra Pradesh, filed O.A. No. 1259 of 1987 before the Tribunal for a direction to promote them as Assistant and Senior Assistant in the cadre of civil services of the State into a separate cadre. The Tribunal by its order dated October 6, 1989 allowed the said Original Application holding that the respondents Nos 4 &5 were not members of the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Service and they were not entitled to be promoted to the post of Junior Assistants or Senior Assistants. The State Government filed an appeal against the order of the Tribunal before the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court by its judgment dated October 9, 1989 dismissed the said appeal holding that there was no provision in the order for promotion of the respondents No. 4 and 5 to the cadre in question. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1.1 The power under paragraph 3(1) of the Order is only to organise a separate unit for purposes of recruitment, seniority or promotion etc., as the case may be. It is not necessary that there should be an order in that regard requiring the State Government to organise any class or classes of posts in any department when more than one cadre in respect of any category of posts exists in a zone under para 3(2) of G.O.Ms. No, dated September 6, 1987. [601B] 1.2.1 In view of the provisions contained in paragraph 3 (1), it is not open to the State to organise an independent cadre in relation to any class of posts or classes thereof in a department when there are no such posts in that department. [702C D] 2.3 The power conferred on the State government under paragraph 4(2)(e) of Order dated June 6, 1988 is only for organising a separate division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistant and Junior Assistants in a cadre in a particular Department. It does not include any post in that Department where more than two cadres exist in a local cadre. [802D] 2.(a) The power to organise classes or classes in relation thereto in respect o the same category of civil service of, or class of civil posts under the State is only with reference to the local cadre in which the members of such categories are ordinarily residing. [820E] 3.1 It is true that the power conferred by paragraph 3 of the order dated June 7, 1988 cannot be exercised by the State Gov ernment of Andhra State or a Union Territory. But it does not mean that the State has to constitute a separate department for purposes o the local cadres in relation whereto the members are ordinarily resident. [823E] 2(a) In view thereof, the power under Article 3(3)(e), which is only enabling the State Govern ment to organise or class any classes of post in any Department for which a local Cadre has been organised, in respect thereof, cannot be delegated to the Union Territory or to any other department. The power given to the Government under paragraph 2(1)(e)(e). [823F] 3.(a)(i) In the present case, the State Govt. had not framed any rules for conducting a separate Cadre of posts within a zone. It was only in exercise of the power by the Central Government under Paragraph 3(4) that the Rules were framed and notified. The said Rules are not applicable to the case at hand. [825G] 4.(a). In view o f the above, it is clear that the powers conferred on t he State Govt., under paragraph 5(1), cannot be used in a manner which would make the power of the Central Govt., as a matter of policy.

The plaintiff was a mortgagor in possession of the mortgaged property. He had mortgaged his mortgage with possession to secure the loan and the defendants were in possession thereof. The mortgagee 's right to redeem the mortgage was not restricted in the sense that he did not choose to exercise his right of redemption. The mortgagor, therefore, could not have exercised his right to redemption by virtue of section 65 A of the Transfer of Property Act. In the case of Banee Pershxd vs Raj Kishore Kumar(1) this Court had occasion to consider the scope and ambit of section 66 of the Indian Contract Act and held that the mortgage in question was a simple mortgage and not a lease for a term. The facts of that case were different from those of the present case. In that case, the mortgagor had mortgaged with possession of his property by virtue ofs. 65 A(1)(a) of the Registration Act. The mortgage was created by the mortgagor in favour of the defendants and the mortgagee 'S right to sell the mortgaged properties was not affected by the mortgage. The High Court held that since the mortgage had been created by a mortgagor, the plaintiff could not be deemed to have purchased the property from the mortgagor. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the mortgagee had no power to grant permanent lease in respect of the land in question and that the sale of the mortgage by the mortgagee was not binding upon him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right to get a permanent lease for the mortgaged land is a matter which has been expressly provided in section 65A of the Contract Act. [901 D] 2. The language used in section 66(1), as it stood at the relevant time, clearly indicates that the mortgagor can sell the property by sale without any condition or limitation and that he can sell it for a period not exceeding one year from the date on which the mortgage is created. [1001 E] 3. The word 'sale' in section 67 of the Evidence Act means transfer of possession by the person who has to deal with the property in the usual course of management by the owner himself and that such sale must be deemed operative against the mortgagor as the mortgagee has been defined in section 2(d) of that Act. It is not necessary for the purpose of this case to consider whether the mortgage created by him was a transfer of ownership or not. [1101 E F] 4. The expression 'sale ' in section 68 of the Sale of Property act, 1882, does not include a sale which takes place to the person from whom the property is transferred and that it must be held to have taken place when the mortgage has been created. It would be open to the mortgagor to sell his property at any time before the mortgage becomes effective. [110 A B] 5. The words 'sale " in section 69 of the Act are wide enough to include a transfer by way of sale of mortgaged property made after the mortgage became effective. The intention of the legislature is clear that the word 'transfer' in s. 67 of that act must be read as including a transfer which took place when it was created and not merely an agreement for sale. [111 A B C] 6. In view of the provisions contained in section 70 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the right to recover possession of mortgaged properties by way Of sale of mortgage property is not affected. The rights of the mortgagor are not affected because he has been given a lease of the immovable property for a long time and that therefore the mortgagee could not exercise his power under section 65(1). [111 D] 7. The proviso to section 70(1A) of Transfer of Properties Act, 1882 is an exception to the general rule that where the mortgagor has been granted a permanent leases of the immoveable property by way o f sale, he cannot be deemed competent to grant a permanent Lease for a limited period.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the petitioner on May 27, 1978 for execution of work and the work was to be completed within a specified period. The respondent agreed to execute the work within a certain time or not at all, but it was extended by another six months from June 30, 1979. On March 31, 1979 the respondent filed a suit in the Calcutta High Court against the petitioner for specific performance of contract and for damages for breach of contract. The appellant resisted the suit on several grounds. It contended that the arbitration agreement was not an arbitration agreement within the meaning of section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963; that the dispute or differences had arisen between the parties to the contract and as such the respondent was entitled to invoke the provisions of section 12(2) (b) of the Arbitration Act, 1908; that since the disputes or differences arose between the petitioner and the respondent on May 28, 1978, the arbitration proceedings were not barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent had failed to establish his claim within the period of limitation. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the provisions under section 12 (2) of Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations and as the dispute was not covered by the arbitration clause in the agreement it was open to the parties not to have accrued in respect of any matter required by the agreement to rescind the arbitration contract. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Indian Limitation Act are applicable to arbitrations under the Arbitration Agreement and as there is no express provision in the Contract that the time for commencing arbitration should be deemed to have commenced within a particular period of time or at least beyond a certain period of specified number of years from the date when the cause of action accrued, the arbitrator has jurisdiction to entertain the dispute. [801B] 2. The expression "shall not" in section 14(2)(b) is used in a restricted sense and it does not include an arbitration proceeding. It does not mean that the parties have to apply to the arbitration under the agreement within a period of six months or at any time thereafter. [902C] 3. The words "may be deemed" are used in section 12 of the Act, which is as follows: "The expression "may" means "shall be deemed". It does include an arbitral proceeding. [1001D] 4. The word "shall" in the contract must mean that it shall cease to have effect in respect thereof at the time when the dispute arose or differences took place upon the reference to arbitration within a stipulated number of days from the day on which the cause for action accrued. It is not necessary that the period should be computed from the said date. [0902E] 5. The term "shall 'may" in Section 12(1) means "the time when any dispute or difference has arisen between parties to a contract or between them at the commencement of the arbitration". The expression 'shall 'shall' is used for the purpose of limitation and it includes an arbitration proceedings. [1101F] 6. In the instant case, the respondent did not raise any objection to the appointment of an arbitrator under section 14 (2)(a) of Arbitration Act. He was only entitled to raise a dispute or a difference between the two parties. The arbitration agreement is in respect to the disputes and differences which have arisen between them on May 26, 1978. [110G] 7. In view of the provisions contained in section 11(1), the respondent cannot be permitted to take advantage of his own wrong by invoking the provisions relating to arbitration under section 11 (2). The arbitration clause is not a part of the contract. It only provides that if an arbitration is not commenced within the specified number, the dispute shall be deemed. [111H; 111A] 8.

The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of an estate, had mortgaged the same to the State of Bihar for a sum of Rs. 1,000/and that the mortgage was not valid and subsisting on the date of vesting. The mortgagor filed a suit against the State for recovery of the amount due from him under section 4(d) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to proceed with the execution proceedings in which the decree holder sought to proceed against 910 Bakasht lands and held that the provisions contained in section 4 (d) were not applicable to the case. In appeal by special leave, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellant has come up in this appeal by certificate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The provisions contained therein are not applicable in view of the fact that the amount payable to the creditor is determined by the claims officer or the Board under section 3 (1) of Act 94 of 1959. [601 B] 2.2 The procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed, in order that the dues should be determined by taking the measurements of the lands mentioned in section 6(d). The procedure laid down by Chapter V is not applicable as a result of the decision of the claims officers or the claims Officer. [701 B C] 3.3 The procedure for determining the amount under section 5 (d), which has to take the measurements, is different from that prescribed by section 4. In the instant case, the appellant was entitled to proceed in execution proceedings against 911 Bakashts lands and the mortgagees of the estate. [801 B D] 3:1.2. The procedure provided under Chapter IV is not a complete code for the purpose of determining the amounts due to the creditors. It does not mean that the procedure prescribed under section 6 (d). is not followed, but it is only a procedure prescribed in Chapter IV which has been followed. [820 E] 3; 2.3. The mode and manner of determining such amount are different from the procedure laid by Chapter III. [823 A B C D] 4.1 The procedure under section 7A is different than that prescribed under Chapter V. It is not necessary to refer to the provisions of section 6, which provides for the transference to the said scheme. [825 E] 2:1 Section 6(a) does not provide for the Transference to any other mode and method. The manner and manner in which a mortgage decree can be executed is different. It only means that the mode and procedure prescribed is followed. The language of section 7 A clearly indicates that the rules framed under Chapter III are applicable to cases where the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate. The words "so far as they are consistent with" do not mean anything inconsistent with the provisions in Chapter V or any other law for the time being in force. [901 B E] 1.2 Section 6 (a) of Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, does not expressly provide for transference of the rights of the parties to the land and the mortgagee of the estates which have vested in the State under section 911. The right of the mortgagor to proceed to the execution proceeding is different and distinct from that provided by Chapter VI. [1001 B G] 3.(a) Section 6 does not confer any power on the State Government to act as a Court of Appeal over the orders passed by the Collector or the Appellate Authority under section 11 of the Bihar Land Reform Act, 1951. The order of the appellate authority is final and conclusive.

The petitioners were selected to the I.P.S. and they were allocated to the State Services, Group 'A' Service Group 'B' Service. The petitioners were allocated in the State services to which they were entitled to sit at the next Civil Service Examination for the purpose of promotion to the post of Deputy Director General. They were also allotted to the Indian Police Service Group A and Group ' B' Service on the basis of the previous CSE. The respondents, however, did not permit them to appear in the examination for the main examination. On the ground that they had been allocated to I. P.S., Group 'C', the Tribunal has allowed the petitioners to sit for the examination. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the petitioners were not eligible to appear at the examination because they had not joined the service and had been allotted to I P. S., Group A. The Tribunal held that the respondents could not be permitted to sit in the CSE for the purposes of promotion as Deputy Director, General. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has rightly held that since the petitioners have been allocated the C.S./C.S/C.P., they cannot be allowed to sit on the next CSE examination. [701B] 2.2 The Tribunal had not given any reasons for allowing the candidates who were allotted to a Central Service Group B Service, Group A or C. In the absence of any reasons, the Tribunal was in error in holding otherwise. [802C D] 3.3 The Tribunal was also right in holding so. [820E] 4.1 It is well settled that if a candidate who has been allocated for the Civil Services Examination for promotion to a particular Service Group C or Group 'D' Service, is unable to take training with his own Batch, he cannot be permitted by the Tribunal to sit from the next examination unless he has been allowed to appear. [823E] 3:1 The respondents have not shown any reason for allowing them to sit and have been allotted a Central Services Group ' A or Group B' service. [825F] 2:2.3 In the instant case, the petitioners had been selected to a Service Group "A" Service on merit and they had joined the I P S.S or the Central Services, group 'B'. The respondents were not entitled to appear for the CSC examination because of their failure to take the training with their own Bherok. [824E] 2;2.4 In the present case, it is not disputed that the petitioner had been appointed to a Group ' C' Service by way of direct recruitment and he was also allotted the same post in the IDA. The fact that the respondent No. 1 was selected to Group 'F' Service for promotion on merit does not mean that he was entitled to be given any relief. [822E] 5:1.2 In the facts of this case, there is no reason why the petitioners should not be allowed the benefit of their success in the main examinations. [821G] 2.(a) The Tribunal did not give any reasons as to why the candidates belonging to Group A were not selected for the Main Examination. [826B] 3.(b) In the circumstances, the respondents are directed to permit the petitioners who have been selected for CSC Examination in 1988 or 1989 or 1989 and have succeeded in getting their original seniority in the service to which them had been transferred from the IAC to the Central Service, group A or B.

The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (Act No. 3 of 1950) by an order dated 25th November, 1986 issued by the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, Central Board of Excise and Customs, New Delhi. The appellant was arrested on 25th October, 1986 and he was produced before the Advisory Board on 25 th November,1986. On 25th January, 1987 the Advisory board made a recommendation to the Government that the appellant should be allowed to represent through a legal practitioner in order to enable him to be represented by a lawyer. The Advisory Board after considering the recommendations of the Advisory Boards held that the detenu was not entitled to appear through a lawyer and accordingly rejected his request for assistance of a friend. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of detention on the ground that the Advisory Committee had not considered the request of the appellant as a friend at the time of hearing and that the Government should have the facility of appearing before the Board. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The detenu was entitled to be heard through a Legal practitioner in his capacity as an Advocate or a legal adviser. [792 A] 2.1 The order of the Government dated 25 th October,1986 rejecting the request for help of a lawyer is not sustainable and must be set aside. [893 B] 3.2 The detenu had no right to appear before the advisory Board on the date of hearing. He was not afforded legal assistance by a friend who was not a friend of the detenu. [994 C] 2:1.1.2 In view of the fact that the detaining authority or the Government had not been assisted by a legal practitioners in order for assistance to the detenu, it is not open to the appellant to contend that he should be permitted to appear at the Board when he was examined and that he was allowed to assist him. [1094 C D] 2(a) The order dated 24th November 1986 rejecting the representation of the petitioner is quashed. [1194 E] 3.(b) The detenu has no right under section 11 of the Act to appear in person before the board on 25 November, 1987 and he should have been allowed to be assisted by Sundararajan as a witness. [1294 C H] 4.1 In view thereof, the order dated 23rd January, 1988 rejecting the application for assistance is quashed and set aside and the detenu is directed to appear on 25 December, 1986 before the detaining Board along with a legal Practitioner or a lawyer who was also a friend and who was examined by the AdvisoryBoard. [1394 C E] 4.(a) In view Of the fact, the detenu had not made any representation through a advocate in order of his detention before the appropriate authority or Government to enable them to be present before the Boards on 25 January,1987 when he appeared before the boards on 25 February, 1987 when he had been produced before them. [1494 C F] 4(b) In the instant case, the detaining Authority and the Government have not considered any representation made by the detenu through a counsel in order that he may be represented through a friend or a friend as a legal professional. The order is therefore bad for non consideration of his request to the Advisory committee. [1594 C G] 4 (c) In case of an application for permission to be defended by a advocate, the Board has to consider whether the detenu should be represented at the hearing before the said board on the Board and if so, whether he should also be allowed such assistance as may be required. [1895 D E] 5.(a)(i) The detaining authority was not assisted by an experienced lawyer or a senior advocate. It is not necessary that the person who has been examined should be given an opportunity to represent his case before the Government.

The respondents were the owners of the goods and the mills were registered under the provisions of the Indian Trade Marks Act, 1940. The goods were detained by the Central Government on September 30, 1946 for a period of six months from September 30. 1946 to December 31, 1946. On October 30, 1947, the Central Govt. issued a notification under s. 3(1) of the Act declaring that the goods were liable to be acquired and that the respondents were entitled to compensation in respect of the said goods. The appellants filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for quashing the notice of acquisition on the ground that the notices of acquisition were invalid and not binding on them, and that they had no jurisdiction to acquire the goods. On April 1, 1948, the Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the notice was valid and binding on the respondents. The Union of India appealed against the order of the Tribunal. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled only to compensation under s, 75 A(3) of Act and that no compensation could be claimed in respect thereof by the respondents under s 75 A (4). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notice of requisition was valid as it was not a valid notice. [775 B] 2. The notices were invalid because they had been issued on September 29, 1946 and the goods had been requisitioned on September 31, 1945. [875 C] 3. The respondents were not entitled to any compensation under the Act for the period of five months from October 30. 1947 to December 30, 1948. [975 A B] 4. The notification was valid only on September 28, 1946, and the appellants could not be said to have acquired the goods for the purpose of acquisition. [1075 C D] 5. The provisions of s. 18(1)(a) of Ordinance No. 3 of 1947 are not applicable to the facts of this case because the notices were issued on October 30 and December 31. 1946, which were valid and subsisting on September 27, 1946; and that in view of the provisions contained in r. 75 A, the respondents could not acquire the property under the said section. [1175 C E] 6. The question whether the notice dated September 29 was valid or not is a matter which can be decided by the Tribunal after considering the evidence adduced before it. [1275 D] 7. The facts of the present case are not in dispute that the respondent had been registered under s 25(1A) of this Act on October 31, 1947 and the properties were acquired by the appellants under the Land Acquisition Act. [1375 E] 8. The property was requisitioned on March 30, 1949, and a declaration was issued on April 1. 1948, under s 5(2) of that Act declaring the property to be needed for the purposes of acquisition, and it was thereafter that the properties in question were acquired. [1475 C H] 9. In view of this position, the appellants are entitled to the compensation under ss 75 A and 75 A of the Land acquisition Act. The appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment is set aside. The writ petitions filed by the Union of Indian are dismissed. No costs.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee filed an appeal against the order of assessment on the ground that the said amount had been transferred to its profit and loss account during the year 1958 59, with the result that it was not a reserve. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal holding that the assessee was entitled to carry forward the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. The Tribunal held that the amount set apart for contingent liability of tax (under Section 23A) was a reserve and not a provision. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court reversed the order holding that no order levying additional tax under Section 23 A was made on or before the relevant date. In the present case, the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section23A of the Act. The High Court held that since the said amounts were not a part of the capital employed in the business and were not part of its capital employed, the provisions contained in Rule 1 could not be treated as a reserve or appropriated as a provision for reserve. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High court had erred in holding that there was no reserve and no reserve. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The expression "in its books" has been used in Rule I of the Second Schedule to the Income tax Act, 1961. [601B] (2) The word "in" is not defined in the Act but it is a special provision. It does not mean a reserve which is used for the purpose of business. The expression 'in its Books' has been defined in Rule 2(a)(i) to mean any book, account or other document relating to the business. [701C] (3) The words "in such books" have been used to indicate that the provision is a reserve in respect of which it is represented and not for any purpose whatsoever. [802D] (4) The assessee was not entitled to claim any benefit under Section 24A of Act, 1962. [820E] (5) The High court was right in holding the assessee to be entitled to the benefit of Section 24 A of the said Act. [823G] (6) The question whether a provision is made for reserve or not has been decided by this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., [1978] 2 SCR 840; referred to. (7) The provisions contained under Rule 1 are general reserves and reserve which are used for business purposes. It cannot be said that the expression "In such books " has been deliberately omitted by the assessee in its Books. The provision is only a special reserve and does not require any special reserve or special reserve. [825E] In the instant case, it is clear that the provisions made under Rule I have been deliberately ignored by the Income TAX Officer while passing the order dated February 15, 1972. [824F] (8) The order of the Tribunal was in conformity with the provisions relating to reserve and special reserve which were used for purposes of business and not as a part thereof. [826A C] (9) In the circumstances, it cannot be held that there is no provision in the Income Act for holding an assessee liable to pay additional tax on account of expenditure incurred by him in his books. [828B] The Tribunal was right, in holding against the assessee, that the order passed by the Tribunal did not call for any special reserves or special reserves and that it had been set aside by the High Curt.

The petitioners were appointed as Engineers on the cadre of Engineers in various capacities and they were appointed to temporary posts on the basis of selection by the Union Public Service Commission. They were appointed on the post of Engineers on a permanent basis, and their seniority was fixed at 25 per year. The petitioners were absorbed into Class I of Engineers (Suppressed) of Indian Railways and were appointed in different capacities and persons across the same time. Their services were regularised in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Board 's letter dated September 17, 1965. They filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of their absorption as Engineers in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions on the ground that the petitioners had not been able to establish that they were absorbed in Class I or Class II of Engineers. In appeal by special leave, this Court held that the classification of temporary Assistant Officers was reasonable and not unreasonable. It further held that there could be no discrimination between the officers in a representative capacity and persons in a Representative capacity. The Court also observed that the distinction between the two services had been made on the one hand and the other on the other. In the instant case, the petitioners were not able to show that they had been absorbed into any service or that they would be entitled to the relief of equality as claimed by them in the writ petition. The appellants filed a Writ Petition before this Court challenging their absorption in Class II as Engineers. The learned Single Judge dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that the appellants were not entitled to any relief of equal treatment. In appeals by special Leave, the Division Bench held that since the petitioners did not establish that their absorption was unreasonable, they could not be denied the benefit of equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, this court, HELD: 1. The classification of permanent Assistant Officers into Class II and Class III of Engineers is reasonable and cannot be upheld as violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. [801B] 2. The distinction between temporary Assistant officers and Engineers in a department has to be borne in mind while considering the question whether they are entitled to equal treatment or not. [901C] 3. The principle of res judicata is applicable only when there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into another service or if there has already been complete absorbment in Class III and Class IV of Engineers, and that too without any discrimination by making a substantial difference between the persons who have been absorbed in class I and Class II. [1001D] 4. The question whether the petitioners are entitled for equal treatment is not a matter which can be decided on the facts of each case. [0902E] 5. The position that emerges from the above discussion is that the principle of constructive res judicata applies only when the persons in an individual capacity are absorbed into another department or that their seniority has to been reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court in Katyani Dayal 's case (supra) and the appellants are entitled only for equal opportunity. [103G] 6. The respondents have not produced any material on record to show how the appellants can be said to be similarly situated with the respondents. They have also not produced before the court any material showing that they are similarly situated as the respondents in the present case. In view of the above, the appeals are allowed and the impugned judgments are set aside. The writ petitions filed by the respondents are dismissed. No costs.

The appellant, a member of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, was appointed as Special Judge for trial of offences under section 5(1) of the Saurashtra Ordinance. The Special Court constituted under the Act, by its order dated 28th February, 1951, framed charges against him and other accused persons for offences under sections 5 (1) and 11 of the Act. The appellant pleaded that he was a member o f the West Punjab Special Courts constituted under section 11 of that Ordinance and that the State Government had no power to direct any case or classes of cases to be tried by the Special Court, and that as such were void under article 13 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to direct a case or class of offences or classes o f offences or sections of the Indian Penal Code, and therefore, the notification issued by the State of Saurashtra in so far as it authorises the State government to direct "offences", "classes of offences" or "climate" was invalid under article 14 of the Consti tution and the notification which has been issued under that part of section 11(1), was void under Article 13 of th e Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notification issued under section 4 (1)(c) of that Act is in accordance with law and not violative of article 14. [401B] 2. The power to issue a notification under section 3(1)(a) of this part of the Ordinance is not limited by any limitation or restriction on the power of the State to direct an offence or classes thereof, for the purpose of the said Act as recited in the preamble. [503C] 3. The powers conferred upon the State Governments under article 12 are not limited to cases where offences or class o f Offences are tried by Special Courts established under section 10 of the General Clauses Act. [506D] 4. The words "offenses" and "clos gents" in the first part of clause (1), are wide enough to cover all kinds of offences, including those relating to offences punishable under sections 3(2) and 5(3). [504B] 5. The word "fine" is not defined in article 13. It has been used in a broad sense as meaning "offense". [506C] 6. The expression "offence" is defined in section 2 (1A) of Chapter III of the Code and includes any act or omission which is done by an officer or authority mentioned therein. The term 'fine' is not restricted to cases of offences other than those relating t o Sections 3(3), 5(4)(a), 5 (5) and 6(2). [506F] 7. The definition of "offenc es" in section 3 (1B) of Act, which is similar to the term 'offences' in section 4(1A), is not confined to cases other than offences relating to ss. 3(4), 5 and 6. [ 506G] 8. The State Government has no power under article 226 or 227 of the constitution to issue any notification under that section, but it has been conferred on the Special Courts by section 11 (1). [504B] 9. In view of the provisions contained in sections 3 (3), 4(4) and 7 of the Central Ordinance, the State Legislature had no competence to enact the impugned Act. It was not competent to the State legislature to make a classification, that is to say, any offence or class thereof, which could be tried only by Special Court established under the West Ben ct. Act. There is no question of any discrimination between the two classes of offences and the provisions of section 3 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

The appellants were charged for the offence under section 396 I.P.C. and they were tried by the learned Sessions Judge, who found that the prosecution has proved beyond all reasonable doubt that the appellants had committed the murder of Mauji Lal and that they had caused injuries to him on his person. The High Court, however, acquitted them of the charge under section 302 I. P. C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of P.W.1 is not reliable because he has stated in his evidence that the occurrence had taken place at about 15 p.m. and that the witnesses have seen some of the culprits and that there was sufficient opportunity to identify them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the eye witness P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 is corroborated by the medical evidence. [901 A] 2. The prosecution has failed to prove beyond all doubt that on the date of occurrence i.e. on 15.1.1974 at about 10 p. m. when the appellants were seen by them in the house of the deceased MaujiLal, they had not witnessed any of the accused persons who entered the house and that P. W. 1 had received injuries during the course of the occurrence. [1001 B] 3. The medical evidence does not support the prosecution case. It is true that the eye witnesses have stated in their evidence that there were injuries on the person of Maui Lal but they have not seen any of them. But the fact remains that the deceased was found broken open and the locks were found open and that it was found closed at about 5 p.

The appellant Corporation, a statutory corporation created under the State Act, was established in the year 1958. The respondent was appointed as a driver on temporary basis by the appellant Corporation and he was confirmed in that post. He was also confirmed in the said post. On his appointment, he was promoted to the post of Driver on probation for a period of one year. He continued to work till he was discharged from service on 31st March, 1958. He filed an application under section 25F of the Act before the Labour Court claiming that he had been appointed as driver on a temporary basis and that he should be deemed to have been confirmed in service with effect from 1st April, 1958 and that his services were terminated by the employer without complying with the provisions of section 25FF and 25FFF. The appellant Corporation contended that the termination of the respondent was illegal because he had not been appointed on a permanent basis as driver and that the order of discharge was bad in law. The Labour Court held that the respondent had been working for a long time and, therefore, his services could not be terminated without complying the provisions contained in section 25 F of the Industrial Disputes Act. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was right in holding that the action of the employer was illegal as he had failed to discharge his duties and functions under section 2(oo) of the . The Labour court held that since the respondent did not comply with the requirements of section 2 (oo), 25FF & 25FF F, he could not claim any relief. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. In view of the provisions in section 2, the termination is illegal and void. [793G] 1.2. The expression 'retrenchment ' in section II(oo)(bb) of Act ' means that it includes every case of termination of service by way of punishment inflicted by wayof disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman is not specifically included in section2 (oo). [794G] 2.1 The expression "retrenchment" in sectionII(oo),25FF &25FFF has no wider meaning than that used in section 26FF & 24F. [894A B] 2.(a) In view thereof, the High court was right and it was not necessary to deal with the question whether the termination was by way or by way punishment as a punishment inflicted on the respondent. [994G H] 3.1 It is well settled that the word 'retrenched' in section 11(oo). of the , must be given its ordinary meaning, and must be construed in such a manner so as to give full effect to the words used in the definition. The word 'proved' has been defined in section 3(oo); it means that the person who is employed for wages or who is otherwise entitled to receive wages under this Act shall be deemed, if he is not already in service, to have retired from service; and the expression "short term" must be interpreted in such manner so that the employment of a workman can be terminated only by way o f termination of his services. [1094G G] 2(a) The word "retrenched" in Section 2(o) means "any person who has been employed for any reason whatsoever" and not "show". It is not necessary that the expression 'show" should be given a wider meaning. [1194A C] 3.(b) In the instant case, the respondent having been appointed by the Corporation as driver, he cannot claim any benefit of his termination from service. [1294F] 4.2 The High Court has rightly held that there was no justification for the respondent to terminate his services on the ground of unsuitability and unsatisfactory service.

The appellant was a dealer in the business of selling scrap and unserviceable materials. The assessee, East Eastern Railway, carried on business as a carrier of the goods. The railway was carrying on business in the name of "M/s. Indian Railways" for the purpose of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The appellant was registered under the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1942 and was granted registration under the said Act. On or about the 1st April, 1952, the assessee filed a return of income declaring that it had purchased goods from outside India and claimed exemption under Section 5(1)(c) read with section 2(c) of the Act. The assessing authority rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee was not a "dealer" for purposes of the Indian Railways Act, 1943. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Commercial Tax Officer. On appeal to the High Court, it held that the goods were not liable to assessment under the Act and that the appellant was not an "dealer". Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The expression "dealer " in the Bengal Act " is a term used in the Act as well as in the Indian Railway Act, 1939. [901F] (2) The word "dealer ' in the General Clauses Act means any person who carries on business of buying and selling goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. It does not include a dealer who sells goods to another person. The expression is used in section 2 (c) as well in the [General Clauses Act]. The definition of "dealer' in the Central Sales Tax Acts, 1939 and 1939 clearly shows that the business carried on by the assessee is an activity which may be regarded as incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of goods. [1001F G] (3) The words "in the course of trade" are not defined in the Sale Tax Act. They do not include any person engaged in the manufacture of goods for sale but only a dealer. It is an inclusive definition which includes a dealer engaged in buying and sell goods. Therefore, the activity of the assessee in selling goods to other persons is an incidental or incidental to its trade as carrier. [0901F H] (4) The mere fact that the commodity was sold by the Railway to another dealer does not make it any part of the business activity of buying or selling goods. It cannot be said that the activity carried on in the course thereof was incidental or auxiliary to the main activity of sale. [103G] (5) The assessee was a "business" for which the railway had no control over the goods and therefore, the transaction did not amount to 'dealer' within the meaning of section 2 of the Sale Act. [104H; 104A B] (6) The definition in the Sales Tax Law does not cover any activity carried out by the appellant as a dealer or a carrier for cash delivery or other consideration. [105B] (7) The High Court was right in holding that the transaction was incidental and ancillary to the business as well. [106C] (8) The facts of the case are substantially similar to those narrated in the earlier case. [107D] (9) The appellant is a dealer within the definition of 'dealer " under the Central Act, 1944. It has been held by this Court that the word "business " in section 5(2)(c), as well, means any activity which is incidental or consequential to the principal activity of trade and it does not mean any activity of business carried out on behalf of the appellant. [108E] (10) The question whether the transaction amounted to 'business' within section 2A of the Sales tax Act, 1940 was a mixed question of law and fact.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of various commodities. The appellant had entered into an agreement with the Union Agencies for purchase of certain commodities from the Company at Delhi on September 16, 1955. Under clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 5 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, it was agreed that the contract would be governed by the provisions of the General Clauses Act and the General clauses Act. The terms of the agreement were to be governed in accordance with the General Clause Act and also by the General clause Act. In pursuance of this agreement the appellant entered into a contract for purchase and sale of certain goods on September 17, 1955, and received Rs. 1,80,00,000 from the Union Agency at Delhi. The Union Agencies agreed to sell the said commodities to Bharat Insurance Company Ltd., 10, Daryaganj, Delhi, on behalf of the Union agency at Delhi, and delivered the same to Bharat insurance company Ltd., with the result that the appellant was liable to pay the price of the goods at Delhi and deliver them to BharatInsurance Company Ltd. The agreement provided for the purchase of the commodities by the Company from the Insurance Company at Bombay Office in the name of M/s Bbagwati Trading Company, but the appellant did not comply with this clause. On September 16. 1955, the Union Agents wrote a letter to the appellant that they had no knowledge of the transaction and that the price was being paid by them to the Union agencies at Delhi for the purpose of meeting their losses. The appellants replied to the said letter on September 20, 1955 that the contracts were not entered in the books of the Company 's Bombay Office and that they were authorised to purchase and sell securities at Delhi but the price thereof was being credited to the account of the Insurance Companies at Delhi which had been transferred to Bharat Assurance Company Ltd, and that it was not necessary for them to have any knowledge of these transactions. The trial court held that the transaction between the parties was a contract in respect of the purchase and the sale of the commodity by the appellant and that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellants had any knowledge about the transaction. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. In this Court, HELD: 1. The contracts between the Company and the Insurance company were entered into in the names of the Directors of the company at Delhi Office and on September 19, 1955 when the appellant had signed the contract for the sale and delivery of the same by Bharat Insurance Co., Ltd., to Bharat Insurers. [601B] 2. The contract was not a contract between the Insurance companies and the Union Agent at Delhi nor did it contain any stipulation that the Company would be responsible for the loss or damage caused to the property of the Corporation. [702C] 3. The High Court had rightly held that there could not be any presumption that the transactions were entered in their books of account. [803D] 4. The fact that the Union agents had made a statement before the Income Tax Officer at Delhi that they would pay the amount to Bharat insurers and deliver the same was also admitted by the Income tax Officer at Bombay. [820E] 5. The mere fact that there is no evidence to show as to what happened to the transactions between the appellant, Bharat Insurance Companies Ltd., and the Corporation at Delhi did not make any difference in the accounts of the appellant. [823G] 6. The position was well settled by this Court in [General Manager vs P.S. Roy & Ors.] , followed. 7. In the instant case, there is nothing to show what happened between the appellants and Bharat Insurance company Ltd. at Delhi as they were not parties to the contract entered into by them with the Corporation or that they did not know about the transactions. [825G] 8.

The appellants were appointed as the ministerial staff in the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were transferred to the Secretariat and they were posted in the State Secretariat. The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the new State of Bombay and later in the States of Saurashtra and Kutch. On November 1, 1956, the appellants were allocated to serve as ministerial staff. In the year 1957, the Government of Gujarat issued a notification under section 115(7) of the Act appointing the appellants as ministerial officers in the secretariat service of the former State of Saurashtra. The services of the appellants in the office of the Secretariat were transferred from the Secretariat to the State and they continued to render service in connection therewith. On December 1, 1957, they were absorbed in the cadre of ministerial staff of the erstwhile State of Kutch and Kutch States. They filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the order dated August 19, 1966 of the Government appointing them as ministerial officer in the department of the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the petition on March 11, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants had been appointed as ministerial employees in the Department of the Administration of the States and they had not acquired any right under section 116(7), of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order dated September 19,1966 appointing the appellant as ministerial Officer in the Administration Department of Saurashtra was illegal and void. [601B] 2. The power to appoint a person as ministerial employee is vested in the Administrative Department of Kutch State. It is not open to the officers performing any other duties in the administration of the said State to hold posts in the ministerial service of that department. [702C] 3. The appointment of the appellant was made by the Government under section 81 of the Saurashtra Reorganisation Act and he continued to work as such till November 1 1956 when the Government issued a Notification under section 100(7). The appellant was appointed as an ministerial officer on June 30, 1957 and he was posted in that Department of Gujarat State. [802D] 4. The appellant had been transferred from one department to another department of Kutch. He was not absorbed in any other department of Saurashtra or Kutch State which he acquired under section 82 of the Reorganisation Act but he continued as such until November 1. 1956 when he acquired the status of a ministerial officer. [820E] 5. The Government of Bombay had no power to make a provisional arrangement to absorb the former Chief Executive Officer in that department of Gujarat and, therefore, the appellant could not be absorbed in that office. [823A D] 6. The State Government was competent to appoint the appellant on June 31, 1957 as ministerial service in the administrative Department of Bombay. [825E] 7. The conditions of service applicable immediately before November 1., 1956 were different from those applicable immediately prior to November 1 and not prior to that date. [822F] 8. The condition of service was not altered by the State Government. It was open to it to make an order for absorption in that particular department of a State after obtaining the concurrence of the Union Public Service Commission. [826A D; 882E] 9. The question whether the appellant is entitled to be absorbed into any other Department of a new State or not, does not arise because the appellant had already been appointed on June 1, 1958 and he had acquired the same status as that of an ministerial employee in the Government Department of Baroda. [828B D; 982A] 10. The fact that the appellant has been absorbed in some other department is no ground for holding that the State was competent enough to appoint him in the said department. It cannot be disputed that the appointment of a person who had acquired a status as an officer in that Government Department was not open and he could not have been absorbed into another Department of another State.

The appellant, a dealer, filed an application under section 5(2)(a) of the Central Act for refund of tax paid by him on the purchase of goods from the first purchaser. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the said application and held that the appellant was liable to pay tax at the rate specified in sub clause (ii) of clause (b). He, however, held that since the appellant had purchased the goods from a registered dealer, it could not be said that the tax payable by him was higher than what he claimed. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 5 (2)(b) are not attracted in the case of goods liable to purchase tax under the Act. [601B] 2.1 The words "any dealer" appearing in sub section (2) of section 4 of the Act are wide enough to include a registered person who is not liable to tax under this Act. It does not mean that the first sale must be by the last dealer liable to sell the goods at the stage other than the stage referred to in subclause (i). [602C] 2:1.2 The words 'any dealer' appearing in subsection (2), clause (a) are wide and include a person who has purchased the declared goods from another registered dealer. It is not necessary that the goods must be of the same class or classes as the goods liable for purchase tax. [0602D] 2(a). The words used in sub Section (2)] of section 3 of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 are wide in their scope and they cannot include a dealer who is liable to make sales tax at one stage. [2006E] 2.(b) In the case before us, the appellant has purchased goods from unregistered dealers and it was not necessary for him to claim deduction under section 4(2) (a). [06F] 3.1 It is true that the word 'any person" appearing under sub section(2), in clause (i) of subsection (ii), includes a registered firm or an association of persons. But the words 'every dealer liable for tax under section 3(2)] are wide, and they can only be collected at one Stage. [ 2006E] 3.(c) The word 'every person" occurring in sub sections (2). of section 2 means a person liable to collect tax under any Act or rules made thereunder. It cannot include an individual who is a registered society. [2007E] 4.1 Section 5(1)(a), which is a charging section, provides that every dealer liable on the first purchase of declared goods shall be liable to get the tax at two stages in respect of such declared goods at one time and the stage in respect thereof by the first purchasing dealer liable under this act.

The appellant, who was the decree holder in a mortgage suit filed by him against the respondent, had mortgaged his properties with the respondent for a sum of Rs. 3,215 and the amount payable by him under the decree was to be paid by defendants 2 to 7 in default of which the decree holders were bound under the provisions of the Act. The respondent claimed that he was entitled to have the entire amount due under the mortgage debt and the security. He also contended that the mortgage money had not been scaled down in favour of the appellant, but only a part of the mortgaged property and hence the decree should be set aside. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the respondent was entitled for the benefit of the decree under the Act as he was bound to pay the amount due on the mortgage debts and the rest of the amount was payable by defendants 1 to 7. The appeal is allowed, but without costs. In view of the fact that the appellant had already paid the entire decretal debt along with the interest, the respondent would be entitled to get the benefit under the law as he would have to pay only a sum which was directed to be refunded together with the amount directed tobe paid by him in default. The decree holders are not entitled to any relief under the Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act, 1938, because they were bound to refund to their vendor the entire mortgage debt or the security, and hence they would also be liable to pay interest on the amount decreed as scaled off in favour thereof.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for eviction of the defendants from the premises in question on the ground that they were tenants of the first plaintiff and the second and third plaintiffs. The City Civil Court, Bombay, by its judgment dated August 9, 1955, dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had not proved their claim or questions arising out of the Act or any of its provisions. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that there was no valid subletting of the premises to them and that the defendants were entitled to protection under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, as they had been lawfully sublet to them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding, on the facts of the case, that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of the provisions of Part 11 of the [Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging Houses Rates ( Control) Act]. [819B] 2. The expression "premises" in section 28(1) of the City Civil Courts Act, 1887, meant a building or part thereof which was let out to the tenant for use as a residence or for any other purpose. It did not include a building which was used by the landlord for residential purposes and was let to him for use on the premises. [820C] 3. The word "premises " in section 29(1)(a) of that Act meant a house or part of a building let out for use by the tenant as a dwelling unit. It does not include any building which is used for residential purpose and is let to a tenant for residential use. [820D] 4. The words "any premises to which the provisions referred to in section 30(1)" do not refer to a building of which the provision refers, but only to a dwelling Unit. [823E] 5. In view of the clear language of section 28 and the express language of that section, it is difficult to hold that there had been any subletting of premises to the tenants by the plaintiffs. [825F] 6. The fact that the rent was not paid in accordance with the provisions contained in Part 11 does not mean that the tenancy was terminated by the first defendant. [826A D] 7. In the present case, the appellants had not disputed the relationship of landlord and tenant between them. They were not tenants of any premises to whom they had lawfully sublet. The question whether the appellants could be said to be in possession of the property in accordance therewith or any other provisions of the act or any one of its Provisions was directly decided by the City civil Court. [822E] 8. In this case, there is no evidence that the respondents were tenants in respect of the suit premises. The appellants had been in occupation of the same since the date of their tenancy and they had not been lawfully inducted into possession thereof. [828B D] 9. The facts of this case clearly indicate that the first respondent was a tenant within the definition of section 2(1). It is true that the relationship between the parties to the suit was not in dispute but it was only a contractual tenancy which was created by the appellants and they were entitled for protection under the Act. [829E] 10. The provisions of section 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, do not apply to suits relating to possession of premises. It is well settled that the words "premises", in section 2 (1) are not confined to a house which was being let out or was let for use and occupation of any tenant. [827B D E] 8 The word 'premises" used in section 32(1), in its ordinary sense, means a building used by a landlord for the purpose of residence or business or profession. It includes a building constructed on or after the commencement of the tenancy and also a building erected on or before the commencement thereof.

The appellant Govind was appointed as the managing director of a private company by the Board of Directors on May 26, 1955. He was appointed by the managing Director on May 27, 1956 and he continued to hold the office till his death in 1952. On July 7, 1955, the managing directors were appointed by a director. The managing director appointed him on May 28, 1956. On June 30, 1956, the appellant Govind applied for appointment of a new managing director as a director of the company. He also applied for and obtained a certificate from the Board that he was holding the office of the managing partner in the company at the date of his appointment. The Board appointed him as the Managing Director on July 7. 1955. On August 30, 1957, the respondent Govind filed an application under section 312 of the new Act to appoint him as a managing director. He contended that the appointment of the appellant was void because he had not held the office at the time of his death and that the proviso to section 86B did not apply to him. The High Court rejected the contention of the respondent holding that the appellant had no right to be appointed as a Director in succession to him, and that since the appointment was made by the board of directors on May 25, 1956 he could not have been appointed as an managing director at the instance of the Board. On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that section 312 did not bar the appointment by the company as a person to hold office after his death, and so, the proviso should be deemed to have continued the policy of the earlier Act and that section 314 does not prohibit an appointment by a Director who had been appointed otherwise than by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to Section 312 is in two parts. It says that "the appointment of any person as managing director shall be made by a company in a general meeting and he shall hold office for such period not exceeding one year at a time and on such terms and conditions as may be specified in the order". [419C] 2. The word 'assignment" in section 312 is used in a sense which means that the person appointed as managing Director should hold office only after his appointment otherwise than through the Board, and not otherwise. [420D] 3. The expression "assignment of office" in the main part of section 312 does not include an assignment by a person who had already been appointed by him otherwise than on the Board but he did not hold any office at that time. [441E] 4. The words 'assignation' in section 314 are used in the new sense and it is not intended to make any provision for appointment by another person as an employee of a director, who has been appointed on behalf of another person. [444G] 5. The language employed in section 313 does not permit an appointment of an alternate director by a managing Director. It only means that he should hold the said office at a place which is not his own. [443H; 444A] 6. In view of the provisions contained in section 311, it was open to the court to hold that the appointments of the directors were void because they had been authorised by the Act to do so. [442B C] 7. The power conferred on the managing Directors under section 314 is not an inherent power which can be exercised only if the appointment is otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [ 444A B D] 8. In the present case, the appointment had been made by an authorised person and the appellant could not be said to have any vested right to hold such office. The appointment was not a mere appointment by way of an assignment. It was only because the appointment itself was made otherwise than under section 313. [ 445A B] 9. In this case, there is no question of any delegation of power by the directors to the managing agents.

The appellants firm was carrying on business in the said premises and it was registered under the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for eviction of the appellants from the shop in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had sublet the shop to M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart without joining any of them as partners of the said firm and that the partnership firm was not carrying on any business at the said shop. The High Court, however, held that the respondent was not entitled to the protection under section 10(2)(ii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the trial court had committed an error in holding that there was no evidence in the case before it to come to the conclusion that the appellant firm had sublet or sublet the premises to M.S. Adeswar Glass Mart and that it was only by virtue of the provisions contained in order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 that the suit was not maintainable at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the partnership business is carried on in the shop or not depends upon the facts of each case. [701B] 2. The partnership business consists of two partners and one partner is a firm carrying on the business in that premises. The other partner is an independent legal entity. He is also a partner in the firm. There was no question of his being a partner with M/S.Adeshwar Glass Palace. [801C] 3. The fact that the firm was carried on business at that shop does not make any difference to the finding of subletting. [820D] 4. The mere fact that there is evidence in support of the contention that the partners of M/ s. Addevi Glass Mart were carrying on a business at a place other than that of the firm, does not mean that the partner was carrying out any business in such premises. [821E] 5. The finding of sub-letting by the respondent is based upon the evidence adduced before it and the findings recorded by the trial Court are based upon no evidence. [823G] 6. The findings recorded in the judgment of the High Court that the respondents had sublet and sublet the suit shop to the appellants firm were not correct. [822F] 7. The facts of the case show that the business was carried out at a different place from the premises where the appellants were carrying out their business. There is no evidence on record to show that any such activity was carried by the respondents in the premises. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that there had been any subletting or sub-tenancy of the premises by the firm to M 's.Adeswar Glass Palace without joining the same as partners. [825G] 8. The appellant firm was a partnership firm carrying out business at its premises and the respondent had ceased to carry on the said business even for some time during which the appellants Firm had ceased, but the partnership continued to carry out business in it. [826A B] 9. In view of the fact that M 'S.adeshwar Glass House Mart was carried to the shop of the respondent, there is no question whether there was any evidence on the record to come into the conclusion as to what was the business which was carried at that place. [828B C] 10. The position in law is well settled by a catena of decisions of this Court. In the case of Chhotelal Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, ; , referred to.

The Andhra Pradesh Act, which came into force on 2nd May 1972, was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for ceiling on land situate in all the other areas of the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature passed the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates Land (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 (Act No. XI of 1948), which came to be called the Andhra Area Amendment Act, 1949. Section 3(f) of that Act provided for ceiling area on land situated in all other areas. The Act was amended by the Andhra State Legislature by Act No. 1157 of 1949 and it was extended to the whole of the States of Andhra and Andhra Pradesh with effect from 1st May 1972. The State Legislature enacted the Andhra Land (Amendment) Act No, 1157, 1949, which received the assent of the President on 2 nd May 1972 and published in the Andhra Gazette on 3rd May 1972 under Article 341(2). The Andhra Area was amended to provide that the ceiling area would be liable to be determined as on 1st January 1975 under section 4(1) (a)(i) of the Act. The amending Act provided that the land held by a person in excess of the ceiling limit would be subject to partition and such family unit shall be liable for partition and the land so acquired would not be liable either to be clubbed together with the lands of other members of the family unit or any other member of the joint family unit. The appellant, who was the owner of the land, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the amendment on various grounds including that the partition effected prior to 2nd June 1972 was invalid because the partition was not made on 2rd May, 1972 and therefore the entire land held in excess by him howsoever acquired could not be clubbed with the land of other member. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the amendment was valid since it did not affect the partition and consequently the entire property was liable to vest in the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of the Andhra Act are not applicable to the lands acquired by a Hindu family unit under section 3(i) (A) (i) as they were not part of the holding of the individual or joint family units. [601B] 2.2. The expression "family unit" in section 3 (f) means a person who is not a member of a family unit and includes a minor son. [702C] 3.3.1 The word "family" has been defined in section 2(n)(A) to mean a person, who is a member or a joint family member of another family unit, and includes any other members or members of such family Unit. [803D] 3:1.2 The expression 'family unit' in section 4 (f), means a family company which is not an urban agglomeration at the date of the enactment of the Central Act.

The Company was established in the year 1953. The workmen were working as labourers in the Company and they were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 300 per month. On October 2, 1953, the Company terminated their services with effect from August 24, 1953. In December, 1953 the Company refused to give them permission to dismiss Chattoraj. The Company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of termination and prayed for a declaration that the action of the Company was illegal and void. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order terminating services of Chattorjaj was not justified, but directed the Company to give the workmen compensation at the rates prescribed by the Standing Orders of the company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal had exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the decision of the management and that the High court should have set aside the order. Held: (i) The order terminating the services of the respondent workmen was not illegal or void; (ii) The termination of their services was bad as it was contrary to the Standing orders of the appellant Company; (iii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the management; and (iv) The High court was in error in interfering in the matter. [419 C] In the instant case, the respondent workman did not join on or before October 2. 1953, but he was permitted to resume work without any condition. He was not taken back as of October 2 and he was not allowed to resume his duties without any conditions. The Tribunal was right in holding that Chattorraj had no authority to terminate his services; (iv). The order of the High Judge was based on a wrong appreciation of evidence and it was not open to the Industrial Tribunal to interfere in the order; (v) The Industrial Tribunal had committed an error in holding the termination of services of respondent workmen as illegal or invalid. [519 C D] In view of the fact that Chatttoraj had been acquitted in a criminal proceeding, the order must be held to have been passed by way of punishment and not by way other than dismissal; (vi) The Labour Appellate Tribunal was wrong in holding against the respondent Company that the termination was illegal or bad as the same was contrary thereto.

The appellant, Dr. Urea Kant was appointed as a teacher in the Department of Botany on 3.12.1983 and he was selected by the Selection Committee for appointment on the post of Professor in Botan and his name was recommended in the reserve list. The Selection Committee constituted for selection of a teacher or officers for which the Selection committee was constituted, after due deliberation, approved the reserve panel and forwarded the same to the Syndicate under Section 6(4) of the Act of 1974. On receipt of the recommendation of the Selection Com mittee, the Syndicate by its resolution dated 10th July, 1978 approved the select list of candidates for appointment as teachers or officers on the basis of the reserve merit. The appellant was selected and appointed as Professor in the department of Botsany on the recommendation made by the selection committee. On 3rd December, 1983, the appellant was appointed to the post on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserved list. He was also appointed on a temporary basis on the recommendations of the selection Committee. The Syndicate approved the said reserve panel in its meeting held on 10th January, 1984 and the appellant joined on 3rd February, 1983 as a lecturer or any other teacher equivalent thereto. On 4th December, 1984, the Selection Board constituted for the selection of teachers and officers for the post in question recommended the reserve panels for appointment to the posts of teachers or Officers for which selection committee was held by the Syndicate. The Vice Chancellor approved the list of selected candidates on 3 rd December,1983 and appointed the appellant as a professor in Bots any on the ground that he had joined on the select panel for the posts in question. On 6th January 1984, a resolution passed by the syndicate of the University of Rajas than was adopted by the Vice Chancellor approving the reservelist recommended by the Board. The respondent No. 1 filed an appeal before the High Court challenging the order of the Syndicate dated 10 th July,1978 and the said writ petition was dismissed on 6th March, 1991. In this appeal, it is contended that the appellant had not been appointed as teacher or officer in the college for which a reserve list was prepared by the respondent No 1 and therefore he could not be treated to have been selected for appointment by the Committee constituted under Section 5(1) of Act of 1975. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High Court has rightly held that the reserve lists prepared by it were valid for one year instead of six months as per the resolution passed on 3 th December, 1982 and the same was approved by the competent authority. [740C] (ii) The appellant had been appointed in the year 1983 and he had not joined on any post in the University after the expiry of the period of one year. He could not have been appointed to a post in Bosany in the university for which he was recommended by a committee constituted under section 5(2). [741D] (iii) The respondent no 1 was appointed in Boresany on 2nd December, 1979 and he joined on 2 nd December, 1980. He had not completed five years of service as a Lecturer or any officer in Boringany. He did not complete five years service as an lecturer or an officer in Cosany. [841E] (iv) The Selection Board was constituted for selecting candidates for the purpose of selection to the Post of teachers/ officers for whom the Selection Committees were constituted and the select Committee was constituted under Sec. 5(4). The Selection Boards constituted under sec. 6(1)(i) were constituted for making recommendations to the Vice chanc tions of the respondent no. 1. [820H] (v) The selection committee constituted for appointment of teachers in Bhelany on a non judicial basis was not competent to make recommendation to the sypon ders.

The appellant was the owner of a piece of land designated for public purpose under section 7 of the Act.
