The appellant filed an application before the State Government for sanction under section 10 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on July 8, 1964. The State Government sanctioned the development plan and sanctioned the same on July 9, 1961. On August 5, 1963 the appellant applied for permission to construct a building in the area designated for a public purpose. The application was rejected by the local authority on September 7, 1964 on the ground that the construction of the proposed building had not been completed within the prescribed period of ten years and that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of sections 4 and 11(3) of the . The appellant challenged the validity of the sanction under sections 10 and 11 of the. Act before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the sanction was not in accordance with law and that it was not a simple one. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of section 4 and section 11(2) of 'the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1964 are mandatory in character and they cannot be read as directory or mandatory. [601B] 2.1 The power under section 11 of 'The Act is not a mere formality but it is an administrative power conferred on the local authorities to carry out a fresh survey of the area within their jurisdiction with a view to revise the development plans in all its stages, and if so required by the State government after the date on which the last development plan was prepared, the same could be given without doing any violation to the development Plan. [701C] 2:1.2 The power conferred under section 13 of the 'the Acquisition Act is a mandatory one. It does not mean that the local Authority can take steps in accordance therewith and if it is satisfied that the land designated as a public purposes under section 4 or 11(4) of . The development plan has to guide itself. [801D] 2.(a) In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 17 of the , because he had failed in complying with the requirements of sections 5 and 11 (3) and 11. [820E] 3.1 It is true that the development scheme was prepared by the Municipal Commissioner on July 7, 1961 but it did not contain any provision for carrying out a new survey of any land designated under section 8 of the said Act. [823A D] 2(b) The appellant had not complied with the requirement of sections 3 and 11 as required by section 4 of the Acquisition Act. It was only after the preparation of the final development plan that the State had to make a fresh assessment of the land in accordance With section 17. [825E] 2 (c) The power to carryout a new development plan is not an administrative one. The power has to be exercised by the Local Authority or by any other authority empowered to carry on such development scheme. [826A D E] 3(a) The State Legislature had no legislative competence to enact section 4(3). It was competent for the local Authorities to carry it out a special survey of land in the manner provided under section 9 of the Central Act and that they could not do so without complying with sections 4 to 16.

The appellant, a British territory was merged with the State of Kutch. The Government of India by an agreement dated January 26, 1950, appointed the Collector of Kutch to take over the management of the Rann and to exercise all powers which were exercisable by the Maharao of Kutch in respect of the said territory. On February 1, 1951, the Collector passed a resolution authorising the Collector to take possession of the land and to sell it for sale to the appellant. The Collector thereupon made an order on March 31, 1951 declaring that the land was not liable to be sold under the provisions of section 3(1) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Code') and directed the Collector accordingly to take delivery of the possession of Rann from the appellant and to pay compensation for the land. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Collector. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the Collector had no jurisdiction to make an award under section 3 (1) (d) of Bombay Land revenue Code, which was not a part of the territory of India and that the award did not purport to be made by the Collector in exercise of sovereign rights and authority. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The question whether the Government of Kutch had any jurisdiction to pass an award is a matter for the High Courts to decide. [601B] 2. The power of the Government to make a reference under section 18 of the Code is not a judicial function and it cannot be exercised by the Government in respect to matters with respect to which Parliament has no power to make laws. It is only when there is evidence to show that the Government had any Jurisdiction or that the dispute was settled, that the jurisdiction of the Court to entertain the reference under sections 18 of Code is limited to cases where the Government exercises sovereign rights over the territory in question and that it cannot exercise its powers under section 12 of the Act. [701C] 3. The word "jurisdiction" used in section 12(1)(d) includes any power which is exercisable by a High Court or by any other court or tribunal in respect thereof. [802D] 4. The expression "jurisdiction " in relation to territory over which the Government has no jurisdiction, includes any powers which are exercisable by any High Court and not otherwise. [820E] 5. The words "jurisdiction of the Supreme Court" in section 3 of the Civil Procedure Code refer to the High court having jurisdiction over the territories over which it exercises sovereign power. It does not mean that the Supreme court has no such jurisdiction. [823G] 6. The powers of the State Government under section 13(1), (d)(i) and (ii) are wide enough to cover all cases where a territory over the subject matter is found to be in existence at all material times remained indefinite, because of the nature of the terrain, the shifting nature of border of what was called Rann. [825G] 7. The jurisdiction of this Court under article 136 of the Constitution is limited only to cases of infringement of fundamental rights and not to matters which are beyond the competence of the executive or legislative authority. [826A D] 8. The provisions of article 136 do not apply to cases in which the exercise of power by the State Legislature to make law is subject to any limitations imposed by the Constitution. [827B C] 9. In view of the fact that the Act does not provide for any limitation on the powers of this court, it cannot, therefore, be said that the provisions are not applicable to cases which are outside the competence or legislative power of this State Legislature. [828A D E] 10. The award of the International Tribunal is not an award within the meaning of article 226 of the constitution. [829E] 11.

The appellant, who was the mortgagee in possession of the mortgaged property, filed a suit on July 12, 1946, for recovery of the mortgage money. The trial Judge decreed the suit and directed that the mortgage be declared as one to enforce the claim to recover the mortgage amount under section 68 of the Transfer of Property Act. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to recover only the mortgage debt and not the mortgage. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) Under section 68(2)(b), the mortgagor is entitled to get the whole amount due from him in respect of the property mortgaged. [601B] (2) The right to sue for recovery is a right to recover money under section 69 of the Act and not a mortgage debt. [702C] (3) Under the proviso to section 68, the mortgagor 's right to get possession of mortgaged property is governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act. [801D] (4) The mortgagee is entitled only to recover from the mortgagor the amount due under the mortgage and not from the mortgagee. [820E] (5) Under Section 68(1)(b) of the Indian Transfer of Properties Act, 1882, a mortgagor can sue for possession of property mortgaged by the mortgagor in respect thereof. He cannot claim any right to enforce his mortgage against the mortgagor. [823G] (6) The proviso to sub section (2), of section 68 is not applicable to the present case because the mortgagee was not entitled to enforce any claim against the mortgagee as he had already sold the mortgaged properties. [825E] In the instant case, the appellant had purchased the mortgaged lands from the original mortgagor and the mortgagee 's rights in the mortgaged land were governed by Article 120 of Limitation Act, 1908. The mortgage money was not payable by the mortgagee to the mortgagee but was due to him as a result of the sale.

The appellants were engaged in the business of transport of passengers. They had been carrying on their business for hire and reward. The appellants were registered as a public service vehicle under section 3(7) of the Act. The respondents were issued with a certificate to that effect. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of the Commissioner of Pune Division, Pune which was dismissed by the Commissioner. The respondent challenged the validity of the certificate on various grounds including the ground that the appellants had not paid any amount from the employees for providing transport facilities and that they were not liable to pay any amount in view of the provisions of section 3 (7) read with section 2(7). The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 4(1)(a) of Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'public service vehicle' has been defined in section 2 (7), as meaning a motor vehicle which is used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. [601 B] 2. The word 'goods" has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules. It does not mean any goods carried by a stage carriage. The words 'goods' have been defined under section 2 of the said Act and it is clear that the transport vehicle provided to the employees by the company would be a public Service vehicle within the definition of the word 'vehicle" in section 3 of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Tax Act, 1958. [701 C] 3. The transport vehicles provided to employees by a private company which are not members of the public but as held by the High Court that such a transport vehicle is not a public services vehicle within meaning of section 2 read with sections 4(7), and therefore, the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public motor vehicle. [801 D] 4. The definition of 'public Service vehicle' in section 4 (7)(a)(b) of Bombay Motor Vehicle Tax Act clearly indicates that the goods carried on any public service vehicles which could not be said to be a private service vehicle within that definition. [820 E] 5. The provisions of the Maharashtra Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1959 are clear and unambiguous. It is not disputed that the tax was levied only on passengers who were carrying on a contract Carriage within the ambit of the charging section. [821 A B] 6. The goods carried in stage carriage are not necessarily covered by the definition. The exemption under Section 4(6) of that Act is not confined to passengers carried on public service. It cannot be said that the vehicles which are used as public service are not a private vehicle within its ambit. [823 E] 7. In view of this clear and categorical finding, the appellant could not have been denied the benefit under section 5(6)(a). [820 G] 8. The High court was in error in holding that the exemption granted by the Government is not applicable to the transport vehicles which were used as private service vehicles within the purview of the levy of tax on passengers carried by road, and therefore the appellant cannot be denied the exemption. [822 A B C] 9. In the instant case, the appellants were carrying passengers in stage carriages and they had been using them for hire or reward. They were not entitled for the benefit. The vehicles which had been used as contract carriage were not covered by section 4 of the Gujarat Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1961. [825 A B D] 9: The appellant was a public sector undertaking carrying passengers within the scope of the definition and therefore it could not claim exemption under the said provision. [826 C] 10: 11. In order to attract the provisions contained in section 5 (6)(b), the legislature has provided that the motor vehicles which can be used as an essential or integral part of public service shall be registered in the State of Bombay.

The appellants, who were the local residents of the village, had applied for a licence under Rule 102. The licensing authority refused to grant a "no objection certificate" and granted a "No objection certificate". The appellants filed an appeal against that order before the State Government. The State Government rejected the application on the ground that the grant was in violation of the principles of natural justice. The appellants challenged the validity of the grant of a cinema licence by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had not made out a case for granting a "NO objection certificate", and that the State government had no power to refuse a cinema license on the same grounds which it took against the grant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The grant of an "no objections certificate" is a matter of discretion conferred upon the licensing authority by Rule 102(2) of the rules and that it is not open to the licensing authorities to refuse or reject a cinema Licence on the grounds which they took against a licence granted under rule 3. [682D] 1.2. The power to grant an "No Objection Certificate" is not a matter which can be exercised by the licensing Authority in accordance with the provisions of Rule 102 (1) of Chapter V of the Rules. [782E] 2.3. The licence granted to a cinema house under rule 102(1) is subject to the conditions specified therein and it cannot be denied or cancelled merely because the grant is in violation thereof. [882F] 1.(a) In the instant case, the licensing officer refused to issue a "NOC" certificate on the basis of an application made by the appellants under Rule 2(2)(b). The appellants had no objection certificate and they did not challenge the grant before the High Court. [820G] (b) The grant was subject to conditions specified in Rule 2 (1), which are as follows: "The licensing authority may refuse a licence if it is satisfied that there is no objection to the grant or refusal of a licence, if it has been satisfied that the application for a cinema is in respect of a site on which the cinema house is proposed to be constructed. [823A] (c) The licensing authorities are not bound by any statutory provisions and they cannot refuse a license unless they have reasons to do so. [825E] 1(d) In view of the fact that the licensing order was passed in violation, the appellants were entitled to an "NIA" certificate under Rule 3. The appeal is allowed.

The appellant, who was the lessee of a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanal, Hosadurga Taluk, and who had agreed to assign the mining lease to him under a contract dated August 3, 1957, filed a suit for specific performance of the contract on September 2, 1957. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the assignment of the mining leases was not an acceptance of the offer made by the plaintiff and that as the plaintiff did not accept the offer he could not be compelled to agree to assign a lease to the defendant before November 6, 1957 and that the contract was concluded on September 3,1957. The High Court held that the plaintiff had no enforceable right under the contract dated September 2,. 1957 and therefore the suit for Specific Performance of the agreement was not maintainable. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the High Court should have dismissed the suit as barred by time. HELD: 1. The question whether a concluded contract is an acceptance or an acceptance does not arise in this case because the plaintiff has no enforceable rights under the contracts. [775 A] 2. The contract between the parties is concluded on October 31, 1957 when the offer was made and the acceptance of its offer by the defendant. It is not necessary that there should be a concluded agreement between the plaintiff or his agent or servant. [875 B] 3. The plaintiff had not accepted the offer either orally or by letter sent to him before November 1, 1957 but he did not make an offer in writing to the plaintiff. [820 C] 4. The defendant was entitled to remain in possession of the lease and the plaintiff could not enforce his right under a concluded lease. [823 D] 5. The suit for injunction restraining the defendant from transferring or assigning any mining lease was clearly barred by limitation. [825 E] 6. The cause of action for filing a suit arose on September 1,1957 when the contract in question was concluded and the defendant had not applied for and obtained the consent of the Central Government to assign mining lease. The period of limitation prescribed under article 31(2) of the Limitation Act is three years from the date of the notice of allotment. [822 E] 7. The time limit prescribed by article 31 (2) is not applicable in this suit because the defendant was at liberty to cancel the offer and to take possession of mining lease before November 2,1957 and that he had no subsisting right to continue in possession after November 2. 1957 when he made an offer. [826 A] 8. The fact that the defendant did not apply for and obtain the consent from the Central government to assign any mining leases to him is a clear indication that the communication of an acceptance was communicated to the appellant before November 3, 1956. [828 B E] 9. In the present case, the communication dated September 1,. 1957 was communicated by the letter dated September 4, 1957 to the respondent and it was communicated on October 30, 1957 by the respondent to the appellants. The communication dated October 31.1957 was communicated after November 6. 1957 and the respondent had not made an acceptance. [829 C] 10. In view of the fact that there was a concluded contracts between the appellant and the respondents, the question whether the respondent could be compelled or prevented from doing so does not really arise in the present appeal.

The appellant was a sugar factory manufacturing sugarcane. He purchased sugarcane from the respondent on August 30, 1966 and the respondent purchased sugarcane for Rs. 1,000/- from the appellant. The respondent purchased the sugarcane from him on August 31, 1966. On August 31/08, 1966 he sold the sugarcane to the appellant and the appellant purchased it on a sale price of Rs. 2,000/-. The respondent filed a complaint before the police alleging that the sugarcane was purchased by him for Rs.. 1,500/- and that the appellant had not paid the price thereof within 14 days from August 31 and August 30. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence under section 3(2)(c) of the Act and issued process against the respondent. On appeal the High Court held that the complaint was premature and quashed the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings because the complaint did not disclose a Cognizable offence and as such the same was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Government under section 2(2) (c) is an enabling provision and it cannot be exercised by the State Legislature or other competent authority. [601B] 2. The word 'may 'shall 'may' in its ordinary sense means that the legislature has no power to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs. It does not include any law relating to the control of sugarcane as also the regulation of the price of sugarcane. [702C] 3. The words 'may "may ' are used in section 2 (2)(b) of Act which is a part of agriculture' and it is clear that the Legislature has no competence to enact the Act or to legislate therein in respect thereof. [803D] 4. The expression 'shall' in section 3 (2) of Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 does not mean that the Parliament had no power under section 11 of the Bihar Sugar Factory Control Act to enact any law regarding the control and supply of foodstuffs and it does not cover any law pertaining to the regulation and sale of sugarcane which is an incidental or ancillary provision. [820E] 5. The object of the legislation in question was to regulate the movement of sugarcane from one place to another and to provide for regulating the prices of sugarcane and for securing equitable distribution and supply at fair availability at fair price. It was not a case where the legislature had no competence under section 4(1)(f) to enact law relating thereto. [823E] 6. The Act does not contain any provision regarding the regulation or sale of cane in the State nor does it contain any provisions regarding the fixation of prices of sugar and for regulating distribution and sale thereof. It is a piece of legislation which is incidental or connected with the control, supply, distribution and distribution at fair value. [825E] 7. The fact that the Act provides for regulation and price of cane at fair rate does not make any difference to the position in regard to the fixation and price at fair rates. [826F] 8. In the instant case there is no evidence on record to show that the respondent had purchased sugarcane at a price higher than the price fixed by the Central Government under the Order. The High Court was, therefore, right in holding that the prosecution of the respondent was not maintainable and the order passed by the Magistrate was liable for being quashed. [828G] 9. In view of the fact that there is nothing to show on record that the State Government had no authority to enact a law relating only to the Control of sugarcane, the High Courts were right in quashing the proceedings as also quashing the prosecution.

The appellant was a manufacturer of sugar and it had been manufacturing sugar in the State of Bihar. The appellant purchased raw materials from its factory at Patna for the first five years from the date of manufacture of sugar. It claimed that the benefit of exemption under Section 8A was not available to it as it did not specify the power under which it was issued. The High Court held that the said notification was invalid and quashed the order of 30th June, 1969. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The expression "in any case" in Section 8 A(2) is wide enough to include within its ambit all sales tax paid on raw materials purchased by it for the next five years. [801B] 2.1 The word 'exemption' has been used in a very comprehensive sense and it includes all sales of goods made by a new industry to a new industrial unit. It is not confined to the sale of goods manufactured by a newly established industrial undertaking but extends only to the transactions of sale of raw materials which are made exigible under the provisions contained in Chapter 3 of the said Act. [901C] 2.(a) The word "exemption" has been defined in Section 2(d)(i) of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1957 (referred to hereinafter as "the Act") and it is not limited to the sales tax payable on raw material purchased by a person for the purpose of manufacturing sugar. [1001D] 3.(b) The expression 'exempt' has not been defined either in Section 3 or in Section 4(1)(a) of Bihar Sales tax Act,1957. It does not include any sale of any goods made exigible to sales tax under the said provisions. [1101E] (c) The words "exempt" have been used for a very wide and comprehensive sense. It cannot be regarded as good law in view of the recent decision of this Court in Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC, 430; referred to. 2.(d) The power under Section 3(a) is not restricted to the grant of refund. The word used in Section 9A has been interpreted by this Court to mean that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant or reduction as permitted by Section 8-A and where the source of power underwhich it was granted is not stated in an order but merely certain words have been incorporated in the Order. [110G] 3(e) The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be used in any manner. It must be regarded in a sense that it has no application to the facts of the case and the question whether the State Legislature had any authority to grant refund is not a matter which can be determined by the Court on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. [111H; 111A] 4.(a)(i), (ii) & (iii)

The appellants were charged for offences under Sections 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. The prosecution case is that the deceased Madda Lakshamandas was having a spear in his hand and A 1 and A 2 assaulted him on his head by A 1, A 3 and A 4. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons of the charges under Sections 147 and 302/149 I. P.C., but convicted them under Section 148 I.PC. and sentenced each one of them to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 302 readwith section 149 I PC. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.1 The prosecution story is that A 1 was attacked by the accused party with spears on his person and A 3 hit him on the head of Madda. He fell down on the road and sustained injuries on his body. The deceased Madka Laksamandas was carrying a spear at the time of occurrence. The medical evidence clearly shows that the injuries were caused by the appellants. [601B] 1.2.1 In view of the fact that the prosecution has not been able to establish that the accused attacked the deceased and the injured persons on their head, the High Court was justified in convicting them under Sections 302 read and Section 34 I.p.C.. [602A B] 2.3 The conviction of the appellant under Section 149 IPC is based on the evidence of P.W. 1, the wife of the deceased, who was injured by A 3. [06B C] 4.1 It is true that the High court has not given any reasons for convicting the appellants but it has come to a conclusion that the appellants were guilty under Section 147 and 149 IPC. [63A B D] 2:1.2 The conviction under Section 307 read with section 34 I PC is based upon the evidence on record of P W. 1 and the eye witnesses to the occurrence. [64B C E] 3.3.1 A person who was attacked on his own body by A 4, A 5 and A 6, is not liable for any offence under Section 304 Part II read with 149 I P. C. The conviction is based solely on the testimony of P,W. 2, the daughter of the accused. [65A B E] 2 3.2 It is well settled that a person who has been attacked by A 5 or A 6 and A 7 cannot be convicted under Section 326 read with 34 IPC unless there are compelling reasons for such an overt act on his part. The evidence of the eye witness to the incident clearly shows the presence of A 1 at the scene of occurrence and the injuries sustained by him on their person. [66A B C] 3:1:1 It was not possible for a person to have been attacked on the body of Madka, Laksamma and A 5, A 4 and A 8 who were armed with spear. The fact that they had assaulted Madka and the deceased also does not make any difference in their evidence. [68B C D] 3;2:1 The High court was justified to convict the appellants on the basis of the testimony given by P, W. 2.2, the eyewitness to the crime. [69A B G] 3.(a) The prosecution has failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt that A 4 had caused injuries on the person of Madho Laksyam who was also injured by a spear and he died due to the injuries inflicted on him. [70C D] (b) The High Curt did not consider the evidence given by the eyewitnesses to the murder of Madkha Laksramandas. It is clear that the eye-witness had not made any attempt to explain the injuries on Madho Lasramandas and the injury sustained by them on his hand.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had entered into an agreement with the Government of India for purchase of certain properties. The assessee was to pay a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- as consideration for the sale of those properties. On or about the date of the agreement, the assessee paid a sum equivalent to the full value of the consideration received by him and the balance amount was also paid by him. The Income Tax Officer assessed the total income at Rs.2,50,000/-. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee had not disclosed the true nature of the transaction and the market value of those items as on the date when the agreement was executed. The High Court upheld the view taken by the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression 'value' in section 2(d) means the price actually received or receivable for the transfer of a capital asset. [601C] 1.2 The expression "value" is defined in section 3(d). It includes all amounts paid by way of consideration and any other kind of consideration. [061D] 1.(a) The expression has been used in section 4(3)(b) to mean the amount actually received by the assessee as on or after the date on which the agreement is executed. [ 605E] 1 (b) The word 'value" in section 5(2) means a price which has accrued to the assessee and which has not accrued to him and which had not accrued or disclosed by him but was subsequently furnished by him, and the burden of proving such fact is on the Revenue. [ 604F] 2.(a). In the instant case, the transaction took place between the assessee on the one hand and the assessee in respect of the transfer and the consideration actually received for the same. The transaction took effect from the date the agreement had been executed. It was not a case where the full amount received by wayof consideration was less than 15% of the value so declared, but it was only a case of an amount which was not disclosed or disclosed in other words, the duty payable on the consideration for transfer was more than what was declared by the appellant. [ 607E] 2.1 In the present case, there is no understatement of the price received by respondent No. 1 and the same has been disclosed and the onus of proving that the transaction had taken place between him and respondent No 1 lies on the assessee. [ 608F] 3.2 It is not necessary to go into the question whether the transaction was a genuine one or not. The fact that the respondent No1 had paid a part consideration for transferring the capital asset does not mean that the transfer was made in good faith. [ 609H; 607A] 2(a). The expression used in Section 4(2)(b), is wide enough to include all amounts received by an assessee as consideration of the full price of the capital assets as on date when a transaction took out of consideration for which the transfer had been understated by the respondent. [ 620B D] 3.(a)(i) The words 'value of the property as on that date' in Section 5(1) are wide enough and include all sums paid by the person who has actually received the consideration. It is difficult to determine whether the transfer is really a genuine transaction or not, because it is possible for the Income Tax officer to determine what was the full market value as on 1st April, 1963. [ 621E] 4.(a), (b)(i), (c) and (d). The words "value of any property" in Section 2(g) are wider than the word 'amount received by a person who had actually received it.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence under Section 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. He was convicted by the trial Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two months. The appeal filed by him against his conviction was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the Food Inspector was not reliable because he had stated in his examination under Section 342 of the Code that the sample of the food article contained in the cash memo was meant for human consumption and, therefore, the conviction should be set aside. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to prove that the articles were sold by the appellant to the Food inspector. [701B] 2. The evidence of P.W. 2 is not reliable since he had deposed in his cross examination that the food Inspector had told him that they were meant for consumption as a medicine for human use and, as such, he could have been prosecuted on the ground that he had written on the cash Memo. He did not say that the Food Inspectors had told them that they had sold the Til seeds to the appellant. [801C] 3. The fact that Tambe was meant only for Pooja and not for Pooja does not mean that it was meant to be used as food. It is true that the prosecution has not proved that the article which was kept for sale was meant as a food. But, in view of the fact that the appellant had stated that he sold the articles to theFood Inspector, it cannot be said that the explanation given by him that the same was meant exclusively for human purposes, was not acceptable. [901D] 4. The mere statement of the P. W. 2 that the black 'Til" seeds were intended for human food is not enough to prove the fact in issue that the quality of the sample was not known to the Public Analyst. [1001E] 5. The Food Inspector had clearly stated in the cross examination as follows: "The Food Inspector has also stated in a letter dated 18th February, 1971 written by him to the accused that he purchased the Til seed from the shop of the accused and sold it for sale to the public analyst. He had further stated that the said sample was meant solely for human purpose and not merely for human medicine. The Public Analyst had clearly mentioned in his report that the samples were meant only to be sold for human necessity. [1101F] 6. The High Court has rightly held that the version of the prosecution is not convincingly satisfactory. It was not proved by the Food Officer that the accused had told the FoodInspector that he intended to sell the Til oil seeds to him and, in fact, he had given the same to the food inspector. The defence taken by the accused was that the report of the Public analyst showed that the milk was meant merely for domestic consumption. [110G] 7. In view of this finding, the High court has rightly come to the conclusion that the story put forward by the prosecution was not convincing and reliable. [111A D] 8. The contention that the Public Food Inspector did not state in his evidence that the Milk was meant mainly for human cultivation is also without any substance. It cannot be accepted that the contents of the report were not proved to be true. [112E] 9. In the instant case, the prosecution had failed to establish that the chillies sold by it were meant exclusively to be consumed as food and, consequently, the appellant was rightly convicted under section 7(1) of Prevention of food Adulteration Act. [113G] 10. The conviction of the respondent under section 13(i)(f) of 'P.C. Act is set aside and he is acquitted of all the charges framed against him.

The appellant, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh, was dismissed from service by an order dated 13th of January, 1966. He filed a second appeal before the High Court against the dismissal of his first appeal on the ground that the order of dismissal having been passed in appeal therefrom and the revision petition having been dismissed on 31st August, 1966, he had ceased to be operative on its own strength and did not exercise jurisdiction vested in it under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the dismissal was not justified because the order dismissing the first appeal from service was passed after the expiry of six months from the date when the appeal was filed or representation made by the appellant was disposed of. In this appeal, the appellant contended that the judgment of the High court is erroneous and the High 'Court should have exercised jurisdiction vested under article 227 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the State Government dismissing the second appeals from service is not a nullity because it was passed in exercise of its jurisdiction under article 136 of the Cons tution of India. [701B] 2. The question whether the dismissal is valid or not has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [802C] 3. The State Government had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal against the order passed in the first instance by an officer in the department and, therefore, the High C ourt was right in holding that it had no power to entertain a second appeals against the orders of dismissal. [901D] 4. The view taken by the High Cou rt is not correct. It has been held by this Court in the case of Raghubir Jha vs State of Bihar & Ors., [1978] 1 S.C.R. 869, that the right to sue accrued on the date of dismissal and the order which was upheld by the appellate authority could not be equated with any propriety or legality. [1001E] 5. The second appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellant who was the decree holder of a mortgage in respect of certain properties, executed a mortgage deed on August 1, 1956. The mortgage deed provided that if the mortgagor had not paid the amount due under the mortgage deed he would be entitled to get interest at the rate of 18% per annum from the date of the mortgage and the mortgagee would be liable to pay interest at 18% p.a. On September 30, 1957, the appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain property on the ground that the mortgage was not a security for the loan advanced by him and that he had not executed any document in respect thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to interest at 15% p., but held that the decree passed by the trial court was not an order of affirmance and that the variation made in regard to the amount of costs was a part of the decree and that it was not necessary for the appellate court to make a variation in respect to the decree. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree of affirmances before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no variation in the decision of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The judgment of the High court is not a decree of reversal but only makes a variation. [601B] (2) The language of section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure clearly shows that the appellate decree passed in the case of an appeal from a decree passed under section 35 is a decree made by the Court which has been confirmed by the lower court in respect thereto. [702C] (3) The words "decree of affirmness" in section 35 are not to be construed as including the variation in regard only to the part of a decree which is a part thereof. [803D] (4) The word 'judgment' in section 34 of the code of Civil procedure has been defined in section 2(2)(a) of the Act and it means "decree made by a Court which had jurisdiction to make such variation". [704E] (5) The expression 'decree of reversal" is not defined in the Code. It does not mean that the judgment of a court which had no jurisdiction to pass an order as to interest which the Court could make under section 34 or 35 of Civil Rules. [777A D] (6) The High court was right in holding that since the appellant had not made any variation in his decision of affirmation, he was entitled only to get the amount from the decreeholder and not to the extent of the variation which was allowed by the appellate Court.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was carrying on business in the name and style of "M/s. M/s M/S. M.K. Agarwal & Co., Ltd., a registered dealer under the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The respondent filed an application for revision against the revisional order passed by the District Judge under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, which was allowed and the revisional orders were set aside. The High Court held that the revisional authority had no jurisdiction to entertain the revision petition under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no power to entertain a revision petition against an order passed under section 50, Provincial Act, and that the revision petitions filed by the respondent were incompetent. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The revisional authority has jurisdiction to decide the question whether a revision application under section 100, Code, Civil Procedure, is maintainable or not. [975A] 2. The power of revision conferred on the High Courts under section25, Provincialised Small Cause Court Act, is a very wide and comprehensive one. It does not confer any power on the District Court to entertain an application under sections 25, and 115, C.P.C., for revision of orders passed by it. [875B] 3. The jurisdiction conferred on a District Court under section 75, Code is a revisional authority. The State Government has no power under section 35, Code to revise the order passed in revision under section 26, Provincialized Small Cause courts Act. [775C E] 4. The powers of the High court under section 24, Code are not appellate and revisional powers conferred on it by section 25. It is a well settled principle that the State Government can exercise revisional power under sections 115, and 25, Code if there is an order of the District Magistrate under section 20, Provincialisation Act. In the instant case, the revisional authorities have exercised their revisional jurisdiction under section 15, Code. [76G] 5. The revision petitions were not maintainable against a revisional order under section 40, Provincialization Act. It was open to the High Curt to exercise its revisional powers under section 27, Provincialising Act. The orders of the revisional courts are set aside and the matter is remitted to the District Courts for consideration as a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution. [75A B] 6. In view of the fact that the impugned order was passed in exercise of revisional jurisdiction, it would be open to this court to consider whether the revision applications filed by respondent were maintainable or they could have arisen out of original suits of any valuation, decided by a District Judge exercising the revisional power conferred on him under section 28, Code and not under section115, Code as contended by the appellant. [77C E F] 7. The order passed is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the State Legislature under section 30, Code or under section 116, Code; it is a revision proceeding which can be filed against an appellate order passed on appeal under section 54, Code read with section 115. [79G H] 8. In this case, there was no question of invoking the revisional powers of a District court under sections 100, 115, code and section 115 of the Code. The impugned orders were not amenable either to the revision jurisdiction of a High Court under article 227 or to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the constitution. [80H] 9. In order that the case should be remitted to a High court for consideration of a petition filed under section 125, Code it is necessary to consider the question as to whether the revisional proceedings under section 60, Code can be entertained by the High Civil Courts under article 226 or 227 of Constitution. The proviso to section 115(1) provides that no revision shall lie against an original order passed after the commencement of the Act.

The respondents were owners of the land in question. The State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Act for acquisition of their lands situate at Jaipur and published on February 8, 1984, acquiring the same from the appellant. The respondents filed an application before the Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur, under section 53 (2) of Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, seeking to acquire the land belonging to them. The Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur by his order dated April 9, 1984 declared that the entire land was needed by them for the implementation of a development scheme at public expense and directed the respondents to acquire their lands within the State of Rajasthan. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority under section 54(2) against the said order of the Special Officer. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on March 13, 1984 holding that the acquisition of the notified land was not a bona fide one and that the notification issued by the State Government under section 51 (1) or 52(l) of Act was invalid. The respondent filed an Appeal before the Division Bench of the High Court against the order of dismissal of his appeal. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that since the acquisition proceedings were initiated in accordance with the provisions of the Rajasthan Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, the notification under sections 52(2), 52(3) and 52(4) of that Act was valid. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court committed a manifest error in holding that section 52 (1)(b) of Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is not applicable to the acquisition proceeding initiated under section 48(2). [605B] 2. The notification issued under section 50(1), as amended by the Rajasthan Housing Board (Amendment) Act No. 8 of 1984, dated February 8 1984, was valid and legal. [606C] 3. The provisions of section 52 of the Land Acqrer's Act, 1956, are not applicable in the instant case because the notification was issued under sections 53(1)(a), 52 (2), 54(1). [705D] 4. The acquisition proceedings initiated by the appellant were quashed on the ground that the land vested in the State government free from all encumbrances and that it was not needed by the respondents for the purpose of implementation of the development scheme. [706E] 5. The question whether the acquisition is valid or not, depends upon the facts of each case. In the instant cases, the acquisition was initiated under sections 48(1 ), 54 (2). The notification under Section 52(i) of 'the Act was issued on February 9,1984 and published in the official gazette on March 7, 1984. The declaration under section 55(1 ) of the said Act was published on March 10, 1984 and published by the Government on March 11, 1984 in the Official Gazette on March 12, 1984 which was published in two newspapers on March 14, 1984 i.e. on March 15, 1984 at Jaipur Bench. The Notification under section 56(1)/52 (2 ), as it stood prior to its publication in the Gazette of February 8.1984, was issued by State Government on April 9.1984 and the notification published in official gazette dated February 10,1984 was published by State government on March 16, 1984 under section 22(1A) of The Act was challenged before the High court by filing a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that there was no infirmity in the acquisition and the land vests in the Government free from any encumbrances.

The appellant was assessed to house tax under the old Rent Act on the basis of the assessment made by the local authority having jurisdiction and in view of the provisions of s.39 of the new Rent Act, he was entitled to the benefit of s..39 of that Act. The appellant filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the building had not become ten years old on the date of the suit and, therefore, the appellant would be entitled to protection of the New Rent Act. On the basis that the appellant was not entitled to get protection of s.,39 as the building was constructed in 1968 and the landlord had purchased it from it during the pendency of the litigation, the High Court held that the new rent Act did not apply to a building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. The High Court also held that there was no change in the cause of action for the appellant and, accordingly, dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of the old rent Act are applicable to a case where the building has been constructed in the year 1968 and it is not necessary to determine whether any amount is due from the tenant under sub section (2) of s.(2), viz., the arrears of rent or damages for use and occupation of the building during that period. [901 D] 1.2. The new Rent Acts are applicable only to a suit where the landlord has purchased the building in 1968 but not in the years from which its constructed construction is complete. [0902 E] 1, 3.3. In the present case, the building having been constructed during the year 1967 and the appellant having purchased it during that year, the question of giving the benefit under s. 39 does not arise at all. [1001 A B] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that the provisions contained in the newRent Act were applicable to the case where a building had been constructed on the land and the building which was constructed on it during this period, but before the assessment of the house tax and water tax, the landlord could not be said to have purchased the premises during that time. [1101 B] 1 2.2 The High Courts were right in taking the view that the old Act did apply to the building at the first hearing of the revision petition and, consequently, the new Act was applicable to it.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was incorporated in the year 1942. The appellant filed an application for reference to arbitration under section 18 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, and prayed that the award be set aside. The arbitrator made an award on April 1, 1937, and the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Patna. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the original agreement was not a copy of the award and that it did not contain any provision for the levy of penalty on an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The arbitration clause in the contract is only a procedural one and does not provide for the imposition of any penalty on a non-tested document. [601B] (2) The award was made by the arbitrator without reference to the arbitration agreement. The arbitration agreement did not refer to arbitration, nor did it contain any provisions for the payment of penalty. It is only an unthamped or inadequately stamped instrument which could be validated and acted upon. [702C] (3) The High court has committed a manifest error in holding that there was no valid reference to Arbitration. [803D] (4) The arbitrator had not applied his mind to the question whether the original document was an instrument or a copy thereof. He did not consider the question of the validity of the arbitration clause and the effect of the agreement on the basis of which he could have awarded the award. [902F] (5) The power conferred by section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1935, is not an absolute one. It does not confer any jurisdiction upon the court to make a decree for specific performance. [1001B C] (6) The agreement was executed by a person who was authorised to execute the arbitration and that the dispute related only to payment of bills. The agreement did no more than refer to the original contract, but it contained only a provision for payment of compensation on an incomplete or insufficient stamped document actually produced in Court.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab. He was placed under suspension by an order dated 30th April, 1979 issued by the Chief Engineer, Public Works Division, Punjab, Chandigarh. The respondent was served with a charge sheet on him alleging that he had committed certain irregularities and negligence in discharge of his duties as Executive Engineers in Public works Department in Public Health Department in respect of a period from 1st January, 1979 to 31st March, 1979. He also alleged that the respondent had committed breach of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules by adopting the proviso to clause (b) of Rule 3.2 and thereby contravened Rule 2(2). The trial court acquitted the respondent on the ground that the prosecution was barred under Article 311(2) of the Constitution since the respondent was prosecuted in a criminal case for offences punishable under Section 161, Penal Code and Section 5(1)(d) read with Section 5 (2) and Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High Court quashed the First Information Report on the basis that the provisions of Rule 1.2 were not attracted to the facts of the present case because the respondent did not commit any breach of rule 2.1.2. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in quashing the prosecution of Mangal Singh Minhas for the offence punishable under Sections 161, IPC and Section 4(1) (d) of Prevention of corruption Act because the provisions contained in Rule 2 were not applicable to the case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that the proviso was not attracted in the instant case as the respondent has been prosecuted in judicial proceedings for offences under Section 5 of the Indian Penal Code. [813E] 1.3 The High Courts were wrong in quashing a prosecution on the sole ground that there was no bar to initiate criminal proceedings against the respondent for the same offence. [713A B] 2.4 The High courts had committed an error of law by holding that Rule 2,2.2 was not applicable in the case because it was not specifically framed for a different purpose. [77C D] 3.1 In view of the above, the High court could not have quashed the prosecution on that ground alone. [78E] 3:1.3 It is well settled that if there is a clear violation of Rule 4, then the High Courts should not interfere with the order of the trial court. [79G] 2:1 The power to frame a rule under Article 309 and the purpose of Rule2 cannot be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general bar to the prosecution in respect thereof. [80H; 81A B C] 3,3.4 In the instant cases, the respondent is not entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause (a) of rule2. The power under Article309 and the object of Rule 9 cannot be construed as laying a down an inflexible or general prohibition against the prosecution for the purpose for which it was provided. [81A B D] 2,3A] 3(b) In the present cases, there is no bar on the prosecution to initiate proceedings for the offences under Sections 5 and 6 of Prevention Of Corruption Act against the appellant. The provisions contained therein are not applicable. [82C E] 4.1 Section 5 and Rule 2 are in the nature of a rule regulating the conditions of service of a government servant contained in clauses (a), (b), (c) and (d). The power conferred on the State Government under Article 310 is to be exercised by the Governor in accordance with the provisions laid down in clause(a) and clause (c).

The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee company was a public limited company within the meaning of section 23 A(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The respondent company acquired and carried on the business of manufacture and sale of "paints" which were not entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. The appellant company claimed that the dividend paid by it in respect of its shares was not distributed as dividends amongst the shareholders but only as dividends. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the company had no right to participate in the profits and gains of the company. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the provisions of section 3 A(2) were applicable to the case and that the income tax authorities had jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23A. The High Court upheld the decision of the Income tax officer holding that section 23AA was not attracted in respect thereof. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The provisions of sections 3 A and 23AA are applicable to cases where the public are substantially interested or beneficially held by the public. [775C] (2) The expression "pinner" used in section 23(1)(a) is not confined to a company which has been substantially interested in the public company, but includes a company whose shares have been acquired and vested in the company under section 3A(2). [776B] (3) The word 'painting' used in the Explanation to sub section (1), as it stood at the material time, is not restricted to a Company which has substantially interested. It does not include a company who has been wholly interested or substantially interested to share its shares. [77C] In the instant case, the appellant company was not entitled either to a higher fixed rate or to have a fixed percentage of dividend as reduced by the amount of income tax payable by it under section 2(2)(a). The Explanation to section 23 (1)(b) is in the nature of an exception to the general rule that where the assessee is substantially interested, he must be shown to have been interested in some other company which was substantially interested and not beneficially.

The appellant, a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1956, had been issued with a notice to show cause why he should not be assessed to tax on the goods sold by him. The appellant filed his reply to the show cause notice and contended that the goods were delivered to Dwarkadas Khetan & Company on behalf of the first appellant and that the sale was made in accordance with the provisions of the Bombay General Sales Tax Rules, 1956. The learned Magistrate held that the delivery of the goods had been effected by the first respondent and that he had not committed any breach of the law. He further held that there was a clear violation of the provisions contained in section 3(1) of the Act inasmuch as the goods which were delivered for delivery at Dharsi Moolji were not sold to the appellant, but were delivered on behalf or on behalf, of Dwarkadans Khetan & Co., and that since the goods have been delivered to the first Appellant, he was liable to pay tax under section 3 (1) read with section 4(2). The High Court held that in view of the fact that the appellant had not sold the goods to the second appellant, it could not be said that the sales were made by him to Dwarakdas Khetan and Company. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The delivery of goods was effected by Dwarkadan Mills through their agents or their agents. It is clear from the provisions that the deliveries were made in the manner prescribed by the rules framed under section 4 (1). [782 A] 2. The goods had passed and they were delivered at Dharsa on behalf and as Dwarkadasi Khetan & company, but the delivery was not made by them to Dwarakamas Khetan. [783 B] 3. The fact that Dwarkadaram asked for delivery of those goods did not mean that he could have sold them to the appellants. It was only when Dwarkada asked for the delivery that the appellants were given an opportunity to deliver those goods. [882 C] 4. The position is clear that the first Respondent had delivered the goods at Dharusa on behalf. He had not taken back the goods and the Mills had sent them to Dharsa. It cannot be said, therefore, that the Delivery of the consignments was made by Dwarakamans Khetan and company in accordance therewith. [982 C D] 5. The High Courts have rightly held that since Dwarkadala Moolji had delivered those goods to Dharsi on behalf the first Petitioner, it was not open to the learned Magistrate to hold that the said delivery was made at Dharaka. [1083 E] 6. In view of this finding, the appeal must fail and is dismissed.

The appellant was appointed as a lecturer of the Government College on June 30, 1964. He was appointed to the post of an examiner of the University. On July 1, 1965 he was promoted as an examiner and was posted at the Government Polytechnic College, Ahmedabad. The appellant was then posted as an Examiner of the said college. He had been appointed as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Public Health Engineering on June 31, 1964 and was also posted to the Government Higher Secondary School, Ahmedabad on July 1. 1965. On August 5, 1966 he was transferred from the Government High School, Baroda to the University of Gujarat. The Government of Gujarat issued a notification under section 6(1) of the Indian Penal Code in exercise of its powers conferred by sub section (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, which was published on August 9, 1966. The petitioner challenged the validity of the notification and contended that he had been wrongly prosecuted for criminal misconduct as a public servant under section 5(1)(d) of that Act. He also contended that the offence committed by him was not a public servants but was an offence under section 161 of the Penal Code. The High Court held that the petitioner was not entitled to be prosecuted for any offence under s.161 of the I.P.C. and dismissed his petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the prosecution had been validly instituted against him because he had not been charged with any criminal misconduct. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding, that the charge of criminal misconduct was not made out by the prosecution and that the appellant was not liable under section 4(1), (d) or 5(2) (a) of Prevention of corruption Act. [701B] 2.1 Section 5(3)(d), which is a special provision for the punishment of dismissal, is an exception to the general rule that if a public officer is dismissed from service on account of misconduct, he cannot be prosecuted under section 3(1). The expression "any other public servant" in this sub section means any person who is dismissed or removed from service. [801C] 2:1.2 In order to attract the provisions of section 4 (1) (d), it must be shown that the act complained of was done by a public official, and that he acted as an officer in discharge of his duty. The word "any" is not defined in the Code but it has been used in the sense of "public servant". [802D] 2(a) In order that the word "officer" must be given some meaning, it must also be shown by necessary implication that he was acting as an Officer in discharge his duty and that it was only a person who was not holding office as a Public servant. [820E] 3:1 The word 'officer' in this clause means any other public officer or employee of the State Government or of any local authority. It is not necessary to show that he has been acting as a Minister or an Officer for the performance of any public duty. [823A D] 2.(a) The word used in section 5 (1)(D) must be understood in the context of the definition of "officer". [823E] 2 (b) In the instant case, the appellant had been working as a Professor in Government Polytechnics and he was appointed by the Government as an Inspector. He did not hold any office or post for the purpose of performing any public duties. The act complained against was done in discharge or in breach of his official position. [825E] (c) In view of the provisions contained in section 4, it is clear that the acts complained against must be done by an officer who is acting as such and not by a person holding office.

The petitioners were engaged as casual labourers in the open line of the Construction Department of the Railways. They were appointed on temporary basis and they were continued to work till they were selected through regular Selection Boards for Class IV staff. The Railway Administration, after having obtained temporary status, had not been able to absorb them permanently. On their absorption, they were given temporary status. In the year 1984, the petitioners were appointed as casual labour in the Construction department of the Railway Administration and they continued to serve till they are selected through a regular selection Board for Class III staff. They filed applications before the Railway Board for regularisation of their services. The Railways refused to regularise their services on the ground that they had not completed 240 days of continuous service. On appeal, the Railway Tribunal held that the petitioners should be treated as temporary employees and directed that they should be absorbed in regular cadre with effect from the date of their initial appointment. In appeal, this Court upheld the decision of the Tribunal. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the railway administration. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Railway administration had no right to absorb the petitioners permanently in regular posts and that they were entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line recruitment. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had erred in directing that the respondents should be given the same pay as was admissible to the casual labourers who acquire temporary status on completion of 360 days by giving them a notice and that the appellants were entitled only to the privileges which they were eligible to have under the scheme. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The scheme for absorption of casual labour is not an approved one. It does not provide for any automatic absorption of the casual labour who acquire permanent status on completing 360 days of service. [901B] 2. The respondents are entitled to the same salary as was payable to the Casual Labour when they were appointed through regular selection Boards for Classes IV staff and that their services were regularised in accordance with the scheme framed under orders of this Court. [091C] 3. The Tribunal had not given any opportunity to the appellants to put forward their arguments and documents before it. It was open to them to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by the casual workers who acquire regular status on completes 360 days from the commencement of continuous employment. [1001E] 4. The question whether the respondents are entitle to get the same benefit as was available to the temporary employees or not is a matter which has been specifically provided for in the scheme itself. It is not necessary that all those casual labourers should be granted the same benefits as were admissible to other casual workers. [1101F] 5. The fact that the Railways had refused to regularize the services of the petitioners on completionof 360 days would not make them entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the Constitution. [110G] 6. In view of the above, the writ petitions are allowed and the respondents shall be given all the benefits as admissible to temporary employees from the dates of their appointment till they complete 360 days in the project or in the Open line. [109H; 110A B] 7. The petitioners were not entitled to get any benefit under Article 14 of the constitution. They have been denied the same treatment and benefits which they are entitled for. [111B] 8. In these circumstances, the respondents cannot be allowed to take advantage of their own wrongs. [112E] 9. The writ petitions filed by the petitioners are accordingly dismissed.

The appellant, a registered association of the Association, was formed by the Association in the year 1956. The objects of the Act were to provide for the regulation and control of the conduct of its business in the country. The object of the legislation was to regulate the conduct and management of the affairs of the associations. The Act provided for the constitution of a Committee consisting of three members, namely, (1) the Secretary to Government, Agriculture Department, ex officio; (2) the Director of Marketing, exofficio; (3) the Chairman, Board of Directors, ex-officio; and (4) the Registrar, ex -officio. The appellant was a member of the Committee. He was appointed by the Central Government as its Chairman on January 24, 1956. On February 7, 1957, he was appointed as the Secretary of the Federation. On March 31, 1958, he made an application to the Central Board of Agricultural Research and Development for permission to open a new market in the State of Maharashtra. The Central Board rejected the said application on April 11, 1959. The Association filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the bye laws framed by it under section 12(1) of the Bombay Agricultural Produce Marketing Act, 1958 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and prayed for a writ quashing the bye law made by the Government under section 11 of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the petition on March 31/1959. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The power conferred on the Central or the State Government under s. 12(2) of Act is not a legislative power but is an executive power conferred by the statute. [723A] 2.1 The power to make bye laws is a legislative function and it can be exercised only in so far as it purports to operate retrospectively. It cannot be delegated to any other authority or body. [824B] 3.2. The powers of the Central and the State Governments under section 13(3) of Bombay Agricultural Marketing Act are not coextensive with that of the power conferred upon them by the rules made under the Act. [923C] 3:1.1 Section 12 (1), as it stood before its amendment by Act No. 11 of 1956, provided for a bye law which was in force at the time when the Act came into force. The said provision was not retrospective in operation and therefore, the power to amend the byelaw could not be exercised retrospectively. [1024F] 3;2.1 In the instant case, the appellant had been appointed as Secretary of a recognised association by the governing body of a recognized Association under section 10(1)(a) of that Act. He had been authorised to make a bye laws in respect of the same subject matter and it was not competent for him to have delegated his functions to the Commission. [1124B C] 3,2.2 The power of the State to make rules under section 9 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961 is not an executive function conferred by section 12 (i) of it. [1223C E] 3(a). In the present case, there was no delegation of powers by the Commission in respect to the matters specified in section 12 of the aforesaid Act. It was not a matter which could be delegated under section 8 of the impugned bye law. The State Government had power to do so under section 14 of the Gujarat Agricultural Produce Market Act, 1962. [1324F G] 3.(a) In the case of a registered Association, the Registrar is empowered to make an order in writing for the registration of a society as its bye laws and it is not competent to do that. The Registrar has no power under section 16 of the Indian Registration Act to make such bye laws.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. The assessee was carrying on the business as a dealer in cotton yarn and was also carrying on business as an agent of the Ukhara Estate. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee for the assessment year 1964 6A to 1966 7A. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeals to this Court, the appellant contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the receipt of compensation received by the UTI Estate from the Ukhra Estate was not part of the fixed assets of the Company and taxable as dividend. The High Court held that the amount attributable to salami received by it for the grant of long term leases after 31st March, 1948, was capital gain arising after 31 st March, 1949 and not part thereof. In appeal to this court, the assessee contended that interest on compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land for public purposes was not capital gains but was income of a capital nature. The Appellate Assistant commissioner held that interest was not taxable as dividends. He further held that there was no question of law raised by the appellant in his appeals and the High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gains arising after the 31st day of March, 1950. In view of the findings recorded by the Appellate Tribunal, the High 'Court held that distribution of dividend out of capital gain was not a capital gain. The appellant appealed to this ' Court. HELD: (1) The High ' Court had no jurisdiction to decide upon any question of fact arising in the case and it could not be said that the finding recorded by it on all the questions was erroneous or illegal. [701B] (2) The expression "other sources" used in section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 means income derived from other sources. [802C] (3) The word "interest" in section 12 of the Act is wide enough to include interest on the compensation received or receivable for compulsory purchase of land. It does not mean that the interest must be deemed to have been earned by the person concerned. [601D] (4) The words "other source" used therein are wide enough and they cannot be construed in any manner to include income derived by the Company from other source. [820E] (5) The language of section 12(6B) is clear and unambiguous. It is not open to the Income Tax Officer to decide whether any part of such capital gain arose after 31 March, 1947 or before the 1st day April, 1956 when the amount received was capital asset.

The appellant was engaged in the business of cutting and removing grass from the forest area. He had been carrying on his business as a wood oil agent for the purpose of manufacturing and selling the timber. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act, which provided that the said wood would be used for the purposes of manufacture and sale of timber. In the notification, it was stated that the wood oil is a forest produce. The appellant filed an application before the Forest Officer claiming exemption from payment of tax on the ground that the trees were not wood oil within the meaning of section 2(f) (i) of Act. The Forest Officer rejected the claim and held that the timber was not wood as defined under section 2 (f) of Forest Act, 1963. He also held that there was no evidence to show that the forest produce was a forest product. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the order of the Forest officer and allowed the application filed by the appellant. In this appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the Forest Department had not produced any evidence to prove that the tree in question was wood oil. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The forest produce is a 'forest produce'. It is a commodity which is used for manufacturing and sale. Therefore, the word 'forest' has to be construed in its popular sense in which it is being understood in the trade. [601B] 2. The word 'Forest produce' has been defined in section 2 of the Indian Forest Act as including any forest produce which is not a forest. It does not include any wood or forest produce, but includes any timber or forest product which is produced for the manufacture and/or sale of such article. [701C] 3. The expression 'forest ' has to bear in mind the purpose and object of the act. Therefore it cannot be restricted in such a manner as to defeat the principle and object which is being interpreted in the sense in Which it is used. [802D] 4. The term 'forest " has to include all wood or forests produce, whether or not cut and removed from any forest area or not. It must also include any timber, or forest products which are produced for sale. [820E] 5. The words 'forest" have been used in the Act as a word of wide import. Therefore the word "forest produce" has to receive its ordinary meaning in the context and the purpose. The definition of forest produce in section 3 (1) (f), therefore, must be construed strictly in the light of the intention and object that it is understood in which the word is used in commercial parlance in which such word is being used. Therefore there was nothing in the statute to show as to what is meant by 'forest'. [820G] 6. The meaning of forest has to necessarily be interpreted in its technical sense. It cannot be limited in any manner it can be understood in that sense in the popular sense. [823E] 7. In view of the definition of 'forest', the word forest produce' is to include wood or trees which are cut and remove from any place within the forest areas. Therefore when the word Forest produce is used, it cannot mean that wood or Forests produce can be used as a forest for the manufacturing or sale of goods. [825E] 8. The dictionary meaning of 'Forest Produce' in the definition is to exclude wood or timber which are not cut or removed from the forests area. Therefore if wood or wood is cut and removal from any other place within that area, it will be covered by the definition. [826A D] 9. In order to attract the provisions of section 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the legislature has used the word wood as a ' forest produce'. The word " Forest produce" is not defined in the Indian Penal Code.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. He was also convicted under s.302 read with s.34 and sentenced as aforesaid. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the accused but reduced the sentence from imprisonment for life to one year. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had not properly appreciated the evidence in its proper perspective and that the judgment of the trial court was perverse. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the High court that the prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was guilty of murder is based on a dying declaration made by Shivlal, the brother of the deceased. [857 A] 2. The evidence of the eye witnesses is not reliable and trustworthy. It is true that the appellant had been acquitted in respect of an offence under section 304 Part I read with sections 34 and 302 readwith section 34 but the High Curt has rightly held that the conviction was based on the dying declarations made by the deceased and the other eye witnesses. [957 A B] 3. The prosecution case is not supported by any reliable evidence. It must be disregarded in this case also because the High Courts have accepted the testimony of the two eye witnesses, who are alleged to have been present at the time when they were brought to the hospital at 5 p.m. and the dying declaration was made by them to the police at 5 a.m., and the evidence of both the eye witness is not trustworthy. [1057 B] 4. The fact that the deceased had been admitted in the hospital does not affect the prosecution case because it has not been shown that the doctor who examined him had given any opinion on the basis of which he was declared hostile. [1158 C] 5. The dying declarations are not supported either by any evidence or by any other circumstances. It cannot be said that the dying statements made by both the witnesses were not reliable. [1259 D] 6. The medical evidence does not support the prosecution version. There is no reason for the HighCourt to interfere with the findings of the Sessions Judge and the order of acquittal.
