[1360 E] 7. In the instant case, the High ' Court has rightly acquitted the accused. [119G] 8. It was not a case where the evidence was of a very weak type. The trial court had wrongly relied upon the dyingdeclaration made by one of the witnesses. There was no reason to interfere in the judgment. [118A B] 9. In view of the above, there is no merit in this appeal and it must be dismissed.

The appellant company 's factory at Jamshedpur was incorporated under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The management of the appellant company was taken over by the Government of Bihar and its employees were transferred to the appellant 's establishment at Jamshedpur. On September 30, 1963, the appellant Company 's union filed a petition in the High Court for a writ quashing the award dated September 28, 1964 of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that it was not maintainable because the dispute raised by the workmen of the company ' s establishment at the Jamshedpur and its workmen represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers' Union were not covered by the provisions contained in the Industrial Dispute Act,1947. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the dispute between the management and the workmen. [701B] 2. The dispute raised was not a dispute arising out of the agreement between the parties but a dispute relating to the conditions of service of the workmen employed in the factory at the work 's company at Jamshedpur and the Tribunal was justified in holding that the dispute was not covered under the Industrial dispute Act, 1948. [801C] 3. The question whether the dispute is covered by an agreement between two parties or not is a matter which can be decided only by the Tribunal in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 10(2) of the Act. [820D] 4. The appellant company has been incorporated under section 25FFF of the Indian Companies Act, 1956 and it has been registered under the Companies Act. It was carrying on business at Jamshedpur for a period of about six years. The workmen of that factory were not employees of the Company at Jamshedpur but were employees of its other establishments. [823E] 5. The company 'S establishment at Ranchi was an undertaking of the Union and it had been running its own unit at Jamshedpur, which was a part of the country. It had been carrying on its business at the factory of the petitioner company at Ranchi. The Company ' s union was not in existence since the date of the said agreement. [825E] 6. The employees of that establishment were not workmen of its own establishment at any time and, therefore, they were not entitled to any special leave under section 20(2)(b) of Industrial Disputes act, 1947, as the workmen 's Union 's unit at Ranchi had been working in Jamshedpur. [826E] 7. The workers of the factory were also employees of their other establishments at Jamshedpur who had made the aforesaid demands and had also paid the normal rate of wages as provided by the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. The union was, therefore not entitled under section 2(b) to claim any special allowance for the extra ordinary leave granted to them. [828E] 8. The Labour Court was right in holding the appellant to be a workman within the meaning of section 2 (b) and that the workmen were not members of the executive committee of the union at Jamshedpur which had been constituted by the union. [827G H] 9. The respondent company ' S establishment at its Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Act and, as such, it could not be said to be an industry within the definition of section 25F of Industrial Dispute act,1947, as it was a case of lay down of conditions of services of the employees of a factory at Ranchi which had come to be represented by its workmen at Jamshedpur in terms of the provisions relating to leave available to the company. [829E] 9 A. The expression 's representative' used in section 2 of the I.N.T.U.C. Act, is not defined in that Act. But it has a wide meaning and connotation. It does not include any person who is directly or indirectly interested in the management of an industrial undertaking. [824E] 10 A.

The appellant, a stage carriage permit holder, filed an application for grant of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Transport Authority granting the permit. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal by its order dated May 3/4, 1963 allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the State Transport Authority refusing to grant the permit in favour of the appellant. The appellant challenged the order passed by the State Government on the ground that the Regional transport Authority had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals against an earlier decision of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the Appellate Authority was not competent under section 64(1) of the Act to entertain and decide the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant had a right to file an appeal against an order granting the permits in pursuance thereof and that the appellate authority had no power to entertain or decide the appeals. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authorities granting the stage carriage permits are not competent to entertain appeals against orders of the authorities granting the same. [601 B] 2. The Appellate Tribunal is competent under Section 64(2) to grant a permit and it has no jurisdiction in respect of an appeal to the State transport Appellate Tribunal constituted under sub section (2). [602 C] 3. The power conferred on the Appellate Tribunals by section 64 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, is not a judicial function. It is only a ministerial act which can be exercised by the appellate authorities. [613 D] 4. The powers conferred on them are not judicial functions. They are not merely administrative functions. The Tribunal has no power under section64 to grant permits and it cannot exercise any jurisdiction in regard to matters with which we are concerned. [502 C E] 5. The order granting a permit is only an ministerial act and does not confer any right of appeal against the grant of the permit or its rejection by the Appellate authority. [511 D] 6. The appellate authorities have no power, under section 65(1)(a) to entertain an appeal from an order passed in pursuance thereto. [504 C] 7. The orders granting a stage Carriage permit are not appealable under section 66 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1945 (old Rules). [503 D] 8. The appeals before the State Appellate Tribunal are competent under sections 64(3) to 64(4) to the Appellate Authorities constituted under section 63 of the said Act. [506 E] 9. In view of the provisions contained in section 64 (1)(b), the appeals before this Court are not maintainable. [500 F] 10. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed.

The appellant filed a petition under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (in short 'the CPC') for setting aside the election of respondent Prakash Vir Shastri. The High Court allowed the petition and set aside the order of the Election Commissioner holding that the publication Exhibit 22 was not proved to be published with the consent of the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1.1 The appellant had been guilty of corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of respondent Vir Shastri and his election agent. He had also committed a corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (in brief 'the Act') which was punishable with imprisonment for two years. [701A B] 1.2 The appellant was not able to prove that respondent Prakash Chandra Shastri or his election agents were guilty of any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (3) read with section 123 of the Act. [802B C] 1.(a) The appellant did not produce any evidence in support of the allegation that respondent Vir Gandhi had committed any corrupt practices in relation thereto. He was, therefore, not entitled to be declared as a candidate for election to the Lok Sabha from the constituency. [901C H] (b) The High court has erred in holding that there was no evidence to prove the fact that respondent Rajiv Shastri or any other candidate had committed an corrupt practice. [1001E C] 2.(a)(i) The allegation of corrupt practices is not proved by the appellant and, therefore the High Court was right in setting aside his election. [1101F G] (ii) The allegations made against the appellant were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. [110G] 3.(b) In view of the fact, that respondent PRAK Vir Shastri had been acquitted by the trial court on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice, the High court was right to set aside his conviction and sentence. [111A B C] 4.1(a)(ii) In the present case, the appellant had not produced any evidence to show that respondent Pratap Prakash Shastri or other candidate Vir Shastri were guilty for any corrupt Practice in relation thereof. The appellant could not prove that he was a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Uttar Pradesh. [112A B E] (iii) The onus of proving that respondent No. Prakash Chandra had been convicted by the court under section 124(3)(b) readwith section 123, is on him. [113B C F] 4.(a). In view thereof, the conviction and sentences passed against the respondent Prakash Shastri are set aside. [114A B D] (iv) The conviction of respondent No,. Prakash Chandra by the High Judge under section 125(3), is not sustainable in law. [115E] 5.2. The appeal is allowed.

The respondent decree holder purchased the property from one Shri. B.K. Jain, who was the auction purchaser for a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- and deposited the sale price with the court on July 17, 1980. The appellant filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale on the ground that the application for delivery of possession was made within one year from the date of the sale and that the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134 of the Limitation Act would be computed from the day of the purchase. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the second application holding that the appellant had not filed an appli cation for setting up a fresh suit for settingaside the sale. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code are applicable to applications under Order 21 Rule 95 and 90 of the C.P.C. and not to applications for setting off the decree within a period of one year. [701B] 2.2 The application for setting it aside was made on July 19, 1980 and the appellant filed the second appli tation for delivery thereof on July 21, 1979. The application was made beyond the period prescribed by the Limitation act. The period of three years from the filing of the second ap plication expired on July 20, 1979 and the application was filed on July 22, 1979 i.e., after a period o f limitation as provided by Article 136 of the Constitution. [801C] 3.3 In view of the provisions of Article 134(b) of the Schedule to the Limitation A ct, the application could not be said to have been made within a year from July 21 1979 and that is why the application filed on 7th July, 1980 was beyond the time prescribed by article 136 of th e Limitation Act. [901D] 4.1 In view thereof, the appeal is allowed and the order passed by the learned Single judge of the Rajasthan High Court is set aside. The second appl ication for setting-aside the auction sale on July 23, 1980 is also dismissed.

The appellant was the first respondent and his election agent. He had been arrested for an offence of harbouring the accused in a defamed case, that is to say, he had not seen the incident of murders having taken place a day prior to the election. The High Court has recorded a finding that the said poster was published on 25th March, 1987 and it was intended to create an impression and did not show any intention to commit the offence of murder. It is this finding which is challenged in this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has recorded findings that the appellant had made a statement on oath before the election officer that he was present at the time when the incident took place a days prior to his election and that he had also seen the wall posters and wall posters. [701A] 2.2 The evidence of PW 1, who is an independent witness, clearly shows that he has not seen any such poster on 25 th March,1987. He has stated in his examination under Section 313 of the Code that he did not see the wall poster together with exhibit P1 and that the same was published by him on 25.3.1987. [801B] 3.2 It is true that the evidence of PWs 1 to 4 clearly shows the fact that they had seen the occurrence of murders in question, but there is no doubt that they have not seen anything about the incident. The evidence also does not show that they were present at any time prior to their election. [901C] 3:1.3 It is well settled that a statement made by an independent person cannot be used as evidence against an accused person unless it is corroborated by other evidence.

The respondent No. 5 was granted permission to develop a hotel on the land in question for the construction of a five star hotel. The respondent No, 5 applied for permission to construct a hotel and the Municipal Corporation had sanctioned the development plan. The Municipal Corporation rejected the application for approval of the revised plan on the ground that it was not prepared in accordance with the direction of the respondent No., 2. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court against the order granting exemption to the respondent no. 5. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order of the Municipal Commissioner. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The decision of the High court is not correct in law. It was not open to the appellants to challenge the validity of the resolution on the grounds that it is contrary to the directions issued by the respondent NO. 2. [701B] 1.2. The order granting the exemption to respondent No 5 was passed without considering the objections raised by the Municipal Council and the appellant No. 4. It is not open for the appellants, in this case, to challenge that order of exemption granted to respondent no 5. 929. The appeal is accordingly allowed. [801C] 1:1.3. The view taken by the High Courts that the respondent had sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground is not sustainable. [820G] 2.1 The High court was, therefore, justified in holding that the order passed by the Commissioner granting exemption should be quashed. [821A] 1.(a) In the instant case, the High Powered Committee had considered the objections of the appellants and rejected the same on the basis of the report of the Development Plan submitted by respondent No 4. The appellant No 5 had not challenged the sanction of the development plans. [822B] 2:1.(b) The High Power Committee had approved the revised development plan submitted by the appellants. It had also considered the objection raised by respondent no, 5 and held that the revised Development plan was prepared in conformity with the directions of the Corporation. [823C] 2(a) The appellant had not questioned the validity or otherwise of the sanction granted to the Development plan submitted before the Municipal Committee. [825D] 2.(b)(i) The respondent no 1 had not filed any appeal against the decision of respondent No 2 granting exemption under section 46 of the Act. [824E] 3.1.(a). In view of the fact that the appellants had not raised any objection to the sanction accorded by the Corporation, the Municipal Board was justified in rejecting the plan submitted on behalf of 929 respondent no 4. 928. [826B] (b) There is no substance in this appeal and it must be dismissed. [828C] 3.(a)(i). The High power Committee had not considered the question whether the revised plans were prepared in compliance with the order dated April 30, 1984 of the Commissioner. [827A] (ii)The respondent no 2 was entitled to rely upon the revised master plan submitted for the development of the hotel and also on the report submitted by him. [829B] 3(a)(iii)The High Court had not properly appreciated the fact whether the appellants were interested in seeing that sufficient area is kept reserved or recreation ground has been taken into account while deciding the question as to the legality or otherwise to the validity and otherwise of a resolution on April 30 1984. [82C] 4.(b). The respondent NO 1 was entitled only to rely on the revised Master Plan submitted for a park or recreation grounds. [881D] 5.(a), (i)The appellant No 2 had not produced any evidence before the Commissioner that the land reserved for a recreation ground was required for public purposes or recreationground.

The appellant union was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of various products. The workmen were employed by the employer for a period of five years from April 8, 1980 to March 8, 1979 when they were reemployed. On April 8. 1980, the appellant union had been closed down an industrial undertaking. In the course of its employment, the workmen were re-employed and the new employees were reengaged. The management issued a notice on May 10, 1980 calling upon the workmen to show cause why their services should not be terminated. The employer filed a reply to the said notice denying the allegations made by the workmen. On June 11, 1980, an industrial dispute was raised by the union that the workmen had been retrenched and that they were being re-engaged in service. The Industrial Court held that the employer had failed to prove that the new workmen were being retrenched and the employer was not guilty of unfair labour practice. The Labour Court held: "The management has failed to establish that the industrial undertaking was closed down or that the employees were being continued re-employment as they were already employed by him. It is true that the management had not established that the existing workmen were not re-employing in service but had closed down and that the said closure was a genuine one. But there is no evidence on record to show that the present management has resorted to closure of the industrial undertakings. The evidence produced before the Industrial Court shows that the employers have not taken any steps to terminate the services of the workmen or to regularise them as they are re- employed by them. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that the appellant Union had failed in proving that the earlier workmen were continued reemployed and that their services were being discontinued. The industrial undertaking has closed down the industrial Undertaking and has closed its work. It was not a case of lock out or closure but had been re-opened. Therefore, the management was guilty of misconduct under Sec. 28(1) (b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947." In view of the above decision of the Supreme Court, it is clear that the question whether the employer has committed an unfair labour practices by imposing lock out and closure was not one or merely a device to determine whether the industrial company was closed or that it was a case where the employer is not guilty. The High Court held in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The question whether there was any lockout or not has been determined by the Industrial Tribunal and the High Court has rightly held that since the employer did not have the intention to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer at the time when it closed down, it had closed its industrial undertaking and that it had not closed down. [601B] 1.2. The fact that the workers were re employed by a new employer is also not decisive of the matter. It has been established on evidence produced by the employers that the old workmen were in employment at the relevant time when they closed down were reemployment as it was now expanding and that there was no change in the circumstances beyond the control of the employers at the date when the industrial activity was started. [701C] 1.(a) The employer had not given any notice to the new workman before the closure was over. It had not been given any opportunity to explain his conduct. [771B] (b). In view thereof, it must be held that there is a violation of Sec.28(1)(b) and 28(2) of The employer has failed in establishing that the change in circumstances beyond control of its industrial undertakings was a device or pretence to determine what the employer would have closed down its industrial Undertaking. [78C] 2.(a). In the instant case, the employer having not given notice to it before the closing down of the undertaking, it could not be said to have closed its undertaking and had closed it. [79D] 3.(b)

The appellant company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 with a view to invest in investments and properties of the assessee company. The assessee company was registered as a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties of its business. On September 30, 1964 the Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 66(1) of the Act calling upon the appellant company to show cause why the income chargeable to tax be not included in the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, security and other properties of their business. The appellant company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the proceedings on various grounds including that the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to issue notice under sections 66(2) and 66(3). The High Court held that the enquiry made by the Incometax Officer was not competent on the question as framed at present. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had erred in holding that the income charged to tax was a dealer within the meaning of section 2(15) of Act, 1922 and that the Appellate Tribunal had no power to issue a notice under s 66(4). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the Income Officer had jurisdiction to proceed with the enquiry is a mixed question of fact and law and it was not open to the High Courts to interfere in the matter on the ground that the relevant material on which the enquiry was made by an officer was not a question of law. [701B] 2. The High court has erred in setting aside the judgment of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner holding that there was no evidence on record to support the finding of the Income TAX Officer that the assessee had incurred losses and profits made or profits made by it as it was a business loss. [802C E] 3. The facts disclosed in the memorandum of association and the statements of the case clearly show that the appellant Company was a registered dealer in investments, properties and securities and other assets of its company. It was not an investor. The Income Tax officer had no authority to issue any notice under sec 66(5) of Income Tax Act, 1961. [602F] 4. The Appellate Tribunal has rightly held that there is no evidence to support that the transactions were not a dealer or an investor and that it was only an investor who was a person in investments. [820G] 5. In view of the fact that the question whether a particular transaction was a trade or an investment, was a mixed questions of law and fact, the High courts have rightly held against the assessee Company. [823A D] 6. The Tribunal has not committed any error in holding otherwise. It is well settled that the provisions of section 66 (1) are mandatory and they do not confer any power on the Income officer to proceed under section 67(2). [823E] 7. In the instant case, the appellant had not been able to show that there were no sales or purchases of shares and securities. The fact that there had been a sale or purchase of shares or securities does not make it a dealer. [825F] 8. The mere fact that some mistake was discovered in the facts of the present case does not mean that the Tribunal has committed any mistake in holding so. [826G] 9. In this view of things, the appeal must fail and is dismissed with costs.

The appellant, a Judicial Officer of the State Judicial Service, was appointed as District Munsif in the Madras Presidency Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953. He was posted to the Madras City Civil Services and was posted at the Madras High Court. On April 28, 1954, he was transferred from the Madras Civil Services to the Hyderabad City Civil Service. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the order of suspension dated January 28,1954, on the ground that the Government had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally and that the order passed by the High court on January 28 1954, was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had a right to have his case referred to and determined by the Tribunal in accordance with Rule 4 (1) (a) of the Madras civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules. On appeal, the Division Bench held that the enquiry was not properly conducted and that it was open to the Government to hold a fresh enquiry and decide for itself whether the charges were well founded or not. The Division Bench further held that since the appellant was appointed by the Governor of the Province, he could not be dismissed from service on the grounds that the findings given by Balakrishna Ayyar J., were without jurisdiction. On further appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no power to decide for themselves whether the findings recorded by BalakKrishna Ayyar J. should be held to conclude the question against the appellant, and that since there was a finding that the charges against the Members of the District Judicial Service were well based or not, the Government could not have passed orders on such charges. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Curt in so far as it relates to the appellant's suspension pending enquiry into the conduct of a judicial officer is bad. [601B] 2. The power conferred by Article 311 of Constitution is an administrative power and not an administrative one. It is not an executive function. It can be exercised only by the Government or its delegate, and in the absence of any such delegation, it cannot be said that the orders passed on such charge are either arbitrary or illegal. [701C] 3. The mere fact that the procedure followed by the enquiry officer was not fair or illegal does not make the order bad. It may be that the power conferred is an executive power and the Government can exercise its discretion in accordance therewith. But it cannot, therefore, be said to have been exercised arbitrarily or mala fide. [801D] 4. The impugned orders are clearly without jurisdiction and they do not call for any interference by this Court under article 226 of the constitution. [820E] 5. The Government is bound to hold an enquiry into grave charges against a member of the service, and if it decides that there was no proper enquiry, it has no power or authority to pass orders on the charge. [823G] 6. In view of the fact that in the present case the High Powered Committee had not decided for itself any question as to whether the allegations were well grounded or not and that there is no question of holding a fresh inquiry, the High powered Committee was bound to consider the same for itself. [825E] 7. The powers conferred by article 311 are not administrative in nature. It cannot be exercised by the State Government or by any other authority. The State Government has no jurisdiction under article 311 to decide on the question whether it is a case of corruption or misconduct. [826C] 8. In the present cases, the appellant has been appointed as a District Munsif and he was posted in the Hyderabad Civil Services as District Munsiff. He had been promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge by the order dated January 27, 1954. The orders were passed on January 27. 1954, and they were not challenged by any party.

The appellant, a legal representative of the deceased person, filed an application under section 24B of the Act for assessment of his income on the ground that he had not died. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and assessed the appellant to income tax on the basis of the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 (as it stood at the material date) in view of the fact that the legal representatives of the estate of the appellant were not liable to be taxed in the hands of the legal representative. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment and assessed him to income Tax on the footing that the death of the said person was caused by his legal representative, and he also held that the provisions contained in section 24A of the Income tax act 1922 (which were later substituted by the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953, with effect from April 1, 1952, were not applicable to the assessment of income tax. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and held that section 24 B was ultra vires the provisions relating to income received by a legal representatives and the liability to pay the tax on such receipts was not liable for assessment under section 23A of 1922 Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the expression "assessee" in section 2(2) of the 1922 Act did not include any person who died, but only a legal Representative of a deceased person. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "person by whom income tax is payable" in Section 24B means a person by whom the income received or of the loss sustained by him or of his death was deemed to have been received by such legal representative and the legal Representatives of a person who cannot be deemed to be liable to pay tax on their income. [601C] 2. The word "person" in the section means a legal practitioner, and includes any other legal representative who can be deemed as having received the income by such deceased person from his legal representatives. [702D] 3. The words "any person in respect of whom income is payable", in section 23B of 1922 are not applicable in the case of an individual who died or was deemed as a legal heir to receive the income. It is only if he has received the amount by way of tax, that the liability would be on the legal heirs and legal representatives who cannot claim any refund due to them. [802E] 4. The legal representative or the legal Representative can be treated as having died in the course of business. [820G] 5. The liability to tax on income received is not in accordance with the provisions for assessment, but it is only when the legal heir or the Legal representative who cannot get the refund due has been treated as a person liable to tax under section 25B of 1961 Act. [823E] 6. In view of this position, the appeal must fail and is dismissed.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Madhya Pradesh. He was appointed as an ex- Ruler of that State by the Government of India and he was recognised by the President as the Ruler of such State. On his death, the appellant became entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in his villages. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of rent or other revenue from him on the ground that he had not been recognized by the government of India as the private property of the appellant and that the appellant was not an ex Ruler of any State. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution was maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 and 228 of the constitution because the appellant had not filed any written statement or evidence in support of his case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the petitioner was an eximi midar within the meaning of article 366(22) of the Indian Constitution. [601 B] 2. The expression 'maufidar' in article 366 (22) means a person who by or under the provisions contained in the Constitution is recognised by, the President to be a Ruler for the purposes of the Union and includes any person who after the commencement of the Act was recognised as such by the Ruler as the successor of such Ruler. [701 C] 3. The word 'mafidar' has not been defined in article 363 of the Government Order dated January 26, 1950. It is a definition which is confined to a person holding land under an ex­ Ruler and includes also any person holding or claiming to be recognised by Government as such. [802 D E] 4. The words 'maffidar' have not been used in any narrow or technical sense. They are only limited to persons holding or being recognised by government as such and the word 'maufidar" has not necessarily to be confined to persons who by virtue of the provisions of article 363(22), have no right to recover rents or revenue. [902 D] 5. The definition of 'mazidar' under article 366 is wide enough to include a person whose property is recognised as an Ruler for purposes of Union and not otherwise. [1001 E] 6. The term 'mazanian' in the definition of "mazidars" has been defined by section 2(m) of that Act to mean a person having a right to receive rent or any other revenue or rent from persons who are recognised as Ruler for purpose of Union under article 363. [1101 E F] 7. The object of the definition is to provide for the continuance of the status of an ex emptionaldar in the State and not to confer upon him any rights which he may have against the Government. [110 A B] 8. The right to collect rent or rent is a right which has been recognised by law as an absolute right. It cannot be denied that the income from the land held by the appellant is not liable to be assessed to land revenue. The fact that the villages in question were assessed to lands revenue does not mean that the villagers had no right, whatever, to recover any rent or Revenue from personsholding land in their villages. [111 A B C] 9. In view of the clear language of article 362(22)(i) and (ii), it is difficult to hold that the provisions relating to the grant of a certificate under article 132(1) are not applicable to the appellant as he was not recognised by his Government as an emptionary of the Ruler. The question whether the appellant could be regarded as an Ex- Ruler or an ex minedee of the erstwhile State of M.P., does not arise for consideration in this appeal.

The respondent was posted at Shillong in the office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. He was transferred to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, Office of the Directorate General, Botsanical survey of India. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of transfer on the ground that the same is vitiated by mala fides and that the Tribunal has exceeded its jurisdiction in quashing the order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was passed malafide and that it was not open to the respondent to challenge the same in a court or Tribunal only where it is passed malafide or where it was passed mala fide or where the transfer is made in violation of any statutory provisions. In appeal by special leave, this Court held that the impugned order of the High court quashing the transfer order was vitiated by malafides and that there was no reason for the respondent not to pass the order at all. Allowing the appeal, this court, HELD: 1. The power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions/guides. It does not empower any spouse to go out from his place of posting and that too without sacrifice of the requirements of administration and needs of other employees. [901 D] 2. The guidelines issued by the Government on 3.4.1986 have no application to the case of a person who is serving at Shillong for a longer period, and that is why the respondent should not be allowed to continue at Shillong till he reaches his place in India. [092 E] 3.1. In view of the guidelines issued in the Government of India O.M. dated 3.04.1986, it cannot be said that the transfer was vitiated on account of mala fides or that the respondent is liable to transfer anywhere in India, particularly when he reaches the place of his choice without sacrifice and needs. [1001 E] 4.2. The order of transferring the respondent from Shillong to Pouri (Uttarakhand) by Senior Administrative officer, Officeof the Director General, Indian Circle, Government of Indias, New Delhi is not a valid order. It is an order of posting which is not in accordance with the guidelines. [1101 E F] 4:1. The transfer is an incident of Government Service and it does not enable any spouse of the administrative needs and the same has to bear in mind this aspect along with the exigencies of administration. [110 A B] 2:1 The order transferring the Respondent from Shillong cannot be sustained as malafide or that it is made by the Director of General, India, NewDelhi. [109 C] 3:2.1 The respondent was transferred from Shillong and posted at Pauri, Assam to Pure, Assam. He had been transferred to Shillong and he reached Shillong on his own request. He has been transferred from Guwahati to Paon, Assam and posted in Shillong. The said transfer is in violation to the administrative guidelines issued for the purpose of considering transfers of an individual officer. [111 D] 3; 2:2 It is not possible to accept the contention that the posting of an employee at a particular station is not permissible under the administrative rules. [112 E F H] 3, 3:1 A transfer is a matter of policy and it cannot interfere with the order unless it is shown that the authority has applied its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The mere fact that the officer has been posted at different places does not by itself make him liable to be transferred to any other station. [113 F H; 113 A B C] 2, 3 & 4:2 The transfer of an officer is a policy matter and it can interfere with only where there is a vacancy in the said station.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with Section 149, I.P.C. and were convicted by the learned Trial Judge for an offence punishable under Section 304 Part I, I PC. The prosecution case was that on January 2, 1977 at about 8.30 A.M., when the deceased Jawahar had gone to answer the call of nature, he found that his father had caused injuries to him. He also saw that the appellants were armed with sticks and A2, A3 and A4 assaulted him with aruval (bill hook) and A5 armed with stick. The deceased Jawahar was lying on the ground in front of the house when he was assaulted by the appellants. The appellants were tried for an assault on Jawahar and his father/mother. The learned Trial judge found that the prosecution case rested on circumstantial evidence, but held that the circumstances proved against the accused persons were not established beyond reasonable doubt. He further held that there was no direct evidence to connect the appellants with the crime. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the motive for the murder was not established and that the evidence was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The circumstances proved by the prosecution are not sufficient enough to establish the guilt against the appellants beyond reasonable doubts. [701B] 2. The High Court has rightly held that it was a case where the motive was not proved and the evidence is not reliable. [802C] 3. The fact that the deceased had been assaulted by A1 to A3, does not make any difference in view of the facts and circumstances of this case. [820D] 4. The evidence on record clearly shows that the accused were armed only with sticks. There was no reason for them to have caused injuries on the person of Jawahar. [823E] 5. The nature of the offence committed by the accused is not established. It is a matter of common knowledge that when the attack on Jawahar was made, he would not be able to give any finding in favour of the prosecution. [825F] 6. In view of this fact, it cannot be said that the case falls within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., and the High court had rightly held the appellants guilty under Section 307 read with section 149, IPC. [826A D] 7. The conviction of the appellant under Section 324 read with Sections 149, is not sustainable in law. He was convicted under Section 323 read with Sec. 34, IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. [822E] 8. In the instant case, the evidence on the record clearly establishes that the first accused had caused simple injuries to Jawahar and he had inflicted a single blow on him. The medical evidence clearly shows the fact that there were no external injuries on his person. He had also received one injury on the head of Jawahar and the other on the left hand. [828E] 9. In this case, it is not possible for the prosecution to prove that the appellant was guilty under Sections 302 read and 307 read. The offence committed in respect of which the appellants had been convicted under Sections 147 and 148 I. P. C., is clearly established beyond doubt. [829F H] 10. It cannot be disputed that the intention of the first appellant was to cause grievous hurt to Jawahar. He did not intend to cause any injury on his body. The act of the second appellant was also an offence under Section 325, IPC read with 307, IPG.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1913. The respondent No. 1 was appointed as a Director of the appellant Bank on June 30, 1969 and he was appointed by the Central Government as a director of the said company. On July 31, 1970, the appellant bank issued a notice to the respondents calling upon them to pay the amount due to it under section 4(e) of the Act. The respondents filed an application before the High Court for setting aside the order of the Tribunal and for quashing the order dated August 30, 1976 passed by the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the said application on the ground that the appellant had not made out a case for striking down the provisions of section 4 (e) as it was not a corporation within the meaning of section 2(e). Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 4(a) of Act XLIII of 1956 is an exception to section 4 of the General Clauses Act and does not apply to corporations created or constituted by any special Indian law. [968B] 1.2 The expression 'any other law ' in section 4 means a law made by the Parliament itself. [1069C] 2.3 The word 'any ' in the context of section 3(e), as it stood on the date when the Act was passed, would mean that the legislature had not intended to refer to any law made either by the Indian Legislature or by the law itself. It is well settled that a law which is made by Parliament itself cannot be said to have been enacted by the Legislature of the country. [99D] 2:1 The word "any ' has been used in section 3 (e), but it does not refer to a law passed by any Legislature of its own country, nor does it refer to an Act of Parliament of India which is a special Indian Law. [100E] 2(a). In the instant case, the expression 'an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom or any special India ' in Section 4 (a) has been enacted as a piece of special law applicable to corporations established by it and not by the legislature itself. The word used in the section is clear that the Legislature had intended to take the said Act into consideration, but it did not refer only to a statute which was created by any other Indian law, but also to a statutory enactment of Parliament. [101E] 3.2 In the present case, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the respondent No 1. The expression "any other Law ' in clause (e)(a) would be applicable to the appellant and not to corporations formed or created by special Indian laws. [103G H; 101A B] 3:1.3 In the case before us, the word 'an ' has not been used either in the Act itself or in the statute itself. There is no doubt that the word "an ' in relation to a corporation established by a special law would refer only if it is created in pursuance of an Act which is expressly mentioned in section 2 (e). [103H; 101B] 3(a)(b) The expression used in clause(e)(c) would not be applicable in the instant cases, but would be confined to corporations constituted or created under a special statute. [104A B C] 3.(a) In the context in which it is used, the words 'any special law ' have been used and not any other law. The words 'an existing law ' are not defined in the Indian Penal Code. [105D] (b) A corporation formed or constituted under a Special Law would be governed by the provisions contained in section 5 of the Banking companies Act, 1949.

The appellant, a manufacturer of sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, filed an application under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for a direction that the price fixed by the Government should be at Rs. 150 per quintal for the whole of India and that the prices should be fixed accordingly. The appellant contended that the fixation of price was arbitrary and unreasonable and that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned notification is not in accordance with law and is bad as it contravenes article 14 of' the Constitution; that the power to fix the price is not a matter of policy or expediency but is an administrative power conferred on the Central Government under section 4 of the Act and that there was no discrimination between the two regions. The power to regulate the prices cannot be exercised by the Central or State Governments in any manner, except in accordance therewith, as provided in article 14. It is not necessary for us to consider whether the fixation is arbitrary or unreasonable. The notification is therefore bad as the price of sugar fixed by it is not adequate and reasonable. [657 C] In the present case there was a discrimination between two regions and the appellant. The impugned notification was issued under section 5 of the said Act, which is in violation of article 14, and the impugned Notification was issued on July 30, 1958. The price fixed for the entire country was not adequate or reasonable. The fixation of prices by the State Government is therefore arbitrary and illegal. [757 D] In view of the economic factors which control the price at a loss, there is no discrimination in effect between two industries in the other areas.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of indexes. The Company had been carrying on its business from one place to another at Calcutta. In the year 1957, the appellant entered into an agreement with the Company for the supply of indexing and indexing materials and for that purpose it paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/- as advance payment. On June 21, 1954, the Company agreed to pay a sum in instalments of Rs..2,500/as advance payment and the balance was payable on July 31, 1955. The appellant paid a further sum of rupees one thousand on August 30, 1956. The company made an application under section 33A of the Act for permission to carry out the work of indexation and indexes at the cost of living index. The Central Government granted permission to the Company to carry on its work of Indexation and Indexing at the rate of Rs... per square metre in respect of working class cost of indexations and indexed material. On July 31. 1955, the Central Government issued a notification under section 32(1) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for the purpose of carrying on the work relating to Indexation at the rates specified in the schedule annexed thereto. The respondent company filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal claiming that the working class of indexed and indexories were equalised by fixing the cost at Rs..1,000/per square metre. The Tribunal allowed the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to get any increase in the dearness allowance at the prevailing rates of living Indexes at 344.1. The High Court held that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding that there was a substantial change in the working classes cost of Indexing and Indexes in regard to the working conditions of indexories at 344.. In appeal No. 88/66, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Tribunal. The State Government appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding on the basis that there were substantial increase in living Indexing in the cost indexes in respect to working class costs of indexets at 344, that the said figures relate only to working classes and not to the corresponding entries in regard thereto. [801F] (2) The High court had erred by holding that since the working standard was Rs.1,500/- per square foot, the Tribunal was justified in holding the appellant to be entitled to increase in dearness allowance for living indexes of the indexes and indexs at 344 and that the High court was not right in relying upon Exhibit 3, which is a part of the annual book. [901F G] (3) The working class and index value of living and index are equalised according to the prevailing market rate of living. The working classes are equalized by fixing their cost at about Rs.2,000/-. The Tribunal had not given any reasons for holding that in view of the fact that the work done by Indexing was less than Rs.500/-per square foot the Tribunal should have granted increase in Dearness Allowance at the prevalent rates of live indexes to the extent of Rs.,200/per sq. metre. [1001F H] (4) The appellant had not produced any evidence before the Tribunal that he was not aware of any substantial increase or decrease in living indexing in his cost index. He did not produce any evidence to show that there is a substantial increase of living scales at 344 or indexes as the prevailing rate of live Indexes. [1101F F] (5) The work done for indexation at 344 was less and therefore the working rates were equalized according to prevailing market rates of both the indexations at 344 as well as indexes, and that there could not be any increase or reduction in living scales.

The appellant, who was appointed as a "Modified" in the erstwhile State of Andhra Pradesh under the provisions of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation Act, 1955 (Act 11 of 1956) as a 'Modification Act' and since he had been appointed as such by the Government as early 1939, he became entitled to be treated as a member of the Board of Hindu Religious Endowments. The appellant was appointed in the year 1939 as an Executive Officer under the Hyderabad City Municipal Corporation Rules, 1955. On the basis of the scheme framed under the relevant provisions of this Act, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the schemes framed under section 63 of the said Act and praying for a direction to the Government to appoint him as an "Mhodified" for the proper administration of the Mutt and its properties. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the scheme was not consistent with the provisions in the earlier Act, but it was only with the object of preventing the implementation of the same by legal proceedings and it was open to the appellant to challenge the schemes on the ground that they contravened the Matadhipati 's fundamental rights under article 19(1)(f) and 19(2). The High court held that the schemes were not consistent With the provisions contained in the latter Act, and since the scheme had been framed under sections 63 of this very Act, it was necessary to consider whether the scheme should be deemed to have been settled or modified under the corresponding provisions of section 103(d) of the new Act. Held, further, that the object and purpose of the Scheme is not to enable the Government or its officers to take over the actual administration of Mutt and their properties but it is only with a view to ensure that the objects and purposes of the Schemes are fully implemented and the scheme is properly implemented. The scheme was framed under an Act which was valid when it was enacted, and the provisions were not warranted by the provisions made in the former Act. The Scheme was framed in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions and the object or purpose of this enactment was to enable Government or their officers to implement the schemes. The object and purposes for which the scheme has been framed are clearly discernible from the scheme itself. It is true that under section 103 (d) the Government can make a reference to the relevant sections of the Act, if it is satisfied that there is no real danger to the public interest or the interests of the general public. But the object underlying the scheme being to enable an Executive officer to takeover the actual management of Mutt, and its property rights, the provisions are not warranted. The schemes framed by the appellant were valid when they were framed under [section 63] of the erstwhile Hyderabad Act. It was only after the scheme came into force that the Government could make a declaration under section 62(d). The scheme did not contain any provision for appointment of an Executive Magistrate and it merely provided for appointment as an officer to be appointed by the Board. The provisions of sections 103 (c) and (d), were, therefore, not applicable to the schemes which were framed in the present case.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi teacher in the school with effect from July 12, 1982. He was appointed on ad hoc basis on July 12 and he continued to serve till 31st December, 1984. The appellant was then appointed on July 13,1982 as Hindi Teacher in the School with effectfrom July 12. He continued to work till 31 st December,1984. On August 30, 1984, the managing committee of the school issued a notification under Section 3 of the Validation Act appointing him as Hindi teachers in the said school with retrospective effect from 7th September, 1982 and he was appointed in the same capacity on ad interim basis. The respondents challenged the validity of the Act by filing writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to regularisation as Hindi Teachers in the schools with effect on July 11,1982 and he had been working with the approval of the authorities for a period of 89 days from July 13 1982. The State Government preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High court. The Division Bench of the Orissa High Court dismissed the writ appeal holding that since the appellant had not been appointed as a Hindi teacher on adhoc basis, his services could not be regularised in view of the provisions of Section 3(2) of the validation Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned judgment of High Court is set aside and it is directed that the respondents shall treat the appellant as regularly appointed Hindi teacher with effect form July 12 1982 and they shall treat him as regularly appoint ed teachers in accordance with the provisions contained in Section 3 (2) and 3(3). [782B] 2. The respondent was not appointed on regular basis as a Sanskrit teacher in school with the prior approval of educational authorities for the period subsequent to 1986. He had been continuing to serve as Hindi Lecturer in the concerned school with full salary, including the salary, but he continued till 31.12.1984. [785C] 3. The services of the appellant were terminated on July 14, 1982 by the managing Committee of the School and he has been working for a long spell out of which he was continuing to work until 31st March, 1984 and he is still continuing to discharge his duties till 31St December, 1985. [885D] 4. The appointment of the respondent as Hindi Pandit in the aforesaid school with its approval by the educational authorities was not approved by the Educational authorities for nearly four years. It was only on July 15, 1982 that the managing authority of the said School issued a letter to the appellant stating that he would continue to serve in the post till 31 St December, 1986 and he would be paid salary and other emoluments due to him as a result of his regular appointment. The said letter was not challenged by the respondent before the Orissa Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the respondent had been appointed on adhoc basis for 89 days continuously without any approval by educational authorities. [85E] 5. In view of this finding, the High Courts were right in holding that there was no approval by Educational authorities to regularise the services of a Hindi Teacher with effect immediately from July 14 1982 and the appellant continued to function till 31th December, 1983. The order of the Tribunal is set-aside and it will be open for the respondent to treat him on regular appointment as Hindi lecturer with effect retrospectively from 7 th September,1982. [86E] 6. In the instant case, the appellant has been continuing in service since July 12 1983 and he continues to serve until 31 st March,1984 when he was selected by the selection committee. The termination of his services is not challenged on any ground. It is only after the expiry of the period of three months from 7 1st December 1984 that the appointment of respondent as a teacher in schools with retrospective date was made and he continue to work upto 31 st January, 1984 when he became qualified for appointment by the Selection Committee.

The appellant was elected as a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti by the Punjab Government. He was elected to the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti on the basis of an election held in February, 1967. The appellant filed his nomination paper for election to the said office. The respondent contested the election and contended that he had not been disqualified under r. 7 of the Rules. The High Court accepted the contention of the appellant and dismissed the Election Petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in holding that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under rules 3 to 7 of Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, as a result of supervision of a Chairman, Vice Chairman or Member, was not a disqualification under r., 8. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the respondent had failed to establish that the allowances payable under rs. 3 to7 were in addition to the payment made by him to the Chairman, and, therefore, he could not be said to have incurred any pecuniary loss. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of r. 3 are mandatory in character and they cannot be held to be directory in character. [801B] 2. The word 'shall' used in r. 4(1) of the rules means that the Chairman or a member of a panchayat Samiti is not disqualified from being chosen as a member for election under r, 8. [902C] 3. The expression 'may 'shall 'shall be construed accordingly. It does not mean that the word 'may' in r., 4(2) must be read as 'may'. [903D] 4. The words 'may "may ' are mandatory and they should be interpreted to mean that it is only a condition precedent for holding an office of profit. [093E] 5. The term 'shall not be construed to mean 'must 'may.' It does mean that 'may be 'must' or 'may. In the case of a member who is treated as a State guest while attending the meeting or while attending a meeting or when attending a meetings or when attend a meeting, or when attended a meeting and when attending such meeting or if attending a Meeting, or if attend a Meeting or when attendance of a meeting is not necessary for the purpose of performing his duties. [1003E] 6. The mere fact that the appellant was disqualified under rule 7 to be paid mileage allowance does not make him an office in profit. It cannot be said that he was disqualified from attending a session or meeting when attending any meeting or, if attending such meetings or, when attending the meetings or if attended a Meeting without attending such Meeting, he would have to incur for his work. [1103F] 7. The fact that a Chairman is not qualified to attend a session of the Samiti does not affect his status as a Member of the Zila Parishad. [110G] 8. In view of the provisions of rule 3 and 4(3) of Rules, 1965, the Chairman is entitled to travelling allowance at the rate of Rs. 100/ per day for the day of departure from the place of residence of the Chairman. [109A D] 9. The Chairman is also entitled to travel allowance at a rate not exceeding Rs. 200/ per month for the days on which he was holding office. [108E] 10. In this case, the appellant had failed in proving that he could be said not to have spent any pecuniary gain for performing his official duties. He had not proved that he would incur for performing the official duties of profit within the district. [107A D E] 9 A. The facts are not similar to those of the present case.

The appellant was inducted into the disputed premises by the respondent on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that he had constructed tin shed and the partition wall was in existence on the open land adjacent to the tenanted building. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the disputed construction was not permanent or temporary in nature, but was made with the consent of the landlord. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to file a suit under Section 10(1)(b) of the Act for eviction on the grounds specified in clause (a) and (c). The appellant filed an appeal before the Division Bench. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that there was no material alteration in the accommodation, and dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has committed a serious error of law in interfering with the findings recorded by the First Appellate Court on the question whether tin shed or the partition walls were permanent or Temporary in nature. [701A B] 2.2 The respondent was not entitled to the protection under Section 13(1) (b) and the High Court erred in interfering therewith. [802B] 3.3 The High Curt has committed an error of fact in reversing the findings of the First Appeal Court on this issue. [901C D] 4.1 In the instant case, the respondent had constructed a tin shed on the disputed land adjacent thereto and it was not a material alteration but a material alterations in the structure or the structure of the tenanted premises. The appellant had constructed the tin shed as it had been constructed by the landlord without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate. [1001E] 2:1.2 In view of the fact that the construction was made by the appellant with the permission of his predecessor in interest, the question of construction does not arise. [1101F] 3:1 The respondent has failed to establish that the structure had been erected on the land adjacent t he open land adjoining to the disputed tin shed. [110G] 2.:2.3 In view thereof, the High court was right in interfering and setting aside the findings on this point. [107H; 107A B C] 3 :1.4 The High Courts were wrong in interfering in second appeal with the finding of fact recorded by both the courts below that tin shed had been built on the site adjacent to it. [108B D] 2.(a) In view, the disputed structure was not constructed by a tenant in the open space and it had become a material change in the nature and character of constructions which could be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation.

The respondent company had filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 28,479/ against the appellant company on the ground that it was not served on the company because it was left at the registered office of the company in Calcutta and the summons were sent to the registered officer of the defendant No. 1 for settlement of issues. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the summons was duly served on Shri Navlakha and, therefore, the summons could not be treated as valid service on the respondent company because the summons had been duly served by the company on its employee at Indore. The High Court held that the notice sent to a gentleman who is described as an office assistant of the Company was not correct and that the service of the summons on Shri Nawlakha was not due to his absence from duty. The respondent company filed an appeal against the decree of the trial court. The appellant company contended before the High Court that the suit was barred by limitation because the notice was sent to one Shri Navrakha who was not an officer duly authorised to accept summons on behalf of the respondent and, as such, the suit could not have been dismissed on the grounds mentioned in paragraph 9 of the petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice sent by the appellant to a competent officer of defendant No 1 for settling issues is valid service and, thus, the trial Court was right in holding that it had no knowledge of the ex parte decree. [701B] 2. The summons were duly served upon the company at Indore on 17 1975 3.40 P.C. and the same was returned to the appellant on 18 1975 4.40 A.D. It is not disputed that the respondent Company had delivered a copy of the suit to the Registrar of Companies, Calcutta. [801B C] 3. The service of summons on the appellant was duly effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code. The company remained in dark and could not take any steps for settlement thereof. [820C] 4. The suit was filed within a period of six months from the date of service of summon on the defendant. The cause of action for filing the suit arose on 1775 when the summons served on defendant No1 were returned to him. The plaintiff had failed to file the written statement within the prescribed time. [821D] 5. The plaint was not accompanied by a copy thereof. It was, therefore. clearly barred by time. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the judgment of the High court is set aside.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. He filed an application under section 145(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for a declaration that he had no right to continue to exist at any stage of the proceedings and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence on the basis of a preliminary order drawn up by him. The Magistrate rejected his application holding that there was no question of breach of peace and that it was not necessary that at the time when a final order was passed, the Magistrate should have given a finding as to whether there was any breach of the peace or not. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish that he was in actual possession on the date of the preliminary order. The High Court further observed that the question whether the dispute could be said to have been settled between the parties would depend upon the nature of the dispute and the evidence adduced by the parties before the Magistrate. In appeal, this Court held: "The question whether there is a breach of law or not has to be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case." (Emphasisours) In Ramarao vs Shivram & Ors.(1), it was observed that there is no doubt that the dispute having ceased to exist, as contemplated under section145(5), Cr.P.C., the Magistrate could have given an order for the apprehension of breach thereof. The appellant had not produced any evidence before the Court to show that he has been in actual physical possession on that date. In view of this finding, it was held that there were no questions of breach as contemplated by section 145 Cr. P.C. and that there could be a breach on the part of the Magistrate to mention in his final order drawn out by him in his preliminary order which was implicit in the final order. It is not necessary for the Magistrate before passing the final orders to give a finding on this aspect of the matter having been recorded by the Magistrate in his order that there had been breach of any peace existed at the date when the final Order was passed. The question whether a breach has occurred at the relevant time or not, depends upon the facts of each particular case and it is not possible to say that the breach of a peace exists at the moment when the preliminary Order was made. In this connection, the decision of the Hyderabad High Court in Ramarao & Ors. vs Shiv Ramrao & Ors., ; , referred to. (Emphasis Supplied)

The appellant, a non resident, was assessed to income tax on the sale of his goods in British India. The Income Tax Officer held that the sales were not taxable under section 14(2) (c), and that the question whether the profits had accrued to it in British Indian territory was not open to challenge in a reference under section 66(1). The appellant challenged the correctness of this decision by filing an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the income tax payable on the sales of goods in the States of Bombay and Bombay was not liable to be taxed at the hands of the appellant, but held that since the sale was effected in British territory, the profits could not be taxed under section 42(1) and that it was not a question of law. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The High court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. [701B] (ii) The decision in Com Missione's case is based on the principle that if a question is raised as to the character of the payments made to the appellant and the correctness or otherwise of such a question was not challenged, the same could be referred to the court under section 44(1), and the finding recorded by it could not therefore be sustained. [601C] (iii) The Tribunal had no power to interfere in the matter when it came to the conclusion that the appellant had failed to prove that the payments were made to him in British territories. [76B] In the present case, the appellant was not able to establish that the transactions were not genuine or that they were not tainted with any evidence. [77C] The fact that the sale took place in British country is not disputed by the Department and it was only a question whether there was any evidence to show that the profits accrued to the assessee in British Kingdom. [78D] (iv)The Tribunal had not given any finding on the question of fact, nor did it give any finding as to its character as to what the appellant could be taxed. [79E] (v)The fact that there was no evidence to prove the character or the character as the income of the assessee was not disputed before the High Court and that in any event the conclusion of the Tribunal that the transaction was not genuine, is not open for challenge. [80F] (vi)The question whether a particular transaction was benami or not was not raised by the appellant before the Tribunal. [81G] (vii)The facts were not disputed on behalf of the Department. The assessee had purchased the goods from the purchasers in British countries and it had been sold in the State of Bombay. It was only after the sale that the assessee sold the goods to the ultimate purchasers, that the profit accrued to them in British States could not have been taxed under sections 42(3) and 42(4). [80H] (viii)The mere fact that some transactions were made by the assessee with the ultimate purchaser in British subjects did not make any difference. The sale was not merely a benami transaction but was also a question relating to the nature of the transactions. [82A B] (ix)The decision in Commissioner of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co.(1) is based upon the principle of law that if there is no evidence, it cannot be challenged as perverse or against the weight of evidence recorded by an authority subordinate to it. The Tribunal was not right in holding that there had been a violation of section 42 (3) of the Act.

The assessee was appointed as a Manager of the mill at the initial stage and he was paid Rs. 75,465 by way of commission to the General Manager. The assessee claimed that he had incurred expenditure wholly or exclusively for the purpose of carrying on business. He contended that the amount of Rs.75,465 paid to him was not an expenditure laid out or wholly and exclusively for his purposes of the business of the assessee and therefore the allowance was reasonable and the allowance should be made on account of business considerations. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected this contention holding that the commission paid to the general Manager was not a revenue receipt but was expended wholly and solely for the purposes of carrying out the task entrusted to him. The High Court held that the expenditure incurred by the assessee in the business carried on by him was wholly and mainly for the benefit of the company and therefore it was not allowable as an expenditure incurred wholly or partly for the business purposes of its business. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether an amount is laid out and exclusively used for the carrying on of business or not has to be determined by the Tribunal in each case. [701C] (2) The Tribunal was right in holding that a sum of Rs 75,467 paid to Shri Vaish was not expenditure laid Out wholly and primarily for the objects of the Company and therefore was not deductible as an item of commission under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act. [802D] (3) The High court was right when it held that a part of the amount claimed by the appellant was not spent wholly or solely for purposes of business of his business. [820E] (4) The fact that the assessee had incurred expenses wholly and predominantly for the object of carryingon business does not make any difference to the question whether the expenditure was wholly or mainly for purposes other than those for which it is laid or exclusively used. [823F] (5) The mere fact that some amount was laid out, wholly and essentially for the use of the purpose for which the assessee was entitled to be assessed does not in itself make any material difference to its character as an amount laid out for the said purpose. [825G] (6) The expenditure incurred on the business is wholly and entirely for the main purpose of the profession or vocation. It cannot be held that it was incurred wholly and purely for purposes ancillary to the main object of the trade or profession. [826A D] (7) The assessee had not made any profit in the past and therefore he was able to secure an order from the account of what he was receiving. [827B C] (8) The amount claimed as expenditure incurred was laid wholly and substantially for the intended purpose of business. It was not, however, a part or entirely for purposes incidental to the business. The Tribunal had rightly held that there was no material difference between the amount laid down in the profit earning account and the expenditure actually incurred by him.

The appellant was employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The appellant was appointed as a workman by the management of the Mill and he was also paid wages at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. He was also given a notice to show cause why his services should not be terminated. The management of Bast Shoo company filed an application under article 226 and article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court praying for a writ quashing the order of termination dated March 11, 1957, by which the Tribunal had rejected the appellant 's representation. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief on the question of representation as well as on the merits of his case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal erred in rejecting the appellant's application for a separate representation and that since the appellant had no faith in him, he should be given an order giving him proper relief on his own choice in place of Fateh Singh. HELD: (1) The Tribunal has committed a serious error in rejecting his application for separate representation. [701B] (2) The High court was not right in holding that since there was no dispute between the appellant and the Union, the Tribunal was justified in rejecting him 's application for an appropriate relief on its own choice. [802C E] (3) The appellant had a right to represent his case before the Tribunal by an officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member. He had no interest in the matter and that the Union had no right to be represented by an authorised representative of his own behalf instead of Fateh singh. [901F] (4) The order of the Tribunal rejecting the application for fresh representation was not correct. [1002G] (5) The fact that the respondent was a member of a trade union and he had no connection with it, is not disputed. [1101B F] (6) The question whether the appellant could be represented in any proceeding under the Act by an agent of a Trade Union or by an employee of a recognised trade union, does not arise because the appellant has no faith therein. [110G] In the instant case, the appellant did not choose to represent the respondent as a member and he only wanted to have his representation heard before the order was passed. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. [107H; 110A B] (7) The appeal must be dismissed.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in dispute. The respondent No. 1, who was the tenant of the appellants, filed a suit for ejectment against Kedar Nath and his heirs from the premises on the ground that Kedar Nath had died during the pendency of the appeal before the High Court. The appellant contended that Kedarnath had no right to remain in occupation of the property as he had a joint interest in the premises and, therefore, the appeal was not maintainable. Held, that the appeal filed by Kedar Nath was incompetent and could be dismissed on the basis of r. 4 of O. XLI, r. 3 of OXLI, rs. XXII and O. XXIX of OLI, and, as such, the second appeal was incompetent. The provisions of 0. XLI r. 33 were not applicable to an appeal filed against a decree in favour of the legal representatives of Kedar Nath. The appeal could not have been taken to be an appeal against a part of the decree passed by the trial court. The second appeal could only be dismissed if it had been filed after the death of Kedarnath and not before the appeal preferred by Kedarnath was pending. The third appeal was, therefore incompetent. [723 B E] In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to any relief under O.XLI r. III of Ol. XLI of , r. II of OLLI, as he was not a tenant of one of the landlords and had a common right to continue as tenants of all the other persons when he had an interest in getting a decree against him.
