[823 C] The provisions contained in 0. XLIV of OLA, r., 3 of 0XLI and r. 41 of Oo. XLI were applicable to appeals filed by the surviving appellants.

The appellant, a tenant of the premises in question, filed an application under section 111(g) of the TP Act for ejectment of the respondent from the demised premises on the ground that he had not paid the rent due to him. The Rent Controller rejected the application and dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the provisions of the lease were not applicable to the tenancy in question and therefore, the appellant was entitled to a decree for eviction. In appeal by certificate, this Court reversed the decision of the High court and held that since the respondent had not complied with the requirements of section 111 (g) and (h), the provisions contained in the TP act would not be applicable to his case. The High Court further held that there was no requirement in English law of a written notice to the lessee of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds of equity and good conscience. In view of this, it is clear that the appellant had not made out any case for eviction under section 112(g). The High court further held: "In the present case, the lease in question was determined by forfeiture and the respondent was entitled only to a notice of termination of the tenancy. The respondent did not make out any ground for eviction on the basis that the notice of forfeiture was not served upon him. He had not filed any written statement or affidavit before the Rent Controller. The appellant has not made any averment in his application that he received the notice from the Rent controller and therefore the provisions relating to notice of the termination of tenancy were not attracted to his application for ejectment. In the absence of such a pleading, the respondent could not have been permitted to raise an objection against the maintainability of the petition under section 110(g), as it was not filed before the Controller." The High Courts held that in view of the provisions in section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, the tenant had no right to challenge the validity of the notice issued by the Rent Control Controller. In this Court, the learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the provision of section 112 (g), which was applicable to a lease executed prior to the coming into force of the Act, was not applicable and therefore it was held that even if the provisions were not made applicable, the tenancy would be governed by the principles of equity. The learned counsel also contended that there being no express provision in the Transfer Act, it could not be said that the lease was determined as per the principles embodied in section 112 of the Contract Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 111(a) of TP Act is a general rule and does not apply to a case where the lease has been determined by efflux of time limited thereby in terms of the principle embodied in Section 111 (a) or (g). [601B] 2.2 The expression 'shall presume that the lessee shall have notice of a termination of his tenancy in writing to the lessor, if he so chooses, to determine the lease on forfeiture and also to show that the lessor has not terminated the tenancy by efflux time limited by efflux period limited by duration limited by the duration limited. [602C] 3.3 The expression "shall presume" is a rule of law which means that the tenant must have notice in writing of a decision of a lease on the termination or termination of a tenancy in accordance with the principles contained in section 114(g); and it does not mean that the landlord has no right, whatsoever, to terminate the tenancy unless he has been given a notice in accordance therewith. [613D] 3:1 The expression used in section 113(g)() of T.P. Act is "shall be presumed" and not "shall have notice". [603E] 2:2.3 In the present cases, the notice under section 106 of the T. P.

The appellant, who was dismissed from service by the Governor of Assam on a criminal charge, filed an application under section 311 of the Government of India Act, 1935 for being heard in respect of certain charges. The High Court allowed the said application and quashed the order of dismissal. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the Governor had no power to dismiss or remove a person from service without giving him an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as required by article 311(2) of the Constitution, and that the High Court should not have interfered with the order passed by the President. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Governor has no power under section 309 of the Govt. of Assam Act to dismiss a person who is dismissed or removed from service on a charge framed against him. [801 E] 2. The expression "reasonable opportunity" in article 311 (2) means that the authority empowered to dismiss, remove or reduce a person or to reduce him or to reduced him or reduce him to rank until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of show cause against such action. [902 A B] 3. The word 'reasonable opportunity' in article 310(2), as it stood before amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, means that if the authority competent to dismiss and removed a person is satisfied that in the interest of security of the State it was not expedient to hold such inquiry, he may be given an opportunity to show cause. [1002 B] 4. The words "reasonable time" in Article 311(1) are not intended to convey any right to the government servant to show that in his interest it is not expedient or necessary to hold the inquiry under the principal clause, that is to say, that in order to give an opportunity, the Governor has to be given a fair opportunity of explaining the circumstances in which he had been dismissed or reduced in rank. [0902 C] 5. The language used in article 309(2)(c) is not intended merely to convey some right to government servant but it is intended to confer on him certain rights and that is only enabling him to give a reasonable time for showing cause. It does not, however, mean that the Government can act under the proviso to clause (2). [09 D] 6. The power conferred by article 309 is not an absolute one. It is not necessary to give any right of hearing to government servants who are dismissed or reduce in rank unless it is reasonably practicable to hold inquiry under article 311. [99 E] 7. The object of the proviso is to enable the Government to take a reasonable and fair opportunity to make representation against the proposed action. If the Government does not consider that there was no reasonable and proper opportunity, it cannot be said that the power conferred on the Governor by article 310 (2)(b) is an absolute right. [100 F] 8. The proviso is not merely an enabling provision but a safeguard against arbitrary exercise of power. It only provides for the giving of an opportunity in regard thereto to show causes and the Government has to consider whether it is expedient or proper to hold that the government should be given reasonable and reasonable opportunity to give such an opportunity. [101 F] 9.

The appellants and respondents 1 to 4, who are the members of Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, filed a suit for declaration that they were entitled to their customary rights in respect of Plots and structures in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants and the respondents 5 and 6 had established their customary right in respect to Plots, and structures on the plots and structures and that the respondents 1 and 4 were not entitled to any customary rights. On appeal by the appellants, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was no adjudication or decision on the rights of the parties on merits as a result of the final order passed by this Court in the appeal. [701B] (2) The respondents 1 & 4 were entitled only to their ordinary rights in the plots, and structure, but not to any other right. [802C] (3) The appellants had established customary rights on Plots or structures in respect thereof. They had also established their existing and recognized customary rights to perform their religious rites, practices, observances, ceremonies, ceremonies and ceremonies, observings, ceremonies or ceremonies, performed minus the functions and ceremonies specified in the Notification issued by the Shia Board on 1st of December, 1956 under Rule 54 1136 (vii) of the U.P. Muslim Wakfs Act, 1936. [901D] (4) The notification dated 1st December,1956 under Rule 936(vii) was issued by a Shia board on 1 st of December 1956 under Section 5(1) of U. P. Muslim Wakf Act, 1937. The appellants were not parties to the proceedings before this Court and they had not impleaded them as party to the writ petition. [1001E] (5) The Notification dated 1 st December, 1955 under Rule 48(vii)(a) was not produced in the earlier litigation either before the Allahabad High Court or before this court. [1101F] (6) The appellant was not a member of Shian community of village Doshipsura and the Shias community of Village Dosipura. The respondents 5 & 6 were not members of the Shian Community of Mohalla, Dosapura. They were not the members thereof. [110G] (7) The respondent No. 1 was not entitled under section 4(1)(a), to claim any customary right or hereditary rights in favour of the appellants. [111H; 111A B] (8) The suit filed by the respondents was not maintainable because the appellants had failed to establish their customary and enforceable rights on the basis of which they could have claimed customary rights under section 5(2)(a). [110B C] (9) The right to property in question is a fundamental right. It is a statutory right. The right is a right conferred by statute. The State Government has no power to make rules for regulating the manner in which such rights are conferred. [112A B D] (10) The State Legislature had no power under section 144 Cr.Pc. to regulate the manner of exercising any right in favour or interest in respect thereto.

The appellant assessee filed a return of income under Section 139 on the ground that loss had not been determined in pursuance of a return filed under section 139. The Income tax Officer, after giving due notice to the assessee, assessed him for set off under sub section (1) of section 24 of 1922 Act and disallowed the claim of set off. On appeal by the Revenue, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the loss had been determined as required under section 24(3) of 1922 act and not set off in accordance with the provisions of sub section(1)(b) of Section 44 of 1922. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The claim for set Off is admissible in law. [701B] 2. The assessee had filed a declaration under section 143(2) of the Act on the basis that loss was determined as per the provisions contained in sub section 3 of section 80 of the 1922 Act. The said declaration was made on the footing that loss has not been computed in pursuance o f the provisions relating to set off and set off, but it was only a notional capital loss. [801C] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the claim for setting off was admissible in view of sub clause (ii) of clause (a) of sub sec tion (2) and sub section 2A of Section 74A of 1922 read with section 80(3). [702D E] 4. The expression "set off" used in sub sec.(1)(a) and (b) are not defined under the 1961 Act. It is a well settled principle that when an assessee has set off against capital gains, he must be entitled to have set off of loss on the same ground as if he had been assessed at the time of assessment. [602F] 5. The wordings used in section 80 are wide enough to include all losses which have not been taken into account for the purpose of computation of the loss. It does not mean that the assessee has to set Off the loss on a particular ground. [783B] 6. In the instant case, the loss was computed under the Act and set Off in accordance therewith. The loss had already been determined by the Income Tax Officer as per sub section 1(2A) of Chapter VI of 1922, but the loss has been determined only under the provisions referred to in sub sections (1)(c) and subsection (2). [783F] 7. In view of the fact that the amount of loss had actually been determined under the provision relating to setting off under section 44(3), the assessee was entitled to setoff under section 80. [784H; 878A B] 8. The question whether the loss could be set off or set off is a matter which has not to be decided in the appeal filed by the assessee before this Court. [780B] 9. In order to appreciate the contention of the Revenue that the losses had been computed under section 79(1) (b), it is necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the 1961 act and the rules framed thereunder. [78C E] 10. The object of the 1962 Act was to provide for setting up of a new machinery for the purposes of carrying forward the loss to the public. It was not intended to give effect to the policy of the legislature. [80F] 11. In construing the provisions in section 79, the Court must be satisfied that the intention of the Legislature was to give retrospective effect to any provision of the law which had been enacted by the Parliament. The language used in the section is clear and unambiguous. It cannot be interpreted in a manner so as to make it retrospective. [79F] 12. In interpreting the provisions, the court must not be satisfied with the intention that the Legislature intended to confer retrospective effect on any provision.

The respondent was recruited to the Defence Science Service on October 12, 1966. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Airport) (Deptt.) Department of Defence Research & Development Organisation (DRDO), Hyderabad. On September 10, 1966, he was promoted as Scientist 'E' in the Defence Engineering Service with effect from October 12. 1966. The respondent was appointed to the defence Science Service by the Government on October 13, 1966 and thereafter he was posted to the Directorate General of Inspection and Production, Ministry of Defence (Airports), New Delhi. On November 10, 1967, he joined the service as Scientist-E in the Department of Military Engineering Services. He retired from service on attaining the age of 58 years. The Government issued a notification dated October 12/1, 1966 whereby the respondent was promoted to the rank of Scientist 'F' with effectfrom October 13/1/1966 and thereafter to the post of Scientist-D. On January 28, 1968, he filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for quashing the order of promotion issued by the Ministry of Finance on the ground that his service as a Scientist 'G' was not governed by the Service Rules. The Tribunal allowed the respondent's application and quashed the order dated October 13.1/1967. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application filed by the respondent for quashing of the order issued by it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the Government under Rule 12(3) of the Service rules is a judicial function and cannot be exercised in any manner. It is not a judicial or quasi-judicial function. [701B] 2.1 The power to make rules is an administrative power. The Rules are framed by the President under Article 309 of the Constitution. The powers conferred upon him are not merely administrative functions but are also administrative in nature. [802C] 3.2 The power of the Government to make a rule is an executive function and can be exercised only if it is shown that there has been some legal or constitutional infirmity in the exercise of such power. [601D] 2:1.1.2 In the present case, the respondent had not been recruited to any of the three units of the Defence Research and Development Organisation. He had not acquired any right to be appointed as Scientists 'F'. The respondent had been recruited only to the four units of Defence Engineering Services on October 14, 1966 when he was recruited in the defence engineering Service. [820E] 2.(a) The respondent could not have been appointed to any one of the units of defence Research and development Organisation. [823C] (b) The power under Rule 13(3)(c) is an enabling power which can be used only for the purpose of making rules. It cannot be used in a manner that it would be misused or abused. [825E] 3.(a). In the instant case, there was no such power vested in the Government by virtue of Rule 12 (3) (c) and the respondent could have been given the benefit of the enhanced age of superannuation to the members of the other unit. [822F] 4.1 It is true that the respondent did not opt for one or the other of the four Units of Defence Training and Development Organization but he was appointed as a part time officer in the same Department on October 15, 1966 which was a separate unit. The appointment of the respondent as Scientist was made by the DirectorateGeneral of Inspection & Production (Dy.C) on October 16, 1966 whereas the respondent retired from the service on reaching the age 58 years on November 10. 1966 and he was given the option to opt for another unit. It was not open to the respondent to have exercised his option in favour of one or other of his members of his group.

The appellant was a member of the Municipality and he had been elected as a member. He was a candidate for election to the Sangli City Municipal Council. The appellant was elected as the Chairman of the Sangli Municipal Council on June 3, 1967. On June 4, 1967, the appellant filed an application under article 226 and 227 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Judge. The learned Judge dismissed the application holding that the appellant had been guilty of corrupt practice and directed his election to be set aside. The High Court held that the election petitioner was not entitled to any relief in view of section 21(1) of the Act as he had failed to prove that the pamphlet was a genuine document. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding recorded by the Judge that the charge against the appellant was proved beyond reasonable doubt and therefore the appellant could not be tried for corrupt practice is erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The election petitioner had been rightly held to have committed a corrupt practice under section 21 (1) read with section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [701B] 2. The charge against him was proved by his own evidence and he was not guilty of any corrupt practice. He could not therefore be tried in view thereof. [802C] 3. The finding recorded on the basis of the evidence adduced by the appellant is based on the evidence of two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses. It is true that the learned Judge had taken into account the evidence about the distribution of the pamphlet and the distribution thereof by it, but he was also not satisfied with the evidence given by the election petitioners in respect of the distribution made by them. [602D] 4. The evidence of the two witnesses examined by the learned trial Judge clearly shows that the charges against the petitioner were proved beyond doubt and the appellant did not make any attempt to prove the charge under section 123(1)(a) of Representation of People Act. [820E] 5. In view of the fact that the evidence on record was sufficient for the purpose of finding out whether the charge was proved, the learned judge rightly held that there was no reason to interfere with the order passed by the trial Judge and dismissed the petition. [823G] 6. The appeal is accordingly allowed.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. The appellant was registered as a dealer under the provisions of the [Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930], hereinafter called the 'Act'. The appellant purchased jute goods from its dealers for the purpose of carrying on business in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The sales tax authorities assessed the appellant to sales tax in accordance with the provisions contained in section 3 A of the Act. The Sales Tax Officer, however, levied a tax on the sale of gunny goods at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per rupee. The petitioner appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who confirmed the order of assessment. The appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Tribunal. In the meanwhile, the appellant filed an application under article 226 in the High Court of Allahabad for quashing the impugned notification dated March 31, 1956. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the impugned notice on the ground that the State legislature had no power to impose a tax in future, and that the impugned Act was not a law in respect of sales tax, and therefore, the impugned Notification was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Validation Act is ultra vires the powers of the legislature under which the legislative competence of the State Legislature under entry 54 of List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule could be exercised by the legislature in respect only of sales of jute products, and not to the sale tax. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is ultravires the powers conferred on the State Legislatures under entry 52 of List I of the Constitution. [701B] 2. The power of the Legislature under Entry 54 of list II or the Seventh schedule to the Constitution is plenary and unrestricted subject only to the same infirmity which attached to it when it was published on March 31 1956, and the impugned notifications are valid. [802C] 3. The State legislature has no power in respect to tax on sale of goods, as recognised by the statute, but has no competence to impose any tax in respect thereof. [601D] 4. The notification dated April 1, 1956 is not a Central Act and it does not affect the powers under entry 53 of List III or the State List. It merely affects the power of taxation conferred on it under entry 55 of List 11. [820E] 5. The word "tax" in entry 54 has reference to the tax on sales of goods which are outside the entry 54, and as there is no other entry in the Seventh Schedules, the State Government cannot impose a duty on the dealer who pays the tax. [823G] 6. The words "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of this Act" in section 2(a) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, are qualified by the words "any other provision of law in force at the time of the commencement" and not "any provision of any other law in existence at the date of the notification." [823B] 7. The language used in entry 52 is clear and unambiguous. It does not mean that the legislature has power to enact a law with retrospective operation, but it does so only with respect to sales of tea products which are within the entry 53. [825G] 8. The expression "any such provision" in Entry 54 is qualified by its terms "any provisions of any law in place at the commencement or in any other manner". [823H; 882A] 9. In view of the language used, it must be held that there was no imposition of tax in relation to sales which are inside the entry 52. The contention that the notification is invalid as it does affect the power conferred on Parliament under Entry 53 of list I or List II of the seventh Schedule cannot be accepted. [824E] 9 A.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court, Ambala for offences under Section 376(2)(f) of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. He was also convicted for an offence under Section 354 read with Section 511 IPC and sentenced as aforesaid. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence from rigorous imprisonment to one of life. In this appeal, it is contended that the appellant had been falsely implicated in a case of rape on the victim 's wife by the father in law of the woman who was a young man. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction and sentences passed against the appellant are not sustainable. [701B] 2. The appellant is entitled to be acquitted of all the charges framed against him. He has been convicted for offences punishable under Section 366 read with 511 IPC. [802C] 3. The sentence imposed by the High Court is excessive. [603D] 4. The appeal is allowed and the conviction and the sentences passed by the courts below are set aside. The bail bonds executed by the appellant shall stand cancelled. He be taken into custody to serve out the remaining part of his sentence. [820E] 5. The order of the High court is upheld. The Criminal Appeal is dismissed. [823A B] 6.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling sugar. The appellant purchased certain lands from the Government for the purpose of setting up a factory at Calcutta. On July 29, 1955, the appellant purchased some lands from its employees for the purposes of setting them on lease. The Company sold these lands to the Government. The Collector held that the compensation payable to the appellant was not a receipt of a revenue nature and therefore, it was not liable to be assessed to income tax under section 18 of the Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In further appeal to this Court, the High Court held that since the entire question was considered by the Tribunal as real and substantial, the Tribunal was right in holding that the amount of compensation received by the appellant related to the acquisition of land during the previous year ended March 31, 1956. The assessee appealed against the order passed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court allowed the appeal and held that there was no liability in praesenti in respect of the additional amount of the compensation claimed by the State Government on the basis that the entire amount of Rs.7,37,190 payable to it was a receipt from the assessee. In appeal to the Supreme Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right, in holding, that the sum of Rs.,7,36,691 deposited by the Government on April 25, 1956 was not an offer or tender of the amount determined by the Collector to be paid to the assessee as compensation. [801B] (2) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide whether the entire sum of money received by it related to acquisition of the land during that year. [902C] (3) The mere fact that the appellant did not receive any amount from the State exchequer in praeenti does not make the payment of compensation payable under section 19 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a receipt for the same. [1001D] (4) The expression "any sum" used in section 18(1)(a) of the said Act means the sum which has been actually paid to or is likely to be received by way of compensation. It does not include any amount that has accrued or deemed to have accrued or had become payable under the provisions of the [Land Acquisition Act]. The expression 'any sum' used in sections 18(2) and 18(3) of that Act means a sum which is actually paid as compensation to the person who has actually received it. [091E] (5) The word "any" in section 19(1) of Land Acquisition, 1894 includes any amount payable under any law for the time being in force or otherwise. [1101F] (6) The words "any amount" used therein are not to be construed as including any amount which has accrued and has become payable by way thereof. [110G] (7) The phrase "any other sum" is not defined in section 2(f) of Act No. 18 of 1956. It is only a part of the total compensation which has actually been paid to, or is expected to be due to, the person entitled to receive it. The expression means "a sum payable under this Act". [110H] (8) In the instant case, the amount was not paid by way Of compensation but was merely an offer and tender of that amount. [111G] The Tribunal has rightly held that in view of the fact that there is a clear distinction between the amount which had accrued or has become due to the claimant on the date when possession of the property was taken by the government, the sum payable could not be said to have been paid as an offer.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant from a shop in dispute on the ground that he was entitled to possession on one or other of the statutory grounds mentioned in Section 12(1) (f) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the compromise decree was not legal and proper. The High Court, however, set aside the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The compromise decree is binding on the parties and it is open to the court to pass a decree for eviction in accordance with the provisions of the act. [901F] 2.2. The tenant in question had withdrawn all his defence against the suit claim. He was not entitled to any relief under Section 12 (1) of Act. [0902B] 3.1 The compromise is binding and it cannot be said that the tenant in dispute had withdrawn any defence against his eviction from a room in which he was residing. [1001F G] 2.(a) The compromise was not lawful. It was open to a Court to pass an order for possession in accordance therewith. [1102B C] 3.(b) In view of the provisions contained in Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the suit must be held to be valid and enforceable. [110G] 2(a) There is no doubt that a compromise decree can be passed only on one ground or other and it can be executed only on the basis of the compromise. But if the compromise is not lawful, the Court has to pass the decree in accordance thereof. [111A D] 3(b) The provisions contained therein are mandatory in nature and do not confer any right upon a party to get an order of eviction against a tenant from any accommodation except on one of the grounds mentioned therein. [112E C] 4.(a)(i) In the instant case, the appellant landlord had withdrawn his defence by filing a suit under Section 13(1)(e) of The Act and the trial court was satisfied that there was no valid compromise decree in respect of the suit premises. [113A D; 113B E] 5.(ii) The High court was not justified in holding that a decree passed for eviction against the tenant on one and other of statutory grounds under Section 11(1), (2) and (3) of 'the Act were not binding on parties. [114E C, 114F] 6.1 In view thereof, the compromise cannot be held as valid unless it is shown that there has been a clear and unambiguous agreement between the parties to suffer a decree in terms of Section 12 of the , the Act or any other provision which prevents the tenant to get a decree against the landlord. [115E C; 115F] 3 (a) In order to get the decree for ejectment against a person who is not entitled under the provisions to have such a decree, the court must make out a case for eviction within the meaning of Section12(1). [115G] 4.2 The compromise cannot therefore be held valid unless there is a clear or unambiguous agreement in terms thereof. It is open for the Court to make out an order to that effect and pass a Decree in accordance thereto. [116A D E] 3: (b) There was no express or implied agreement in the compromise for the protection of a tenant based upon public policy. The condition precedent for passing a decree under Section12 (1), is not satisfied by the compromise, but it is clear that there had been a specific provision in the Act which prevents a tenant to obtain a decree from the landlord and this was clearly a case where the compromise was legal and valid. [117E] 3; 4.3 The compromise could not be held invalid unless it was shown that the parties had withdrawn their defence against eviction.

The assessee company, a public limited company, had purchased shares of the company in Elphinstone Mills Ltd. for Rs. 12,00,000/ and paid a dividend of Rs. 10,00/. The assessee company claimed that the loss incurred by it was not reasonable but was only a capital loss. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the losses incurred by the company were not in the relevant accounting years. On appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal held that the amount of Rs.. 12,000/- paid as dividend was a capital expenditure and not a capital profit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the assessee had suffered a loss of Rs... per rupee on account of depreciation in the value of the shares purchased by it during the relevant year and that the Income tax officer should have held that in view of the losses previously incurred by him, he should not have declared dividend for the year in question. Dismissing the appeal, this Court ^ HELD: (1) The assessee had made a profit of Rs 12,50/ per rupee in the previous year and the loss was incurred by its Directors during the accounting years in question and that it was reasonable to expect the company to declare dividend for that year in respect of its total income. [701C] (2) The fact that the shares were purchased for the purpose of acquiring the managing agency of a company does not mean that the profits made in the earlier years or to the smallness of profit made in previous years or the smallity of profits made during the year would be less than the statutory percentage of the total income of the assessee. [801D] (3) The mere fact that there was no commercial profits in the accounting year does not necessarily mean that it is reasonable to believe that the company would declare dividend in respect thereof. [820E] (4) The word 'having regard only to' which the loss actually incurred by a company in earlier years and to smallness or to its smallness, cannot be used as a term of arty. It must be remembered that the business consists wholly or mainly in the same accounting year and it is not possible to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering the two matters mentioned therein. [823E] The word "having regard" in the context of the provisions of section 23A (1), should be understood in the sense that it does not say 'having regards only 'having regarding losses previously made in earlier year or to small times of its income on account thereof. It is not necessary to consider whether the loss sustained by the assessee was reasonable and if so, what was the amount actually transferred to a reserve fund under section 23 A (1). [823F] (5) The words 'having relating to losses previously suffered by the Company in earlier periods or to smaller times of their income on any previous year or for smallness cannot be construed as indicating that the same were not reasonable and, therefore, the loss must be considered to have been incurred by such company in subsequent years or for largeness. [825G] (6) The expression 'having about losses previously done in earlier period or to larger times of the income on a previous year shall be deemed to have occurred if the profits were not less than that declared by a Company which is more than the prescribed percentage of its aggregate income. It would, therefore be unreasonable to expect that the Company should declare dividend at a rate higher than that fixed by it for the relevant years or so as to reduce the amount to less than what was actually paid by it on account whereof the loss had been incurred.

The appellant, a displaced person, filed an application under section 12(6) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 (U.P., Act No. V of 1954), before the District Judge, Aligarh, for setting aside the award made by him and for setting it aside. The District Judge allowed the application and set aside the order of the Civil Judge. The appellant filed a revision under section 39 of the Act before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision on the ground that the decision of the arbitrator was not final. Hence, this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 37 of the Land Acquisition Act provides for an appeal against the order passed by the District judge under section 9(6). It is clear from the language of section 37 that the provisions of sections 46 and 47 of the .Act are not applicable to arbitrations under section 13(4) of, the Act. [701B] 1.2 The expression "any dispute as to title" in section 12 (6) must be read with section 37 of , the Act and if it is so read it would mean that it makes the applicable to the proceedings before the arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. [802C] 2.3 In the instant case, the question whether the decision was final or not has been decided by the Civil Court as it emerges after appropriate proceedings. The expression 'any dispute ' must be construed as having been determined by the arbitrator as it emerged after appropriate proceeding. [820G] 1.(2) The word "any" in sub section (6), of section 12 of the , does not mean that the jurisdiction of the civil court to decide the question of title is not final or conclusive. It only means that the civil courts have no jurisdiction to decide such question. [823C] 3.1 In the present case, there was a dispute as regards title and the question as to whether the Civil judge had jurisdiction to deal with the matter under section 37(4), did not arise at all. The dispute was between the parties and it was only in respect of the right of the appellant to raise the objection that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction. [825D] 3.(3) In the case before us, there is a clear distinction between the two sections. It is well settled that the question regarding title and its finality cannot be decided by a civil court unless it can be determined by a competent court. The question whether a particular dispute as regard title or otherwise has been determined in accordance with the provisions contained in section 37 (4) must also be determined in the manner provided in section 36 of the 'Act. [826E] 3(a) In view of the fact that the Civil Courts have no power to decide any question of law, it is not open to the civil Court to go into the question about title or the finality of the decision. [827C] 4.2 It is true that the High court has jurisdiction to go behind the award and to decide whether a dispute has been finally determined by an arbitrator under section 36(4). But the question is whether the civil judge had no power, in law, to decide that question. The civil courts are not bound by the decision as it stands on the merits of the case. [828E] 4.(b) In order to determine the question relating to title or finality of an award made under section 38(4)(a), the civil Judge has no jurisdiction, in view of section 36 (4). [826F] 5.(c) The High court had no authority to decide a dispute under section 48 of the A.P Act. It was not open for the civil Courts to go beyond the scope of section 39 and to determine whether the question raised by the appellant was finally determined or not.

The respondent Corporation issued a resolution on the basis of the educational qualification for promotion to the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent corporation. The respondent Corporation passed a resolution dated 27th January, 1988 promoting the petitioner as Superintending Engineer and also promoted him as Superintending Engrer. The appellant challenged the said resolution by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned resolution was not violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The classification made by the respondent Corporation is arbitrary and discriminatory in nature and violative of Article 14 and16 of the constitution. [701B] 2.2 The classification of the appellant as a separate category was not permissible in law. It was not a case where the classification was made among the members holding the same post on a basis other than that in the case before the respondents Corporation, the classification made amongst the members held the same posts on a principle and in the absence of rules and regulations, the said classification could be made among those who are degree holders or diploma holders. [801C] 3.3 The classification was not arbitrary but was based on the educational qualifications prescribed for the post. It is well settled that the classification can be made amongst those who were degree holder or diploma holder Junior Engineers and degree holders. In the absence thereof, the impugned decision of the respondentCorporation cannot be sustained. [901D] 4.1 There is no dispute that the appellant was appointed as Superintending Engineers in the year 1988 and was promoted to the said post on 27th February, 1988. The promotion to that post was made by way of a resolution passed by the Corporation in 1988. It may be stated that the respondent No.2 was not competent to make such a classification. [1001E] 4.(a) The impugned resolution dated 28th January 1988 was passed by a duly constituted board of officers and it was not challenged by any person. [1101F] (b) The appellant was not qualified for promotion as Superintending engineer in the post held by him on 27 th February,1988. He was not eligible for promotion on the ground that he had been promoted to that rank only on a regular basis. [110G] 4(c) The respondent corporation could not have made any classification contrary to the provisions of section 64 of the Act. It cannot be said that the rules and regulation framed under section 64 were not in accordance with law. [111H; 111A C] (d) The classification between the two categories of Junior Engineers was not valid as it was based upon the educational and other qualifications prescribed by the regulations. [112B D] 5.(a)(i) The power to make a classification is vested in the executive authority. It can be exercised only if there is a violation of any of the provisions or rules made under section 65 of the . [111A C; 111D] (ii) The exercise of power by executive instructions cannot be held to be arbitrary or violative of article 14 and 15 of the '[112E] (iii) The word 'authority' in section 64(1)(a) is not defined in the Act but it has been used in a broad sense. It does not mean that the authority can act as an executive authority for the purpose of making classification. The power conferred on the executive authorities to make classification is not arbitrary or unreasonable. [113E] 6.(i) In the instant case, the appellant had been appointed as Executive Engineer and was posted in the office of the Executive Engineer. He had been working as Superintending Engineering Officer in the department for more than five years. The post of Superintending Engineer was a selection grade and he was entitled to be promoted to such higher grade.

The appellant was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Orissa in the State Judicial Service on 16.7.1987 and he was posted at Cuttack. He was transferred to Cuttack from Cuttack on 17.8.1988. On 18.9.1989, he was transferred from Cuttack to Cuttack. The Chief Justice of India by his order dated 19.10.1990 transferred him to Cuttack and posted at Bhubaneswar. In the meantime, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the transfer order dated 16.11.1991. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to be considered for promotion as Chief Justice. On appeal by special leave, this Court held that the transfer of the appellant from Cuttack was not justified and directed the Union Government to consider his case for promotion in accordance with law. Allowing the appeal, this court, HELD: 1. The power of appointment is vested in the Central Government under Article 124(1) of the Constitution. [801B] 2. The expression "cadre" has been defined in Article 366(3) as meaning a cadre comprising all posts in the service and every post in the Service shall be deemed to be a cadre included in that cadre. [901C D] 3. The word 'cadre' is not defined in the Constitution but it is used in Article 233 of the constitution. It does not include any post in any cadre. The definition of the expression "joint cadre" is wide enough to cover all posts and every cadre has a constitutional obligation to be exercised by the Union government. [1001E] 4. The words 'cadre ' have been defined under Article 366 (3) of Constitution as meaning an existing cadre comprising of various categories of posts in that service and any other post in that Service. [091F G] 5. The term "jachelors" is not a word of art, but it has to be understood in the sense that it includes all posts which are created by the President or Governor under Article 233. [1101A D] 6. The Constitution does not permit the creation of any post for the State Government. It only provides for appointment of Chief Justice and the appointment of a Judge is made by the Governor. [110B E] 7. The appointment of the Chief Justice is not an executive function. It is only an administrative function. There is no question of appointment of any person as Chief Justices of the Supreme Court or the High Courts in the case of the State Public Service Commission. [109G H] 8. The post of Chief Justices and Judges of the Higher Judicial Services is a cadre consisting of various posts in different services and it has been stated that the Chief Justices or Judges of this High Court are not members of the service. [108A D E] 9. The function of appointment to the higher judicial service is only administrative function and not executive functions. It cannot be said that the appointment to a post is administrative in nature. [107B C] 10. In view of the fact that the post of the Judge of this Court is a subordinate office, it cannot be held that there was any element of immediacy in the matter. [106C D E; 108A B] 9: The Chief Justices are not part of the executive or judicial service. They are members of all the services and they are members only of the Executive or judicial services.

The respondent was appointed as Enquiry Officer under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi particle Settlement dated 19th October, 1966. The respondent was promoted to the post of Assistant Executive Engineer on ad hoc basis by order dated January 18, 1988. He was confirmed in the said post on February 20, 1988 and he was reverted to his substantive post on March 31, 1989. On April 1, 1990, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned order of punishment. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent had not raised any objection against continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon as an official of the bank and therefore the respondent was estopped from raising such a contention for the first time in a writ peti tion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had committed manifest error in holding that there was no valid appointment to the respondent and that the order imposing punishment was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment and directing payment of all consequential benefits. [701B] 2.2 The High Cour t had committed a manifest error by holding that since the respondent did not raise any objection to continuance of his enquiry by an Enquiry Officer, he was estopped to raise such a plea for the second time in the writ petitio ner. [802C] 3.3 The High cour t has committed a patent error by observing that the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge is without jurisdiction and therefore, it is liable to be set aside. [820D] 4.1 It was not open to the appellant to raise any further objection against the continuance of enquiry by a second or third party non official. The question whether the respondent could have raised such a ground for the continuance o f the enquiry was left open to be agitated before the competent Disciplinary Authority. [823E] 3:1.2 In the present case, the appellant had not challenged the order of dismissal passed against him by the disciplinary authority. He had only challenged the validity thereof on the ground that the said order was without any jurisdiction and that too on technical grounds. [825F] 3;2.3 It is true that the learned Judge of the High C ourt has committed an error in directing payment to the employee of the salary etc., but he has not done so because the learned judge of the Division Bench had not gone into the merits of the case and therefore it was open to him to raise a contention before the learned single Judge of t his Court that the appellant was estopped by his conduct from raising any objection. [826E] 4:1 The order of the Disciplinary Authority is, therefore, liable to quashed and set aside on the technical ground that it was without authority or competence. [822F] 2:2.4 The learned Single judge of t he High Court had committed an illegality in directing the payment of salary etc. to the Respondent. [828B] 3 :1.5 In the instant case, there is no dispute that the Respondent was appointed by the Managing Director of the Bank as a Enquiry Officer and he had been appointed by him as a Disciplinary Authority and he has been so appointed by a de facto officer. The learned Judge has not committed any error in allowing the writ pet ition. [829B] 4;2:1 It is well settled that the power vested in the disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer cannot be exercised by the Disciplinary authority unless it is shown that there is an appointment to an office which is defective or illegal. [827C] 2 :1 The learned single judge has committed manifest illegality in holding the impugned action of appointing a second Enquiry Officer as a disciplinary Authority and therefore he had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the learned Chief Executive Officer.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the 'Corporation ') had applied for sanction under section 336 of the Act for construction of a building or any work in that zone. The appellant submitted his plans and plans. The plans were approved by the Corporation on March 31, 1967. On April 1, 1968, the appellant applied for permission to construct a building on the land in question. The Corporation granted sanction for the erection of a new building on that land. The application was rejected by the Commissioner on May 10, 1967, and the appellant filed an appeal against the order of rejection of his plans. In the meantime, the Corporation issued a notice under section 337 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (Act LXVI of 1957) to the appellant asking for sanction for erection of new building. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the appellant on May 11, 1967 and also the rejection of the plans submitted by it. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Corporation had not complied with the provisions of section 14 of the Development Act and that the sanction was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The sanction for construction is a mustard and mustard plan. It does not contain any provision for a particular use of land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Development Plan. [601B] 2.2. The sanctioned plans are prepared under section 7 of the Town Planning Act,1957 (Act LXI of 1957), and the Development Rules, 1957. The plan is prepared under sections 7 of that Act and it has come into operation. [702C] 3.3. The sanctioning authority must give a reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 before it comes into operation, and if he does not give such an opportunity of placing any objections or suggestions, which have all to be given an opportunity to place any objections and suggestions, then the Corporation will have to be afforded an opportunity for placing any objection or suggestions. [802D] 4.4. The Commissioner is justified in rejecting the plans and Plans submitted by the appellants on May 12, 1967 when he had already approved the plans. [820E] 5.1 The appellant has not been able to establish that any land or part of a road which is prohibited for an indefinite period, was acquired by the Municipal Corporation under section 14. [823F] 4 A.2 The Development Act does not provide for any such use of any land and building otherwise as in conformity therewith. It only provides for a special purpose. [825G] 5 A.3 The appellant cannot be permitted to construct any building on his land or any part thereof, unless the plans provide for a specific use of the site for which he has been authorised to construct such building. [826C] 4A.4B] 5:1.2 In order to sustain the validity, the Commissioner must give an opportunity in place of placing objections and suggestion, which has all to been given an adequate opportunity to the appellants to make representations or suggestions or making any representation or suggestions which have any substance or substance or truth or substance. [827C] 6.3 It is not necessary that the appellant should be permitted, as a matter of right, to construct the building on its land or on its site. The Development Rules do not provide that the appellants should be allowed to construct buildings on their land or upon its site, unless such plans provide that they should be given a reasonable opportunity of putting forward any objections, suggestions or representations which have no substance or substances or truth and substance. It is only if the plans are approved by it that the Development Authority will have the right to construct building on it. [828E] 6:1 The appellants cannot be allowed, as they would have been permitted to build a building in that area or on their site, if such plans are not approved by them.

The appellant No. 1 was the Secretary of the judiciary and he was a member of the judicial staff of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. He was also a member in the judicial service of the State of Madhya Bharat. The appellant No, 1 was an advocate practising as a lawyer at Indore. He had been convicted by the Special Judge under section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code for having committed an offence punishable under section 5(1) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay fine of Rs. 500/- in default of payment of fine, he was also convicted by a Special Judge for the offences under sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case as alleged against the appellant No 1 is that on the night of the 8th March 1949 at about 9 p.m., the appellant Nos. 1 to 3 were found in possession of certain currency notes from his house and were arrested by the police authorities. On the basis of a secret information, the appellant was apprehended and he made an application for bail before the Special Court. The Special Judge rejected the application on the ground that the appellant had not been able to establish the falsity of the allegation made by the prosecution against the accused persons and therefore the conviction of the appellant no. 1 under section 6(1)(c) readwith section 5 of the Act was illegal. The High Court, however, acquitted the appellant from all the charges framed against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution had failed to establish that the currency notes were handed over by the appellant to Nagindas when the raid was organised and were the instruments of the crime of the members of the public. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The conviction of appellant No 2 under section 4(1), 5(2) read along with section 161 is not sustainable in law. [601B] 2. The evidence given by Shanti Lal Ahuja, the Additional District Magistrate and the High court clearly establish that Nagindash had been entrusted to Naganias when they were organised and had been handed over to Nagundas. [702C] 3. The fact that Nagania had been arrested on 8th April 1949 is not in dispute. It was only after the recovery of the currency note from Nagindasi, Naginda and Nagindai, the prosecution case was established against the appellants No. 2 and 3. [801D] 4. The facts disclosed by the witnesses are quite clear that Nagunda had come to know about the illegal gratification received by him from Naganianas and he had been given a receipt of Rs 10,000 in cash. He also knew that Nagaianas had been apprehended at the time when the search was organised. [820E] 5. The mere fact that the money was not recovered from Nagundasi is not sufficient to establish his guilt. [823G] 6. The recovery of currency notes by Nagindattas and Naganiis in the bedroom of the accused No.1 and the recovery thereof at the instance of Nagindanas, cannot be said to be a true version of the prosecution story. [825H; 801A B] 7. The trial court had rightly acquitted the appellants. [826B] 8. In view of the fact that there was no evidence on record to establish any falsity of allegation made against the respondents, the conviction under section 3(1A) read alongwith section 5 and section 5A of the P.C. Act cannot be sustained. [822E] 9. The appeal is allowed.

The plaintiff was serving the State Police as a constable in the Police Department. He was convicted by the Additional District Judge, Patiala for an offence under section 325 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months each. The appeal filed by the plaintiff against the judgment of the first appellate court was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The order of the Additional Sessions Judge is clearly illegal because it has been passed without jurisdiction in view of the provisions of section 16(2) of the Punjab Police Act. [801B] 2.1 The High Court was right in holding that the order of dismissal was not legal and valid. [902C] 3.2. The High court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the first Appellate court. [1002D] 3:1.3. In view of section 17(4) of Punjab Police Rules, 1934, the High court could not have interfered with the judgment and decree of the trial court. The provisions of the said rules are mandatory in nature. [092E] 2:1 The order passed against Kahan Singh by the Superintendent of Police, Patiala is illegal because he was not a member of the police force. [1102F] 3;2.1 In view thereof, the appeal filed against the order dated 20.4.1976 dismissing the appellant from service was rightly dismissed. [110G] 2.(a) The High Cour t had no power to interfere in the matter of punishment imposed on Kahan singh. [108A] (b) The order is not illegal because the appellant was a member in the police Force and he was acquitted by the criminal court. He could not be tried again for an alleged offence under Section 325 readwith section 34 IPC. [107B] 3.(a)(i) In view, of the fact that the trial judge had given a finding that the appellant had committed offences punishable under sections 325 read With section 34, I.P.C., the High C ourt was justified in interfering with the sentence imposed on the appellant. [109A B] (ii) The appeal against the decision of the High cour t is not maintainable because the order is a result of misappreciation of evidence and is based on no evidence. [106B] 4.(a). In view Of section 17 of the Act, the question whether the order was illegal or void does not arise. [105C] (iii) The appellant had been convicted by a criminal court for an offen ce punishable under section 302 read with sections 34 IPC and sentenced as aforesaid. He had also been acquitted by a competent court. In the present case, the appellant has been convicted for an act of murder and sentenced with imprisonment for life. [104E] (iv) The facts in this case are not similar to those in the instant case. The appellant was convicted under section 307 read with Section 34 IPC on the ground that he had been acquitted from the charge of murder. He, therefore, could not claim any relief against his conviction. [103A B C] 5.(a), (b)(i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v) and (vi) of section 34 read with Sections 34 IPC, are clearly distinguishable. The judgment in the case of a criminal trial is not applicable to the facts of this case. [101B D] 6.1 It is true that the High Cou rt has jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to interfere only when there is an error apparent on the face of the record or if it is based upon no evidence or where the findings are perverse. But the High Courts have no power under Article 227 to interfere even with the findings of fact recorded by the courts below.

The respondent assessee, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea garden tool tools and requirements, had purchased the goods from the appellant. The respondent assessee claimed that the transactions were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to sec. 24(1) of the Act. The Income Tax Officer held that the transaction was speculative in nature and therefore the losses suffered by the respondent assessee were not speculative in a speculative transaction within the definition of explanation 1 to section 24(2). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that since the transactions entered into by the appellant were speculative in character, the loss could not be set off against the profits made by the assessee. The High Court held that there was no actual or physical delivery of the commodity or the scrips. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the facts and circumstances of the case showed that the sale transactions were in a commercial transaction and therefore, the losses incurred by the company could not form part of the trading loss. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The explanation does not apply to transactions which are speculative in any other business. It is only where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, that the loss, if any, would be a loss in a transaction of the same nature. [801B] (2) The word 'sales' has been defined in explanation 2(a) to section 2(c). It is not necessary that the goods are actually delivered by the seller to the buyer but laid only out and the sale proceeds thereof could be set aside if there was actual or actual delivery of goods. [901C] (3) The expression 's sales ' in a business can be considered as speculative transactions in any one of the three ways mentioned in explanation 1. It must be remembered that the word 'sale ' has been used in Explanation 2 to section 4(a). In the case of an ordinary transaction, it is not possible for the assessee to prove that the trading transactions were not genuine or that they were not made by a person who had purchased goods from another person. [1001D] (4) The fact that the sales were speculative and the losses were incurred in speculative transactions does not make any difference because the sale of the goods was not speculative. [091E] (5) The mere fact that some transactions were made by one person to another person cannot be a reason for holding that the losses had been incurred in speculation transactions. [1101F] (6) The facts and the circumstances show that the assessee had purchased some of the commodities from other persons and had sold them to others. [110G] (7) The assessee was not entitled to have the loss set off under any other head in speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set Off against a profit in a sale transaction. [109A B] (8) The question whether the transactions are speculative or speculative in the nature of a business does not arise from the facts of the present case and therefore it is necessary that there should be actual or constructive delivery of commodities or the shares sold to others, cannot be set back against a loss incurred in a trading transaction. The assessee had also purchased some other commodities from another persons and the transactions which were not completed by the sale were speculative. The losses incurred in such transactions could not therefore form part and parcel of the business.

The appellant, a candidate for the election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the constituency of the Punjab Vidhan Sabha, was elected as a member of the Legislative Assembly. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the returned candidate on the ground that he had not been duly nominated by the Returning Officer and that he was not qualified to be chosen to fill up the seat reserved for him under section 33(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that the nomination paper of the appellant was invalid because it was signed by a proposer and seconder in a prescribed form and subscribed by the candidate himself. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 36 does not define the word "signatures" but only defines the word 'signature". [601 A] (ii) The word "writing" is used in the sense of making a signature and it is not defined in the Act but it is used as a verbatim meaning given to the word. It is not necessary that the word must be so construed as to make a signature or mark. [602 B] (iii) Section 33(2) does not say "writing". The word 'signing" is not used in any technical sense and it means writing by a person who has signed the nomination papers. It only means signing the nomination form. [063 C] (iv) The words "writing " in the form" are not defined either in the General Clauses Act or in the Special Clauses Act. [20064 E] (v) Section 3 of the General clauses Act does not refer to any other document which is required to be signed by the proposer and the seconder. It merely says that the signature must be in a particular way. The word must mean " in writing". [065 C] In the instant case, the nomination was made by the appellant himself and he had signed it as a proposer. He did not sign the nomination forms. He was not authorised to do so. [ 20064 E F] (vi) Section 4 of the Representation of the People Act does refer to the general policy of the act which is of the essence in making a signatures and it does not show that the writing of a mark is to be so signed as to give effect to the special definition of "signing".

The appellants were employed as "Skilled Workers" in the Company 's establishment on September 20, 1972. They had been working for more than 240 days in a year and had not abandoned service of the Company during that period. The Company was terminated from service by the appellants on October 22, 1972 and they were re-employed elsewhere. On September 19, 1972, the appellants filed an application under section 33(A) of the Act before the Industrial Tribunal for reinstatement with full back wages. The Industrial Tribunal after considering the evidence adduced by the parties held that the appellants had abandoned service and had abandoned their services and accordingly directed the Company to reinstate them in service. The appellants challenged the said order of the Industrial Court before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the termination of the services of the appellants was illegal and invalid and that they were not entitled to any relief. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned action was not justified because the appellants were not interested in the service of their Company and had voluntarily abandoned the service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of services of a workman is illegal and void as it amounts to retrenchment. [601B] 2. The word 's employment' has been defined in section 2(oo) of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 which reads thus: " 'S Employment means any employment by the employer or any other person whether for wages or not, in connection with the affairs of the company, and includes a strike, lockout, lock-out, strike, riot, strike or lockout. [701C] 3. The expression 's service' has not been defined either in section 3(oo)(i) or in any other provision of this Act. It is well settled that the word ' employment' means any service by a workman for wages and includes any appointment by a company on behalf or under any other arrangement, whether for remuneration or not. [801D] 4. The words "any person" have been defined to mean any person who has been employed in connection With the affairs or management of the undertaking or any work connected with the business of the employer. It does not include a workman who is employed in the undertaking. The definition of 's services in section 10(oo), therefore, clearly shows that the employment must be for wages. [820E] 5. In the instant case, the appellant had abandoned his service and he was not interested to abandon his service. He had voluntarily left the service and did not intend to abandon the service during the pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court. [823A D] 6. The appellant having failed to discharge his duties as a workman in accordance with the provisions of section 10 (oo) and 10(o), the question whether he was entitled to reinstatement or not does not arise at all. [825E] 7. In view of the fact that the appellant did not abandon his services during the period when he had abandoned the services, it cannot be said that the action on the part of the respondent Company was illegal or invalid. [826A D E] 8. The Labour Court was right in holding that there was no abandonment of service and the appellant having abandoned his services, the action was clearly illegal and bad. [827B C] 9. In order to appreciate the contentions raised by the learned Counsel for the parties it is necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 (Bombay Act No. XIV of 1947) which are as under: "Section 10(0). "Save as otherwise provided in this Act or any law for the time being in force, no workman shall be retrenched by the Company unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against such retrenchment and has been afforded an adequate opportunity of making representation.

The appellant, a public trust, was the owner of certain properties. The trust was created by the Government of Bombay in exercise of powers under section 36(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, which came into force on January 1, 1950. Under section 36 (b), the Charity Commissioner appointed under that section shall be deemed to be a Judge for the purposes of section 36 and the provisions of that Act shall apply to all proceedings before him. The appellant filed an application in the High Court for setting aside the sale held by him. On February 15, 1951, the High court dismissed the application holding that the sale was not valid under section 37(a). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High 'Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the auction sale held in execution of a decree for sale as prayed for by him and that the order passed by the Charity commissioner was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that since the sale in execution proceedings was not a decree within the meaning of section 37 (a), it was competent to set it aside under section 38(b) of that act. [701 A] 2. The power of the Charity Commissioners to set up an enquiry as to whether a judgment delivered by a Division Bench of a single Judge is liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on a reference made on a question of law arising before him, was not vested in the Chief Justice of the High Courts. [801 B] 3. The powers of the Chief justice of a Division bench or a single judge are not limited to examining the question whether a particular judgment is relevant for deciding the question of fact arising before it. [820 C] 4. The jurisdiction which is vested by the Charter of the Court in the Court of the District Judge in execution proceeding is not affected by any decision of the Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court. [823 D] 5. The learned Judges of the Division Bench were right in setting aside a sale held without jurisdiction and that they had no power to set them aside on a proper case. [825 E] 6. In view of the fact that the judgment was delivered by the High' Court after due consideration of the points before it, the question as to what is the correct position in law would not arise at all. [822 C] 7. The judgment of the learned Single Judge was based on a wrong assumption that the appellant had agreed to abandon the execution proceeding and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the amount specified in the proclamation of sale for which the sale had been ordered, and that he had agreed not to abandon, the execution proceedings and to continue with the execution. [826 D] 8. The fact that a Division Judge or a learned single Judge has no power under section 35(a), to set-aside an auction sale on a finding that the amount mentioned in the Proclamation of sale was insufficient to discharge the debt due by the trust, does not mean that he can exercise his jurisdiction under section 34(b). [826 E] 9. The language used in section 36 is clear and unambiguous. It is well settled that the powers of a Judge or an Division Bench are not unlimited. In the present case, the learned Judges have held that the auction was valid under the law and the High Curt had no authority to set down any enquiry as a singleJudge or a Division Court. The view taken by the learned Judge is clearly erroneous. [828 E] 10. It would be open to the appellant to raise all contentions before the Chief Judge of the City Civil Court, Bombay, in regard to the validity of the sale and the correctness of the decision of that court on the question.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935 and he was promoted to the post of Senior Clerk on June 5, 1935. He was promoted as Senior Clerk in the year 1936. The appellant was promoted on June 7, 1935 to the said post. On July 11, 1935, he was posted at the Railway Station at Kanpur. He joined the Railway Service on June 9, 1935 as a Clerk and was promoted in the month of January, 1934. He filed an application for voluntary retirement under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules. The Railway Board by its letter dated November 30, 1962 informed him that his request for voluntary retire ment from service was not accepted by the Government. On June 11, 1964, he submitted a representation to the General Manager, Northern Railway, Kanpur requesting that his case be considered under Rule 2046 and that he should be given an opportunity of being heard in respect of the proposed retirement. The General Manager rejected the request on July 12, 1965. He challenged the order of retirement before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to voluntary retirement from service with effect from June 4 1964 and that the order passed by the Railway Board dated November 29, 1962 was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the impugned order of compulsory retirement was bad in law as it was not based on any statutory provision or a rule framed under proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution which is inconsistent with it. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power conferred by Rule 2 (2) to retire a Government servant after he has completed 30 years qualifying service and has not attained the age of 55 years is inconsistent With the power conferred on the Railway Administration under Article 77(1) of Pension Rules, 1950. [601B] 2. The rule does not say that the retirement shall be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. It only says that the power to retire an officer who has completed thirty years qualifying serv ice, and has never attained the Age of 55 year is inconsistent. [702C] 3. The language used in Rule 2 of Pension rules does not mean that the retiring Government servant should be retired at any time after he had completed 30 year of qualifying service. It does not speak of retirement at any stage after he was over 30 years of qualifying servi cation. [803D] 4. The word 'providing' in Rule 2047 has no parity with Rule 2. In the instant case, the appellant had completed thirty five years qualifying s ervice and had not attained his age of superannuation which is consistent with Rule 2041 of the Rules. He had completed only 30 years service on June 3, 1935 but he was retired at a time after attaining the age o f superannuation. [903E] 5. The expression 'prov ement' in rule 2(1)(h) and (i) of pension rules does no more than make it clear that the retire ment is to be made on the basis of the date of retirement. It is not a case where the retiring government servant has completed the age 55 years. [1003F] 6. The words 'proved' in the rule are not to be interpreted in any manner and they do not mean merely to make it retrospective or equitable. [1101G] 7. In view of the above, the order dated November 28, 1962 is bad in the eye of law and is liable to be set aside. [110H; 1102A B] 8. The order dated June 4/6, 1964 is not violative of Article 14 of the constitution. It has been issued under Rule 19(1), which provides that the date on which a Government Servant attains the age specified in Rule 19 shall be determined by the President. [111G H; 1103A B C] 9.

The assessee, a registered firm carrying on business in the mills at Raichur and accused Nos. 1 to 3 were partners of the assessee firm. The assessee was assessed to income tax under section 5 of the Act on the basis that the activity which the assessee carried on at Raichur was part of their business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter called the 'Act'). The assessee claimed set off in respect of the chargeable accounting period ending March 31st, 1943 and 23rd November, 1942. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim of set off on the ground that the assessee had not incurred any deficiency in profits during the chargeable chargeable accounting periods and, therefore, set off was allowable under section 7 of the Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1944. The High Court held that the amount of the excess profits which accrued to the assessee during the relevant accounting period could be set off against the chargeable business profits for the chargeable period ending 31st March, 1943. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1. The expression 'accounting period' in section 5 (1) means the period commencing on or before the 31st day of March, 1941 and ending on or after that date. [701B] 2.2 The expression "accounting year" in section 7(1)(a) includes any accounting period beginning on or subsequent to the 1st April, 1943 but ending on the 31 st March, 1944 but ending with the 31St day of January, 1941. [802C] 3.3 The expression used in section 6 (2) means a period commencing from the 1 st April, 1942 and ending before the date on which the assessment is made.
