[820D] 4.4 The word 'account " has been defined in section 2(d)(i) of that Act as follows: "(1) any sum payable by an assessee to his account shall be setoff against the amount due from him under this Act for the purposes of the business carried on by him at Raichur or accused Nos 1 to 4." [820E] 5.5 The expression has been used in the Act and it is not necessary that the liability to set off should be determined on that basis. [821F] 6.6 In the instant case, the assessee was entitled to set up a set off of profits during accounting period commencing 31st December, 1940 to 31st January, 1943 under section 4(1). The assessee had claimed setoff of profits in respect thereof during the accounting period and the same was allowed by the Appellate Assistant commissioner. [823G] 7.7 In the present case, it is clear that the business of the appellant at Raichur had been started from the beginning of 1940 and ending with 31st May, 1943, and therefore, the question whether the activity of the Appellant at Raichur could be said to have been part of his business within its meaning or not was a question of fact. [825G] 8.8 The High court has rightly held that there was no material on record to show that the activities of the firm were part of the manufacturing activity of oil in their mills at Bellary and, consequently, set Off profits during those chargeable accounting years ending March, 1942 to 31 st December, 1941 could not be said as a part of its business within that period. [826C] 9.9 In the circumstances, the High Court was right in holding that the appellant had incurred any liability for the assessment year 1943 4 to 31St March, 1940 and that the question of law raised by the appellant was not open to be decided on the facts of this case. [827G] 10.10 The High Courts have rightly held against the assessee.

The appellants were appointed as Civil Engineering graduates on the basis of a competitive examination held by the Kerala Public Service Commission. They were selected and appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Mechanical Engineering Department. The KPSC was directed to prepare a common list for Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering. The appellants filed an appeal before the Division Bench of the High Court against the judgment of the learned Single Judge. The Division Bench allowed the appeals and set aside the judgment and order of the Kerala High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The judgment of a Division Bench is not correct in law. It is well settled that when a common seniority list has been prepared and published, it cannot be said that there was any violation of the principles of natural justice or that the appellants were prejudiced because of the non-compliance with the directions given by the High court. [701A B] 1.2 The judgment in Civil Engineering (Civil) case is not applicable to the facts of this case as the appellants had not challenged the seniority list prepared by the Public Service commission. They did not challenge the seniority lists prepared by them. Therefore, they were entitled to a direction to prepare separate rank lists for Civil engineering and Mechanical Engineers. [801C] 1.(a) The judgment is distinguishable on facts. (b) The appellants had filed an application before the High Power Committee of Kerala for approval of their names in the seniority List prepared by it. They had also filed a representation before the Government of Kerala. The Government of India, after considering the representations and the objections raised by the KP SC, rejected them on the ground that they were not aware of the fact that the KPsSC was prepared by a common rank list for Engineering (Electrical) and Mechanical engineering. [820A B C] 1(a) In view of the decision in Civil Appeal No. 1149/80 decided on 28th April, 1980, the appellants cannot challenge the inter se seniority list. [821B C] 2.(b) It is not necessary to clarify whether the appellants are entitled to any relief or not. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had not made out a case for interference with the judgment. [823C] 3.(c) The High Power Committees of Kerala and the Government have not given any directions to prepare the common list. They have not done so. Therefore there is no question of giving any direction to the appellants to prepare their separate rank list. There was no reason why the appellants should not be directed to make a common gradation list for the Engineering (Elect) and Electrical engineering. The appeals are accordingly dismissed. No costs.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for dissolution of partnership accounts and valuing at Rs.150 only on the plaint allegations made by the plaintiff in the suit for partition of business and valuations at Rs,150. The plaintiff alleged that he had been ousted from the business and he was entitled to get a sum of Rs.50 only on his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint. The trial court rejected the claim of the plaintiff holding that the valuation put by the defendant before it was not correct and that the plaintiff had been excluded from the partnership business. On appeal, the High Court held that the value of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction and accordingly allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The plaint allegations are vague and do not disclose any cause of action. [701B] 2. The valuation put in by the appellant before the Income tax department is quite reasonable and does not require an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the case. [802C] 3. The value of a suit cannot be determined on the basis of the valuation given by the assessee before it is put to any valuation under section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, 1961. [601D] 4. The court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter and to take into consideration the statement in the plaint which is arbitrary and unreasonable. [820E] 5. The High Court was not right in rejecting the plaint on the ground that it did not disclose a correct valuation of any particular item of property. [823G] 6. The suit for declaration of accounts and valuation of assets at Rs.,150 only was rejected by the trial court. [825A B] 7. The defendant had been directed to pay the amount of Rs,50 only as his share of the profits for a specific period by way of profit for the year 1979 8. The respondent No. 1 has not challenged the valuation of his property at Rs..150 only. He has also not challenged that valuation put up by him before the court. He had been asked to place the valuation on his claim at Rs...150 only, and he had not challenged it. [822B] 7A B C] 8. In view of the fact that the plaint averments made by respondent No 1 in the present case were vague and did not contain any decision to the contrary, the trial Court was right in holding that as the valuation was put by him on his behalf before the income tax department, he had no interest. [826C] 9. The facts of this case are quite different from the facts of the present appeal. It is true that the appellant has not shown any decision at all to the effect that the estimated value of his share was Rs..50 only. [828D] 10. In the circumstances, the valuation made by him in the case before the High court cannot be said to be unreasonable or arbitrary. [827E] 11. The Court is bound to accept that the proper valuation put on his suit for declaring accounts and valued at Rs .150 only is correct and not arbitrary. The appellant has failed to show any decision of the court to the value put by respondent no. 1 in his plaint. [829F] 12. In this case, the plaintiff has not produced any evidence to show that he was ousted from business or had taken all the accounts and other properties at Rs,.150 only for a different period by referring to the proceedings of the income Tax department. The fact that respondent No1 had been prevented from presenting his valuation on behalf of the appellant does not mean that the court has jurisdiction to consider the matter. [824E] 13. In order to find out whether the valuation is correct or not, it must be fair and reasonable and not unreasonable. It must be a fair and just valuation.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of various kinds of "traditional industries" and had set up its industry in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant company, it is stated, had been granted a certificate under section 12(1)(i) of the Act for the period from 1st April, 1981 to 31st March, 1981. The said certificate was issued on the basis that the appellant company had setup its industries within the specified areas and had started production after the explicit instructions of 12.1.1 962/87. The State Government by a notification dated 23rd January, 1982 exempted certain industries from the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958 with effect from 1 st April,1981. The exemption was granted to such industries on the condition that they would not be entitled to any exemption under section 22D of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1981 and that they were eligible for the exemption under the said notification. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification was prospective in operation and the appellant had not opted for the scheme of deferment of tax under section 11(1) of Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the exemption granted by the notification dated 1st March 1981 was retrospective in operation; that the said exemption was not available to the industries covered by rule 14 and that the Director of Industries had no power to grant a certificate to the appellant under section 23D of Act; that since the exemption was given to such industry, it could not be said that the appellants were eligible to avail the benefit of the exemption. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The notification dated 24th January, 1981 is prospective in nature and does not set out any condition for the grant of a certificate. [601B] 2.2 The words "trained industries" used in section 12 (1)(ii) are to be read into the notification itself and all that the conditions for the said purpose are set out in the notification themselves and all those conditions for exemption have to be set out clearly and only if they are not specifically mentioned in the said rule. [701C] 3.3 The words 'trained industry" used therein are to refer to a particular industry which is covered by the exemption clause. It does not mean that the industries specified in the Notification itself would not apply to them. [802D] 4.1 In the instant case, the appellants had been given a certificate on the ground that they had already availed the benefit under section 20(2) of Central Sales tax Act, 1956. The notification was issued only for the purpose of extending the exemption and not for the purposes of granting exemption. [820E] 3:1.3 In view of the fact that the notifications were issued only to extend the exemption to such units covered by Rule 14 and not on the terms of the scheme, it cannot be said to be retrospective in nature. [823A D] 2:1 The appellants are eligible for exemption under rule 14. [822E] 2(a) The notification itself provides that the benefit shall be available only to those industries which have set up their industry within the notified areas and specified in column (3) of Schedule below who have setup their industries within specified areas. [821A D E] 3(b) The appellants were not eligible for a certificate as they had not availed the exemption from the operation of rule 14, because the notification did not provide that they should be eligible for any exemption. The condition prescribed in the rule was that the certificate issued by the Director would be valid only if it is found that the company has set up a new industrial unit which is not eligible to get the benefit. [825E] 4(c) The words used in rule 14 are clear and unambiguous.

The petitioners were appointed as Additional District & Sessions Judges on the basis of merit cum seniority cum senioritycum-merit. They were promoted to the post of Additional District and Sessions Judge by the Full Court of the High Court. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of Rule 7(a) and (b). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not fit for promotion on merit cum merit basis but they were appointed to temporary posts in accordance with qualifications laid down under Rule 7 (a), namely, by selection and after completion of a minimum of ten years judicial service. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had erred in holding that Rule 7 was not applicable to the appointments made by the Delhi Higher Judicial Service as well as by the High Curt. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding so. [601B] 2.1 The High C ourt was right on the ground that the appellants were appointed regularly and after completing a minimum ten years of judicial service in accordance to the rules of recruitment prescribed under Rule 16(2) of the Rules. [702C E] 3.2 The High Courts were wrong in holding otherwise. The appointments made on merit basis by the Selection Committee were not in accordance either with the qualifications laid out under Rule 8(2), namely that the promotees were appointed on the recommendation of the Full court of the Delhi Judicial Service or on the recommendations of the Selection Board. [802F] 3:1. The appointment of the respondents was made on the advice of the Government and they were not selected by the Public Service Commission. They had completed ten years service in the judicial service and they could not be appointed as temporary Judges. [820G] 2:2.3 The High courts were wrong, in holding, that the appointments were made on merits cum seniority basis so much so that persons found fit for promotions were ignored as in the case of direct recruits, namely, from amongst members of Delhi Judicial Services, who had completed not less than ten years' service in judicial service, but were appointed by the Governor. [823G] 3;2.4 The High Power Court was right, in treating the appointments on merit as being made on a regular basis and holding that they were regularly appointed on a substantive capacity to a temporary post of District & Session Judge. [825H] 4.1. In view of the above position, it is not possible for us to hold that the appointment of respondents was illegal or invalid. [826A D] 3,2.5 The High power court was wrong in treating them as being appointed on regular basis. [822B] 4:1 It is well settled that a person who has completed ten year of judicial Service cannot be placed at a higher post than a District and Session Judge unless he has been selected by a duly constituted Selection Board for appointment to the Delhi Superior Judicial Service. [828C] 3(a). The power of the Governor under Rule 6(1) is not an absolute power but it is an absolute one. It is only in exceptional cases where the Governor is satisfied that there are compelling reasons for doing so, he can direct the appointments to be made on regular posts. [829B C] 4(b) In the instant case, the High Power court was correct in holding the appointments of respondents as temporary judges and not as permanent Judges. The power under Rule 5(1), therefore, is not a absolute one and it cannot be exercised by the President or Governor. The Governor has no power to direct the appointment to any post. [827C] 4.(c) In view thereof, the impugned order of the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court is set aside and the appeal is allowed.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to tax in the hands of the Ambala Flour Mills. The Income tax Officer, who had passed an order assessing the income of the appellant as "an association of persons ' under section 31(3) (c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, set aside the assessment and directed that the income be assessed in the names of the two partners of the firm or any other person. The Tribunal held that the Income tax officer was competent to make the order of assessment and reassessed the income in the light of the findings of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court allowed the appeal, set it aside. In the present appeals, the appellant has challenged the correctness of the decision of the High Court on the question whether the Income taxes Officer was competent under section 33A to make an order of reassessment or reassessed. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court had no jurisdiction to direct the Incometax Officer to amend any assessment made on the appellant. [701B] 2.2 The power of the appellate Assistant Commissioner to make a direction for assessing the Income income in respect of the income earned by the appellant was not barred by the law of Limitation. [802C] 3.3 The High Courts had no power under section 34(1) (a) of Income Tax, 1961 to direct that the assessment should be made on an association of individuals or a member of the association of person or a firm or a partner of such individual or a company. [820D E] 4.1 In the instant case, the Income TAX Officer had no authority to make any order of reassessment in respect thereof. He was not competent under Section 33A of the Act to make such an order. The Appellate Assistant commissioner had no powers to direct re-assessment in the absence of a direction by the IncomeTax Officer to make fresh assessment on the assessee or any person in consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction contained in an order passed by the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner. [823E] 4:1 The power under Section 34(2) (b) is not a power which can be exercised only if there has been a change in the assessment made by the income tax Officer. It is not open to the Income Taxes Officer to direct reassessment of the assessee on the ground that the business was carried on by an association or a person of persons or a joint family of which he was a member. [825E] 3:2 The Income Tax Officer had jurisdiction to make orders of re- assessment and reassess. He could not have made any order in respect thereto. [826A B] 4;3:1. In view of the provisions of section 34 (2) of Act, the Appellate Tribunal was competent and could not give directions for assessing income in favour of the joint family. [828B C] 3(a) The High 'Court had no inherent jurisdiction to issue a direction to assess the income on an Association of persons under section 32A of Act. [827C] 4(b) The Income TAX officer was not empowered to make reassessment or reassess. The power conferred by section 34A is not an absolute power which could be exercised in favour only if it had been exercised in accordance with the provisions contained in section 33B of Act and the assessment had to be made under section 27 or 32B of the said Act. The order of the Tribunal was therefore, without jurisdiction. [829E] 5:1 It is true that the Appellate Authority had no such power. But it was not open for the Income Incometax Officer to have made a direction in respect to the income which he could not be assessed under section 26 or 32A. [822F G] 3 (a)(i) The order passed in the case of the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow vs Ram Chandra and Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the plaint schedule properties. The plaintiff claimed that he was entitled to get a decree for partition on the basis of the value of Rs. 15,00,000 as the value thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the valuation of the plaint was not correct and that the appellant had no right to amend his valuation for the purposes of court fee. The High Court held that the plaintiff was entitled only to a sum of Rs., 15,000 on the plaint and the court fee paid on the memorandum of appeal was not payable on the ground that the value was not fixed under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of the High Court in respect of the valuation made by him for the purpose of court fees. The Division Bench of the Madras High Court allowed the appeal holding that it was open to the plaintiff to amend the valuation for payment of court Fees on his memorandum of appeals and the memorandum thereof. In appeal, the appellant contended that the court fees paid on plaint and memorandum of cross appeal should be taken as the valuation in respect thereof. Held, that the trial court had jurisdiction to determine the value under section 8(iv) (b) and it was not open to it to go into the question whether the valuation should be adopted for determining the value. The Court fee paid by the appellant on the Memorandum of appeal could not be taken into account in computing the court Fees payable on plaint or memorandum of crossobjections.

The appellant, a public authority, issued a notice under Section 16(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on 18.4.1989 calling upon it to show cause why the plans submitted by them should not be rejected and the plans should not continue to be in conformity with bye law 16.4.. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the notices issued under Section 17(1). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notices were invalid as they did not comply with the requirements of Byelaw 16. 4.8.2 and 16.5.8, but allowed the writ petitions. In appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had erred in holding that bye law 17.1 applied only to a case where the plans were not in conformity to Bye laws 16.3.4, and that the NDMC did not raise any objection to the construction work according to the plans. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "external walls" in bye law 15.4 does not mean that they are located on external walls. [601 A] 2.1 The expression 'external wall" is a term of art and includes any structure or structure which may be erected on external wall. It does not include any structure, or structure, whether or not constructed on external surface thereof. [702 B] 3.2 The expression used in byelaw 16 has to be understood in the context of the specific objectives of bye laws 16 and that it is a general rule that the construction should be made on external side walls. It must be clearly understood in its ordinary sense. [803 C] 4.3 In the instant case, the appellant had not raised any objection against the construction of the building. The NDMC did raise no objection to such an application. [820 D] 5.1. The High court was right in holding, that the plans filed by the appellant were not consistent with bye laws and that they were not within the meaning of Bye law 16, and therefore, the requirements for the pedestrian walk way and Podium could not have been satisfied. [823 E] 4: 1.(a) In view of the clear language of byelaw 17, it is not possible to hold that the appellant was entitled to a reasonable opportunity of being heard before the NDMC had rejected the plans on the ground that they did so in violation of Bye Law 16. (b) The High Cour t was right when it held that the requirements laid down by bye law 18 were not satisfied. (c) In the present case, there is no dispute that the plan submitted by the appellants was not consistent to bye laws 17.4 and that as the plans did not contain any provision for the retaliatory measures, they could not be accepted. [825 E] 2.(a)(i) The appellant had made a representation on 18th April 1989 to the NDMC seeking permission to commence construction of a building in accordance with Bye law 15, but it was rejected by the NDMC on the premise that the same would be at the risk of the appellants being not consistent or in any other manner. [826 A B] (ii) The appellants had made an application for sanction of plans under byelaw 18. The appellant did not make any such application and therefore the plans could not continue beyond a height of 15 metres. [827 C] 3.(a). In view thereof, the appellants were entitled to have their plans approved by the Chief Fire Officer, Delhi Fire Service, New Delhi. [828 E] (b)(i), The appellant was not entitled to any relief under bye law 14.

The plaintiff, who was the owner of a motor business in respect of which he had entered into an agreement with the defendants for purchase of a new motor car and a licence for the sale of a number of motor cars, applied to the Court for a decree for partition. The Court passed an order on April 6, 1948, that the suit be dismissed. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and decreed his claim to the extent of Rs. 1,00,000/=with interest at the rate of 12% per annum from March 31, 1946, up to March 31st, 1946. The plaintiff appealed to this Court against the judgment of the High court. HELD: (1) The suit was not barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure. [601B] (2) The cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit was barred under order II, Rule 2(4). [602C] (3) The plaintiff having abandoned his claim for accounts of motor business after March 31 and not actually of all businesses up to the date of the final decree, he is bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree. [613D] (4) The plaint in the second suit was clearly barred under section 2(2), of Civil Code. [502E] (5) The High Court was right in holding that the cause of actions in the first suit was different from the cause for partition and that the plaintiff had abandoned his claims to account in respect thereof. [511F] (6) The second suit is barred under article 2(1)(a), (b) and (c). [503G] (7) The question whether the cause was different or not does not arise in the present case because the cause is different from that of the two Suits. [504A B] (8) The facts are not similar to the facts of the present suit. The cause for filing the second suits was different and distinct from the causes of action for partition, and the cause thereof was different.

The appellant was engaged in the manufacture of salt works and he had been working as a contractor for the purpose of carrying on the business of salt. The appellant was also doing the work of salt work in the said salt Works. He was also carrying on his business of manufacturing salt. On April 9, 1952, the appellant was employed by the Salt Works Department as an agent for the manufacture and sale of salt Works and he was also working as an Assistant Engineer in the Salt Factory. The Chief Inspector of Factories, Bombay, issued a notice to the appellant under section 6(1) of the Indian Factories Act, 1948, calling upon him to show cause why his licence should not be cancelled. The respondent filed a reply to the said notice and contended that the salt works were not covered by the definition of the word " factory " in the Act. The High Court held that the appellant had no intention to carry on any business of manufacture and that the word 'factory " did not come within the definition. On appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The word ' factory " is defined in the Factories Act as meaning a factory which carries on any manufacturing process or any other kind of work. [601B] (2) The words 'factory ' are used in the sense of an office or establishment and not in the ordinary sense of the term. It does not mean that the business carried on by the appellant is not one of the two kinds of work mentioned in the definition, namely, the manufacturing process. [701C] (3) The expression "factory" has been defined in section 2(k) of Act LXIII of 1948 as meaning any factory which is engaged in any manufacturing activity. It means a factory or any kind of business carried out by the manufacturer or his agent. [802D] (4) The definition of 'factory' in the Bombay Salt Works Act, 1958, does not include any factory or other kind thereof. [820E] (5) The term "factory " is used in relation to the manufacture or production of salt and it includes every kind of building or part of a building or an establishment which carries out any manufacturing operation. It is not necessary that the said word ' must be given a meaning different from the ordinary meaning of the expression ' factory ' in the Indian Salt Works. [823E] The word "factory ' has been used in connection with the manufacture, production and sale thereof. The word employed in the section includes any premises which are used for the manufacturing or production by the assessee himself. [825F] (6) The intention of the legislature is clear that the words ' factory or establishment ' have to be given the meaning that they mean a factory as defined in s. 2(s). It does include all factories which carry on the manufacturing activity and every kind thereof whether it carries out manufacturing process, or any type of work, but does not exclude any premises where the manufacture is carried on. [826C] The words "factory or establishment " have to necessarily be given meaning that it carries on the manufacture itself. It cannot include any premises wherein the manufacturing operations are carried on and every type of activity which is carried out in the factory or in the establishment.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in the Department of Technical Education, on deputation to the Polytechnics and he was posted at Devangere Chetty. He was promoted to the post of Instructor in that department with effect from November 28, 1949. On his promotion to the said post, he was confirmed in that post by the Director of Technical education, Mysore. The respondent was promoted as Instructor on deputation from the Polytechnic at Devagere Chetty and he continued to work in that Department till November 28 1949 when he was so confirmed. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his reversion to the parent department. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in that cadre, but it held that the order of absorption in the department of TechnicalEducation was not justified and that he was entitled to be treated as a break in his service with effect on November 28 1950. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of reversion is not an order of appointment or transfer. It does not create any right in favour of the respondent. [701B] 2. The appellant was appointed to the Department as Instructor and he had been working as such till November 30, 1949 when his services were terminated. He continued to serve in that office till November 31, 1949, when he resumed duty on deputation. He did not hold any post of Tailoring Instructor in any other department for a long period in that Government. [801C] 3. The appointment was made by the Government as Instructor. It is not disputed that the appellant had been appointed to that Department on deputation and he joined the Department on November 30 1949 when the respondent was so appointed. He, however, continued to hold any other post till November 29, 1949 and he could be absorbed only in that of Tailing Instructor. [820G] 4. The Government of Mysore, by a notification dated December 12, 1949 had directed that the promotions of the appellant as Instructor should be made from the post held by him on November 27, 1949 subject to the condition that he would continue to hold the said posts till November 27 1950 when he assumed charge of Tailor Instructor in his department. [823G] 5. The question whether the respondent could be treated to have been absorbed in the service of the Department or not was a matter which should be decided by the Public Service Commission and it is open to the Government to take such action as may be necessary for doing so. [825A B] 6. In view of the fact that the services of the respondents were terminated on November 29 1950, the appellant could not claim any right to the absorption in that service. [822B] 7. The case of the State Government was that the appointment of the Instructor was made under a mistake of law and it was not open to him to take action as he had already been absorbed into the Department. [821C] 8. In the present case, the respondent did not acquire any right or privilege in his favour. He could not be absorbed permanently in that Service by reason of the order dated February 19, 1964, which was passed in 1955. The State Government had no right to absorb him in that particular department. It was open to it to take appropriate action as it may consider necessary for the purpose of giving effect to the decision of the Public Services Commission. [824E] 9. In this case, there is a clear distinction between the two classes of employees who were absorbed in another Department and those who were appointed to such department. They were not absorbed permanently or temporarily in that Departments. The fact that they were absorbed permanently on November 26, 1949 was not disputed by the respondent before us. [826C] 10. In order to appreciate the question whether a person is entitled to absorption in any department of technical education from a particular date, it is necessary for this Court to examine the scheme of the Act and the rules framed thereunder.

The appellant was born on 17.5.1950 and he had been residing in India since then till the date of his marriage with the respondent. The respondent married the appellant on 16.6.1951. He was living in India for a period of five years. On 15.7.1951, the appellant married one Smt. Roshni Devi and she was born to her. After the marriage, the respondent married another girl who had been born to the appellant. The appellant filed an application for guardianship before the court on behalf of the foreigner. The High Court allowed the said application and directed the appellant to be given in adoption by the recognised social or child welfare agency in India. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1.2. The provisions of Section 5(3) of the Act are mandatory in nature and they have to be strictly complied with. [601B] 2.1 The provisions contained in Section 5 (3) are mandatory and they must be strictly adhered to. [702C] 3.1 In view of the fact that the appellant was a minor, the provisions of section 5(4) are directory in nature. [803D] 3.(a) The provisions relating to adoption by a recognised social welfare agency are mandatory. [777E] (b) The provision contained in section 5 (2) is mandatory and it must be complied with before any application for appointment of a foreigner is made. [78F] 3(c) The procedure laid down in section 6(3)(a) is directory in character and the same must be followed by every effort to find out the child from adoption. [77A D] (d) The appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 5 of the .[777E C] 4.1 Section 5 of Act provides that if a person is born to another, he shall be given an opportunity of being heard before any adoption by such agency is made and if he does so, he may be given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against his appointment. [76B D] 3 (a) In the instant case, the High Court has not properly appreciated the provisions contained under section 6 (3)(b). The appellant had been living in the country for a long time and was able to gather information as to who are the biological parents of the child. [773E C; 77A D E] 4.(a)(i) In view thereof, the application for grant of guardianship made by the foreigner for adoption by recognised social Welfare agency is not maintainable. [779B] (ii) The High court has committed a serious error in holding that the provisions relating thereto are mandatory as also the procedure laid under section 9(3). [773A D; 77E] 5.(a). In view, of the facts and circumstances of this case, it would be in the interest of justice to allow the appellant for adoption of the respondent by recognised Social Welfare agency. [1978F] (iii) The application for custody made by a foreigner for taking a child in adoption is not competent. [1977G] 6.(a), (b)(i), (c) and (d). (ii), (e) and 5(2) are procedural requirements. They have to comply with the provisions laid down under section 4 of the , but they must make it, before any such application for the guardianship is made, by a person who has taken a child from the recognised Social welfare agency. The procedure prescribed in section 9 (3), therefore, must be adhered to and if it will be in interest of the children to have the child study report, the same should be supplied by the recognized social welfare agencies. [780E] 6(a) It is not necessary that there should be a reasonable time for making an application to the court so that the principles and norms as also norms as to the procedure prescribed under section 8 (3).

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Limited, Calcutta, is a company incorporated under the Companies Act and it has been carrying on business in order to facilitate its business. The Company was registered as a private limited company under the provisions of the Companies (Court) Act, 1956. It had entered into an agreement with the Company for providing certain facilities to its employees including the appellant, which were to be provided by the Company. The terms and conditions of the agreement are set out in the Schedule to the agreement. Clause 2(a) of the said agreement provides that the Company shall pay to the workmen at the rate of 20% of the gross profits for the year 1965 66 on the basis of the percentage of bonus payable for the accounting year 1965 67, as determined by the Tribunal. The company was also required to make up the balance available and allocable surplus in accordance with the provisions contained in the agreement within a period of six months from the date of the notice given by the employer. The workmen were not paid any amount under section 7 of the Act. The Tribunal held that the amount of Rs. 65,764 was not an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the ground of commercial expenses and therefore, it was not a deductible surplus. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal had rightly rejected the claim of the workmen for deduction of bonus from gross profits. [849B] (2) The High Court has committed an error in holding that the Tribunal was justified in disallowing the claim made by the Unions on the principle adopted by it. [950C F] (3) The question whether the amount paid to the employees under section 37(1) of Income tax Act is deductible from gross profit or not, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [1052D] (4) The workmen are entitled to get the bonus at 20% for the years 1965 66 and 65 respectively on the principles set out by this Court in Indian Oxygen Ltd. vs Their Workmen(1), that the amounts paid to them under section 6 and 7 of Act 67, should be deducted from gross salary for the purpose of computation of the available surplus and allocability of the surplus. [1152E] (5) The amount of bonus paid to employees under sections 6 and 37(2) of Act 68 is not an expenditure allowable under section 36(1). [1153F] (6) The amounts payable to the workers under section 5 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, are not deductible from the gross profit.

The appellant was appointed as a Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on July 7, 1975 and he was promoted to the post of Deputy Commissioner. He was posted as a Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in 1972. The Government of Tamil Nadu by its order dated November 29, 1974 directed that all the promotions gained by him should be made from time to time. On September 19, 1975 the appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner and he joined as a Commercial Tax Officer on July 30, 1975. He filed an appeal against his promotion before the Appellate Tribunal which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the order of the Government retiring him from service. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order passed by the Government was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order made by the State Government and that the appellant should be reinstated in service. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of promotion is not a punishment. It does not amount to an adverse entry. It merely amounts to an order of reversion. [701 A] 2. The power of the State to make a compulsory retirement on the ground of misconduct or inefficiency is not an absolute power but is an administrative power. It is a power which can be exercised only if it is shown that there was some material before the Government to come to its conclusion that the charges were proved. [801 B] 3. The mere fact that the Government had arrived for the enquiry cannot by itself make any difference in the present conduct of the employee as a Government servant. It would not be an error of law apparent on the face of the record. [820 C] 4. The State Government was entitled to take into consideration all the history of the service and to come out with its conclusion whether there was any entry in the service book to his promotion as Deputy Commissioners or that he had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. [823 D] 5. The fact that there were no entries in the confidential file of the petitioner shows that the petitioner was not only aware of the existence of the entry but also that he was aware of it. [825 E] 6. In the present case, the appellant had been promoted as a Joint Commercial Tax officer on July 19, 1974 and he had completed 25 years of qualifying service. He had been posted as Deputy Commercial Taxes Officer in 1957 and posted as Member of Sales Tax appellate Tribunal in 1970. The promotion was made by an order dated September 19. 1975. The said order was passed after the appellant retired from service on November 29. 1975 and his promotion was set aside by the High Commissioner. [826 C] 7. In view of the fact that a large number of employees had been appointed to the posts of Deputy Commissioners, it is difficult to sustain the order dated October 19, 1976. The impugned order cannot be sustained in law. [827 D] 8. The question whether the appellant could have been promoted to a higher post or not was a matter which would have to be decided by the appropriate authority. [828 E] 9. In this case, there is no material before him as to what was the nature of his duties and how he had performed. He has been posted to a different post in the same cadre. The allegations against the appellant were not substantiated by any evidence. There was nothing on record to show that he could have rendered himself liable for punishment under the rules. [829 E] 10. In order to appreciate the contentions raised by the learned Counsel for the State of Tamil Pradesh, it would be necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the rules and the material placed before the High Powered Committee. The Rules are in two parts. They provide for the promotion of officers to a post carrying pay scale. [824 E] 11.

The appellants were plying their buses on the routes in question. The Regional Transport Authority of Andhra Pradesh, which was constituted under section 68F(1) of the Act, granted permits to them for plying their vehicles on the route in question and also issued a permit in favour of the appellants for plying them on the said routes. On June 10, 1963, the appellants filed an application before the Regional Transport Authorities for grant of permits in respect of the said route. The applications were rejected by the Regional Authority on June 10. 1963. The appellants challenged the validity of the schemes and also the orders passed by the State Transport Undertaking on the ground that they were not allowed to ply their buses at the routes which were already nationalised under section 69F(2) of Act, and that the Regional transport authorities had no power to issue a permit for plying the vehicles on those routes. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the schemes were not vitiated by non compliance with the requirements of section 68 C and the Rules made thereunder. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The scheme framed by the Corporation is a self-contained one and it cannot be called in question on the grounds that it was inconsistent with the provisions of section 69 F(2). [601B] 2.1 The schemes are not vitiated either by non application of mind or by reason of the fact that they are not allowed by law to ply the buses on those route. [602C] 3.2. The schemes were framed under section 70 C and 68D of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue permits for plying any vehicles on such routes. [063E] 2:1.1 Section 68F (1) provides that the State Government may by notification in the official Gazette direct that the provisions contained in sections 68C and 68 D shall not apply to any route or part thereof, whether it is a public service vehicle or a private service vehicle. The power of the State transport authority to issue such permits is subject to the condition that the scheme framed under Chapter 70F(3) is subject only to the conditions that the permit issued by the Government for plying such vehicles shall not be cancelled or modified except as provided in section 68C. [2006E] 3:2.1 In view of the provisions made in Ch.68F(l), the State Governments are competent to issue the permits under Ch. 68D and the rules framed thereunder, but there is no power conferred on them by law either to issue or not to issue any permit for such vehicles. [ 2006E] 4:2 The State Government has no power under section 72C of the Andhra Pradesh Road Transport Corporation Act, 1988 to issue permit for a private vehicle. [2007E] 5:2 In view thereof, the Regional Government is competent to grant permits in favour or otherwise to ply on the notified routes. It cannot be said that the permits issued by it are inconsistent with any provision of the A.P. Road Transport Corporations Act, 1989. [2008F] 3;3:1 The State transport authorities have no power either to cancel or modify the schemes framed under sections 68 C & 68D.

The appellant, a dealer registered under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, was granted a declaration form in respect of certain sales to him. The said declaration form was furnished by the purchasing dealer and the prescribed authority had issued the declaration form. The appellant filed an application for registration as a dealer under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act on November 21, 1957. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant on November 22, 1957 and the appellant filed a revision petition before the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the said declaration forms were not required to be furnished by a dealer who had issued them as required under section 27A of the Orissa Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the proviso to section 5 (2)(b) of Orissa Sales tax Act, 1948, which provided for the exemption in respect thereof, did not apply to the sales made to a registered dealer and that the appellant had furnished a declaration in writing by the selling dealer or by such person as may be authorized in writing in this behalf by such dealer. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The proviso to s. 5(1)(a) of Bihar Sales Tax, 1947 is not inconsistent with section 5 of the said Act and the rules made thereunder. [601B] 2. The expression "any other person" used in the proviso is a word of wide import and it does not mean any person who has been authorized to file a declaration under the provisions of the Bihar Sales tax, 1947. [702C] 3. The words "any person" appearing in the said proviso are not intended to cover a dealer whose turnover is specified in the purchasing certificate form. It is only when the prescribed particulars are furnished by such a dealer that the goods in question are specified in his purchasing certificate forms. [803D] 4. The word "any" used therein does not refer to any person other than the registered dealer who has issued the certificate of registration as required for resale by him or in the execution of any contract. It only means that the declaration forms must be furnished with a prescribed form and good and good reasons for rejecting the claim. [903G] 5. The language used in section 5 is clear and unambiguous. The conditions mentioned therein are not mandatory but only directory. The condition is that the dealer should produce a true declaration in the prescribed manner and within the time specified therein. [1003E] 6. The requirement of the proviso cannot be complied with by the dealer who is required to furnish a declaration as required by section 5. [1101F] 7. The assessee has not produced any other evidence to prove that the sales were for the purposes mentioned in the declaration Form. It was only when such a certificate forms are furnished well and good, and if it was substantially complied with, the proviso would have no application. [110G] 8. The provisions of section 5A(2) (a)(i) of Act do not apply. The notification issued by the Commercial Tax Officer under section 4(1) of that Act is in terms to enable the dealer to produce a declaration forms and it is only if such a declaration is furnished well, well and sufficient reasons for rejection of the claim are given, the Sales tax authorities would have jurisdiction to make an order of assessment. [100G] 9. The power conferred on the Commercial Taxes Officer under s. 4(2), therefore, cannot be exercised by the Salestax Officer in respect to any dealer who does not possess a valid declaration form and it can only be exercised if such certificate forms and good reason are furnished.

The State of Bihar has filed a counter affidavit in response to the direction given by this Court on 26th February, 1979. The State of BIHAR has furnished to us a list of cases pending in each of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 and 5th March, 1979, which have been filed before the Magistrates or the Sessions Courts, as the case may be, for a period of over five years. In addition to the particulars given in the counter affidavit filed by Bageshwari Prasad Pande, Superintendent of Police, the State Government should provide him a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail and if any application for Bail is made, the Magistrates/the Sessions Courts may provide him an opportunity to make an application. The High Court has directed that on the next remand dates when they are produced before the Magistrate or the sessions Courts, the Magistrate should dispose of such cases as expeditiously as possible and in accordance with the broad guidelines indicated by us in our judgment dated 12th February 1979. In view of the directions given by us on 26 th February, 1978, we direct that on 31 st December,1978 and 5 th March,1979, the District Magistrate shall provide him with a lawyer for his own cost and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State of Patna within three weeks from today. The District Magistrate will furnish to us within three days from today particulars as to the number of cases in each district as on 30th December, 1979 and 5nd March, 1980, which are pending investigation for more than six months.

The appellant landlord filed an application under section 29(2) of the Act for obtaining possession of the land. The tenant contended that he had not acquired any right to terminate the tenancy and therefore the notice was bad in law. The High Court held that the provisions of section 34 (1) were applicable to the present case, and that the landlord had terminated the tenancy by one year 's notice. The appellant filed an appeal against this order before the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the appeal holding that the termination of the tenancy was not in accordance with the restrictions imposed by sub section (2) A of section 29 of the Amending Act and therefore, the landlord was entitled to terminate his tenancy by a notice given under section 34(1). In the present appeal, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had erred in holding that sub section(2A) of section 31 of the amending Act applied to the facts of this case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Amendment Act are applicable to all cases where notices given before and after the commencement of the amendment were given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the said Amending Act. [601 A] 2. The proviso to section 34 of the principal Act is not retrospective in operation. It does not affect any right of the landlord to terminate a tenancy by giving notice under section 31(2). The proviso does not apply to cases where notice might have been given before or after the coming in force of Amending Act, but it applies only when the period of notice has expired and the right to terminated the lease has accrued to the landlord. [701 B] 3. The language used in sub section A of the Principal Act is clear and unambiguous. It is not necessary that the notice should have been issued before or at least after the termination. The words "the date on which the tenancy has actually terminated" are not to be taken into consideration for determining the right of landlord in the matter of termination of tenancy. [801 C] 4. The word 's end' is not defined in the Amending Acts. It means that the date on or before which the right is acquired by the landlord becomes extinguished and the tenant acquires a vested right to obtain possession of land. [820 D] 5. The expression "the day on which" occurs in sub Section (2A), must be understood in the sense that it does not include any period after the date of termination. It would mean that the tenancy is terminated before or even after the expiry of the period specified in sub clause (1). [820 E] 6. The right to terminating a tenancy under section 32(2)(a) is not an accrued right to the tenant but it is only when he acquires a right to continue in possession and the landlord acquires a subsisting right to termination the tenancy. It cannot be said that the legislature intended to apply the provisions to all situations where notice given before the commencement or even thereafter had not been given. [823 E] 7. The object of the enactment was to provide for a period of three years from the date when the tenancy stood terminated and the tenancy continued till the termination thereof. It was, therefore, necessary that notice should be given before terminating the tenancy under sub section 1 A of Section 32(1) of that Act. The provision is not applicable to cases in which notice might be given after the lapse of three months from the commencement. [825 E] 8. In the instant case, the appellant landlord had not terminated the contractual tenancy and the respondent was not entitled to obtain any possession of his land. He had no right to get the benefit of the protection afforded by sub Section 2A of section 32 (1), as he had already terminated the said tenancy. The respondent was therefore entitled to have the protection of sub section 2A. [826 A B] 9.

The petitioners, who were the daughters of Khadim Ali and their mother, were members of a family. They had been allotted houses in the two houses by the Custodian under section 7 of the Act. The Custodian had made an order on January 10, 1952, declaring that the properties had already vested in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. The petitioners filed an appeal to the Custodian against the order of January 10. 1952, and they were unsuccessful. On appeal, the Custodian confirmed the order. In revision, the High Court held that the property was evacuee property and that the petitioners could not be declared to be evacuees. It further held that since the properties were evacuee properties, the petitioners had no right to have a larger share in the houses. The High Court also held that there was no question of any adjudication by the Central government on the basis of the order passed under section 8 of the , and therefore, the petition was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to declare the properties as evacuee property because he had not been declared to have been excluded from the purview of the provisions of the . Held, further, that the order made under section 6 of the Evacuee Property Act was a nullity and could not have been challenged by the petitioners. The appeal was therefore incompetent. The appellants were not entitled to any relief in this Court. The petition must be dismissed. The appeals are accordingly allowed and the orders passed by the High court are set aside. The order of the Custodian dated January 10/11, 1952 is upheld. The properties which had been acquired under the provisions Of section 8 are evacuee property. The respondents will pay to the petitioners compensation in accordance with the provisions contained in section 7(2) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976.

The assessee Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The assessee Company had entered into a joint venture with a view to manufacture yarn from wool tops. The company had also entered into an agreement with the selling agents for the sale of yarn tops and the selling agent agreed to share losses in the net profits ascertained in the manner stipulated in the agreement. The agreement provided that the agents would be entitled to the amount paid to the agents. The Company was not able to sell yarn to the selling agency and therefore the assessee Company could not claim any deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the agreements were not contracts of agency but were contracts of sale and therefore they were not covered by any authority cited before it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The agreement was a joint contract between the assessee company and the sell agents for sale of goods tops, and the sale agent agreed that he would be bound to pay the amount in question to the sales agents. [701B] (2) The agreements were merely an agency to conceal the real intention and the commercial venture. It was not a joint enterprise. The agreements did not create any agency or relationship between the parties. The mere fact that the agreement was an agency of the assessee would not make the agreement a joint undertaking. [801C] (3) The Tribunal had erred in holding that the assessee was not entitled to claim deduction under Section 10(1)(xv). [702F] (4) The High Court was right in holding, on the facts and circumstances of the case, that the contracts of Agency were not contract of agency. [601D] (5) The assessee company had entered a joint business with a large number of other persons who were carrying on the business of selling agents. It had also been found by the Tribunal that the transactions amounted to a joint and several venture for the purpose of the business and therefore it was not an agency or a partner thereof. [783F] The assessee was entitled to deduction under s 10(l)(xv), as the agreement did not amount to a Joint venture. [784H; 801A B] (6) The mere circumstance that the parties entered into another joint venture for carrying on business of sale of cloth and yarn would not take the case of the Revenue unless it is established that the transaction amounted to an agency, or a partnership firm. [78B] In the instant case, the assessee had entered in a joint agreement with a third party and had also agreed to pay a sum of Rs. 50,000/to the selling agencies. The payment was not made by the selling Agency to the assessee but was made by him to the purchasing agency. Therefore, the payments were not in excess of the reasonable return as contemplated under the Act and therefore there was no question of any deduction.

The appellant, who is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling sugar. The assessee had purchased certain goods from its registered office at Madras for sale in the State of Tamil Nadu. The sales were effected by the assessee in the course of inter se trade between the assessee and its customers. The appellant claimed that the profits earned by it during the accounting year of which the income was assessable, were not included within the accumulated profits of the company. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had not disclosed the true and correct facts to the Income Tax Officer and therefore, the question referred to the High Court was answered in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "accumulated profits" in section 2(6A) (e) of the Act, 1961 applied only to the case where the income earned by the company during the year of account of which its income was assessed, and not to the previous years. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression " Accumulated profit" in Section 2( 6A) means profits earned from business of manufacture or sale of goods. [950 A] 2. The word "accumsulated profits", in section 3(6B), means profits which had accumulated profits for the previous year of the accounting years of which income was chargeable, and includes profits earned during the previous financial year of any assessee. [1052 B C] 3. The words "accompulated profits " are not defined in the Act. They have been used in section 4(6) of that Act. It is clear from the definition that the word " Accumsulated profit " has to be understood as meaning " profits earned or received by a company during any previous year". [952 C] 4. The question whether the provision of Rs. 18,950 constituted income during the relevant accounting year was not directly related to the question whether accumulated profits could take in current profits for that year. [095 E] 5. The High Court has rightly held that since the assessee did not disclose the true facts to Income Tax Department, it was open to the Appellate Tribunal to refer the case to the said court. [992 G H] 6. In the present case, the appellant had purchased some goods from the registered office of the respondent company during a period prior to the accounting Year of which it earned profits. The income derived by the appellant during the aforesaid accounting year is not directly relatable to the issue of the reference application. It was only in respect of the question of its admissibility that the provisions of Rs 18,0950 were applied to the present controversy. [982 G] 7. In view of the fact that the appellant did not state the questions of law which could be referred to it, and the respondent had not furnished the true information to the income tax Department, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was right in holding that the provision for Rs 180950 constituted profits. [1003 A B] 8. The Tribunal was right, in holding, that the amount of Rs 19,925 constituted profits because the appellant failed to state the question as to whether accumulated profit could take into account when determining the accumulated profit. [1012 C] 9. In this case, it is not disputed that the accumulated income for the accounting period of which was assessable under section 2 (6A)(e) was not included in the accumulated losses for the relevant year of assessment. The respondent company had purchased the goods from their registered office and had also purchased the same from its branch offices. [103 D] 9 A B C,C] 10. In a recent decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. V.B.D.C., , referred to.

The plaintiff was the owner of a land measuring about 200 years in Mouza Nala, and he had been granted a permanent settlement of the estate of Burdwan. The defendants claimed to have dealt with the lands under a Lakheraj grant made prior to 1931. The Trial Court held that the defendants were not entitled to fair rent for a long time without any assertion of title. The High Court held in favour of the defendants, and dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that the plaintiffs had no title to the lands. [901 D] (2) The plaintiffs were not able to establish their claim under a lease granted in 1931, but they could only prove that the lands were Malis and not Malis. [0901 E] (3) The defendants had failed to establish that the land was not Malat or that they held under a jahajari grant made before 1931. They had been in possession of the lands for a considerable long time, and that they did so to the knowledge of the plaintiff prior to 1932. [1001 F] (4) The mere fact that the predecessors of the plaintiffs were in possession would not make them entitled to the fair rent. [1102 A B] (5) The claim was barred by reason of article 131 of the Limitation Act, and since the defendants had not claimed any right under a title, they could not be said to have established their claim.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of agricultural land governed by the Tenancy Act, alleging that he was an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy act and that the respondent had purchased the land in question from one Shri. S.B. Datar, who is a member of the petitioner 's family. The trial Court framed issues on the basis of the pleadings and evidence adduced by both parties. The appellant filed his written statement denying all the allegations made against him and contended that he had purchased agricultural land from one S. B. Datar and that he has not been able to prove that he is an agriculturist as defined in section 2(c) of the Act. The Trial Court framed issue No. 1 on the ground that the appellant was a member and that his father was a tenant under the respondent and that since the land was purchased by him from one Sh. Siri Ram, who was not a member, he could not be treated as an agriculturist. On appeal, the appellate Court held that the suit was barred by section 85A of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act and that it was not barred by the provisions contained in section 85 A of the said Act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether a person is an agricultural agriculturist within section 85(1) of Tenancy Act or whether he is a agriculturist within Section 85(2) of that Act has to be decided and dealt with by the competent authority under the Tenancy Ac t. [801B] 2. The expression "agricultural land" in section 3(c)(i) of this Act means any land which is used for agricultural purposes but does not include any land held by a person as an agricultural labourer or a tenant. [908C] 3.1 Section 85A provides that the competent authorities under the Rajasthan Land Reforms Act shall decide and deal with all questions arising in a properly constituted civil suit, which are required to be settled, decided or dealt with under the provisions of the tenancy Act. [1009D] 2: The expression 'agricultural land' has been defined in Section 2(a) of th e Tenancy Act as meaning any land used for agriculture purposes but not including any land on which agricultural land is used by a member for agricultural purpose. [1108E] 3:1 The word "agricultural" has been interpreted in the context of the provisions relating to the Tenancy Acts and it cannot be construed that the civil Court has no jurisdiction to decide or deal with such issues. [1209F G] 2(b) The expression used in section 86A of Tenancy act is a term which is required to refer to the competent court under the Act, i.e., the Civil Court has exclusive jurisdiction to settle, decide or dealt any question which is require to be determined and dealtwith by a competent authority. [1309F] 3(b)(i). The expression has been used in the Tenancy Law as meaning "agricultural produce" means agricultural produce. It does not mean that the land is agricultural produce but it includes any land other than agricultural produce, i s also agricultural produce which is defined in the Act and which is to be dealt with according to the provisions made in the said law. [1409F H] 3.(ii) The word 'agricultural produce' has not necessarily to refer only to agricultural produce and not to agricultural land. It cannot be interpreted to mean that agricultural produce is agricultural land, i n the absence of any provision in the statute relating to agricultural production. [1510H; 1511A B] 4.2 Section 85 A(1)(a) provides that where a person has purchased agricultural produce from one person for his own use and the purchase is made by another person for the purpose of agriculture, he shall be deemed to have purchased such produce on payment of market fee as may be fixed by the State Government in this behalf.

The assessee company was carrying on the business of heavy engineering. The two undertakings were incorporated by the reconstruction of the business already in existence, and the new undertaking was formed by reconstruction of its business already existing. The assessee company is a new industrial undertaking which has been registered as a new undertaking under section 15C of the Act. The three undertakings are not separate and distinct from each other. The four undertakings were independent and distinct. The five undertakings were not formed by the amalgamation of the two undertakings. The High Court was right in holding that the two units could not be said to be one undertaking. The view taken by the High Court is clearly erroneous. It is true that the three undertakings were separate and separate entities, but the fact that they were independent entities cannot be held to be conclusive. In order to appreciate the contention of the assessee it is necessary to refer to the facts of the case before us. The appellant company was incorporated on April 1, 1948. The business already started in existence and the two undertaking were distinct and separate. The new undertakings were formed by a reconstruction of business already with one undertaking and the same was not formed. The question whether the two industrial undertakings could be said not to be formed out of the existing business of the appellant company is no longer res integra. In the case of [S.R.A.T.C. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, Bombay & Anr.] (supra), this Court held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 10C(2) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The facts in that case were different and it was not a case where the two companies could be treated as one undertaking, but a new company which had been formed by an reconstruction of it, and since the two concerns were distinct, they could not claim exemption under Section 15C(1) of that Act. In this case, the two Companies were separate entities. The third unit was incorporated in the year 1948 and the three units were independent. The second unit was a new business already having been registered with the Income tax Department. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there could be no question of exemption under [section 15C] of the Income Tax Act, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High court had erred in holding the two mills to be separate and independent. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly held that both the units were distinct from one undertaking as formed by them. [813C] 2.2 The High Courts have committed a serious error of law in holding both the companies to be different. [713D] 3.3 The High courts have committed an error of fact and in holding two mills not being separate, the High Courts were right in taking the view that the new undertakings could not form part of the old undertaking. [77F] 4.1 In the instant case, there is no dispute that both these units are distinct from the new industrial undertakings. It was also admitted by the assessee company that the old business already stood in existence. The only question which arises for consideration is whether the new unit could be considered to be a new one or not. [78F] 3:1.2 In the present case, it is not disputed that both units were separate. They were independent units and they were distinct. It cannot be said that both of them had been amalgamated with each other by reconstruction. The amalgamation was not in existence at all. [79G] 3;3.3.4 The High Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Director, therefore, fell within the ambit of section 15 C(2). [78A B] 2:1 The assessee is a company which has already been registered under section 30C(i) of Income Tax. It does not fall within the mischief of section 10B(2)(ii) of income tax Act.

The inamdar, who was in possession of the lands under a grant from the inamdars, filed a suit for declaration that the inams were not liable to be resumed. The trial court decreed the suit and granted a decree declaring that the inamdar was entitled to resume the inam lands. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court reversed the decree holding that the Inamdars had no right to resume land after resuming the melwaram. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the grant was not adverse to the inam holders and that the order of resumption was illegal. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The inamdar is entitled to continue in possession as a permanent alienee from the lands after resumption. [601 B] 2. The Inamdars were not entitled to resumed the lands by virtue of section 44B(2)(a) (i). They were not tenants under the inam and they were not protected by section 44 B(2) (a) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908. [613 C] 3. The grant was in contravention of the provisions of the Act. The lands were resumed under section 44 A(2), but the inamees were not able to resume them. [501 D] 4. The inams were regranted to the Government under section 45 B(1)(a). The inamdars were, therefore, entitled to resumption of the inam land after the resuming of the melaram. [511 C] 5. The High Court was in error in holding that there was no alienation of the Inam lands by the inames and that they were also not tenants. [452 D] 6. The fact that the Government had granted a lease for a term exceeding five years does not make any difference to the question whether an alienee could acquire prescriptive title to the kudiwaram rights in the inam villages under section 4 of the Estates Land (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948. [454 E] 7. The word 'land' is defined in section 2(i)(a), which reads as follows: "2.(1) "land" includes any land held by a person for a religious or charitable purpose whether before or after the commencement of this Act and also includes any waste land, whether used for agricultural purposes or not; but does not include any land which is not included in the definition of 'land". [502 F] 8. The words "any other land" are defined in sections 2(ii)(a)(i) and (iii). It is clear from the definition that the word 'lands' includes all lands held by persons for a charitable purpose, whether before, or after, 1934. [453 C] 9. In view of section 4(2A), it was not open to the State Legislature to resume lands after the expiry of the term of the grant and thereby defeat the provisions contained in section 44 C(2). [454 D] 10. The expression 'land" is defined under section 2 (i)(b) which reads: "land' includes any right, title or interest in land held under a lease granted before 1934 but does include any right to resumption after the grant has been extinguished by adverse possession of such land." [503 F] 11. In the instant case, the inamers were not in possession and they had become impossible of performance as an endowment to the temple or temple concerned, as contemplated by section 4 (2)(b). The Inamdar was not entitled under section44 B(3) to resume inam lands after their resumption. [403 F H] 12. In order that the Inams were not adverse in nature, the State had to resume all the lands and the inams should be deemed to have been resumed. [544 G] 13.

The appellant Corporation was assessed on the basis of the gross annual letting value at which the tax was levied and collected by it. The Municipal Tax Officer, Indore City, passed an assessment order on the ground that the total annual letting values were not liable to be included in the assessment list prepared for the year 1952 53 and 54. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of the said assessment order before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the resolution passed by the Indore Municipality was invalid because it had been adopted for the years 1953, 1954 55 and 54 and that the tax levied on the gross letting value was saved by sec. 2(c) and therefore the appellant Corporation could not be said to have adopted the assessment lists prepared for 1952 53 for the two years in question. The appeal filed by the Corporation against the judgment of the High court was dismissed by this Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the decision of the Indore Municipal Tax Committee was not binding on the appellant and that since the resolution had been passed by it, the assessment order could not have been challenged in a writ petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution. HELD: 1. The resolution passed in the year 1953 was valid and legal. [701B] 2. The power to levy tax is an administrative power conferred on the Municipal Committee and the Municipal Board cannot be said that it has no power to impose any tax at all. [602C] 3. The word 'tax' used in sec. 73 of the Act means a tax which is imposed by law. It does not include a tax on the annual letting Value or the amount of tax assessed thereon for a particular official year. The expression 'tax" has been defined in section 2(b) and it includes a tax levied under the old Act. [802D] 4. The term 'taxation' is used in the sense that it is imposed on the rateable value of buildings or lands or both, which are assessed to property tax. It is not an administrative duty. It merely means a duty imposed by statute. [820E] 5. In order to appreciate the scope and ambit of the expression 'Taxes" occurring in secs. 73 and 74 it is necessary to refer to the relevant provisions of the 1954 Act. The definition of 'taxing authority' in section 3(c), which defines 'taxes ' as including a tax imposed by a statute, includes a duty on the property or both. [823E] 6. In view of the fact that the word 'Taxation" is used for the purpose of the general revenue administration and not for any other purpose, it cannot be held to have been so construed as to include a duty of excise. [825F] 7. The words "taxes" in sec.(6) are not intended to cover taxes which are imposed by the statute. It only means that the taxes levied under a statute are not to be regarded as tax imposed on property or property and therefore they cannot be treated as tax. [826C] 8. In construing the word "taxation" in section 73 of The word "fee" has to be given its natural meaning. The legislature has used the word, 'taxal' in a sense which means that it must be regarded by the legislature as a tax and not a duty. [828D] 9. The language employed in sec(6) is clear and unambiguous. It cannot be interpreted so as to exclude taxes which were imposed by an Act of Parliament or by any other law. [827E] 10. In interpreting the word `taxation', it has to take into account the fact whether the tax is levied on property and if so, what is its nature and extent. The meaning of the word must be given their natural meaning in a manner which would include taxes imposed by statutes. [829F] 11.

The assessee Company was wound up at about the end of the year ending on March 31, 1950. The assessee Company had been wound up on April 1, 1951, and a winding up order was passed on June 30, 1952, under section 10(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment years 1953 2, 1954 3, 1954 4, 1954 5, 1954 6, 1954 7, 1954 8, 1954 9, 1954 10, 1954 11, 1954 12, 1954 13, 1954 14, 1954 15, 1954 16 and 1954 17. The question whether the sale of chemicals and raw materials was a trading or not, came up for consideration before the High Court in a reference under section 66(1) of that Act. The High Court held that the transaction was not a trading one but a sale in the course of business operations, which were carried on by the assessee Company, and that the transactions were not sales in the ordinary way of business or trade, and therefore, the assessee company was liable to tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High court had erred in holding that the sale was a commercial transaction, because the sale did not amount to a trading activity, and since the transactions did not constitute a trading, the question whether they were sales or not could be answered by reference to the Memorandum of Association under which the assessee was woundup. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The mere fact that the business of the Company was being carried on in the normal course of trade operations does not make any difference, because it is a trading and not a sale. [601B] 2. The transactions were for the purpose of putting an end to the business, and the assessee had been put on its own behalf, and it was only when the goods were sold that the sales were made in the regular course of the business operations. [702C] 3. The transaction was a sale within the meaning of section 10 of the Act. It was not an adventure in the nature of trade or commerce. The sale was for the purposes of carrying on any trading activity. The goods were purchased by the Company, but it was not for the business purpose. [802D] 4. The fact that there was a sales in ordinary way and raw material did not make no difference because the transactions had been made for the manufacture of matches and raw chemicals and the raw materials. [820E] 5. The facts are not similar to those of the present case. The business of manufacturing, selling and selling chemicals was being conducted by the appellant Company, which was a part of its trading activity in the business. It is not a trade or commercial undertaking. The sales were for purposes of sale. The profits earned by the company from the sale were not taxable under section 9(2)(a) of Income tax act. [823E] 6. The position that emerges is that the assessee is carrying on a trading business, but the transactions are not sales and the transactions do not constitute an adventure or trade in the trade. [825F] 7. The word 'business' has been defined in section 2(d) of Act 1 of 1922 as meaning any business carried on with a view to carry on any trade or business. The expression 'business ' has been used in section 10 and it is not necessary that the activity should be carried on for the sole purpose of earning profits. [826E] 8. In the instant case, the transactions took place in the year 1942, and they were not trading in the books of the assessee. The income derived by the business was not taxable as a trading receipt. The profit earned by it from the business could not be regarded as a trade. It could not therefore be said that the profits earned from the trading activity were not income derived from the trade or that the income derived therefrom was not liable to be taxed under section 8(2).
